en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Commentary on the Middle Collection (Majjhimanikāya), the Second Fifty.
1. The Chapter on Devadaha.
1. The Commentary on the Devadaha Sutta. 1.
They "divine" (dibbanti) because they sport with the strands of sensual pleasure, frolic, or dwell therein by virtue of their capacity for victory.

They are called "devas" (rulers) because they desire to conquer their adversaries; they shine with the splendor attained through the power of merit as they exercise their authority—bestowing honors such as positions of sovereignty and receiving offerings—and as they conduct affairs by instructing others in their respective interests.
For indeed, while delighting the people through the four bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*), they themselves rule (*rājanti*) with the aforementioned special qualities.
They shine and are resplendent; thus they are called "kings. "Therein" means in that market town. "She" refers to the lotus pond.
"That" refers to that lotus pond which has received the name "Devadaha"; some say it is because [the town] is not far from it.

"All" refers to every kind of feeling, such as pleasure and so forth. "In a former life" means in a previous birth. "By way of the condition of karma performed" means by way of the karma that was done.
"Dependent on karma" means born from the fact that karma serves as a condition.
By this, he shows that all feelings whatsoever must be experienced precisely as the fruit of karma. Therefore, he said "by this," and so forth.
"Stated without specifying" means the matter was stated without distinguishing them by name, such as: "Bhikkhus, there are some recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine. "Specifying" means...
"Monks, the Nigaṇṭhas speak thus"—by qualifying it in this way, he shows [the following].
"Kalisāsana" means defeat. For "kali" is said to mean misfortune; since it "proclaims" (*sasati*) and "spreads" (*vippharati*) misfortune, it is *kalisāsana*, which is defeat.
Alternatively, "kali" refers to the class of defilements such as anger and pride; because of those, speaking improperly is *kalisāsana*. That—
One who wishes to establish [the point] wishes to clarify it. How can those who do not know whether an action has been performed or not performed know that it is such?
And how can those who do not know the classification of actions know their ripening?
They might know the state of the ripening being completed, yet they do not even know the very antidote to evil action.

Showing the point that they will not know how to abandon those [unwholesome states] and the method for accomplishing wholesome karma, he said: "The same principle applies even to further questions. 2.
Furthermore, in the *Cūḷadukkhakkhandha Sutta*, by the phrase "this being so," the fact that those Nigaṇṭhas lack such knowledge is indicated.
Thus it is clearly explained because the preceding teaching proceeded in that manner. For it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
"‘Evaṃ sante’ means ‘this being so,’ that is, while you are thus ignorant.
Nevertheless, in order to show that this meaning, when stated here, is appropriate as it connects with the subsequent teaching, [the text says]: "Of Mahānigaṇṭha..."
The meaning is that [the mind] is peaceful in truthful speech; thus it is said. "Of this much ground" means of the aforementioned fivefold measure of causes. 3.
Here, "thick smearing" refers to being colored many times over, not merely being coated like a cloth; thus he says: "by thick... as if smeared.
This has already been stated and need not be repeated; it is according to the method already explained therein.
The intended meaning is that it should be known.
Because such [knowledge] does not exist for these Nigaṇṭhas, he speaks by way of supposition, thinking, "There might be a time of knowing.
By that, they would be able to know thus, and their vision would be true. Since for them...
It shows that their vision was not true, and therefore they did not know. "At the four times" means at these four times:
the time of cutting open the wound, the time of searching for the arrowhead, the time of extracting it, and the time of applying medicinal charcoal to the wound opening.
"In the pure end" means in the pure portion; in the sense of the complete wearing away of suffering, it refers to the state of being free from suffering.
The meaning: "By means of a single simile" refers to this one simile: "Just as for one pierced by an arrow, the time when the pain becomes manifest is at the very moment of being pierced.
"Three meanings" refers to these three points: whether we existed in the past or not; whether we committed evil deeds or not;
and whether we committed such-and-such evil deeds or not. "By means of four similes" refers to the similes of the incision of the wound-mouth and so forth.
By means of four similes. "One purpose" refers to the single purpose stated in such passages as, "this much suffering has been worn away.
For that is called one purpose because of its commonality in the state of wearing away suffering. 4.
But these Nigaṇṭhas, having given rise to the perception, "I am pierced by suspicion," [said]: "To bring back" means to return, that is, to carry it around.

5. "Of those who believe the doctrine of the past" means: of those who believe the doctrine of Mahānigaṇṭha concerning the past, which occurs as follows: "Sirs, indeed the Nigaṇṭhas have previously committed evil kamma. "Because of its being real" (bhūtattā) asks:
does it proceed by taking as its object a meaning that is exactly as it has come to be, without error? The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.
“Saha dhammena” means *sahadhamma*; that which belongs to it is *sahadhammika*, just as in the term “vinayika.
Here, “dhamma” is intended in the sense of a cause; thus he says, “with its cause, with its reason. It is a counter-argument (*paṭihāra*) because it strikes back or repels;
a debate itself is a counter-argument, hence “vādapaṭihāra”; the meaning is that it is a reply. Therefore he says, “a debate involving a counter-response.”
The meaning is: having reversed the instruction, making it back to its original state. Regarding the word "of them" (*tesaṃ*), this should be understood as a repetition, as in:
"he shows them what is called the doctrine that cuts off their faith.
Ignorance (*avijjā*), lack of knowledge (*aññāṇā*), and delusion (*sammoha*) are synonyms. Or, "by ignorance" means by ignorance acting as the instrument (*karaṇabhūtāya*).
"By ignorance" means by not knowing. "By delusion" means by being bewildered, by great stupidity.
While you yourselves are currently experiencing painful feeling resulting from your own self-inflicted injury, believe perversely—thinking, "Whatever this is... [etc.
...is caused by what was done in the past"—and thus adopt the distorted grasp known as the doctrine of pre-existence (pubbekatahetu).

7. "Seen in this very life" (*diṭṭhadhamma*) refers to that which has become directly manifest; the fruit to be experienced therein is called "to be experienced in this very life" (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*).
Therefore he said: "It yields its result in this very personal existence (*attabhāva*).
By "application" (*payoga*) is meant either physical application or verbal application. By "exertion" (*padhāna*) is meant striving, a mental effort. In a proximate other existence...
It is impossible to ripen [the result] even in this life, let alone to show it at a distance; thus it is said, "in the second or third existence.
Because it brings about birth, it is beneficial to pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanīya*).

Since that resultant feeling is exclusively desirable because of its nature as a resultant, he says, "it gives a desirable object as its result. "The opposite" means that which gives an undesirable object as its result.

“Produced” means produced together with another kamma. “To be experienced in the future life” means to be experienced either in the next birth (upapajjavedanīya) or in subsequent lives (aparāpariyavedanīya).

Even though this is so—meaning that while “to be experienced when fully ripened” is indeed said to refer specifically to what is to be experienced in the present life (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya)—nevertheless, there is a distinction here, because “to be experienced when fully ripened” refers to a specific kind of present-life experience.
To demonstrate this, it was said: “This is the case here,” and so forth. Within seven days from the day it was performed. Therein means:
regarding the giving of the result of karma to be experienced upon ripening within those seven days.
Having plowed once, he sat down with a hungry heart. As she was coming, he said: “The meal has been brought late.”

Without giving rise to mental distress, he rejoiced in the merit performed. Seeing it shining, he wondered, "Is this too of that same nature, or is it merely a fabrication of my mind, or is it truly gold? Investigating thus, he struck it with a staff.
Because of the presence of fierce *yakkhas* in the vicinity of Rājagaha, they circulated a proclamation of a thousand pieces of silver in the city. His passion arose.
It bit her on the crest. "Having informed the king" means having related that occurrence to the king.
The story of Mallikā should be told according to the method found in the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*.
It was performed even at the point of death, let alone earlier than that, and in past existences as well. Here, it refers to the result that has already been produced.
It is called "certain" because its existence is inevitable. It is "to be experienced in the next life" specifically because it gives its result in another becoming.
It is described here as a "quality produced in this very life," and not as a "result produced in this very life," because of its nature as liberation (*vimutti*).

It should be understood as "to be experienced when fully matured," since it does not deviate from the characteristics of being "to be experienced when fully matured" as stated below. It is "one that gives fruit very quickly."
By this, he shows that through its association with the capacity to produce a result, karma is "to be experienced upon ripening" (*paripākavedanīya*).
Because it has the four or five aggregates as its fruit, karma leading to the non-percipient realm (*asaññābhava*) is said to be "much to be experienced" (*bahuvedanīya*);

because it has a single aggregate as its fruit, karma leading to the non-percipient realm is "little to be experienced" (*appavedanīya*). Some, however, [say] that formless-sphere (*arūpāvacara*) karma [is so called] because its fruit is to be experienced over a long period of time...

They say that "much-to-be-experienced" (*bahuvedanīya*) is [kamma] of the sense-sphere, while the other is "little-to-be-experienced" (*appavedanīya*); or alternatively, kamma pertaining to the fine-material and immaterial spheres is "much-to-be-experienced," whereas limited kamma is "little-to-be-experienced.
"Kamma with result" (*savipāka-kamma*) means that which is capable of producing a result when the convergence of other conditions occurs;

it does not mean that the result has already begun. "Kamma without result" (*avipāka-kamma*) refers to types such as "become-kamma" (*ahosi-kamma*) and so forth, which are incapable of ripening due to the deficiency of conditions.

8. Regarding "of those [karmas] to be experienced in the present life, etc.": because it is impossible for the ten types of karma—beginning with that to be experienced in the present life—to undergo a change of nature through external intervention, karmas remain exactly as they are by their own inherent nature.
In this context, the intervention of the Nigaṇṭhas is useless; thus he says, "fruitless. This refers to the exertion of the Nigaṇṭhas, which is a form of wrong effort.
The doctrine that [effort] cuts off exertion is a teaching that proclaims a state of fruitlessness.
"By the reasons stated by others" means by those very reasons through which they point out the faults in the doctrines of the Nigaṇṭhas.

For it is not possible to demonstrate the faults in the doctrines of others without a reason endowed with its defining characteristic (lakkhaṇa). Therefore he said: "having [the arguments] together with their reasons. [This refers to] the Nigaṇṭhas.

“Discourses and counter-discourses”: these are the discourses proclaimed by the Nigaṇṭhas themselves as the exposition of their own respective doctrines, and the counter-discourses spoken by their disciples [in response].
“They come upon grounds censurable by the wise” means that in various instances they encounter and reach grounds worthy of censure by wise and learned people, thinking, “This is the fault here.”
The meaning: This is the summary of the meaning regarding the phrases "its meaning" and so forth:
"By the method already stated, through reasons adduced by others, the doctrines of the Nigaṇṭhas have become possessed of their respective causes;

thus, by demonstrating the lack of conviction in those doctrines, and by withering them through the drying up of the moisture of the conventional expression of 'perfection of cause,' they come under ten censurable designations, such as 'doers of evil deeds' and so on."
9. "The cause of association" means the cause for the occurrence of association arising according to one's wish in various places.
Since that association has the characteristic of necessity (niyati), it is said to be "the cause of the state of necessity.

For the occurrence of necessity is a fixed regularity, like a gem strung on an unbreakable thread that cannot be split. "The cause of the six classes of birth" refers to the dark class of birth (kaṇhābhijāti) and the blue class of birth (nīlābhijāti).
Among these classes—namely, the red class, the yellow class, the white class, and the supreme white class—the cause for birth is the mark of birth (*jātinimitta*).
"Associating with evil" means associating with the base.
Regarding the term *anaddhabhūta*, he states that here the word *addha* has the same meaning as the prefix *adhi*: "Anaddhabhūta..."
"Unconquered by suffering": just as a state of existence in the woeful states (*āpāyika*) is overwhelmed by great suffering, this human state is not so;

thus it is said: "The human state is called 'unconquered by suffering'. [This refers to] the exhaustion resulting from the various kinds of ascetic practices described by the passage beginning with "he is naked" (*acelako*). If this is so, how can they be "bearers of the ascetic virtues" (*dhutaṅgadharā*)?

He said, “But those who... and so forth. For in the Dispensation that leads to liberation, energy (*vīriya*)—when it is practiced by being based on the turning away from existence—is called right effort (*sammāvāyāma*), because it is undertaken according to the method, even if it causes the body to become exhausted.
“The Elder” refers here to the Elder Mahārakkhita mentioned in this context. The three successes are the successes of human birth, of the deva realms, and of Nibbāna.
Or, it refers to the attainments of virtue, concentration, and wisdom. "Right at the tip of the razor" means right on the very top of the head;

the intention is that [the attainment occurs] even when the razor has been removed from the top of the head. "This one" refers to the person described by the passage beginning with "born in a family of lords.
He said, "one born from the womb of a slave," and so forth, because not everyone who goes forth preceded by honors attains Arahatship. "A silver ring."
A silver finger-ring. "By even the mere scent of *goraka* and *piyaṅgu*" means by the mere scent of the *kapittha* bark and *kuṅkuma* flowers.
He said, "The happiness that comes by way of the Dhamma and in accordance with the rule is 'Dhamma-happiness,'" referring to it as "the happiness of requisites from the Saṅgha...
[etc. ...paccaya-sukha. "Uninfatuated" means not overcome by craving. Now, in order to show that state of being unovercome and its fruit, he says: "Righteous..."

“‘Hī’ and so forth was said. ‘Of this’ refers to the origin [of suffering]. For that [origin], being the cause of the suffering of the five aggregates, is stated as something immediate and directly perceived. Therefore he said, ‘of present ones,’ and so forth.
‘Formations’ (saṅkhāra) is the name given to powerful energy and exertion because it performs its function with particular intensity once it has been undertaken. ‘Exerting’ means applying oneself.”
For one who is practicing [the path]. "Dispassion occurs through the path" means that there is a fading away of the cause of suffering by means of the Noble Path.

Therefore he said, "This is what is meant. By this, the practice that is pleasant and characterized by swift direct knowledge (*sukhāpaṭipadā khippābhiññā*) is described, because of the fact that awakening is attained very quickly and without difficulty due to the rapid understanding of the path.
"The mode of equanimity" refers to equanimity regarding energy (*vīriyūpekkhā*). [Regarding] *saṅkhāra*...

In this context, "he exerts" means that he exerts himself toward the formative activity of striving (*padhāna-saṅkhāra*) for the purpose of dispassion, as a sign for the fading away of the source of suffering.
How so? By means of the exertion of the Path, he exerts himself—that is, he makes effort—through the effort within the Noble Eightfold Path which performs its four functions.
"He looks on with equanimity" refers to the application of balanced energy, through which the energy is neither over-exerted nor too lax.
By not performing any activity, he looks on with equanimity. Therefore he said, “developing equanimity.
And since the development of equanimity here is indeed the development of the Noble Path occurring in that manner, he said, “he develops it through the development of the Path.
In this context, the construction of the words of the text should be understood as follows: “He understands thus. How? [He understands] the formation...”
“Through my exertion of the formations, there comes to be the fading away of this source of suffering;
through my equanimity while looking on, there comes to be the fading away of this source of suffering. This should be understood as the preliminary investigation of one who is practicing.

In that context, “exertion of the formations” refers to the energy for instigating the effort of meditation by means of the easy way of comprehension through the method of full understanding (*sammasana*).
“Shown” means that the pleasant way of practice with quick direct knowledge has been shown.

By the phrase “looking on with equanimity,” it is shown that even for someone who exerts energy that is not too intense, there comes about the fading away of the cause of suffering as they apply themselves to insight.
In both cases, it should be understood that the fourth way of practice alone is elucidated. Now, regarding the passage: “For one whose... pe...”.
By the phrase “he develops equanimity therein,” the practice of those very individuals is shown by way of those same modes of progress (*paṭipadā*).
By these modes, the destruction of suffering is elucidated through the wearing away of the cause of the suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*).
11. “With a bound mind” means with a connected mind. “With thick desire” means with a thick craving-desire. “Having transgressed” means...

"Having passed beyond. "Actors" refers to those who perform according to the rules of a troupe of actors; "dancers" refers to others. "Joy arises" [with the thought]: "He has renounced such a woman as this!
"May it be cut" means may it become two-fold. "May it break" means may it shatter.
By both phrases, "may it be cut or may it break," he speaks of destruction alone. "Having known" means having understood by means of preliminary knowledge (*pubbabhāga-ñāṇa*).
"Both of these" refers to the cultivation of equanimity toward the burning of formations (*saṅkhāra*).
"Of one who sends forth" means of one who exerts effort. "With reference to that" means with reference to the fact that the way of practice leads to deliverance from suffering.
Like an arrow-maker straightening an arrow, the yogi straightens the mind. [The mind may be] crooked like a cow's urine or curved like the crescent moon.
The mind is like the tip of a ploughshare because it bends [toward its object]. Energy is like a firebrand because of its burning and scorching.
Faith is like oil in a vessel because of its lubricating nature. The supramundane path is like a bending staff because it bends the mind toward the object of Nibbāna.

The straightening of the mind by means of the supramundane path should be understood as occurring through the clear realization of development (*bhāvanābhisamaya*). [This applies to] those who have abandoned the two extremes.
The "middle way of practice" refers to the breakthrough realization through the piercing of the mass of defilements by means of abandonment.

As for the other way of practice, which is "slow direct knowledge," when these two types of monks are described in terms of the two aforementioned types of "quick direct knowledge," the other is also implicitly described by way of the method of characteristic transfer (*lakkhaṇahāranaya*), due to the commonality of the practice itself. This also applies to those who travel together.

Or rather, the practice has indeed been stated by way of the preliminary practice (*pubbabhāga-paṭipadā*) in the passage beginning with, "It is not that what is not yet firm is of no use," and so forth.

As for the statement, "But the practice leading back [to the world] (*āgamanīya-paṭipadā*) was not stated," this should be understood as referring to the fact that it was not stated specifically for one who is equanimous (*ajjhupekkha*).
"Instruction on departure" (*nikkhamana-desanā*) means the instruction on the means of departure. The rest is easily understood.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Devadaha Sutta* is completed.
2. Commentary on the *Pañcattaya Sutta* 21.
Regarding the word "some" (*eke*) here, the term "one" (*eka*) has the sense of "a certain person" (*añña*), not the sense of "number" and so forth; demonstrating this, he said "some" (*ekacce*).
Furthermore, that which is stated in the Pāḷi as “there are” (santi) demonstrates, by virtue of the actual existence of those proponents of views, their unbroken continuity;
and from that, it shows how his own teaching performs its function through the loosening and removal of their false graspings, as well as its truthfulness.
Even among those who are ultimate ascetics and brahmins, there is not even a trace of being limited to the past or future eons.
He said, "There is not," beginning with the words, "by way of having entered the wandering life.
They are called *aparantakappino* because they construct (*kappenti*) the future limit (*aparanta*) by way of eternalism and so forth; they themselves are the *aparantakappikā*.

Since they construct the future limit by means of craving and views that have been established previously, and then conceptualize it through the power of repeated practice, they do so by means of those [views] which have become fixed attachments established subsequently.
They seize, adhere to, and misapprehend by means of the graspings of craving and views; therefore it is said: "Having conceptualized and discriminated the future limit (aparanta), they seize it.
The acts of conceptualizing and seizing should be understood as occurring through the influence of craving and clinging (upādāna), for clinging has craving as its condition.
And this has been stated in the Mahāniddesa, both by way of summary and in brief: "By way of craving and views..."

By way of craving (*taṇhā*) and views (*diṭṭhi*). Or, by way of the false grasping of one who adheres to eternalism and so forth through craving—which is both a supporting condition (*upanissaya*) for views and co-nascent (*sahajāta*) with them—and through views that serve as their support.
Here, the word "other" (*apara*) denotes the future time because it is intended to refer to objects belonging to the future.
[This refers to] a conceptualized entity (*kappanavatthu*) distinct from the aggregates (*khandha*) such as form (*rūpa*) and the rest.
Since the word *anta* (end) denotes a "part" (*bhāga*) when it signifies non-existence (*abhāva*), he says: "the future portion of the aggregates.
And by the word *kappetvā*, he means the completion and final establishment of the absence of dogmatic insistence through craving regarding that future limit.
*Ṭhitā* refers to the non-abandonment of that adherence.

“Anugata” means followed along step by step by way of making it an object; it occurs in the future. “Ārabbha” means having taken as an objective support (*ālambitvā*). For the future is the domain (*visaya*) of that view.
Precisely because it is its domain, it is the place where that [view] comes and is its object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*);

thus it is said, “having come to (*āgamma*), depending upon (*paṭicca*). “Designation-terms” (*adhivacanapadāni*) are terms of conceptual description (*paññatti*); for example, the word “Sirivaḍḍhaka” applied to slaves and others.
*Adhivacana* (designation) is a term for the process [of naming] that functions by making the mere word its basis.

Alternatively, the prefix *adhi-* signifies "above"; *vacana* means "that which is spoken. Thus, "speech above" (*adhivacana*) refers to a designation being made known above [or in relation to] the material phenomena that serve as the basis for grasping;
the meaning is "derived designation" (*upādāpaññatti*). Therefore, the sense is "terms that illuminate designations. For this is merely a designation.
It is called "the self and the world," and it is not an ultimate reality (*paramattha*) like form, feeling, and so forth.
Or, because they function as exaggerations, views are called "resolutions" (*adhimutti*).

For views proceed by superimposing upon intrinsic phenomena (*sabhāvadhamma*) such non-existent entities as permanence, primordial nature (*prakṛti*), substance (*dravya*), the soul (*jīva*), and the body (*kāya*). They are said to "assert" because—
Having adhered to the view, "This alone is the truth; all else is false," they say, "This is the Dhamma, this is not the Dhamma," and so forth, engaging in disputes.
The use of the present tense is intended to show that the activity of such dispute remains uninterrupted even to this day.

One who possesses perception (*saññā*) is called a "possessor of perception" (*saññī*); thus it says "one endowed with perception. One for whom there is no disease or breaking up is "healthy" (*aroga*).
The sense of "eternity" (*nicca*) should be understood as a synonym for "health" (*aroga*).

Or rather, the proponent of a speculative view (*diṭṭhigatika*) asserts eternity by way of being free from disease—that is, by way of being changeless—hence he says, "Healthful means eternal. "By this" refers to the statement: "The self is percipient and healthy after death.
There are sixteen theories of a percipient self: the fourfold set on the material, the fourfold set on the immaterial, and the fourfold set on the finite.

The "tetrad of absolute happiness" (*ekantasukhīcatukka*): by means of these four tetrads, sixteen theories of those who maintain the existence of consciousness after death (*saññīvāda*) have been explained.

Within these very [tetrads], by means of the first two tetrads, eight theories of those who maintain the existence of consciousness and eight theories of those who maintain neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññīnāsaññīvāda*) are to be understood.

The seven theories of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*) refer to [the cessation of existence] in the human state, the state of sense-sphere deities (*kāmāvacara-deva*), and the state of fine-material-sphere deities (*rūpāvacara-deva*).
Seven annihilationist views (ucchedavāda) are taught by way of proclaiming the annihilation of a being after it has passed away from the fourfold immaterial existence.
It is said that "annihilationism is based on the state of existing" because annihilation is impossible for that which is non-existent;

thus, "existing" means "that which is presently found. Because one grasps [the self] thinking, "As long as this self is not annihilated, it exists indeed," there is destruction without arising (nirudayavināsa).

Here, "cutting off" (uccheda) is intended; thus he says "severance" (upaccheda). Destruction (vināsa) means specific loss or non-existence, and since that is the passing beyond the range of vision of both the fleshly eye and the eye of wisdom, he says "non-appearance" (adassana);

for the word "destruction" is conventionally established in the world in the sense of non-appearance. "Departure from existence" (bhavavigama) means the going away from its own nature—that which is cut off by way of being without arising or destruction.
It does not remain by its own inherent nature alone.

"The five doctrines of Nibbāna in the present life" (diṭṭhadhamma-nibbāna-vādā) are doctrines that proclaim the attainment of Nibbāna in the present life by means of the enjoyment of the pleasure of the five strands of sensual desire and by means of the enjoyment of the pleasure of the fourfold form-sphere jhānas.
"The present life" (diṭṭhadhammo) refers to [the world] as seen by knowledge that functions as vision.

A phenomenon that has been apprehended. In this context, even that which is not within the range of the sense faculties becomes, by virtue of its being clearly manifest, as if it were within the range of the sense faculties;
thus it is said: "‘Seen phenomena’ (diṭṭhadhamma) refers to directly perceived phenomena (paccakkhadhamma). For this very reason, it is stated:
"This is a designation for the individual existence (attabhāva) acquired here and there. It is peaceful in three ways, beginning with the phrase "possessing perception" (saññī).
The meaning of "eternal" (*sassata*) is that which exists in these modes—as having perception, as being without perception, or as neither-perceiving-nor-not-perceiving—and is always apprehended.
There are three views, beginning with "the self has perception. These constitute one view by way of the self of the eternalist (*sassatavāda*).
The other two are those known as the annihilationist view (*ucchedavāda*) and the view of Nibbāna in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammanibbānavāda*).

There are two kinds of seeing. As for the statement, "Having been three, they become five," this is easily understood because it was stated by way of a summary as "one" in the sense of being a present reality (*santattha*), whereas here it is stated by way of the analysis of the designatum (*saññī*) and so forth; therefore, it was not cited in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*). 22.
Regarding the phrase *rūpīṃ vā*: if the intended meaning here were that "one who has form" (*rūpī*) means "one for whom form exists" (*rūpaṃ assa atthi*), then [the following would apply].
One must become a self that is dissociated from form, because form, like perception, is "belonging to the self" (*attaniyatā*).

For in the passage, "the perceiver is the self," it is not the perception that is the self. Thus it is stated in the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*: "In that context, it is said 'having grasped the perception occurring therein as perception.
This being so, how is it that [the text] says, "one grasps the kasiṇa-form as the self"?
But this should not be viewed thus: "He possesses form, therefore he is 'possessed of form' (rūpī)";

rather, he is "possessed of form" because his nature is to be affected by change (ruppanasīla). And here, "being affected by change" refers to the attainment of specific qualities through the increase or non-increase of the kasiṇa-form over time;
and it cannot be said that this is absent, because distinctions such as limitedness and vastness do exist. If...
Is it not the case that, in this way, the inclusion of this doctrine within the eternalist view (sassataditthi) is untenable? No, it is not untenable;
for after the dissolution of the body, the self is intended by him to be without change. For thus it is said: "He is healthy beyond death.

Alternatively, there is no fault even if he is called "possessing form" (rūpī) on the grounds that "form belongs to him. For even a distinction established through conceptual construction (kappanā) [is sufficient].

Because it shows a designation by way of the owner—as in the expression “the body of Silāputtaka”—or because that which is subject to deformation (ruppana) or whose nature is deformation is "form" (rūpa), and he possesses that, he is "possessed of form" (rūpī), as in the phrases “the self” or “phenomena possessed of form.

Having established this, the statement “he grasps the kasiṇa-form as the self” is indeed logically consistent, since the self has the nature of form; thus it is said: “he grasps the kasiṇa-form as the self.”
Regarding "formless" (*arūpin*), the meaning should be stated as appropriate according to the method already explained.

Since there is no reason for grasping what is contrary to it while abandoning what is peaceful and subtle, one who possesses [such a view] is a "possessor. Apart from the "possessor of speculative theorizing" (*lābhitakkī*), who grasps "the kasiṇa-form is the self," all other theorists are included by the very term "possessor of grasping.
This includes both the "speculative theorizer based on hearsay" (*anussutitakkī*) and the "pure speculative theorizer" (*suddhatakkī*).
Because there is no restraint on reasoning, one might at some time grasp even the kasiṇa-form as the self; thus it is said: "He grasps both kinds of forms indeed.
For the pure reasoner, the grasping of both has not been established, and therefore that statement is subject to doubt.

The space resulting from the removal of the kasiṇa, the consciousness of the first immaterial attainment, the base of nothingness which is the state of non-existence, and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are the signs for the immaterial attainments.
"Excluding the aggregate of perception": this was stated with the intention of making perception one's own (internalizing it).

However, if the meaning were explained according to the method stated in the passage "whether possessing form," then without setting aside the aggregate of perception as external, one should simply say "non-material phenomena.
"By way of grasping them as mixed" means by taking together the signs of both material and immaterial attainments.
Regarding the phrase “a single self,” there is the perception occurring therein, which is apprehended as “perception.

For this proponent of a speculative view, having attained the meditative attainments of the fine-material and immaterial realms, stands by grasping their respective signs as being material and immaterial;
therefore, he generates the dogmatic adherence that “it is both material and immaterial,” either like those who maintain an internal self through mere reasoning alone.
Taking material and immaterial phenomena together as a mixture, one holds the view: "The self is both material and immaterial. Regarding the phrase "by means of mere speculative grasping":
because they have reached an extremely subtle state—like phenomena that have reached a residual subtlety after the formations [have ceased]—they are incapable of performing their own functions;

thus, like a collection of pillars, walls, hands, and feet, it is neither material, because it does not transcend the nature of matter, nor is it immaterial, because it does not transcend the nature of matter.

Thus it is by way of the grasping of views that have arisen. Alternatively, the meaning should be understood according to the mutual opposition of positions, as in the method to be explained for the fourth doctrine concerning the finite and infinite, which is also based on gain. However, the distinction here is this:

in that case, the third and fourth doctrines were intended by way of differences in place and time, whereas here they are distinguished by way of differences in time and subject matter. By way of difference in time...
And here, the occurrence of the third position is due to the non-simultaneous appearance of the signs of the material and the immaterial;

whereas the occurrence of the fourth position is due to a distinction in the basis (*vatthu*)—namely, by way of reasoning that "the self is one" from the collection of material and immaterial phenomena.
This is to be understood according to the method that will be explained therein.

Although a second view is also obtainable by way of one who has attained the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*)— since diversity of perception arises through the different absorptions for one who holds such views regarding the eight attainments—
nevertheless, because perception presents itself in a single form within the attainment,
he said, "The first view was stated by way of one who has attained. For this very reason, the term "one who has attained" is used here.
It is said. Or rather, the meaning should be understood by way of one who has attained only a single meditative absorption (samāpatti).

Although a differentiation of perception (saññā) may occur through the differentiation of absorptions, because of the gross diversity of perceptions regarding external, manifold objects, he is called "one possessing diversity of perception" (*nānatta-saññī*).

Thus it was said: "The second view [is explained] by way of those who have not yet attained absorption. By way of an unextended kasiṇa, there is "limited perception" (*paritta-saññā*); by way of an extended kasiṇa, there is "immeasurable perception" (*appamāṇa-saññā*).
To demonstrate this, it is said: "The third view is that the self is the size of a thumb-joint, or the size of a grain of rice, or the size of a mustard seed," and so forth.

Because one perceives the self as limited through such demonstrations as "the self is the size of a thumb, or the size of a barley grain, or the self is the size of an atom," one is called "one who perceives the limited" (*parittasaññī*).
Because one professes the all-pervading nature of the self, like Kapila, Kaṇāda, and others, one is called "one who perceives the immeasurable" (*appamāṇasaññī*).
The meaning here should be understood in this way:
"this" refers to the aforementioned doctrine of self (attavāda) beginning with "either possessing form," and so forth. "Some" means certain individuals.
"Transcending" means surpassing; this genitive case is used in the sense of selection. The construction is: "some assert the kasiṇa of consciousness."

Therefore he said: “Perceiving... [and so on]... they assert. In that context, the phrase “having set aside perception, the remaining three” refers to taking the complete tetrad of perceptions; others say it refers to eight.
“Both of those” means both of what was called the “eightfold perception. This will become clear later in the passage beginning with “four who perceive forms,” and so forth.
He will explain it further below. For he will say: "In terms of divisions there are eight, but in terms of meaning there are seven perceptions.

"Therein" refers to this phrase: "Or rather, this. They are able to transcend [the lower stages] because their qualities—such as faith—are cultivated through seeing the danger in those [lower states] and seeing the benefits in what lies beyond them; conversely, they are unable to do so otherwise.
It should be understood that only those who are capable are included here, because it is possible to describe the specific distinction that will be explained by way of them alone.

Furthermore, in order to show through a simile that the transcending of these [beings] by those who are capable occurs in accordance with the power of their own knowledge, the passage beginning with “But of them...
was stated. In that context, “immeasurable” means having an immeasurable object; it is the state of having an immeasurable object.
It should be understood by way of its arrival, or because its object is infinite; for it does not grasp the measure of even the supreme infinity as being "infinite" with respect to its object.
Having reached the imperturbable (*āneñja*)—so called because it is unshaken by pleasure or pain and because it is a specific development of dispassion toward form—one remains there.
Those who remain while asserting "this is our self" [are those who have attained it]. One makes the consciousness-kasina one is the base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana*).
Some proponents of speculative views say that it is the self. Therefore he said: "First, in order to show the base of infinite consciousness.
Others, however, say it is the consciousness occurring in the space cleared of the kasiṇa, which serves as its object. For that kasiṇa is called the "consciousness-kasiṇa" by way of attention;
and since that consciousness is both consciousness and a base (āyatana) in the sense of being an object, it is called the "base of infinite consciousness" (viññāṇañcāyatana).
And it is so called. The phrase "the base of nothingness is one" follows this same method.
Regarding the word *tad* (that): the letter *ya* functions as a euphonic conjunction (*sandhi*), as he says, "that which is this.

"A resort of views" (*diṭṭhigata*) refers to the view expressed in such statements as "the self is percipient," as previously stated. For a view itself is indeed a "resort of views," as in the expressions "a resort of liberation," "a resort of formations," and so forth.
Or, because there is no further going, "gone by means of view" (*diṭṭhigata*) is simply the state of having gone;
the meaning is "merely the grasping by means of view. Or, *diṭṭhigata* is a mode of view. For worldly people accept that the words *vidha*, *yutta*, *gata*, and *pakāra* are synonymous.
"Condition of view" (*diṭṭhipaccaya*) means the cause of view; ignorance (*avijjā*), etc., is the "basis of view" (*diṭṭhiṭṭhāna*). In that context, ignorance also...
For it is a basis for views by way of being a decisive support (upanissaya) and so forth. As it is said:

"Bhikkhus, the uninstructed worldling, who has not seen the Noble Ones and is unskilled in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones," and so forth. Contact (phassa) too is a basis for views. As it is said: "That too is conditioned by contact.
Perception (saññā) too is a basis for views. As it is said: "For conceptual proliferation (papañca-saṅkhā) has perception as its source."
Applied thought (*vitakka*) is also a basis for views. As it is said: "Having fashioned reasoning among views, they speak of two things—truth and falsehood.
Improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) is also a basis for views. As it is said:
"As he attends in this way, one of the six views arises: 'I have a self,' which he regards as true and established."
“View arises. “Having a view as its object” means the pentad of the aggregates of clinging which has become the object of the view.

Therefore he said: “One regards form as self,” and so forth. Because there is no object of view apart from form, feeling, and the rest, he shows this very point by not taking anything else [as the object], saying:
“By this condition, this specific kind of seeing is grasped.”
Alternatively, it should be understood that by the mention of "condition" (*paccaya*) here in the phrase "by this condition," the object (*ārammaṇa*) is also included.

"That very same" refers both to the mode of view (*diṭṭhigata*) and the condition for the view (*diṭṭhipaccaya*). In the phrase "of perceptions of form" (*rūpasaññānaṃ*), the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning with.
The word *evaṃ* has the sense of "manner"; thus, the meaning is "of those perceptions stated in the manner beginning with 'if there are perceptions of form.'"

“Unblemished” (*nirupakkilesā*) means being free from the defilements such as the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). “Supreme” (*uttamā*) means having reached a state of excellence; for that very reason, it is “best” (*seṭṭhā*);
and because it is best, and because there is nothing superior to it, it is “unsurpassed” (*anuttariyā*). “Is declared” (*akkhāyati*) means it appears.

Since the perception of the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana-saññā*) is mentioned separately, and since the perception of the fourth formless attainment does not enter into this doctrine of perception, [the text says] “if they are perceptions of the formless realms... (*yadi āruppa-saññānan-ti*).
By this [phrase], it is stated that there is "perception of the base of infinite space" and "perception of the base of infinite consciousness.

By the other two, however—namely, by these two phrases, "whether they are perceptions of unity" and "whether they are perceptions of diversity"—the section on those who have attained meditative absorption is likewise explained here;
such is the intended meaning. From the perspective of divisions, there are eight perceptions, as they are comprised within two sets of four.
The intention is that, setting aside the term "perception of unity," there are seven perceptions in terms of meaning when including what has not been previously mentioned.
Therefore he said: "The one who has attained [jhāna]... is indeed included.
"Included in perception" means either gone by way of perception or gone into the inclusion of perception. Furthermore, even though it is not a "gone-to-view" (diṭṭhigata),...

Because it is apprehendable, it is said to be "together with a speculative view. That which is made by coming together through conditions means that it has been produced by coming together with the conditions that serve as its causes, and thus by that very state of being caused;
the meaning is "dependently arisen. It is gross because it is conditioned, owing to the presence of arising, passing away, and change. For that of which arising is discerned...
Arising is discerned, and the alteration of that which persists is discerned. For one who sees this as having a nature of breaking up moment by moment, the evident transformation would be gross.
And herein, the states of the Path and Fruition are not to be demonstrated, because they are not to be contemplated in that manner;
for even those [Path and Fruition states], being conditioned, are susceptible to the same treatment as the others.

Because it is impossible to prevent [the arising of suffering]. For indeed, from the statement “through the fading away and cessation without remainder,” since even the Path possesses the nature of an escape, it is precisely Nibbāna that is pointed out here as the counter-correlative by way of being the cessation of formations, taking it in the sense of “that wherein they cease.
Thus, regarding the statement “there exists what is called Nibbāna, which is cessation”: “There is, monks, [Nibbāna]...”

One should speak by bringing forward the scriptural passage: “unborn, unbecome, unconditioned. “A seer of Nibbāna” means a seer of Nibbāna by way of the realization through direct experience (*sacchikiriyābhisamaya*);
for that very reason, through the accomplishment of the purpose of the other realizations, he has transcended that which is conditioned.
23. Regarding the eight views on non-percipient beings: this was indeed stated below with reference to the method found in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*.

It is said: “By the term ‘percipient,’ the eight doctrines of non-percipient [beings] are expressed. However, here only four doctrines are extracted. Therefore he says, “non-percipient,” and so forth.
This same method applies later to the passage, “among the eight doctrines of neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient beings.

Because when perception exists, there is the grasping of feeling through it, it is said: “Perception is a disease in the sense of being an affliction. This is because it is joined with the sting of suffering.
Perception is a boil because it drips with the impurity of the defilements, and because it swells, ripens, and bursts through arising, aging, and dissolution.
This matter occurs precisely because of being corrupted by hatred; thus he said, "In the sense of being accompanied by hatred, it is a boil.

Perception is an arrow because it produces affliction, pierces within, and is difficult to extract; this matter, having entered into the individual existence (attabhāva) — [the rest of the passage follows].
By way of "establishment," he said: "In the sense of having entered, it is a 'dart' (salla).

Since consciousness, at the moment of seizing rebirth-linking, seems as though it has come from somewhere, it is said: "Coming by way of rebirth-linking. "Going" refers to the course of existence (pavatti).
Since that is the functioning within those various destinies (gati), it is said: "Going by way of death"; [it is also described] by way of growth and by way of dense continuity.
This is the meaning. Therefore he said, “successively. For consciousness, as it proceeds successively by way of continuity, is the “strengthening of delight”;
or else, depending on the other three aggregates, it attains growth, stability, and greatness. Or, by way of increase, it is *gati* (going);
by way of casting off, it is *cuti* (falling away); and from there, by way of the successive occurrence of form, it is *upapatti* (rebirth).

One should connect [the terms] as follows: "growth" (*vuḍḍhi*) by way of the maturation of the faculties; "increase" (*viruḷhi*) by way of the state of having performed and accumulated that respective kamma;
and "abundance" (*vepulla*) by way of the production of the fruit of that kamma. By the words "Granted indeed...
(*kāmañca*), etc., it is shown that the objection beginning with "except for form" (*aññatra rūpā*) was stated by way of a formal definition (*lakkhaṇa*); and this...

The method [of the previous question] might apply because its object is not distinguished; however, in order to show that this present inquiry has a distinguished object, it is said: "But this question...
and so forth. "In these many aggregates" refers to the four aggregates already mentioned, beginning with form and feeling.
By the phrase "apart from form," it is shown that there is no occurrence of consciousness anywhere without some form.

It is illuminated. By means of the exhortation regarding the distinction of existence, it is illuminated that even for form (*rūpa*), there is no occurrence apart from consciousness (*viññāṇa*) by its very nature;

thus he said: "In the formless existence (*arūpabhava*) there is form, and in the non-percipient existence (*asaññābhava*) there is consciousness. Regarding the phrase "of one who has attained cessation" (*nirodhasamāpannassa*):

even for one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling (*saññāvedayitanirodha*), consciousness exists. [This is so] according to the shadow of the literal expression (*byañjanacchāyā*).

"You reject this meaning" means that if you take only the literal sense (*saddattha*) and do not grasp the intended meaning (*adhippāya*), [you would be treating] the sutta as being of interpretable meaning (*neyyattha*).
And here, the first position is based on the case of a being reborn in the non-percipient realm (*asaññabhava*);

whereas the second is based on taking perception itself as the self, according to the method stated in the passage "one regards perception as self," and then regarding another perception—which exists as its "belonging" (*kiñcana*)—as the self.
The second position is that which proceeds on the basis of non-existence, [claiming] "one is non-percipient.

Likewise, the third position proceeds by grasping all material phenomena together with perception—or even both material and immaterial phenomena—as the self. The fourth position proceeds solely by way of speculative grasping.

Regarding these, whatever is to be said should be understood according to the method already stated below. Also, in the case of the neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient position, within the non-percipient state...
The first position is established by asserting the existence of a subtle perception that is incapable of performing the function of clear perception throughout all stages of a being’s birth, death,

and rebirth-linking. The second position and those following it proceed by asserting, according to the method stated in the discussion on non-percipient beings, that there is a nature of perceiving by means of that subtle perception.
In this way, the existence of these doctrines should be understood here. The rest is exactly as previously stated. 24.
Since there can be no arising of knowledge where there is no perception, it is said: “Non-perception is delusion”;
the meaning is that the state of non-perception is the occurrence of delusion. [The term] *niyyānika* is used frequently in the sense of “by which one is led out,” as in “how they lead out.”

The word *viññātabba* is a term denoting the instrument of the action (*kattusādhana*). Thus, he says: “It is ‘to be cognized’ (*viññātabba*) because one cognizes it,” the meaning being that cognition (*viññāṇa*) is the act of cognizing.
Therefore, the phrase “merely by what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized” should be understood as “merely by the measure of the cognitions of what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized.
For this reason, he says: “merely by the occurrence of perception through the five doors,” because of its state of being free from conceptualization (*nibbikappa*).
The meaning is: by means of an application of development that is equal to the occurrence of perceptions belonging to the five doors.
"By the mere occurrence of gross formations" means by the occurrence of gross formations.

And here, "gross formations" refers to the states of meditative attainment (samāpatti-dhamma) culminating in the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana). "Attainment" (upasampada) refers to those who, having seen the fault in both perception and the state of non-perception, [enter] the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana).
Even when praising it, they describe its accomplishment, acquisition, and attainment as being merely the acquisition of the fine-material jhānas;
for them, that [attainment] turns out to be a ruin because it lacks the proper means. Therefore he said, "Destruction," and so forth.
"Emergence" refers to emerging after having previously entered a similar attainment. For them, there is no attainment at all, because it has not been reached.

It is not declared that [the cessation] is to be attained even through the occurrence of gross formations, including the occurrence of formations pertaining to the base of nothingness, because it is to be attained by transcending those as well.
In the phrase "of formations" (*saṅkhārānaṃ*), the genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*).

"The remainder" (*avasesā*) means they are the remainder insofar as there is no state of subtlety beyond this; thus they are so called because they have reached the state of subtlety. Therefore he said:
"Formations that have reached the state of extreme subtlety by way of mental cultivation. "This" refers to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;

it is called "to be attained" because it is designated as such upon the occurrence of corresponding formations. It is "conditioned" because it is produced by conditions through their coming together and combining.
[This is stated] because it will later be said: "Those recluses and brahmins who proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being..."
Having taken together [the various views] as they revolve within his own intelligence, he said, "Therein," because it was spoken by the Blessed One thus.

He stated, "Therein" means "in the seven doctrines of annihilationism," using the locative case. To show that those who remember what is above are "those who remember what has gone above," he said, "What is called 'above'...
and so forth. "Those who remember" refers to those who, having made an aspiration for a certain place, do not obtain it there.

"Knowing. "Asatti" means longing or wishing. "Pecca" means in the other world. "Like the analogy of the merchant" is said because one proceeds with an expectation of specific fruits included within existence (*bhava*).

"From the fear of selfhood" (*sakkāya*): "selfhood" (*sakkāya*) refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*), so called because it is a collection of phenomena existing in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*) that is considered a "good body" (*santo kāyo*);
[it is from] fearing that. "Mā khīyi" means do not waste away; do not go to destruction. Do not...
"Do not sink down below. "Do not be blown away by the wind into the sky; do not break and fall. "Bound with a leash" means bound by a leash.
The "solid post" and the "stake" refer to *sakkāya* (personality-belief), because it is difficult to release.
The "rope" refers to one who holds to views, because it revolves around that [belief]. The "stick" refers to views, because it renders one incapable of cutting them off.
Craving is like a rope because it binds; for it is bound together by way of making an object and by way of being possessed.
Therefore it was said: "by the rope of craving inserted into the handle of views. 26.
By means of his own skill in teaching and according to the inclinations of those to be trained, the Blessed One [refuted] the forty-four doctrines of those who speculate about the future.
Having summarized them as five by way of enumeration—since they are included here and there within those [categories]—and concluding according to that enumeration, he said, "These very five bases.
Therein, because they are the sign of suffering, they are called "bases" (*āyatana*) in the sense of being the cause for various views;
thus it is said, "These very five causes. By way of the "percipient" and so forth, three are the doctrine of annihilationism.
The four [theories] have been divided. But where does the other—the doctrine of Nibbāna in this very life—fit in?
Since it was not divided as a distinct category, he asks: "In which of the theories as they were divided is it included? In the summary (uddesa), however, it was indeed taken as a distinct category:
"Some, moreover, assert Nibbāna in this very life. The other [the opponent] [places it] in the theory of perception of unity or the theory of perception of diversity.
Showing that [the views] are included within [others], he said: "The unity... should be understood," and this was stated according to convenience.

For the first, the doctrine of Nibbāna in the present life (*diṭṭhadhamma-nibbānavāda*), is included within the doctrine of those with perception of diversity (*nānattasaññīvāda*); the other four are included within the doctrine of those with perception of unity (*ekattasaññīvāda*). 27.

"Designated as a past aggregate-section" means the past, designated as an aggregate-section of the prior limit (*pubbanta*). It has as its object the phenomena (*dhamma*) in which one previously dwelt.
In this context, "conception" (kappanā) is intended; therefore, the word *pubba* here denotes the past time.
Furthermore, there is no basis for conception apart from the aggregates such as form (*rūpa*), and the word *anta* denotes a portion (*koṭṭhāsa*). Hence it is said:
"having conceived the prior limit (*pubbanta*) designated as the past portion. And the phrase "having conceived" means the capacity for craving and adherence toward that prior limit.
He speaks of its final completion. "The rest as well" refers to such [views] as "speculations about the past" (*pubbantānudiṭṭhi*).

"Of the kind previously mentioned" means of the kind mentioned in the passages beginning with "those who hold speculations about the future" (*aparantānudiṭṭhino*). It is called "self" (*attā*) because the conceit "I" (*ahaṃmāna*) is placed therein;
it is called "world" (*loka*) because merit and demerit, along with their results, are experienced (*lokenti*) therein; and it is so called by way of those various specific modes of grasping.
He said, "The designation is made by depending [on something]," meaning: "having grasped any one among form and so forth as 'self' and 'the world.
It is eternal (*sassata*) by way of its existence at all times. "Deathless," "constant," and "stable" are synonyms for that very same thing. It is "deathless" (*amara*) due to the absence of death;

it is "constant" (*nicca*) because it persists at all times due to the absence of arising; it is "stable" (*dhruva*) in the sense of being firm and devoid of change. As it has been said, and so forth...

He elucidates the meaning as it has been stated by means of the texts on the analytical knowledge of exposition (*niddesa-paṭisambhidā*). And this meaning is expressed by way of the fivefold view of a personal body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*):
"One regards form as self, one regards feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness as self.
Furthermore, [it is also expressed] by way of the fifteenfold [view], beginning with "possessing form" (*rūpavanta*), etc.
The meaning can also be understood as follows: by means of the view of personality (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), they grasp four or four aggregates as "self" and designate those other than that as "the world.
Likewise, they grasp one aggregate as "self" and designate those other than that as "the world.
This is how the meaning should be seen here. By the phrase "this is the same method," it is shown that just as [in the case of] "form and so forth..."
Having grasped a certain [self] as "self" and "the world," the meaning stated is: "it is eternal... [and so on] ...it is permanent. In this way, he extends the same principle to such meanings as:
"it is not eternal, it is impermanent, it is unstable, it is annihilated, it perishes, it does not exist after death";
and "it is both eternal and impermanent, neither eternal nor impermanent," and so forth.
The four eternalists consist of three who are so by way of their attainment and one who is so by way of his reasoning; thus there are four.

A non-Buddhist (tīrthika) who has attained knowledge of past lives but possesses dull wisdom recollects only a mere hundred thousand births; one of middling wisdom, ten eons of world-dissolution and evolution (saṃvaṭṭa-vivaṭṭa-kappa);
one of sharp wisdom, forty eons of world-dissolution and evolution, but not beyond that. Recollecting in this manner, he...

He asserts that both the self and the world are eternal. But the rationalist, having reached his conclusion through reasoning, following his investigations, and relying on his own ingenuity, asserts that both the self and the world are eternal. Therefore it is said:

"Three [types of eternalists] by way of their gains, and one by way of his reasoning; thus there are four types of eternalist doctrines. And by this very same principle, the doctrine of fortuitous origination is like the doctrine of eternalism.
If it is asked why it is not analyzed in two ways, it should be understood as being because it has been rejected.
And here, in the doctrine that "the self and the world are eternal," this is the demonstration of its irrationality:
for if the self or the world imagined by the opponent were eternal, then because of its lack of modification, it would not abandon its prior form.

For the eternalist (sassatavādī), instruction would be entirely purposeless, since it would be impossible to bring about any specific improvement for anyone, and thus there would be no reason to turn one away from what is harmful or to engage them in what is beneficial.
Furthermore, how could such instruction proceed, given that there is no modification [in the self]?
And in this way, actions such as giving and so forth, as well as actions such as violence and so forth, are impossible for the self, which—like the pure sky—is unchanging. Likewise...
For the eternalist (*sassatavādin*), the very basis for the experience of pleasure and pain is untenable because of the absence of bondage through karma;
since birth and so forth are impossible, how could there be liberation?

If, however, he should say that it is merely a phenomenon (*dhammamatta*) that arises and perishes for him, by virtue of which this conventional expression of "action" and so forth occurs—even in this case, because of not abandoning the prior form...
It is impossible to establish that there is merely a self-nature for one who is stable;

for those states which constitute his condition might be either different from him or non-different. If they were different, then even when those states have arisen, there would be no distinction whatsoever in him.
For it is precisely this [self] that is intended as the one who acts, experiences, passes away, and is reborn. Therefore, he remains exactly in that same state.
The aforementioned fault remains; moreover, the conceptualization of phenomena (*dhammakappanā*) would also become purposeless.

If, on the other hand, [the self] were non-different from them, then since the self—which is non-different from states characterized by arising and passing away—would necessarily undergo arising and passing away just like those states, what opportunity would there be for its permanence?
Alternatively, if those states were permanent just like the self, then bondage and liberation would be impossible; thus, [this position] is simply not tenable.
Regarding the doctrine of eternalism: there is no proponent here capable of stating a pure logical justification for the eternal nature of phenomena;
and since speech devoid of logic does not satisfy the minds of the wise, this doctrine of eternalism is indeed rejected by the discerning.
Regarding the "seven annihilationist views" (*ucchedavāda*), they have already been shown in their essential form below. In that context, two types of people adopt the annihilationist view:
the one who possesses [supernormal powers] and the one who does not. Therein, the "one who possesses" refers to one who possesses the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*);

having seen with the divine eye the passing away (*cuti*) of an Arahant, he does not see their rebirth (*upapatti*). Or, it refers to one who can see even the mere passing away of ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*).
He is able [to see the present], but because he lacks prior practice or fails to perform the preliminary work (*parikamma*), he is unable to see rebirth.
Thus, he adopts the annihilationist view (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), thinking: "In each and every instance, the self is annihilated.

Like the king who took his daughter's hand in marriage, he says: "Who knows the next world? The scope of life extends only as far as the range of the senses. He is one who gains nothing [beyond this].
Either through greed for sensual pleasure, or by means of mere reasoning—thinking, "Just as leaves fallen from a tree do not rejoin it, so too all beings undergo death without rebirth;
beings are like bubbles on water"—one adopts the annihilationist view (ucchedadiṭṭhi). In that regard, what was stated below concerning the human state:
“Having passed away from the state of existence as a deva of the sense-sphere, the state of existence as a deva of the fine-material sphere,
and the fourfold formless state of existence, seven annihilationist views were taught by way of asserting the annihilation of a being. In that regard,

it is indeed appropriate that in the first three doctrines the phrase “with the breakup of the body” is stated, referring to a personal existence included within the five-aggregate existence (pañcavokāra-bhava).

Because those doctrines have arisen, it is not appropriate [to apply] the phrase "with the breakup of the body" to the four doctrines beginning with the fourth, which arise in dependence upon a personal existence included within the fourfold existence (*catuvokāra-bhava*). For indeed, immaterial beings (*arūpī*) possess no body.

This is true; however, by means of the conventional usage current in the realm of form (*rūpa-bhava*), the holder of wrong views (*diṭṭhigatika*) superimposes the conventional term "body" even onto the immaterial realm.
He said, "With the breakup of the body. Just as views were formulated by those holding to wrong views, so too did the Blessed One demonstrate them.

Alternatively, the designation "body" (kāya) should be understood as referring to the formless state of existence, which consists of a collection of phenomena such as contact and so forth, because it exists as a formless body.

Here it is asked: [What about] the second and subsequent doctrines, which establish the non-existence of the entire range of states of existence, such as the form of celestial beings in the sense-sphere realm?
"The state of being speculators regarding the future limit (*aparantakappika*) is appropriate because those doctrines have the future period as their object;

however, it is not [appropriate] for the first doctrine, which establishes the annihilation of the human existence that is directly present to the proponents of views, because its object is the present.

If this is so, then just as in the case of the second and subsequent doctrines, the state of being speculators regarding the future limit is appropriate because they effect the annihilation of one's own successive future rebirths already included within each preceding doctrine, so too—
And it is said: "But, sir, this self is not completely annihilated by that much," and so forth.

Since it is the annihilation of the human existence in the future that is intended, it is logical that even the first doctrine is classified as "speculation concerning the future" (*aparantakappika*).
Thus, among those who speculate concerning the past (*pubbantakappika*), all [the doctrines] are included here by way of proclaiming the annihilation of everything that has come from the past.
The teaching has been concluded. These annihilationist views were presented below among those who speculate about the future limit (*aparantakappika*).
These annihilationist views were stated there in various places for the purpose of showing that [the being] is annihilated right then and there, and that there is no further existence beyond that.
For his conviction is that "beings are like bubbles on water."

"Here" (*idha*) refers to those who speculate about the past (*pubbantakappika*). "Right here" (*idheva*) means that [the self] is annihilated and destroyed right within this human existence and so forth, by way of perishing and passing away.
Thus, the term "speculators about the future" (*aparantakappika*) includes those annihilationists (*ucchedavāda*) whose primary concern is the non-arising [of the self] in the future.
Conversely, the term "speculators about the past" (*pubbantakappika*) includes those whose primary concern is the annihilation of the self right here, after it has come from the past. From this...
The statement "it does not go further," however, is a demonstration of the meaning implied by that [previous] sense.
The doctrine of partial eternalism (*ekaccasassatavāda*) is that which proceeds with the view that among sentient beings and conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), some are eternal.

That [doctrine] is fourfold, arising from those who have passed away from the states of existence as Brahmakāyika, Khiddāpadosika, and Manopadosika deities, as well as from those who arrive here through reasoning; thus he said, "the four types of partial-eternalist doctrines."
“‘Eternalists regarding some conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra)’—this was stated by way of showing the true nature of those phenomena which they grasp as being eternal;
it was not, however, by way of showing their doctrine of eternalism regarding some [phenomena]. For their view is that what is considered eternal is exclusively the unconditioned (asaṅkhata).
Thus it is said in the Brahmajāla Sutta: ‘Whether it be called mind (citta), thought (mano), or consciousness (viññāṇa), this is the self...’”
“Eternal, stable, permanent, not subject to change, it will remain exactly so for all eternity.
For it is impossible for one who is not insane to maintain that a thing which he himself admits to be conditioned by causes is eternal, stable, and so forth.
By this, [it is shown that] things characterized by arising, passing away, and stability might be eternal, or they might be impermanent.

By the passage beginning with "it might not be so stated," the irrationality of the theory of the sevenfold predication (*sattabhaṅgavāda*) as it has been propounded is demonstrated. Herein, this demonstration of irrationality is as follows:

if it were said that "by whichever intrinsic nature a given phenomenon is said to exist, by that very same intrinsic nature that phenomenon does not exist," and so forth, then there would be the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekantavāda*); but if it were said [that they exist] by different [natures], then there would be...

It is not the doctrine of non-absolutism (anekantavāda); nor is it appropriate here to assert that there is a state of being connected with other locations and so forth, because such a thing is established for everyone in the world and thus free from dispute. As for those who say:

"Just as when a golden jar is fashioned into a crown, the state of being a jar perishes, the state of being a crown arises, yet the state of being gold remains; in the same way, some property (dhamma) of all things..."
“Nothing perishes, nothing arises; rather, the intrinsic nature (sabhāva) remains. They should be asked:
“What is that gold which remains constant in both the jar and the crown? If it is the visible form (rūpa) and so forth, then like sound, it is impermanent.

If it is the collection of visible form and so forth, then a collection is merely a conventional designation (sammuti). It cannot be said that such a mere designation exists, does not exist, or is permanent.
Because it is not apprehended by way of an ultimate intrinsic nature (*paramattha-sabhāva*), the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekantavāda*) would not hold.

Furthermore, the phenomena (*dhammā*) must either be different from the possessor of those phenomena (*dhammin*) or not different. If they were different, the possessor of the phenomena would not be impermanent through the impermanence of the phenomena, because of their difference.

For instance, visible forms (*rūpa*) are not the eye-consciousness (*cakkhu-viññāṇa*) due to their difference, nor does the term "eye-consciousness" apply to visible forms; what then is the conceptualization of phenomena?
It would be pointless [to speak of] the permanence or impermanence of a phenomenon (*dhammin*), because such a distinction cannot be established if it is not distinct [from its attributes];

for if it were non-distinct from those things possessing arising and passing away, then since the presence of arising and passing away would belong to that phenomenon just as they do to them, what opportunity would there be for its permanence?

Or else, even those [attributes] would incur permanence just like the phenomenon. Furthermore, the self (*atta*) and the world (*loka*) would be of a nature that is permanent, impermanent, or indescribable.
Because it professes existence in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), it would be like one of the forms such as "permanent" and so forth, or like a lamp and the like.

For it cannot be said that a lamp or similar things—which possess the nature of arising and passing away—have a nature that is permanent, impermanent, or inexpressible, any more than one can say that the soul has any of the forms such as "permanent.
Thus, just as with the sevenfold predication (*sattabhaṅga*), the other predications are likewise impossible.
It should be understood that the doctrine of the sevenfold predication (sattabhaṅgavāda) is untenable.

In this context, those doctrines which proceed thus: "The Lord is eternal, other beings are impermanent"—such as the doctrine of the Lord (Issaravāda) and others—are called partial-eternalism regarding beings (sattékaccasassatavāda).
Those doctrines which proceed thus: "Atoms are eternal and stable, while dyads and so forth are impermanent"—are [called partial-eternalism regarding matter].

The theorists of partial-eternalism (saṅkhārekaccasassatavādā) are, for example, the followers of Kaṇāda and others. But is it not the case that [they hold] "some phenomena are eternal, some are non-eternal"?
In this doctrine, the determination of the non-eternality of the eye and so forth is simply the realization of things according to their true nature;
how then can this be a wrong view? Who says that "the determination of the non-eternal state of the eye and so forth" [is a wrong view]?
"Wrong view"? However, it is the adherence to the eternal existence of certain phenomena that are actually non-eternal which constitutes wrong view here.

Yet, by its occurrence even for a single moment, this [wrong view] corrupts the realization of the non-eternality of the eye and so forth, because of its state of being conjoined with them—just as clarified butter mixed with poison fails to perform its own function due to being contaminated.

It does not deserve to be placed on the side of right view. Alternatively, even though the eye and so forth are determined to be non-eternal, they are grasped by those with wrong views as having the nature of a superimposed "living being" (jīva);

therefore, it is impossible to deny that the comprehension of such [entities] constitutes wrong view. For it is said in the Brahmajāla Sutta: "Whether it be called 'the eye'... or 'the body'... [and so forth].

"...my self," and so forth. And having established this, the objection that "the doctrine of analysis (vibhajjavāda)— which proceeds by stating that some phenomena are eternal and some are non-eternal according to the unconditioned and conditioned elements respectively—
would consequently become a doctrine of partial eternity (ekaccasassatavāda)" finds no footing, because it correctly accords with the true nature of phenomena without distortion.

*Amara* means "does not die. What is it? It is the view and speech of one who holds to a speculative position (*diṭṭhigatika*) that is without limit, according to the method beginning with "I do not say even this.
The various kinds of tossing about by means of such immortal views and speech constitute *amarāvikkhepa*. One who possesses this is called an *amarāvikkhepika*.
Alternatively, *amara* is a certain species of fish; because it [the fish] surfaces and dives, etc., [it is so named].
Just as one running about in water does not reach a firm footing, even so this doctrine runs hither and thither and does not reach a firm footing;

thus it is "eel-wriggling" (amarāvikkhepa), and he who holds such a view is an eel-wriggler. This doctrine proceeds in four ways because it is caused by desire, lust, and delusion regarding the pursuit of false speech;
therefore it is said: "Four types of eel-wrigglers have been stated. Is it not the case that here, all four kinds...

The Amarāvikkhepika, failing to understand as they truly are phenomena such as the wholesome and so forth, as well as the triads concerning the world beyond and so on, merely resorts to evasive diversion whenever he is questioned on various points; thus his status as one who holds a speculative view is established.
For one does not become a holder of a speculative view merely by resorting to evasion when ignorant of the matter asked about, as would be the case for someone simply unwilling to speak.
