"Is it appropriate?"—it is not by the mere act of evading the question that his state of being a "view-possessor" (*diṭṭhigatika*) is intended;

rather, it is by way of false adherence (*micchābhinivesa*). For one who is falsely adhered to the view of eternalism (*sassata*), due to dullness of intellect, fails to understand things such as the wholesome (*kusala*) and the like, as well as the triad of the next world and so forth, as they truly are;
thus, regarding a matter not understood by himself, [he asks] another...
He falls into evasion because he is unable to provide an explanation and out of fear of telling a lie and so forth.

For it has been stated that his doctrine is included within the view of eternalism (*sassatadiṭṭhi*). Alternatively, due to his lack of understanding and lack of faith regarding merit and demerit, as well as their respective results, he maintains the conviction and preference that "it is appropriate and excellent to resort to evasion when questioned on those matters."
For one who, having generated [this view], adheres to it, this arisen view should be regarded as a single, distinct view, like the "sevenfold negation" (sattabhaṅga) view.
It has been stated accordingly: "The view and speech of one who follows a course of views are without limit.
But how is it included within the eternalist view (sassatadiṭṭhi)? Because there is no adherence by way of annihilationism (uccheda). "There is no..."
Someone who knows things as they truly are [might think] this because the world is full of dispute;

however, the notion that “it is exactly thus” is indeed found here as a trace of eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi), by way of grasping at the contemplation of phenomena through another perspective, which has been current in the world since beginningless time.
It is called *anto* because one’s own nature (*sabhāva*) goes to or reaches its end there; it is a limit. That which possesses such a limit is *antavā*. Thus he said:
“With a limit” means: the construction is that it occurs to a person for whom the kasiṇa has not expanded.

The second doctrine is the doctrine that “the world is infinite. The third doctrine is the doctrine that “it is both finite and infinite. The fourth doctrine is the doctrine that “it is neither finite nor infinite.
It is with reference to these very four proponents that the *Brahmajāla Sutta* states: “The finitists [hold] the finite and infinite...”
It is said: “They proclaim to the world [views] on four grounds.
In that regard, it is appropriate to call the first three proponents *antānantikas*, since their views proceed by taking as their object finitude, infinity, and both finitude and infinity.
But how can the last one be called an *antānantika*, given that his view proceeds by way of negating both of those?
This is precisely because it is a doctrine that functions by way of negating both [the finite and the infinite].
For even the doctrine of negation has as its object the finite and the infinite, since it proceeds with reference to them. Others say:

"Just as in the third doctrine, through the process of confusion, both finitude and infinity are possible for this very [world], so too in the doctrine of the logicians (takkī-vāda), both are possible due to the distinction of time."
Both are stated by way of mutual negation. How so? For finitude is stated by the negation of infinity, and infinity by the negation of finitude;
and there is no third position between finitude and infinity because a difference in time is intended.
This is what is meant: since this self, known as the world, [is perceived] by meditators who have attained specific distinctions...
"Because at some time an infinite [world] was seen by a witness and he remembers it, therefore it is not finite.
But because at some time a finite [world] was seen by those very same witnesses and they remember it, therefore it is not infinite.

And just as this is applied by way of the reasoner who relies on what has been heard, so too should it be applied, as appropriate, by way of the reasoner who recollects past births and others. For this reasoner, because his state is preceded by non-increase...

Because the counterpart signs (paṭibhāganimitta) lack direct perceptibility due to their state of having been developed—that is, by virtue of the time at which they were developed—one rejects the view that "it has an end" by remaining at the level of mere hearsay and so forth;
yet, by virtue of the time at which they have not been developed, one rejects that "it is infinite.

However, this is not because of an absolute non-existence of having an end or being infinite, as is the case with the expression "neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient" (nevasaññīnāsaññī), and it must necessarily be so.
This must be understood in this way; otherwise, the fourth position would merely fall on the side of confusion.

For there is no mode of self-existence that is free from both finitude and infinity; moreover, the proponent of reasoning follows the path of logic, and neither of those two is incompatible with a single [self] when considered according to the difference in time.
"The subsequent tetrad" refers to the tetrad of perceptions beginning with "perceiving unity."
"Exclusively happy" means happy in an absolute sense. However, because that happiness of his is unmixed with suffering, he says "continuously happy.
"Only exclusively happy" is said with reference to the abundance of his happiness.
"In the seven past births" is said because it is impossible to recollect more than that by means of the knowledge of recollecting past births (*jātissarañāṇa*).
“Just such a one” means a personal existence (attabhāva) endowed with happiness. For one who remembers that [existence] as being thus endowed with happiness, it is like the present;
and for one who remembers a past birth while being touched by suffering here and now, it is the same.
“Of all” refers to both those who possess [supernormal powers] and those who rely on reasoning. By the word “thus” (tathā), the phrase “of all” is drawn forward [to apply to the subsequent clause].
The sense-sphere [consciousness] is called "neither-painful-nor-pleasant," "not exalted," and "not manifest";
thus he says, "by way of the fourth jhāna. That which has the fourth jhāna as its cause, or that which is produced by it, is "belonging to the fourth jhāna" (*catutthajjhānika*).
"Of one who is neutral" means of one who has become neutral, or of one characterized by abundant neutral feeling. It refers specifically to the state of being neutral.
This is for one who recollects how he himself previously attained a state of neutrality. "Partial-eternalists" refers to those who maintain the doctrine of partial eternalism;
for they are partial-eternalists by way of referring to specific persons (puggalādhiṭṭhāna). This same method applies to the others as well.
Since the doctrine of fortuitous origination is included within the category of eternalism, it is stated that "there are two kinds of proponents of fortuitous origination."
28. *Diṭṭhuddhāra* (The Extraction of Views): This refers to the extraction of the words by way of showing that the aforementioned views are not conducive to liberation (*aniyyānika*).

*Paccattaṃyeva ñāṇaṃ* (Knowledge within oneself alone): This is knowledge within one's own self, independent of others. Since that knowledge is directly experienced by oneself, he says "direct knowledge" (*paccakkhañāṇa*).
*Visuddhi* (Purification): This is the purification of knowledge through the removal of defilements (*upakkilesa*), just as gold is purified by the removal of impurities.
He said: “‘Pure’ means ‘free from defilement. Because it is free from the darkness of the defilements, it is luminous and radiant;
thus it is said: ‘‘Bright’ means ‘effulgent. This is so even according to external systems, because of the attainment of meditative absorption (jhāna).
Thinking ‘we know this,’ by way of a false grasp such as ‘the self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, all else is vain,’ [they fall into error].”

Having merely cultivated a portion of ignorance, and based precisely upon that very misconception as it was grasped—thinking, "We know this matter in that way"—they simply introduce and insert a nonexistent element of knowledge into that false grasp, as if it were present there.
That is not knowledge; it is merely wrong view. And what is this so-called wrong view? It is the view that the self is eternal.
And because of the state of wrong adherence expressed by the passage beginning with “the world and so forth,” he said: “That too... [is] the meaning.
Referring to that knowledge which serves as the decisive support (upanissaya) for the view, he said: “Because its characteristic is mere knowing, it is merely a portion of knowledge.
For even knowledge can indeed serve as a decisive support for a view, since both one who possesses it and another may develop wrong adherence in various ways accordingly.
"Because of not transcending and because of not overstepping. "Non-transcending" (*anupātivattana*) means that by this [condition] they do not transcend; therefore, it is "non-transcending.
"From the condition of clinging" (*upādāna-paccayato*) means from the state of being a condition for clinging. By this very metaphorical designation of the fruit, he speaks of clinging itself.
If all views mentioned in the *Brahmajāla Sutta* are here being discussed, then such being the case, this discourse...

He said, “In the *Brahmajāla Sutta*, they are identical,” beginning with the words, “But in the *Brahmajāla*... Because of the statement, “Apart from form, apart from feeling, they merely run around after identity (*sakkāya*),” it is the view of identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) that is presented here.
The *Brahmajāla* has already been explained, since the sixty-two views mentioned therein are also included here. [This refers to] the adherence to eternalism and annihilationism.
It is preceded by adherence to a self (*attābhinivesa*), because it proceeds from such views as "the self is eternal" or "the self is subject to annihilation.

30. Regarding the statement "The sixty-two [views]... are shown," how is this meaning demonstrated by the textual passage beginning, "Here, monks, a certain person..."? It is because it characterizes the grasping at views concerning the past and the future for one who has not yet abandoned the view of a personal identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*).

"By relinquishment" means by suppression. Regarding the statement, "Having attained and dwelt in the third jhāna through the cessation of the fourth jhāna," it is not the case that one who has fallen away from the fourth jhāna attains the third jhāna;
rather, the third jhāna occurs by way of retrogression for one who has emerged from the third jhāna and for one who has emerged from the fourth jhāna. Therefore he said: "This..."

“*Panetthā*,” etc. This should be understood as being of the same nature. The meaning is that the statement, “The rapture of seclusion ceases,” should be understood as being spoken by way of emergence and cessation (*vuṭṭhāna-nirodha*), just as in the passage, “Due to the cessation of non-sensual pleasure.
“Grief consisting in the exhaustion of inferior jhāna” refers to grief accompanied by the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). For that [grief] brings about the exhaustion of jhāna.
“Workability” (*kammanīyabhāva*) means the state of being capable of action regarding the attainment of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), as if one has already entered that absorption.
It is called “mental grief” (*domanassa*) because it is like mental grief due to its lack of joy (*somanassa*).

The rapture (*pīti*) mentioned again in the phrase “rapture born of seclusion arises” is the rapture of the first two jhānas. “The place from which shade departs” refers to that location which is being overcome by the heat of the sun.
“Shadows depart. In this context, by the phrase “shadows in the sun,” he refers to the place where the conditioned elements designated as “sunlight” are abandoned.
Therefore, he says, “In whatever place,” and so forth. 31.
“Spiritual happiness” (nirāmisaṃ sukhaṃ) is the happiness of the third jhāna, because it has cast far away the bait of sensual desire (kāma).
32. "Neither-painful-nor-pleasant" refers to the feeling of the fourth jhāna, not any other kind of equanimity-feeling.
33. "Without grasping" means not apprehending anything at all through the sense of "mine-ness.
"Conducive to nibbāna" means it is suitable for the attainment of nibbāna, or because it is a one-pointed means that does not run counter to nibbāna itself. Therefore he said, "it is beneficial."

"In all cases" (*sabbattha*) means in regard to all phenomena belonging to the three planes. "This" (*etaṃ*) refers to this suppression of the defilements through the aforementioned cultivation of serenity (*samatha-bhāvanā*).
[Objection: Since there has been no drying up of attachment in all cases, how can it be called a "path conducive to Nibbāna"?
[Response: It is not so; such is the intended meaning. "In all cases" (*sabbattha*) [here] means in regard to everything, such as the view of past lives (*pubbantānudiṭṭhi*) and so forth.

"By way of non-grasping" means by way of not grasping through craving. For where the grasp of craving has been liberated, there the grasps of views and conceit become as if dried up, because they are associated with it. For such a person, the path leading to Nibbāna is indeed near, not distant.
Therefore it is said: "A helpful path has arisen. And for such a person, [the notion] beginning with "I am at peace" [arises].
He says, “‘Speaks out’ means he reviles with overweening pride,” because the view of self-identification stands on the side of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
He says, “‘Grasps at this very thing,’” because there is no restriction [to a single object], and thus it is stated as “even the eighteenfold [grasping].

The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. Since the existence of the remaining forms of grasping is established by implication whenever the grasping of views (*diṭṭhupādāna*) exists, that alone has been specifically mentioned.

"The sphere to be known" means that Nibbāna, the cause of cessation, is to be known. "Of two spheres" refers to two spheres such as the eye-sphere and so forth. Nibbāna is shown by way of negation (paṭikkhepa) according to the inclinations of those to be trained.

"Does not find a footing" means it does not take a stand. "Beyond this" means beyond this Nibbāna. "Stream" means craving. "By way of the negation of formations" means by way of the negation of the four great elements, which constitute a portion of formations.

“Consciousness” (*viññāṇa*) means that which is to be known by distinguished knowledge. For that very reason, it is non-demonstrable, not cognizable by the eye, and beyond the range of the sense-faculties.

“Endless” (*ananta*) means that which has its limits removed; the meaning is “eternal. “Radiant on all sides” (*sabbato pabhaṃ*) means luminous everywhere due to the absence of the darkness of defilements.
Alternatively, there is the reading “radiant on all sides” (*sabbato papaṃ*), meaning it falls or shines forth from every side. By means of those things reckoned as the forty meditation subjects...

It is said that one must enter by descending from the bathing places into the lake of the Deathless (*amata-sara*). It is called "liberation through non-clinging" (*anupādā-vimokkha*) because one is liberated therein without clinging to or grasping at any phenomenon (*dhamma*).
It is also called "liberation through non-clinging" because by means of it one is liberated without clinging;

this refers to the supreme path (*aggamagga*). Furthermore, because it is proximate to liberation through non-clinging, the fruit of arhatship (*arahattaphala*) is also termed "liberation through non-clinging."
It has been stated. The remainder is easy to understand.
The elucidation of the hidden meaning of the commentary on the *Pañcattaya-sutta* is completed.
3. Commentary on the *Kinti-sutta*.

34. "Existence" (*bhava*) is limited; "non-existence" (*abhava*) is great. For this prefix *a-* has the sense of increase, as in such expressions as "restraint and non-restraint" (*saṃvarāsaṃvara*) or "fruit and non-fruit" (*phalāphala*).
Therefore, "the cause of existence and non-existence" means the cause of either a small or a great existence;
the meaning is that one looks back toward that [existence]. Hence he said: "In this or that existence, I shall experience pleasure," and so forth.
35. Since a dispute among worldlings arises concerning the supramundane factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*), it is said:

“Both mundane and supramundane [factors] have been explained. For even mundane factors conducive to enlightenment are a specific cause because they are the proximate cause for the attainment of supramundane states; thus, they are considered superior to other mundane phenomena.
"In these thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment" is stated without distinction.

"There is a difference in meaning" means that there is a differentiation in meaning because of the specific realization of the factors conducive to enlightenment; for it is not the body and so forth that are to be developed, but rather mindfulness alone that is to be developed.
"A difference in phrasing" refers to the distinction in expression. "For this reason also" means by way of this logical justification as well.

Now, demonstrating that reasoning, he says: “The meaning and the phrasing,” and so forth. Therein, “having brought together” means having brought together from other suttas, and having brought together by means of the words of other suttas.
“Otherwise” means from another source; the sense is: having made it depart from what is real (*bhūta*).
“The state of being wrongly established” means the state of being placed not according to reality. “Both the meaning and the phrasing are merely the cause for making [the meaning] known.”
Because it is the cause for awakening to both the meaning and the word without error. 37.
Here, in the context of the Dhamma and Vinaya, *satipaṭṭhāna* is understood as "the very establishment of mindfulness";

in terms of meaning (*attha*), they are identical because the meaning is grasped exactly as it is. In terms of phrasing (*byañjana*), there is a difference due to the distinction of gender, arising from the absence of a common etymological derivation.

Showing it by means of a distinction in phrasing, he said: “Whether you call it ‘the establishment of mindfulness’ (satipaṭṭhāna) or ‘the establishments of mindfulness’ (satipaṭṭhānā), you have applied it incorrectly.
“Trifling” (appamattaka) means minute, slight, and light; it is not something heavy.

Because there is no fault in what was spoken—even though it could have been stated without emphasis—having instead applied it with emphasis and a resonant tone, he said: “It is possible to attain nibbāna.”

This was stated for the purpose of making it known that the misapplication of the phrasing (*byañjana*) does not constitute an obstacle to distinction; [the Buddha] attained final Nibbāna only after answering questions regarding the four paths. This statement—“But this is merely trifling”—was said with reference to the phrasing of the Suttanta.
38. Now, why did the dispute arise on the fourth occasion? The intention is that their statements agree both in meaning (*attha*) and in phrasing (*byañjana*).
Regarding the dispute over perception (*saññā*): although they agree both in meaning and in phrasing...
Furthermore, their perception (*saññā*) is not yet purified; showing that a dispute has arisen on account of that perception, he says "I...

and so forth. By the phrase "The same method applies," he extends the principle that their knowledge (*ñāṇa*) functions thus: "I say this is the foundation of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*)," and "This one says, 'This is the foundation of mindfulness. This is the meaning.
39. "One should not hurry for the sake of reproving" means that one should not reprove [the other] very quickly.

"Therefore" means because someone, by way of a wrathful nature, resists in this manner; therefore. "One of non-clinging view" means one who does not grasp firmly because, having taken up [an idea], he does not adhere to it;
thus he is one of non-clinging view. "As if swallowing" means as if swallowing and putting down [into his stomach].

"Affliction" (*upaghāta*) means affliction of the mind, like the blow of an axe. "Like one whose wound is touched" means that just as pain arises when a wound is touched, so too does mental suffering arise.
"Even after saying it twice, he releases [the matter]" means that he is one who relinquishes well;
the intention is that he releases it even at the mere mention of the censure. And by way of speaking, there is weariness of body and mind.
"Of such a nature" means that although he may have spoken words of vexation to the accuser by not releasing [the matter] immediately, his inherent character is one free from anger and so forth.

"Equanimity" (upekkhā) is the state of looking on with equanimity toward that person, thinking, "He will be known by his own karma. One is said to "despise equanimity" because of failing to look on with equanimity toward that person's misconduct.
40. "Shifting of statements" (vacanasañcāra) is the presentation of a statement otherwise through the medium of slander. "Contempt for views" (diṭṭhipaḷāsa) is due to grasping at opposing positions.
*Laḍḍhi*: This, moreover, is the state of being unsatisfactory to the mind, the state of not pleasing the Teacher’s mind.
*Kalahā* (quarrel) is a conflict that has arisen by way of producing a legal dispute (*adhikaraṇa*); it is the preliminary stage of a brawl.
"By which cause" means by which Dhamma, by the Teacher’s instruction. It is with reference to that very thing that he says: "The Dhamma."
“The quality of reconciliation is intended. Herein: “in accordance with the Dhamma” means here [in the phrase] “and in accordance with the Dhamma.
“Dhamma” refers to the discourse of the Fully Enlightened One as it proceeds in such a way that those who have fallen into dispute come to be persuaded. Therefore he said:
“the making of persuasion for those bhikkhus. That very discourse, when spoken by a bhikkhu, is called “anudhamma” (conformity to the Dhamma).
It is a practice that is irreproachable. Therefore it was said: “That indeed he explains as ‘name’. “Anyone whatsoever” means whoever. “In accordance with the Dhamma” means having a valid reason.
As for the word *kiṃ*, which has another meaning here, he says: “another. “His” refers to the bhikkhu who has practiced according to the method already stated;
the meaning is that his practice cannot be censured by anyone. All the rest is easily understood.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning (*Līnatthappakāsanā*) of the Commentary on the *Kinti-sutta* is completed.
4. Commentary on the *Sāmagāma-sutta* 41.
“Divided into two” (*dvedhikajātā*) means having become divided, having developed a schism. “Split into two” (*dvejjhajātā*) means having reached a state of duality.
*Bhaṇḍana* (quarrel) is so called because by means of it people revile and abuse one another; it is a state of hostile mind. *Taṃ* refers to that quarrel.
*Dhamma-vinaya* refers to the sacred word (*pāvacana*). *Vitujjantā mukhasattīhi* means piercing with the arrows of their speech.
*Sahitaṃ me* means my speech is "sahita"—coherent, well-knit, connected in its sequence, and meaningful. Therefore he said, "connected with the goal" (*atthasaṃhitaṃ*). *Adhiciṇṇaṃ* means practiced.
“Viparāvattaṃ” means turned back by way of seeing the contradiction; the meaning is that it has been overturned and corrupted.
Therefore he said: “By way of long time... pe ... turn back. “Pariyesamāno cara” means wander about, going here and there, and train yourself.
If you are able, untie right now the knot of fault that I have bound. “Maranameva” means death itself, by way of mutual destruction.
“Nāṭaputtassa ime” means these [disciples] belong to Nāṭaputta; since they are his students, he says “antevāsikesu” (among the resident pupils).
*Paṭivāna* is the turning back from a previous practice; those whose nature (*rūpa*) or characteristic (*sabhāva*) is that [turning back] are called *paṭivānarūpā*.
Therefore he says, “of the nature of turning back. *Kathana* is the explaining of the meaning. *Pavedana* is the making known by bringing forward reasons and examples for it. Not...
"That which leads to non-peace" means that which conduces to the absence of peace; that very thing is "conducive to non-peace," and [the phrase refers] to that.
Having been raised up, it stands as a monument (*thūpa*) because it serves as a cause for establishment; thus he said, "with its monument broken" means "with its foundation broken.
Alternatively, "monument" (*thūpa*) should be understood as the state of the Dhamma’s leading out [to liberation], in the sense of being raised above all other phenomena.
Thus, in the system of the Nigaṇṭha, even that which was considered indivisible has become divided and utterly destroyed, being entirely non-existent;
therefore, it is called "a ruined heap" (*bhinnathūpa*). That very state of deliverance is the refuge for those desiring liberation from the suffering of saṃsāra;
since that is absent here, it is "without refuge" (*appaṭisaraṇa*). Thus, the meaning here should be understood as "in that ruined heap, there is no refuge."
“Taking the teacher as authority” means being authoritative by acting as the teacher’s own standard (the teacher’s closed fist).
“In various ways” means in diverse manners. Having stated, “No dispute arose,” he shows the reason for its non-arising by saying, “For the Teacher...
having made it a cause for non-dispute, he attained final nibbāna. To explain this, he says, “By the Blessed One...,” and so forth. And a foundation.

And there are the supports (*avassaya*), namely the Great Authorities (*mahāpadesa*) for determining: "This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction," as well as the modes of answering questions (*pañhabyākaraṇa*); for it is by relying upon these and depending on them that those who uphold the Dhamma and Vinaya reach a definitive conclusion.
Thus, when someone asks about a matter in the Vinaya based on a Great Authority from the Suttanta, [it is resolved] through the four modes of answering questions.
Because its form has been well-determined by way of that [method], it is said, "By that very means," and so forth, meaning that the Dhamma-Vinaya is thus able to perform the Teacher’s task here;
the intention is that it is a fit vessel for the sublime teaching. 42.
It is called a "discourse-offering" (*kathāpābhata*) because it must be brought back after having been entered into, and because the truth must be made to function as the root offering.
The meaning is that the primary cause is the discourse on the Dhamma. Those by whose means the dispute arose are themselves the proponents of what is not Dhamma;
let it lead first to harm and suffering for them.

Then, as for the question, "What about other gods and humans?", the answer is that it serves as a basis for defilement through a succession of accusations. Therefore he said: "As in the Kosambaka Khandhaka," and so forth.
43. "Taught through direct knowledge" (*abhiññā desitā*) means having known through distinguished wisdom (*abhivisiṭṭhāya paññāya*), they have been awakened to it.

"Having the nature of depending" (*paṭissayamānarūpā*) means pointing out that they depend, relying with a sense of reverence; hence he said, "dwelling in dependence" (*upanissāya viharanti*), meaning dwelling by making [the Teacher] their most venerable support.
"Laid down in the *Parivāra*" refers to the passage: "for the sake of livelihood, for the cause of livelihood."

Having determined this, those [rules] which were established in the Parivāra-pāḷi by way of a mixture [of categories] were indeed formulated by the Blessed One according to the recitation of the Vibhaṅga, as in the words: "And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule.
Excluding those, all the remaining training rules are called the *adhipātimokkha* (the primary Pātimokkha); this is according to the maxim of "the cow and the ox" (*gobalībadda-nāya*).
It should be understood as "it is said," because even those [minor rules] possess the nature of being governed by the *Pātimokkha*.

"In this regard, this is the method" means that this method which is about to be explained applies to the state of being minor regarding the easy abandonment [of faults]. "Those" refers to choice foods.
"Whoever" refers to either a monk or a nun. "As a basis for an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)" means whatever serves as the basis for an offense of wrong-doing.
"Ten" refers to the fact that the transgression of a root-offense is slight by virtue of its being easily abandoned.
"The preliminary path" refers to the mundane path (*lokiyamagga*). "Therein" means in that arising of dispute based upon the preliminary path.

"Luminous knowledge" (*obhāsañāṇa*) is the knowledge that serves as the cause for the arising of the luminosity. Furthermore, in that context, he [perceives it] as having the nature of the perception of the path.
Because it is heard that "the path is fourfold," he says, "The first path," and so forth.
In this way, having abandoned [the path] without doubt or suspicion, one is unable to explain the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
"The shrine was not seen" refers to the stupa built by him. [He praises] that which stands in a blameworthy state of being an ordinary person (*puthujjana*).
Because one has adopted the state of an Ariyan, yet by adhering to, grasping, and asserting that wrong view, both heaven and the Path have indeed been obstructed. For it is said:
“He who praises the blameworthy, or blames him who is worthy of praise;”
"He gathers misfortune with his mouth; through that misfortune, he finds no happiness.
For by this [statement], even hypocrisy is seen there, as he says, "I shall explain a meditation subject capable of leading one to Arahantship in a single moment";
however, regarding the others, there is simply nothing to be said. "Having torn out" means having extracted.

“Then those bhikkhus,” and so forth, is the remainder. Having caused [them] to grasp the statement, “They partake of the Deathless who partake of mindfulness directed to the body,” as a wrong grasp, he said, “To this extent, indeed, will the Deathless have been partaken by you. 44.
“Evam” (thus) is a characteristic of the manner; it is not a restriction of the manner. Therefore, for this very reason, whatever dispute...
"It would arise" is what is meant. A mind that occurs toward a venerable person as "venerable" is called *garu* because its object is venerable;

it is *garu* by virtue of being associated with that [object]. Its state is *gārava*, which is "veneration" or "the act of honoring. That which lacks this is *agārava*. Therefore he said, "devoid of veneration" (*gāravavirahito*).
*Patissaya* is said to be "reliance," which is living in a humble manner through the veneration of one who is venerable; its opposite is...

"He is without deference," he said; "he is without support, living in a lowly manner. Here, in order to show how this person is indeed disrespectful toward the Teacher, the passage beginning with "But here" was stated.

In that context, the phrase "does not attend at the three times" and so forth is a complete description showing the whole without remainder; however, the establishment of disrespect through its individual components is as follows:
The undertaking of the training rules in general is the basis; their distinction is the specific difference.

This same method applies to the others as well. "He does not go with due care" means he does not go with a sense of reverence. It is performed specifically for the Saṅgha because it is included within the Saṅgha;
just as when something is given for the sake of the Saṅgha and accepted by a single bhikkhu, it is indeed considered given to the Saṅgha.
He is one who does not fulfill the training and lacks respect for it. Therefore the Blessed One said: “One who does not fulfill the training.
As for the root of dispute that has arisen within one’s own assembly, it is specifically called “internal” because it must be settled by oneself and because it brings harm to oneself.
This same method applies here to the term “external” as well.

46. "Six bases" (*chaṭṭhānāni*) means six roots. Just as the state of being the subject (*adhikatta-bhāva*) belongs to the methods of settling (*samatha*) by way of their application, so too the state of being subject to them belongs to disputes and the rest;
thus he said: "For the purpose of pacifying... [etc.]... legal issues" (*adhikaraṇāni*). By this, he indicates that the word *adhikaraṇa* has the sense of an object (*kamma*).
Alternatively, the methods of settling (*samatha*) are "subjected to" (*adhikarīyanti*) therein by way of their application.
Legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*) refer to disputes (*vivāda*) and so forth.

A dispute, having arisen merely as such, leads subsequently to harshness; thus, based on whatever matter it first arose, following the course of that dispute, it pursues that very matter or another, like a chronic disease rooted in its origin.

Having been established, as it increases and reaches the stage of a legal issue arising from contention (*vivādādhikaraṇa*), it is said to "increase further. When it reaches the stages of accusation, offense, and duty, the increase of the contention is indeed manifest.
Therefore it was said: "That contention, having reached the four types of legal issues, increases further.

"Of those that have arisen, of those that have arisen" means of those that have occurred, of those that have occurred. "For the purpose of settling" (*samathattha*) means for the purpose of calming (*samanattha*).
“By means of the eighteen grounds” is a term for a characteristic, just as in the expression: “If they were to give me diseases, this medicine should be given.
Therefore, those who dispute on account of any one of these are said to be “disputing on the eighteen grounds.
*Upavadanā* means abuse; *codanā* means an accusation.
It is called *sammukhāvinaya* (settlement in the presence) because it is a settling [of a dispute] in the very presence of the legal assembly (*adhikaraṇa*).
It is *yebhuyyasikā* (decision by majority) because it is the performance of a formal act (*kamma*) by a majority of those who speak according to the Dhamma within the assembled assembly.
It is the coming together of the Sangha of performers through their harmony, not merely the mere presence of the individuals who perform the act. *Bhūtatā* means truthfulness.
For here the word *dhamma* has the sense of "truth," as in such expressions as "one who speaks the Dhamma" (*dhammavādī*). It is called *vinaya* because one is disciplined by it;
it refers to the procedure taught by the Blessed One for the settlement of various legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*). The presence of that *vinaya* is "presence of the *vinaya*" (*vinayasammukhatā*).
Adversaries regarding the matter known as the subject of dispute are "adversaries regarding the matter" (*atthapaccatthika*); of them...
[This refers to] those who are adversaries. The presence of the Saṅgha is lacking because the settlement is effected by persons authorized [by the Saṅgha].
"That" refers to the legal issue arising from a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*). It is endowed with five factors as stated in the passage beginning with "he does not proceed through favoritism.

Among the secret methods such as the *guḷhaka*, a secret ballot (*salākaggāha*) should be conducted when the assembly is full of shameless people; a public ballot (*vivaṭaka*) should be conducted when the assembly is full of conscientious people.

When there is a dispute among fools, one who whispers into another’s ear [is considered a witness]. Regarding that action for which those who speak according to the Dhamma are in the majority, that is called a *yebhuyyasikā* (decision by majority);
thus he said, "by the majority of those speaking according to the Dhamma," and so forth.

"Decided in this way" means decided by way of confession after pointing out the offense; however, as for the remedy (*paṭikamma*), it belongs to the settlement of legal issues concerning offenses (*āpattādhikaraṇa*).
It will come from another. "Unbecoming for a recluse" means it is not suitable for a recluse, something that recluses ought not to do;

in that case, regarding transgression or violation. "Concealing" means while hiding it. Because of the abundance of evil, he is an evildoer (*pāpiya*); the formal act to be performed against such a person is *tassapāpiyasika*.
There is no settling by means of *sammukhā-vinaya* alone without the admission [of the offense], because it cannot be settled without such an admission or a formal acceptance (*khanti*).

"In this regard" refers to the confession of the offense. "Acting upon what has been admitted" (*paṭiññātakaraṇa*) is the verbal action consisting of the performance of the act—such as saying, "You should exercise restraint in the future"—and that which proceeds by way of granting the probationary period (*parivāsa*) and so forth, once the state of having committed the offense and other factors have been admitted.
“According to what is appropriate” means according to the method stated as “by two, four, three, or one.
“In this” refers to this sutta, or to this investigation of serenity (*samatha*). “The method of exposition” means the mere outline of the exposition.
Therefore he said, “But the detailed account,” and so forth.
47. It has been stated only in brief, not in detail as in the Samathakkhandhaka. By the word *tathā* (thus), the term *dhammā* (phenomena) is drawn forward;
here the particle *iti* has the sense of "beginning with," meaning "by this manner beginning with [this]," so it is said.
Because the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhammā*) are exclusively blameless, there is no state of being non-dhamma (*adhammabhāva*) regarding the Blessed One’s...

Having shown that speaking by omitting or adding to the manner in which [the teaching] was taught constitutes an act not in accordance with the Dhamma, he says, "The three foundations of mindfulness," etc., in order to demonstrate its state of being non-Dhamma.
"Leading out" (niyyānika) means it proceeds as something possessing miracles and being unopposed. By the phrase "just so," [he refers to] "thus for us," etc.
It draws out the meaning already stated. That which is done according to what has occurred... [is] called *dhamma* because of its being done in accordance with the *dhamma*;
by way of the opposite of what was stated, that which follows is *adhamma*. This is called *vinaya* because of the restraining, abandoning, and reflecting upon lust and the other defilements.
This is called *avinaya* because of the non-restraining of lust and the other defilements. This is called *vinaya* because of acting in accordance with the discipline (*vinaya*).

The opposite of what has been stated is non-discipline (*avinaya*). Since all disciplinary acts (*vinayakamma*) are unshakable precisely through the perfection of the subject matter (*vatthusampatti*) and so forth, he said:
“Perfection of the subject matter... this is called discipline”; it should be understood as non-discipline by way of its opposite.
Therefore, he said: “Failure of the subject matter,” and so on.
In the sense of leading one toward right practice (*sammāpaṭipatti*), the Dhamma as previously described is itself the "guide" (*netti*);
for that very reason, it is called the "rope of Dhamma" (*dhammarajjū*) because it serves as the cause for proceeding without slackening, just like a rope for a living being.

According to the method of the Suttantas, first of all, the ten courses of wholesome action (*dasakusalakammapatha*) are thus called "Dhamma. Or let that alone be the "guide of Dhamma"; whatever [is taught] here in this [context]...

The construction is as follows: having brought in the passage from the *Vaṇṇanā* beginning with “the thirty-six factors conducive to enlightenment,” [one considers] whether it was spoken according to the Dhamma and the Vinaya, or whether that very [passage] itself is the guide to the Dhamma (*dhammanetti*). By means of that guide to the Dhamma, it accords;
by means of that aforementioned guide to the Dhamma, it converges; the meaning is that it possesses the very same characteristic. Thus is the Dhamma which constitutes the basis for dispute.

When one determines that "this is *dhamma*," "this is not *dhamma*," "this is *vinaya*," or "this is not *vinaya*," it is shown that for some there is indeed a legal issue arising from a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*), because the methods for its settlement have not been brought to completion. 48.

"But this" refers back to that legal issue arising from a dispute. Although the section has reached [the point of] explaining the meaning, [it continues]: "By two"—meaning by even two monks residing in whichever monastery where the legal issue arising from a dispute has arisen; [they must be] more than two.
49. "In the vicinity of the aggregates" (khandhasāmanta) means being proximate by way of being an aggregate of offenses (āpattikkhandha).

"Vicinity of an offense" (āpattisāmanta) refers to the preliminary stage of the offense to be committed. He said, "An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) prior to the first Pārājika," because physical contact through lust for sexual intercourse is the basis for that wrong-doing.
For the remaining three Pārājikas, there is only a grave offense (thullaccaya) in their preliminary stages.

50. Having investigated and having made an effort. The legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) has been shown there, specifically because it is intended that [the matter] be dealt with based on a formal admission.
52. The basis for the formal act (*kamma*) has been shown; the intention is that this is not yet the method of settlement (*samatha*).

[Objection: But is this not the section concerning the methods of settlement? [Reply: True. However, it is said "In such a case... and so forth, in order to show that when the cause of the method of settlement is shown, the method of settlement itself is effectively shown.
53. "This legal act" (*idaṃ kamma*) refers to the legal act described by the words, "This [act] of ours who have fallen into quarreling," and so forth.

"Similarity to the *tiṇavatthāraka* (covering over as with grass)" indicates that it is designated by that name because of its resemblance to it—just as one says, "This is Brahmadatta"—even though it is merely in form that it is called a *tiṇavatthāraka* legal act, and not because the entire procedure for performing it is identical.
Therefore he said, "In the Khandhaka," and so forth. [The text continues: "For householders, by the inferior..."

The concealment and denial is, for example, as in the case of saying, "There is no sesame ball. This is an offense incurred through the act of deceiving during a legitimate formal agreement (*dhammika-paṭissava*).

"Of this" refers to the legal issue arising from a duty (*kiccādhikaraṇa*). Its settlement occurs solely by means of resolution in the presence of the accused (*sammukhā-vinaya*), because it is settled precisely through the presence of the Saṅgha and so forth.
54. Because of the statement regarding the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala-sacchikiriyā*), the right view of the path of stream-entry is taught in the Kosambiya Sutta.

However, since it is stated here simply as "he dwells having attained similarity in view," it is said that "it should be understood that in this sutta the right view of the fruit of stream-entry is what is being discussed.
That the lightness or heaviness of an evil deed is to be understood by its being slight or grave—that is, by its being mild or sharp—is why he says:
"Aṇu means slightly blameworthy; thūla means greatly blameworthy. The rest is easy to understand.
The Elucidation of the Meaning in the Commentary on the Sāmagāma Sutta is completed.
5. Commentary on the Sunakkhatta Sutta 55.
It is called "higher knowledge" (aññā) because it understands the noble limit known through the lower paths; it is the wisdom of the path. Because it is the state of its fruit—

The wisdom of the supreme fruit (*aggaphala-paññā*) and the right intention (*sammā-saṅkappa*) and other factors associated with it are called "higher knowledge" (*aññā*); thus he said, "Higher knowledge is Arahantship.
It is described by four phrases, as in the passage beginning, "The Blessed One has been served by me," and not by a single phrase alone.

Showing that mere conceit—the thought "I have attained the supramundane state"—is overestimation (*adhimāna*), he said, "Those who perceive themselves as having attained what they have not attained," and so forth.
56. "This is the occasion" (*idaṃ ṭhānaṃ*): this refers to the more exalted knowledge of rise and fall (*udayabbayañāṇa*), which serves as the conventional cause for illumination and so forth.
For, by virtue of its being more exalted, it deceives the practitioner of insight because, acting as a condition for the wisdom of the path and fruit, it is difficult to discern in its true nature.
Therefore he said: "It is unmanifest darkness. "This question" (*imaṃ pañhaṃ*): this discourse is profound and connected with the supramundane.
The meaning desired to be known by oneself. "Having mastered" means having mastered merely by way of acquiring the Piṭakas.

Therefore he said, "without knowing. "Contaminating" means either allowing the poison of the defilements (*kilesa-viṣa*) to descend, or serving conditions that are unhelpful and contrary to the Dispensation (*sāsana*).
"Thus for him" means: because of their doing so in the manner described, for this mind, by way of teaching the Dhamma...
For one who has set out [on the path], "changeability" (aññathābhāva) is the lack of desire to teach. "That" refers to the aforementioned meaning.
"This" refers to what was stated thus: "In him too there is changeability. 58.
It is called *āmisa* because it is touched (*āmasīyati*) by defilements; here, the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca kāmaguṇā*) are intended as the *āmisa* included within the world.
Since the nature of the bait of sensual pleasure (*kāmāmisa*) is established even when the nature of the bait of the round of existence (*vaṭṭāmisa*) is obtained among those [objects], he said:

"In those which have become the bait of the round of existence, the bait of sensual pleasure, and the bait of the world. For the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) are the "bait of the round" because they increase the round; they are the "bait of sensual pleasure" because they are to be desired and because they are seized by craving for sensual pleasure;

and they are the "bait of the world" because they constitute the state of being bait for the world of beings for the most part. "Similar to the strands of sensual pleasure" means conforming to the strands of sensual pleasure.

Connected with the strands of sensual pleasure. "Connected with the immovable attainments" means connected with the lower formless attainments which are intended here as "immovable" (āneñja) because they are free from the agitation of the defilements.

"One such as this" refers to one who is intent upon, inclined toward, devoted to, and leaning heavily toward the requisites that consist of worldly material things. "To this extent" refers to those people who possess such faith.
"By seeing them and by the inclination toward their occurrence": "the head has emerged" means that, due to the desire for gain, it is as if the head has protruded outside.
"The belly has burst open" means that because of the excessive abundance of what is to be obtained, the belly becomes distended like a bag being filled with too many goods.

59. Just as the first two formless attainments are called "imperturbable" (*āneñja*) because they are unshakable by their own opposing defilements (*kilesa*), so too are the others. That which was spoken of is the bond of worldly material things (*lokāmisa-saṃyojana*) that has been removed.
60. *Nighaṃsanti* means they delimit [it], thinking, "This is just this much. By "glue" (*silesena*) is meant glue such as that used by leather-workers;
there is no need even to mention the diamond-paste glue (*vajira-lepa-silesa*). That which is "broken" is the bond of imperturbability (*āneñja-saṃyojana*) that has been shattered and dispelled.
Because there is no regard for those attainments, having transcended them. Because it is not connected with his underlying intention (ajjhāsayena), it is said:
"He is like a rock split in two. Therefore he said: "The thought 'I shall enter that attainment' does not arise.
61. *Vantaṃ* means discarded; the meaning is "abandoned" (*vissaṭṭhaṃ*).

62. Regarding the phrase "one who has attained the higher attainments" (*uparisamāpattilābhī*): here, "higher attainment" (*uparisamāpatti*) refers specifically to the attainment of the fruit of Arahatship (*arahattaphalasamāpatti*).

For an Arahant, the attainment of the fruit of Non-returning (*anāgāmiphalasamāpatti*) occurs simultaneously with the realization of the Path; for those in training (*sekkhā*), the lower attainments of the fruits have been stilled.
However, as for worldly attainments, they have been relinquished through the abandoning of attachment; thus it is said: "Below... [it] does not arise."

63. The teaching begun with “There are these five cords of sensual pleasure, Sunakkhatta,” and concluded by praising arahantship with the words “a person who is rightly intent on Nibbāna,” is followed by the teaching beginning with “But it is possible,” which is said to have a separate connection (*pāṭiyekko anusandhi*).
Therefore he says, “As below,” and so forth. In that context, as for the one whose taints are destroyed...

The construction is: "one who has attained the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*)," or alternatively, it should be construed as "thus for one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) and who is a dry-insight practitioner (*sukkha-vipassaka*).
This [latter view] is rejected in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*). To show the reason for that rejection, it was said: "For one who has attained the absorptions," and so forth.

Just as a dry-insight practitioner who is overweening in his conceit (*adhimānika*) considers himself to have the same capacity for practice (*samāna-yogakkhema*) as one who has attained the absorptions, due to the perception of having reached what he has not actually reached.

Because there is no difference [between them], thus the dry-insight practitioner who has destroyed the taints (khīṇāsava) is one who has achieved the same goal (samānayogakkhema), owing to the absence of distinction in their state of having destroyed the taints.
Therefore it is said: "When one who has attained the meditative attainments (samāpatti) is mentioned, the other is also mentioned.

"Of two bhikkhus" refers to one who has attained the meditative attainments and is conceited (adhimānika), and the one who has destroyed the taints. For this very reason he says: "First, of the worldling (puthujjana)," and so forth.

“By whatever part” means by whichever portion. Even though for one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), an unsuitable object does not serve as a condition for the arising of defilements because they have been entirely eradicated, it may nevertheless be an obstacle to dwelling in peace due to its discordant nature;
thus it is said: “Even for one whose taints are destroyed, it is indeed unsuitable. Therefore he says: “Poison, namely... poison indeed. By this—

This shows that "just as the measureless state is to be abandoned because it gives rise to unsuitable states, so too, even though it has been fully understood, it must be abandoned because, due to the absence of any specific benefit, it remains of a single uniform nature. Therefore he said, "For not," and so forth.
For one should not be unrestrained, because of its unsuitability. "Only by one who is properly engaged" refers to an object of a similar nature.
One must indeed act with mindfulness regarding looking and so forth.

(64) It is called "the poison of ignorance" because it corrupts the continuity of that [consciousness] where it itself falls and arises by way of its lack of clarity, and because it is the root of suffering, which is reckoned as poison. It is said to "be corrupted."
By inducing intoxication through such acts as those that ought not to be done, one produces a corruption. "Anuddhaṃseyya" means he would afflict.

For lust, as it arises, afflicts the mind by not allowing an opportunity for the occurrence of wholesome states of consciousness; being thus, it withers and causes it to fade away, like the vomiting out of the moisture of faith and serenity, thereby preventing the growth of serenity and insight.
Therefore he said: "He would dry it up, he would cause it to wither. "Sagahaṇasesam" means...
The meaning is: "having left a remainder of the poison that was to be taken. *Analaṃ* means "not sufficient" or "not capable.
Regarding the word *sūka*, since it is stated in the Pāḷi as a synonym for *sūka* (awn), he says: "and the awn of rice, etc., is *sūka*.
The latent poison of ignorance (*avijjāvisadosa*) should be regarded as not yet abandoned because it produces great harm, just like the extraction of a dart accompanied by its residue (*saupādāna*).
The unwholesome... [and so on]... should be regarded as a time of lack of restraint, because of the state of not preserving one’s personal existence (*attabhāva*).
Turning back to the low life after having renounced the training is like death, because of the departure from the life-span comprised by higher virtue (*adhisīla*).
Committing an offense is like the suffering of mere death, because of its state of afflicting the aforementioned life-span. By this same method...
Regarding "the correlation of similes": here, the extraction of the arrow of the residual-less (anupādisesa) is like the elimination of the poisonous corruption of ignorance;
the time when [the wound] is suitable... pe ...and well-restrained is like the non-abandonment of the training;

and the absence of death when the wound has not become suppurated due to those two factors is like the non-committing of any particular defiled offense—this is how the application of the simile should be understood.

65. Regarding the phrase "by means of mindfulness" (*satiyā*): since it was not specified here as "noble" (*ariyāya*), he said, "mindfulness follows the course of wisdom" (*paññāgatikā*), and so forth. And here, mundane wisdom (*lokiyā paññā*) is intended, not supramundane; thus he said, "by means of purified insight-wisdom" (*vipassanāpaññā*).

Demonstrating the power of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), which consists in being well-restrained and is the cause for the six faculties—with the mind as the sixth—not being led away even by objects that are most exalted and resemble those of the devas, he says, "one who acts with restraint" (*saṃvutakārī*).

It is said that because of the fullness of his supreme mindfulness, just as there is non-restraint for one who lacks restraint, so too does he guard the doors of the eye and other senses by the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajañña*), performing his functions such as seeing.

"Having known thus" means having known by means of the wisdom of the Path (*maggapaññā*) accompanied by the wisdom of insight (*vipassanāpaññā*) in this way: "Acquisition (*upadhi*) is the root of suffering. It is called *upadhi* because suffering is acquired (*upadhīyati*) through these.

He said, “The defilements (kilesa) are so called because of the phrase ‘through the abandoning of the acquisitions of defilement, one is without acquisitions (nirupadhi). For that very reason, since suffering is grasped by means of them, the defilements are also called ‘clinging (upādāna)’;
thus he said, ‘the meaning is “without clinging. The complete exhaustion of the acquisitions (upadhi) is the destruction of acquisitions (upadhisaṅkhaya), which is Nibbāna;
thus he said, ‘in Nibbāna, which is the state of the destruction of acquisitions. As for the word ‘as an object (ārammaṇato)...’”
Having made that the object, he is liberated through the liberation of fruition which has that as its object. As for the phrase "he will apply the body to the substrate of sensual desire":
thinking "I shall indulge in sensual desires," he would direct the body toward it;
let alone the application of the body, there is no such reason for him to even arouse the thought. The rest is easily understood.
The explanation of the *Sunakkhattasutta*, which clarifies the meaning of the hidden points, is completed.
6. Commentary on the *Āneñjasappāyasutta* 66.

Because of their momentary dissolution, they are not permanent and not stable; thus, they are "impermanent. For that very reason, they are "not to be resorted to," meaning they should not be relied upon by the wise.
They are impermanent (*aniccā*). Showing that this meaning of impermanence should be understood as being delimited by arising and passing away, he said:
"They are impermanent in the sense of having existed and then ceasing to be"; the meaning is: because they perish after having arisen.

And since this impermanence and the emptiness (*tucchāditā*) to be mentioned later are common to both kinds of desire, he said: "Both objective desires (*vatthukāmā*) and defilement-desires (*kilesakāmā*)."
"Empty and void" means they are separate from those things such as permanence and essence because of their absence within the self.
However, these are not like space, which is called "empty and void" because it is entirely devoid of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). Rather, he says "but not...
and so forth to show that these are merely empty and void because they lack permanence, essence, and the rest. [He adds: "For there is no such thing as an 'empty fist' that does not exist."
This is stated according to worldly convention (*lokasamaññā*); worldly convention is mundane discourse that should not be transgressed.
Because it does not appear due to its limited manifestation, he said, "‘False’ (*musā*) means ‘that which causes disappearance. Or, in the sense of deceiving, it is *musā*.
For these [objects], although their true nature is foulness and so forth, they appear to fools as beauty and so forth, and thus they cause the grasping of them as beautiful and so on.

They deceive sentient beings by means of their apparent reality. "Having the nature of perishing" means that because they are subject to momentary dissolution and have only a brief manifestation, they are of a character that does not persist even while appearing as if they were visible.

Therefore he said, "like a field," and so forth. It should be understood that here the word *dhamma* (nature) is a synonym for "intrinsic character" (*pakati*), as in such passages as "subject to the nature of birth" (*jātidhammā*); the same applies to the word *sabhāva* (essence).
*Mosadhammā* means having the nature of stealing; the meaning is that they have the inherent quality of seizing wholesome goods.

*Māyākataṃ* means made by means of illusion (*māyā*), presented through illusion and so forth in the form of water, jewels, and the like; it is called "made by illusion" because, though possessing one nature, it appears as something other than what it truly is.
Therefore he said, "Just as," and so forth. [This refers to] a science performed only within the range of vision, not...
Regarding the phrase "beyond that," it is said: "It appears in such a way even to one standing within the range of vision. This was stated by way of the knowledge of concealment (*saṃvaravijjā*).
Having thus shown the illusory nature of sensual pleasures through their temporary character, the passage beginning with "And just as" is now stated to show it by another manner as well.
It refers to the perception of sensual pleasures—which have impermanence and so forth as their intrinsic nature—as having an intrinsic nature of permanence and so forth.

It should be understood as being accompanied by perversion (*vipallāsa*). "Because they entice the foolish" means because they are the cause of perversion for those blind fools who have not fully understood the basis [of these sensual pleasures].

It is stated—"sensual pleasures pertaining to the present life are the five strands of human sensual pleasure"—because the Blessed One spoke with reference to humans or while standing in the human world. And for that very reason, it is said: "those pertaining to the future life..."
"Excluding those, the remainder," and so forth, was said. In this context:

"pertaining to the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammikā*) means those for which there exist objects that are of a directly perceptible nature in the present life. "Pertaining to the future life" (*samparāyikā*) refers to perceptions arisen with reference to sensual pleasures of the future life.

That wherein the command is maintained by coming together is "the domain" (*dheyya*); it is the locus for the operation of the command. "The domain of Māra" (*māradheyya*) means the domain belonging to Māra.
Because of the manifestation of its sovereignty. Therefore he said, "By which," and so forth. "Apprehended" means apprehended by way of the relationship between object and subject;
the meaning is that it is apprehended by way of being an object and by way of making it an object.
Therein, apprehension by way of making it an object is the act of grasping it as "this is mine" without distinction; however, apprehension by way of being an object is—

They say that "experiencing the object" means experiencing it according to its constituent parts (*bhāga*). However, with reference to the grasping of both [the object and the parts] by way of craving and lust (*taṇhārāga*), it is stated:
"Both of these are included. "Māra" refers to the defilement-māra (*kilesamāra*).

To the same extent that he is the defilement-māra, to that same extent the son-of-devas-māra (*devaputtamāra*) also brings him under his own power. "With reference to that" means with reference to the designation of the person (*puggala*) by way of the Dhamma.

For individuals who have not abandoned their distortions (*vipallāsa*) and are intent upon sensual pleasures are called "the domain of Māra" (*māradheyya*) because it is the sphere of Māra’s sovereignty;
likewise, showing that they are also called such by way of being Māra’s dwelling place and pasture, he said, "Just as for a cloth," and so forth.
"Nivāpa" means what is sown; that itself is the seed, thus "sown seed" (*nivāpabīja*). "Tet" refers to the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*). "Yattha" means in which place.

Because it exists in the mind (*manasi*), it is called "mental" (*mānasa*); thus he says, "arisen from the mind. Furthermore, those factors such as ignorance (*avijjā*) and so forth are included in the canonical text (*pāḷi*).
For, showing that hostility is dependent upon partiality just as pus is dependent upon blood, he says, "in the object that is cherished," and so forth.
In the phrase "those here" (*te dha*), *iha* is merely a particle; [as in the passage]: "In this world, monks, having eaten..."

As in the case of the words “*assa*” and so forth. “The world of sense-desire” (*kāmaloka*) refers to the world of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāraloka*) consisting of the strands of sense-pleasure, or the world within which the strands of sense-pleasure exist.
“Having resolved with the mind” means having generated the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāganimitta*), which is the object of jhāna, by means of the meditative mind.
It is called “limited” (*paritta*) because it is, as it were, cut off or confined by the defilements, owing to its inability to suppress them. Of that...

"By way of rejection" means by the rejection of the state of being limited (*paritta*). It is called "measureless" (*appamāṇa*) because it does not abandon even the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) and immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*), which are themselves measures, due to its suppression of those factors that act as measures for evil states.

He said "the fine-material sphere and the immaterial sphere" to indicate that which is sublime (*mahaggata*) by way of such rejection. Even sublime jhāna is [not measureless] because of the non-abandonment of defilements by way of their total eradication (*samuccheda*).
It is not even called "well-developed," let alone "limited jhāna"; thus he said: "Well-developed...
this is a name for the supramundane alone. "By means of this" refers to the word "well-developed.
"That very way of practice" refers to that very way of practicing jhāna which brings about the abandonment of covetousness and so forth. It serves as the means for attaining arahantship.
Or, when insight (vipassanā) or the access concentration (upacāra) that serves as its means is present in the fourth jhāna, the mind becomes serene;

thus he said: "Arahatship... or access concentration. "Confidence through resolution" refers either to the thought, "I shall attain Arahatship this very day," because one has entered the path of insight (vipassanā), or to the thought, "I shall produce the fourth jhāna this very day."
Or, it is confidence consisting in resolution because the mind is concentrated through access-concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*).
"Confidence by acquisition" (*paṭilābha-sampasāda*) refers to the confidence consisting in the attainment of either Arahantship or the fourth jhāna.

For even acquisition is called "confidence" because, by overcoming the turbidity of the defilements, it brings about a state of great clarity in the mind. "Conditions" (*paccaya*) refers to ignorance and the rest, which are the conditions for name-and-form (*nāma-rūpa*).
“Sabbathā” means in every way: by way of their origin, their passing away, their gratification, their danger, and the escape from them.
“Āsā” (hope) is an aspiration by way of resolute conviction (*adhimuccanavasena*). Therefore he said: “Hope is established; one obtains resolute conviction.
“Pādaka” means a footing or basis (*padaṭṭhāna*). “Defilements settle down” refers to the defilements associated with the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) being suppressed by way of suppression.
They subside. "Mindfulness" means that the mindfulness which brings about access concentration becomes established.
"The course of formations": because it proceeds with equanimity through meditation, these factors beginning with the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena proceed with a single flavor;
thus, the course of formations included within the arising of the mind of meditation appears clearly and manifestly. "Arising of consciousness" means...
It is an arising of consciousness through meditation (*bhāvanā*). It becomes as if immersed, like something adhering to a lump of clay or a lump of sealing wax.

One becomes concentrated by means of access; one becomes concentrated by means of access-jhāna (*upacārajjhāna*). This twofold mode of resolving is called "confidence through resolution" (*adhimokkhasampasāda*).
When that confidence exists—meaning when there is this confidence through resolution regarding either the characteristics of insight (*vipassanālakkhaṇa*) or access-jhāna.
When it exists. However, for one who attains either Arahatship or the fourth jhāna, their mind is indeed serene;

this is serenity through attainment in the literal sense (*nippariyāyato*). Nevertheless, even though this is so, the passage beginning with "But here" was stated in order to demonstrate precisely this [type of serenity] in the present context.
The phrase "For insight... and so forth is an explanation (*samatthana*) of what was previously stated. In that regard, "by means of wisdom" (*paññāya*)...

"By means of the wisdom of arahantship. "Of resolute conviction" (*adhimuccanassa*) means of the act of placing faith and exerting oneself. "Access" (*upacāra*) refers to access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*). The construction is:
"the cause for the resolute conviction toward the immovable attainment" (*āneñja-samāpatti*).
"Even now" (*etarahi vā*) means right now. "Or the immovable" (*āneñjaṃ vā*) means the fourth jhāna. "Attains" (*samāpajjati*) means he reaches it.
With the words "This indeed," etc., he explains in detail the meaning stated in brief.

He says, "Or alternatively," as another alternative, showing that the realization of arahantship is effectively attained when there is the cultivation of the supreme path (*aggamagga*), and that it is precisely the wisdom of the supreme path that must be resolved upon for that purpose.
In this regard, just as, for example, the various components of the building materials brought together for the sake of a palace...
Showing that just as one who cannot afford a gabled house simply cannot build it, so it is in this case, he said:

"If he does not succeed in that, he enters the imperturbable (āneñja). Or else, he realizes the Four Truths by way of attaining the lower paths, or he enters the imperturbable; for both are supported by their respective causes.
*Tatra* means "in that," referring to the aforementioned attainment of distinction, namely, "one resolves through wisdom, or enters the imperturbable (*āneñja*).
*Ayaṃ yojanānayo* refers to this method of application which is now being stated. *Evaṃ hoti* means that the mental aspiration occurs in the manner now being described.
*Kiccaṃ* refers to the duty of one who has gone forth. *Tato* means from the attainment of Arahatship. *Osakkitamānaso* means one whose mind has shrunk back.
"It does not stop in between" means it does not stop on the plane of non-concentration.
Now, in order to clarify the meaning just stated by means of a simile, the passage beginning with "Just as" was spoken. Herein, this is the summary of the meaning:
just as for that man who is intent on catching a wild elephant in the forest, there is no need to mention his catching hares, antelopes, and so forth as he retreats; even so, for this [meditator]...
For a bhikkhu who is intent on attaining arahantship, there is no need to mention falling back from that state and entering the fourth jhāna;
"the same method applies" refers by extension both to the application of the aforementioned simile and its correlation,
as well as to the application to the development of the path and the realization of the Four Noble Truths.
The particle *yaṃ* is a term that illuminates the meaning of the cause; or, it is the nominative case used in the sense of the instrumental, which is why he says, "by which reason.
That which is worthy of leading to that [result], or that which has that as its purpose, is "leading to that" (*taṃsaṃvattanika*). "Consciousness" (*viññāṇa*) refers to resultant consciousness.
It approaches a state of imperturbability (*āneñja*), thus it is "approaching the imperturbable" (*āneñjūpaga*). Just as wholesome [consciousness] approaches a state of imperturbability...
In this way, even that resultant consciousness (*vipākaviññāṇa*) would come to possess the nature of imperturbability (*āneñja*).
Therefore he said: "The meaning is that it would be just like the wholesome [consciousness]. "Some" refers to the residents of Abhayagiri.
They claim that even the resultant consciousness is wholesome, as it were. "It would have that very name" means it would be named "imperturbable," just like the wholesome [consciousness]. And here—
In the first alternative, "leading to the imperturbable" (*āneñjūpaga*) is stated by way of similarity to it;

in the second alternative, for that very reason, it is stated by way of its conventional designation (*tatsamaññatā*). As for the meaning of this: because of its similarity to the imperturbable, even during the time of its fruition it would bear that same name;

such is the meaning as it was stated. "By this method" means by the method thus described. For here, the resultant consciousness whose cause is the formative action (*abhisaṅkhāra*) of the imperturbable is called "leading to the imperturbable."
Because it is stated, "consciousness exists," it is explained by giving it that very name. Regarding the phrase "also of arahantship":
by the word "also" (api), it should be understood that the meaning includes both the cultivation of the highest path and the cultivation of the lower paths.

"Falling back by way of concentration" is mentioned because the teaching was delivered after demonstrating the method of serenity (samatha) with the words, "he might dwell with a mind that is vast and exalted."
67. "This bhikkhu" refers to the bhikkhu mentioned in the second discourse on the appropriate way to the Immovable (Dutiya-aneñjasappāya-sutta).
Having stated that he is "more wise," it is said—"he comprehends by combining both meditation subjects together"—in order to demonstrate this.

For in the case of the former [discourse], by means of the form door, only visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles were treated under the heading of "those sensual pleasures pertaining to the present life," and so forth.
The inclination toward insight (vipassanā) has been established; however, this is done by way of all material phenomena (rūpadhamma), beginning with the words, "Whatever kind of form...

For when the Blessed One teaches a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), he first shows the practitioner's inclination toward development (bhāvanā) in accordance with the strength of that meditator's causal capacity;
subsequently, as his knowledge expands extensively, [he comes to understand] it without remainder.
He grasps the Dhamma. "By the warding off of form" means by the complete transcendence through the cultivation of dispassion toward form.
"In all cases" means in all three immovables (*āneñja*) and so forth.
"More wise" means superior in wisdom. "Combining all three meditation subjects together" refers to the strands of sensual pleasure and all phenomena of form.

Regarding "perception of sensual desire": having brought together the phenomena included in the three types of persons as explained in three ways according to their meditation subjects, one takes them all collectively as "all this is impermanent" and contemplates them thus:
"Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation. Therefore he said: "Both these are impermanent," and so forth.

Regarding the statement that "both" is said by way of the eight single sections divided into those pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*) and those pertaining to the future life (*samparāyika*) through the perception of form and the perception of the formless, he says: "Having condensed it by way of [the division into] 'pertaining to the present life'... etc., it is called 'both'.
Regarding "by way of craving and views": by way of delighting in craving, thinking "this is mine"; and by way of delighting in views, thinking "this is..."
“...this is my self”—thus one should not delight [in it]. By the phrase “the same method applies,” he extends this meaning:
that one should not, by way of craving and views, delight in it as “this is mine, this is my self,” nor persist in it by clinging to it, swallowing it, and making it one's final conclusion.
The phrase “by warding off sensual desires” is stated for the purpose of showing the path of approach and for the purpose of praising it.
For him, the repelling of form is proximate; even more so is the transcendence of the base of infinite space.
With that transcendence, all those retrogressions by way of insight are stated together, because of such statements as, “Both these are impermanent.
(68) Here, “of one’s own” refers to the meditation subject of the base of nothingness. They cease through the cessation of the desire and lust bound up with them.
But at the moment of attainment, it is also by way of non-arising. Therefore he said, "having reached the base of nothingness.

"In the sense of being insatiable" means by way of its superior nature, that is, by way of the state of not bringing satisfaction to the meditative attainment (jhāna-samāpatti). "That very path of practice" refers to the cultivation of the base of nothingness.
The regression by way of concentration is mentioned because the third immaterial meditation subject has been stated [in the passage] beginning with "where these... and so forth.
"Herein, 'oneself'" refers to the meditation subject of insight characterized by the attention to emptiness (*suññatā-manasikāra*), which consists of two aspects.
"The method of practice mentioned above" refers to the meditation subject of the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*) mentioned immediately prior.

It is stated [here] because the attention to emptiness is preeminent in this development of serenity (*samatha-bhāvanā*). As it is said: "In the second base of nothingness, falling back occurs by way of insight."

70. In the third base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*), there is the meditation subject of insight (*vipassanā-kammaṭṭhāna*) known as the mental application on emptiness (*suññatā-manasikāra*) consisting of the fourfold tetrad.
"In this" means in this section concerning the contemplation of emptiness. "Somewhere" means in some place, at some time, or regarding some phenomenon;
or alternatively, "somewhere" means internally or externally. "One's own self" means one's own person. "This indeed, sir... [etc.]

By stating, “Brahmā... the master, the father of those who have been and those who will be,” and so forth, he says “of anyone” (*kassaci*) etc., demonstrating that he does not see a self as imagined by others, nor anything belonging to anyone.
Therein, “another’s” (*parassa*) refers to what is understood as “another person” or “another being.
Regarding the phrase “nor mine anywhere” (*na ca mama kvacani*), he says “the word ‘mine’ (*mama-sadda*)” because it is used in an improper sense.
“Setting that aside,” he says; and regarding “another”: this refers to one other than oneself.

By way of the conceit, “There is another person who has prepared for my sake, and through him everything succeeds for me”—thus, in accordance with the imaginings of certain proponents of false views—one does not see another as a self, nor does one see that [other] as something belonging to oneself. Demonstrating this, he said, “And nowhere,” and so forth.
And herein, “I am not anywhere” means he sees the non-existence of his own self.

“Because there is nothing belonging to anyone” means he sees that his very self does not belong to anyone else. Furthermore, these two phrases—“I” and “mine”—should be connected respectively with each instance of “there is.
“Nor is there a self of another anywhere” means he sees the non-existence of another's self.
“‘There is no “mine-ness” (kiñcanatā) whatsoever in that other person or in myself’—thus he sees the non-selfhood of both others and himself.

In this way, the emptiness of self and what belongs to self regarding the aggregates internally and externally, as well as their nature as a mere heap of formations, is seen through the apprehension of the fourfold emptiness.
‘The method explained below’ refers here also specifically to the meditation subject of the base of nothingness.”
