He speaks thus. It is specifically by way of insight (vipassanā) that "falling back" is described, because of its distinctive nature as the vision of the fourfold emptiness, and because this act of attention has that as its primary focus.
Here, "oneself" refers to the meditation subject of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. "All perceptions" refers to the perception of form and the perception of resistance.
They say that all perceptions without exception cease in this way: the perception of diversity and the three lower formless perceptions.
However, others maintain that because of the qualification "stated below," the perceptions of the fourth jhāna and so forth mentioned here are also included among "perceptions.

As for the word "that," it refers to the mere conventional designation [of cessation], since the cessation of those perceptions of diversity and so on occurs precisely by means of the warding off of sensual perceptions.

Because of the accomplishment of the goal. The "falling back" by way of concentration is mentioned because the development of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception constitutes a subject of meditation for serenity (*samatha*). 71. "The fivefold cycle of kamma" refers to the continuity of kamma together with its requisites as it has come down:
in the previous kamma-existence, there is delusion (*moha*), which is ignorance (*avijjā*); accumulation (*āyūhana*), which is volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*);

hankering (*nikanti*), which is craving (*taṇhā*); approaching (*upagamana*), which is clinging (*upādāna*); and intention (*cetanā*), which is becoming (*bhava*). Thus is the succession of kamma described.
"Na āyūhitam assa" means it would not have been volitionally produced (*cetita*), nor fashioned (*pakappita*).

In this way, the fivefold round of result (*vipākavaṭṭa*)—consisting of present consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling—would not proceed, because its cause would be unproduced.
"Sace āyūhitam na bhavissati" means if it were not volitionally produced, nor fashioned...
It may be so. That which "exists" is that which exists from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*). Therefore he said, "it is real" (*bhūta*).

For it is called "real" because it is produced by conditions. "I abandon that" means: by abandoning the desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*) bound to it, I abandon and relinquish it precisely through the process of establishing its quality of non-arising in the future.
Regarding the term *parinibbāyī*, it is stated as "he would attain final Nibbāna" (*parinibbāyeyya*) because it refers to the past sense along with its conceptualization.
Alternatively, the reading is *parinibbāyeyya nu kho*, which has the same meaning.

"Nothing was said" means that nothing was stated in its specific form, because the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is an object only for the highest knowledge due to the subtle state of the remaining formations.
However, because he wished to make known the distinction by means of this method, it is said that the Blessed One thought:

"Seated right here in this assembly, Ānanda, being skilled in the connection of topics, will ask a question concerning the rebirth-linking and the attainment of Arahantship of a bhikkhu who has made the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception his foundation; by means of this sequence of questions..."
“I shall teach that matter. Since what is intended here is the process of withdrawal (*osakkanā*), there is a teaching with distinct flavors; thus, a connection based on a question is posed.
For if that [connection] were absent, this teaching would be broken by a fracture in its continuity, and a teaching with distinct flavors is not the practice of the Buddhas.
“Dependent upon insight” (*vipassanānissita*) means supported by that. “Of that bhikkhu”: it is called “clinging” (*upādāna*) because one clings by means of it.

It does not attain final Nibbāna because of the failure to abandon that which ought to be abandoned. Therefore the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, even states (dhammas) are to be abandoned, how much more so non-states (adhammas).
The phrase "the best of acquisitions" (upādānaseṭṭha) is intended to show that the existence of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the highest of all existences;
it is not intended to deny that the noble state is the best of acquisitions.

73. "Depending" means: depending on a state included within existence (*bhava*), and depending on that which is included therein, the crossing over the flood was taught by the Blessed One. "Oh, how wonderful this is! Oh, how marvelous!
Since the teaching in all nine instances has come down according to the vehicle of serenity (*samatha-yānika*) alone, and because no foundational jhāna is mentioned here, it is said:
"A noble disciple is a noble disciple who is a dry-insight practitioner (*sukkha-vipassaka*). This applies to all nine meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

“Having brought them together, one comprehends” is stated on the assumption that comprehension can also occur by taking the factors of jhāna— though acquired through successive attainment— as objects.

The phrase “as far as personality (sakkāya) extends,” which is spoken here in reference to the formations belonging to the three planes, is stated with the intention of referring to a complete, exhaustive inclusion.
"This is the Deathless": because it occurs with reference to Nibbāna, the Deathless, this Arahantship has the flavor of the Deathless. Therefore he said:

"This is the Deathless, the Peaceful; this is the Sublime. Furthermore, because it is stated that "the mind was liberated without clinging to anything," the liberation of the mind through non-clinging is elsewhere in the Sutta called Nibbāna.
"Of three bhikkhus" means of those who are threefold according to the difference in their adherence.
The reason why there is no shifting back for one who stands having made [the position] a foundation should be understood by the method already stated below.
"Having combined" means having properly joined them together, having defined them without confusion in their respective places. It is called "well-spoken" regarding that which is to be spoken.
Because it was spoken without leaving anything out.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Obscure Meaning) for the commentary on the *Āneñjasappāyasutta* is completed.
7. The commentary on the *Gaṇakamoggallānasutta*.
74. Just as the lowest step-sill is called the "last" for one descending, so it is called the "first" for one ascending;
thus it is said: "As far as the final body of the staircase means as far as the first step-sill.
"Having cleared the site" means the procedure for clearing the site of the palace according to the method taught by a master of site-science (*vatthuvidyā*).
"Having done so. "In this regard" means in the construction of the palace. One who can pierce the tip of a hair-split into seven parts is called a "hair-piercer" (*vālavedhi*).

"Providing the locations" means providing the sites for the Vesākha-maṇḍala and so forth. "By means of making fists, etc. refers to methods such as making a fist with the thumb, grasping with the fingers, piercing with the fingers, and so on.
"Counting in this way": one is simply one; two twos are four; three threes are nine; four fours are sixteen.
"Sixteen," and so forth—thus we shall train in counting. 75.
"They are deceitful" means they are possessed of guile and hypocrisy for the purpose of keeping the discipline unstained. They do not overstep that self-restraint even for the sake of their lives;

this is the absence of the fault of their birth. 76. "For the sake of being endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension" means by means of mindfulness and clear comprehension which accomplish constant abiding.
"For the sake of attainment. But surely those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) have reached the fullness of mindfulness and the fullness of wisdom;
how then is their mindfulness and clear comprehension something to be accomplished through effort? To this he says, "For there are two," and so forth.
"Constantly abiding" means they frequently abide in meditative attainments (samāpatti); therefore, at whatever moment they desire, they enter the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti).
By the reverse of what was stated, those who do not dwell constantly should be understood. Therefore he said, "In that regard," and so forth.
He is unable to apply himself because it has not been practiced. "Thinking about that" means thinking: "The novice has no lodging, and the forest is full of dangers such as lions;
what indeed will become of him? "Of such a kind" means of this sort, similar to the aforementioned novice.

"One whose taints are destroyed" (*khīṇāsava*). "These phenomena" (*ime dhammā*) refers to the phenomena such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth mentioned in this sutta. "Having adverted" (*āvajjitvāva*) means that he will be able to attain [the meditative absorption] precisely because of his own adverting to the purity of his virtue and other qualities.

To show the connection for the statement, "These, Master Gotama," the passage beginning with "It is said, regarding the Tathāgata... was stated. "In this way" (*evam*) means he began to speak in the manner beginning with, "These, Master Gotama."
"In present-day teachings" means in teachings that are not ancient. For those [teachings] were composed by one's own ingenuity after merely fashioning them through conjecture.
It is "supreme" and "excellent" because of its antiquity, its completeness, and its absolute capacity for deliverance. Therefore he said: "Among them...
the meaning is 'the supreme'. The rest is easily understood.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning (*Līnatthappakāsanā*) for the Commentary on the *Gaṇakamoggallānasutta* is completed.
8. Commentary on the *Gopakamoggallānasutta* 79.
"Kamma" itself is "kammanta"; because that [work] exists here, the place for performing work is called "kammanta."
Therefore he said, “the place of activity. By those qualities means by the qualities of the Buddha.
Since these have omniscient knowledge as their foremost, he said, “by the qualities of omniscient knowledge. “In every way, entirely” means in every mode without remainder;
this is the extent of the classification of the qualities, and it means without omitting even a single mode among them. “Entirely in all categories” means...
"By all those portions of qualities, without exception and leaving nothing remaining.
"Even that which occurred" means even the quarrel that occurred at Kosambī on account of the monks residing there. That too was settled right there, at the very place where it arose.
"But at the time of his parinibbāna" means, however, at the time of the parinibbāna of this Fully Enlightened One.
To show how the monks became even more harmonious and how a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) arose, the passage beginning with “sixty-eight” was spoken.
They were exceedingly and perpetually tranquil due to their attainment of supreme peace.
*Anusaṃyāyamāno* means knowing thoroughly, investigating, and becoming weary of [the world] step by step. Alternatively, the reading is *anusaññāyamāno*; therein—
Having changed the letter *ya* to the letter *ña*, it is explained [as such]; thus he said, "while wandering about. 80.
"The very first question" means precisely the question asked by Gopaka Moggallāna.
For he asked, "Is there any monk who is the essence of your teaching? with the words beginning "by those qualities," and so forth. And this [Buddha] called that very person "the refuge."
He asked by way of a synonym. "Without a refuge" means in the absence of such a person as you who might awaken the bhikkhus;
thus it is "without a refuge. "Those for whom the Dhamma proclaimed by the Tathāgata is their refuge" are those who have the Dhamma as their refuge.
Therefore he said, "The Dhamma is the support."

81. "It comes" means it comes by way of being expressed through speech. Regarding transgression (*ajjhācāra*)—which is defined as the overstepping of the basis (*vatthu*) and is divided into categories such as heavy, heavier, light, and lighter—the term "offense" (*āpatti*) is used;

thus he says: "An offense... [etc. ...is simply the transgression of an instruction. "In accordance with the Dhamma" (*yathādhamma*) means conforming to the Dhamma. "As instructed" (*yathāsiṭṭha*) means as taught.
In the phrase "it is not the Dhamma" (*dhammo no*), the particle *no* is used for emphasis, as in: "It is certainly not equal to ours."
[This is] as in such passages as, “There is [something] by the Tathāgata,” and so forth. For that very reason he said, “Dhamma alone causes one to act.
(83) “Just as it is with protectors and guardians like you”—thus he wishes to exalt himself under the guise of expressing confidence.
He said, “This is wholesome,” because when there is the forgiving of the evil of reviling the Noble Ones, no obstacle exists. “Gonaṅgalamakkhaṭo” means a monkey with a cow’s tail.
84. This [person] deceives the intended purpose as it was originally undertaken when he speaks by praising even that which is not praiseworthy;

the construction is: "It is not possible to protect the alms-food in this way, lest there be an obstacle to the alms-food that ought to be given by the rejection of these words. Regarding the word *idaṃ*: "No, brahmin... [and so forth].
"Thus the Blessed One," and so forth, is the teaching. "Making it internal" means making it included within Nibbāna, or making it the proximate cause for that contemplation (*nijjhāna*).
For that contemplation occurs by way of sensual lust (*kāmarāga*). "Here" refers to this section of the Sutta.
"All-inclusive jhāna" is said even while acting thus, [thinking]: "May there be no obstacle to the mundane and supramundane [attainments]."
Because it is taught as encompassing everything—the path-jhāna, the fruition-jhāna, and all that pertains to the fine-material sphere—it is called "the jhāna that includes everything.
In the phrase "yaṃ no mayaṃ," *no* is merely a particle. However, in the phrase "taṃ no," *no* has the meaning of "our" (*amhākaṃ*).
He is envious because he is preoccupied with his own status as one intent on royal duties;

because of his dull wit, his mind is overwhelmed by the envy directed toward Vassakāra, and thus, failing to reflect even upon the meaning that has been fully stated, he says, "He spoke only a partial portion. The rest is easily understood.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Gopakamoggallāna-sutta* is completed.
9. Commentary on the Mahāpuṇṇama Sutta 85.
Regarding the phrase *tasmiṃ ahu*, it means "on that day"; thus he says, "on that day. The construction is:

"having become endowed with the fasting of the outsiders (*bāhiraka-anaśana*)—that is, by means of the ascetic practice (*sāsana-kīla*) consisting of the total non-eating of food (*sabba-so āhārassa abhuñjana*)—by means of fasting. By the word *vā* (or), [the text implies] the method of drinking milk, honey-mixtures, and so forth.

He embraces [them]. It is called *uposatha* because one must dwell having approached it; it is the recitation of the *pātimokkha*. It is called *uposatha* because one must dwell having become endowed with and possessed of it, or because it must be made to dwell within one’s own continuum;
it is virtue (*sīla*). Or, dwelling having approached the practice of fasting and so forth is *upavāsa*, which is the *uposatha*.
He says: "In such a specific class of elephants, ‘uposatha’ is a mere conventional designation. Thus he speaks: "Uposatha..."
"In such passages as 'the Nāga king named...,' it is a designation. According to the method already stated, that which they observe (upavasanti) therein is the *uposatha*, namely, the day.
Furthermore, this *uposatha* [is so called] "by way of the fullness of the month" (*māsapuṇṇatāya*), that is, by virtue of the state of the month being complete.
"Full" (*sampuṇṇā*) means entirely full; for by means of that night, the month becomes completely full without remainder. It measures (*māti*) time divided into months, fortnights, and so forth.
Because it appears as if diminishing, the moon is called "Mā. "Ettha" means "in this night. It is called "Puṇṇamā" because it has become full, with its phases complete;
for it is so named due to the fullness of the moon and the fullness of the month. By this, he shows its status as an *uposatha*.
A "place" (*desa*) is that where the fruit is seen or where it corresponds; thus he says, "A place is a cause. They explain everything.
They speak of every kind of thing they have personally grasped; they are unable to speak [of what they do not know] because it is outside their domain.
"In the courtyard of the palace" means in the open space in front of the palace. "In the manner stated above" should be expanded according to the method stated in the *Sekha-sutta*.
86. Regarding the phrase "Are these...?", he says that "nu" here indicates doubt: "It is spoken as if it were a question of uncertainty."

The passage beginning with "By one who knows," etc., should be understood as being intended to demonstrate the manner of the question, not to indicate that the Teacher, the questioner, was himself ignorant.
For the Blessed One knows [the answer]. It is asked while appearing as if one were ignorant;
he asks while standing in hypocrisy, as if knowing the true nature of things as they are. Therefore he said: "What will the Elder do with such words?"—this refers to the reason.
The intended meaning is "because they have been well-abandoned. "Rooted in desire" means rooted in the desire of craving (*taṇhā-chanda*); for craving is the origin of suffering.

It is either a wholesome perception—meaning a perception that is firm, clear, and skillful—or a wholesome volitional formation—meaning a formation that is sharp, firm, and clear; it is consciousness that is perfectly purified, vast, and sublime.
The phrase "the same method applies to perception and the others" extends this principle [to the remaining aggregates].
But why is the teaching here presented solely by way of the future tense? To this he says, "Because...

and so forth. "The designation of aggregates for the aggregates" refers to those things denoted by the word "aggregate," which possess the intrinsic natures of being affected (ruppaṇa), experiencing (anubhavana), perceiving (sañjānana), volitionally constructing (abhisaṅkharaṇa), and cognizing (vijānana).

The designation "aggregate" (*khandha*) has no [other] basis [than this]. By how much? By what measure of meaning; the intention is: of what kind among such meanings as "heap" (*rāsa*), "part" (*bhāga*), and so forth?

"Cause-cause" (*hetu-hetu*) means a cause that functions as a causal condition (*paccaya*). For it is the state of being a supportive factor in the sense of a root (*mūla*) among the co-nascent phenomena, such as greed and the rest.

In the non-figurative sense, it has the meaning of a cause (*hetu*); yet, because the state of being a condition (*paccayabhāva*) is seen even in earth and other elements through the figurative application of the term "cause," it is stated as "the cause that is a cause" (*hetu-hetu*) by distinguishing it with a second word for "cause.
Ignorance (*avijjā*) is the common cause (*sādhāraṇa-hetu*) because it is a shared condition for meritorious formations (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) and the rest;
[it is the cause] "by way of its basis (*ṭhānaso*)" for the undertaking of kamma in the past, future, and present...
Regarding the phrase "the cause as result," although other conditions exist here, because it determines desirable and undesirable results, karma is its primary cause;
thus it is said: "Wholesome and unwholesome [karma] are the supreme causes for the giving of their respective results.

The meaning of "the great elements are the causes" is also expressed by the phrase "the great elements are the condition"; this is because the words *hetu* (cause) and *paccaya* (condition) are synonymous.

Because they have the same meaning, a condition itself is a cause; thus, it is called a "causal condition" (*paccayahetu*). And that which is the cause of the aggregate of form is precisely what is stated to be its condition for its manifestation.
Therefore, he said: "In this context, 'causal condition' is intended.

To the extent that a conditioning phenomenon is a condition for the arising and the persistence of its own conditionally arisen effect, to that same extent it exists as such by way of its own nature and designation.
"It deserves to be called a condition even for making known" means that it is fit to be designated as such.
To show, by way of analysis, the meaning stated in the Canon (Pāḷi) without analysis, the passage beginning with "Therein, the earth element... was spoken.

Therein, "for making known" means for the purpose of awakening [the mind] through such modes as "with cause" or "without cause. Since all such awakening occurs through knowledge as a seeing, it is said: "for the purpose of seeing."
"Contact" (*phassa*) means the state of being endowed with contact. Here, it refers to the arising of a contact capable of performing its own specific function;
for once contact has arisen, it becomes the condition for a corresponding kind of feeling.

It is precisely for this purpose that the Blessed One gave this teaching by way of reference to a person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*); therefore, the word "contact" pertains to two time periods, namely the present and the past.
It should be understood thus: when there is contact, one feels; what is meant is that feeling has contact as its condition. The same method applies to the other two terms as well.
For just as with feeling, so too for perception and mental formations (*saṅkhāra*), contact is the specific condition, because they do not exist in its absence.

By the inclusion of "volition" (*cetanā*), the phenomena of the aggregate of mental formations are indicated, because that [aggregate] is predominant due to its conformity with the act of accumulating (*āyūhana*).

[The intention] is grasped. For indeed, in the *Suttantabhājanīya* and in the *Saṅkhārakkhandhabhājanīya*, it is volition (*cetanā*) alone that is specified by such expressions as “volition born of eye-contact,” and so forth.

Regarding the phrase “of the consciousness aggregate (*viññāṇakkhandha*)”: here, in order to show that consciousness, at the beginning of a single existence, is a condition for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), it is said, “First, by means of rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhiviññāṇa*),” and so on. In that context, for one who is born from a womb...

With reference to the occurrence of materiality for one who possesses mental constituents (*sabhāvaka*), it is said, "by way of the upper limit," because at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), materiality does not exist beyond thirty [moments].

Now, in order to show the conditionality of mentality-materiality (*nāmarūpa*) for the consciousness of the course of existence (*pavatti-viññāṇa*) by way of the doors, it is said, "at the eye-door," and so forth. But is it not the case that contact (*phassa*) is also a condition for consciousness?

Why are only three aggregates stated to have contact as their condition? This is true; however, while contact accompanied by consciousness is a condition for feeling and the other aggregates, it is not so for consciousness itself. Therefore the Blessed One said: "The meeting of the three is contact.
Just as contact is a specific condition for consciousness, so too is name-and-form a specific condition for consciousness.
“Consciousness. Therefore, in order to show this distinction, it is stated that consciousness alone is the condition for name-and-form, and not contact.
87. As long as personality-view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) arises, there is no end to the round of existence; thus, one who has not abandoned personality-view wanders about in the round.
Hence he asks, “But how, venerable sir? while inquiring about the round. And just as with the demonstration of personality-view...

He said: "The question concerning the round (*vaṭṭapucchā*), and likewise the question concerning the turning away from it (*vivaṭṭapucchā*) which demonstrates its breaking up; thus, one asks about the turning away [by saying] 'there is no personality-view (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*'). 88.
This 'taste in form'—the seeing of it as it truly is—is the convergence of full understanding (*pariññābhisamaya*), and it is included within the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*)."
He said, "Form": "By this, both the penetration of full understanding and the truth of suffering have been explained.
Because of the statement, "That form which is impermanent," etc., its state of impermanence and so forth constitutes the danger therein;

and because it exists in dependence on conditions, that condition is the truth of origination. Thus, by the abandoning of origination, there is the transcendence of danger; this is indicated by the mention of "danger" (ādīnava).
He states the accomplished goal: “The penetration of abandoning and the truth of the origin.
And because Nibbāna, the escape from all conditioned things, must be penetrated by way of the clear realization of actualization, he says:

“By this, there is both the penetration of actualization and the truth of cessation. “In these three instances” refers to the three points of clear realization regarding suffering and so forth, as previously described.
"Those states beginning with right view" refers to the eight or seven states known as the Noble Path, beginning with right view.
"Penetration by means of development is the truth of the path" means the truth of the path that occurs through the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of development.
"In the remaining phrases as well" refers to such phrases as, "This is the gratification of feeling," and so forth.
89. In this context, "one's own" is used because it is immediate and directly perceptible; thus, one's own aggregates (khandhas) are designated as "internal.
Because they are the opposite of those, it is said that "external" refers to the conscious bodies of others.

"In all signs" means in all signs such as forms (rūpa-nimitta) and so forth. These, moreover, whether bound to the sense faculties or not bound to the sense faculties, possess that same essential nature.

He says: "It includes even that which is not bound by the faculties. Since feeling and the other [aggregates] are included here by the mention of consciousness itself due to their inseparable nature, it is said:
"in this body possessed of consciousness. Alternatively, "body" (kāya) means a collection of aggregates (khandhasamūha). 90.
"Abiding in what is non-self" means abiding in the portion of the aggregates, which are devoid of a self and have the intrinsic nature of non-self; taking that as one's support...
"Having performed the deeds that were done": "In which self (attani) standing [do they exist]?
means in what kind of self will they show their result, or ripen? By this, he shows that because there is no agent or experiencer, actions belonging to the side of a self are untenable;
furthermore, because the aggregates (khandhā) are momentary, it would entail the faults of the loss of what was done and the acquisition of what was not done.
In this regard, the method for resolving such objections is as follows: first, the clarification of the connection with the path of action by way of the destruction of life.
For among conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), whose nature is to cease moment by moment, who is it that kills, or what is it that is killed?

If it is the continuum of mind and mental factors (*cittacetasikasantāna*), then because it is formless (*arūpa*), it is incapable of being disturbed by means of cutting, breaking, and so forth, nor is it capable of being disturbed. Now, if it is the continuum of material form (*rūpasantāna*), [it is likewise not the killer].

Since it is insentient, it is like a piece of wood or a log; therefore, one does not generate the demerit of taking life through cutting or other such acts in its regard, as one would with a dead body.

Furthermore, the preliminary effort (*payoga*) for taking life—such as the striking of blows and so forth—might occur in relation to past formations, future ones, or present ones. Among these, it cannot occur in relation to the past or the future, because those...

Because of their non-existence [in the future], and because of the momentariness of formations (*saṅkhāra*) in the present—since they have a nature that ceases by their own inherent power when facing destruction—any effort would be purposeless.
Furthermore, since destruction is devoid of a cause, death is not caused by such efforts as striking with a weapon;
and since formations are inactive (*nirīhaka*), to whom would that effort belong? Because of momentariness, it belongs to that which perishes at the very same time as the intention to kill.
Since it does not persist until the conclusion of the action, to whom does the bond of the kamma of killing belong?
It is said: the aggregate of formations designated as a "being," accompanied by the aforementioned volition of the killer, kills.

On account of the application of the act of killing set in motion by that [volition], there arises—devoid of heat, consciousness, and the life-faculty—the basis for the conventional usage of the term "dead" at the moment of performing the aforementioned act of killing.
The collection of material and immaterial phenomena that is destined to arise, or the entire continuum of consciousness and mental factors, is what is "slain.

Even though this [continuum] is not the direct object of the act of killing, because its existence in the five-aggregate realm depends upon the material continuum, when the material continuum has ceased due to the application of another's effort to cut off the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*)—by means of the production of a heterogeneous obstructive material phenomenon generated by that effort—a severance occurs; thus, it does not constitute the taking of life.
It is not impossible; nor is killing without a cause, nor is the preliminary effort (payoga) useless.
This is because, due to the application made toward present formations, the aggregate of formations that ought to arise immediately thereafter does not arise in that way.
This is because, among momentary formations, it is "momentary death" that is not intended here by the term "death," but rather "continuity-death" (santatimaraṇa).
And because it possesses causes in the manner already described, death is not causeless; nor is the act of taking life devoid of an agent,
for even though the formations (saṅkhāra) are inactive, they are present merely as contributing factors, and since these causes are determined to produce their respective corresponding results,
the conventional designation of an "agent" is established— just as one says, "the lamp illuminates" or "the moon, the maker of night, shines."

And the taking of life is not intended for the mere collection of mind and mental factors that coexist with the intention of speech, because it is admitted [as such] only when established by way of a continuum (*santāna*);

and since the accomplishment of purposeful action is seen in the case of lamps and so forth as they proceed by way of a continuum, one is indeed bound by the kamma of taking life. For this very reason, in whichever continuum the volition (*cetanā*) of taking life occurs—
It proceeds within that very same continuum; through the convergence of other conditions, its fruit arises in another existence in states such as hell.

Thus, there is no destruction of what has been done, nor is there the arrival of what has not been done. By this method, the analysis of the connection with the courses of kamma for actions such as taking what is not given should be understood accordingly.
"All grasping at views belongs only to one who has fallen under the power of craving," thus he said, "by the predominance of craving.
"In this and that state" refers to the states of the Dhamma being shown by me. "The natural meditation subject" is the meditation subject being taken up and cultivated in the presence of that elder.
"Another new meditation subject" [is that] according to the teaching of the Blessed One.
Another new meditation subject has been taken up. The rest is indeed easy to understand.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Mahāpuṇṇamasutta* is completed.
10. Commentary on the *Cūḷapuṇṇamasutta*.
91. Regarding the reduplication "tuṇhībhūtaṃ tuṇhībhūtaṃ," he says "yaṃ yaṃ disaṃ" and so forth, because it is spoken out of a desire for detailed explanation.
In the phrase "anuviloketvā," the prefix *anu* also signifies a desire for detail;
thus the meaning is "having looked here and there. For this very reason, he says, "having looked from this side and that. He says "asanto nīco puriso" means "an asappurisa" (an untrue person).
“An evil person, a base person. He is an *asappurisa* (an untrue person). He is unable to know that *asappurisa* because he does not know the qualities of an *asappurisa* as they truly are.
“Endowed with evil qualities” means endowed with base qualities such as bodily misconduct, lack of contentment, and so forth.
One who has devotion (*bhatti*) toward an *asappurisa* is an *asappurisabhatti*. Therefore it was said: “Association with an *asappurisa*. This is the quality of an *asappurisa*.

By dropping the final member of the compound, *asappurisa* (an untrue person) means one whose nature is to think like them; thus he says, "one who thinks with the thoughts of an untrue person," which means one who thinks what is ill-thought. "The counsel of an untrue person" refers to the deliberations and investigations of wicked folk.
"The speech of an untrue person" refers to the four kinds of wrong speech. "The action of an untrue person" refers to the threefold misconduct of body.
The "view of a bad person" (*asappurisadiṭṭhi*) specifically refers to the ten-based wrong view; one who possesses this is said to be "possessed of the view of a bad person.
"Giving by a bad person" (*asappurisadāna*) refers to giving without due care and so forth. The meaning of all these methods is understood from the canonical text itself.
Although the volition such as "I shall kill a living being" certainly involves the harming of another, it is nevertheless [classified] according to how it relates to oneself...
It is for the sake of one's own suffering, and not so for another; in order to show this meaning, it is said, "he thinks for the sake of his own suffering.

This shows that although a person experiences a portion of the powerful or heavier ripening of evil through such thoughts as "such-and-such" or "so-and-so," he does not experience it in the same way that another would. Therefore, he said:
“For the harm of others”: “Having taken” means having taken [them] as companions in evil deeds.

“Carelessly” means having acted without respect. To show that disrespect for the gift to be given is a sign of lack of faith, while disrespect for the person is a failure to honor them, he said: “He does not honor the gift to be given,” and so forth.

"Without making it an object of the mind" (*acittīkatvā*) means not having it placed in the mind, that is, not honoring it. For one who honors places the object to be honored within the mind, and does not cast it outside.
Alternatively, "making an object of the mind" (*cittīkaraṇa*) refers to the practice of performing a marvelous act, namely the act of esteem.
Its opposite is "not making an object of the mind" (*acittīkaraṇa*), which is the act of non-esteeming. "Cast away" (*apaviddha*)—
Like something to be discarded, such as leftover food; therefore he said, "as if desiring to discard it," and so forth.
"As if casting away a disease" means as if one were to sweep a disease from the body of a sick person with rice and other foods and cast that disease into an anthill.
"Certainly the fruit of this gift will come to me alone"—thus for one who holds such a view.
He holds the view that there is rebirth; however, this person does not hold such a view, which is why it says, "he does not hold the view of coming back. Therefore it says:
"he gives without being one who expects a fruit.
Granted, this person may be possessed of the evil qualities such as unrighteousness (asaddhamma) and the like as previously described, yet by all of those...
In order to show that wrong view is a great offense, it is said: "By means of that wrong view, one is reborn in hell.
"By way of the opposite of what was stated" means that the meaning in the bright side (sukkapakkha) should be understood as the reverse of the meaning stated regarding the dark side (kaṇhapakkha).
In such passages as "the world with its devas," the word *deva* refers to the devas of the six sense-sphere realms; so it is here as well.

He said, "The gods of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara-devā). If it is asked why the gods of the sense-sphere are mentioned here when Brahmās have been mentioned separately, it is because the fruit of giving is intended here;

thus, the mention of the gods of the sense-sphere is made. Furthermore, within that category, the inclusion of the six sense-spheres should be understood from the mention of their greatness as gods and so forth.
"The prosperity of the three families" refers to the greatness of the Khattiya family and the others.

Regarding "the prosperity of the three families," it should be understood that not only the excellence of lineage itself is intended, but rather the excellence of longevity, beauty, health, wealth, sovereignty, and so forth, is also intended there;
for these too are achieved through the power of sublime merit consisting of giving.

This has been stated solely by way of the pure round of existence (*suddhavaṭṭa*), because the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭa*) is not touched upon even in the bright fortnight. For faith and the other [faculties] are the mundane accumulations of wholesome qualities.
Thus it is intended here. The remainder is easy to understand.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Cūḷapuṇṇamasutta* is completed.
And the commentary on the Devadaha Vagga is finished.
2. Anupada-Vagga 1. Anupada-Sutta Commentary 93. "One who possesses psychic power" (iddhimā):
this quality is manifest by itself, even without being heard from another, through such acts as the shaking of a palace or traveling among the devas.

Because of their manifest nature; and because the qualities such as being a proponent of ascetic practices (*dhuta*) are likewise manifest in this same manner, due to the manifestation of those qualities and their being determined by others.
"The qualities of one possessed of wisdom" refers to specific distinctions of quality brought forth by the various divisions of wisdom.
For these, for the most part, are not within the domain of others. Therefore he said: "It is not possible to know them without being told."
"Dissimilar" refers to worldlings (*puthujjana*) who are full of improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*).
Because they have not abandoned lust and hatred, they smear over existing virtues in others and proclaim only non-existent dispraise; thus it is said: "Dissimilar... they speak.
That which [is the knowledge] of the eighteen elements as they truly are—in terms of their arising, their passing away, their gratification, and their danger—
Understanding—this is skillfulness regarding the elements (dhātu-kusala-tā). The same method applies to skillfulness regarding the sense bases (āyatana-kusala-tā).

Skillfulness regarding the twelve factors of dependent origination, beginning with ignorance, is skillfulness regarding dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda-kusala-tā). "This is the proper occasion and cause for this fruit;
this is not the proper occasion and not the cause"—thus, knowing the proper occasion as the proper occasion and the improper occasion as the improper occasion, according to reality...

Understanding—this is skill in what is possible and impossible. Furthermore, one who has gone forth from here, having proceeded by means of knowledge—which is named "wisdom" because it moves without attachment through the full comprehension and clear realization of these elements and so forth—is called "wise.
Thus he said: "One is wise for these four reasons. It is "great" because it encompasses great purposes.

"One who has wisdom" (*paññā*) "is his" means he is "of great wisdom" (*mahāpañño*). Since this same method applies to the remaining terms as well, he says: "The meaning is 'endowed with great wisdom and so forth.

"Diversity" (*nānatta*) refers to the diversity and distinction among those qualities of great wisdom and so forth, by virtue of which the Elder is celebrated as "of great wisdom" and so on. This [refers to] any particular immaterial phenomenon (*arūpadhamma*).
"Greatness" is to be understood by way of the accomplishment of its function; thus, demonstrating that accomplishment of its function for him, he said:
"She possesses great wisdom because she grasps the great aggregate of virtue," and so forth.

In this context, [greatness] is to be understood by way of greatness of cause, greatness of condition, greatness of support, greatness of classification, greatness of function, greatness of fruit, and greatness of benefit.

And the greatness of the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) should be understood. In this context, the causes (*hetu*) are non-greed and so forth; the conditions (*paccaya*) are shame (*hiri*), dread of blame (*ottappa*), faith (*saddhā*), mindfulness (*sati*), energy (*viriya*), and so forth.

The supports (*nissaya*) are the fixedness toward the enlightenment of disciples (*sāvakabodhi*), the enlightenment of paccekabuddhas (*paccekabodhi*), and perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*), as well as the distinguished persons who possess them.

The classification (*pabheda*) is the division into conduct (*cāritta*) and so forth. The function (*kicca*) is the dispelling of opposing factors by means of the "removal of that factor" (*tadaṅga*) and other methods. The fruit (*phala*)—
The attainment of heaven and the attainment of Nibbāna; the benefit consists in being dear and agreeable, and so forth. This is the summary here;
the detailed exposition, however, should be understood according to the method set forth in the *Visuddhimagga*, in the *Ākaṅkheyya Sutta*, and other such texts.

In this same manner, the greatness of the aggregate of concentration and the other aggregates should also be determined and understood as appropriate. Furthermore, the greatness of the "proper and improper occasions" (*ṭhānāṭṭhāna*) and so forth is due to their vast range of application.
This is to be understood. In this regard, the vast scope of the possible and the impossible will become clear from the *Bahudhātuka Sutta* itself.

The various dwellings (*vihāra*) and attainments (*samāpatti*) should be understood according to the method established in the section on the aggregate of concentration (*samādhikkhandha*). The noble truths (*ariyasacca*) should be understood according to the method presented in the *Saccavibhaṅga* and its commentaries, as they encompass the entirety of the Teaching.
The foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) and so forth should be understood from their respective *Vibhaṅgas* and the commentaries thereon.

And it is so by the method already explained. This is because the fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala) constitute the accomplishment of great benefit, great happiness, great welfare, and great security from bondage;
and because they are peaceful, sublime, subtle, beyond the sphere of mere reasoning, and to be realized by the wise.
Furthermore, the direct knowledges (abhiññā) possess great equipment, a great range, a great function, great power, and a great accomplishment.
Furthermore, its greatness should be understood from the accomplishment of great purposes, such as the crushing of intoxication regarding Nibbāna.
Regarding the term "vast wisdom" (*puthupaññā*), the meaning should be understood here according to the method already stated. However, this is the distinction:
knowledge proceeds toward the various aggregates, [discerning] thus, "This is called the aggregate of form... pe... this is called the aggregate of consciousness. Thus, [it is vast].
Knowledge proceeds in dependence upon the differentiation of the five aggregates. Regarding these as well: "The aggregate of form is of one kind;
the aggregate of form is of eleven kinds. The aggregate of feeling is of one kind; the aggregate of feeling is of many kinds. The aggregate of perception is of one kind...
[and so on] ...the aggregate of consciousness is of one kind; the aggregate of consciousness is of many kinds."

In this way, knowledge proceeds by depending on the differentiation of each aggregate (*khandha*) according to its singlefold nature and so forth, as well as according to distinctions such as the past and so on.

Likewise, knowledge proceeds by depending on the diversity of the sense bases (*āyatana*), [understanding]: "This is called the eye-base... pe... this is called the mental-object-base (*dhammāyatana*).
Among these, ten bases belong to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), while two belong to the four planes [of existence]."
"In various elements" means: "This is called the eye-element... [and so on]... this is called the mind-consciousness-element.
Among these, sixteen elements belong to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), while two belong to the four planes. Thus, knowledge proceeds dependent upon various elements.
It should be understood that this is stated by way of the clung-to (upādiṇṇaka) elements; for [this knowledge arises] in Paccekabuddhas and in the two Chief Disciples.
Knowledge proceeds by way of the differentiation of the elements that are clung-to (upādiṇṇaka-dhātu) alone;

and even that, moreover, only partially and not exhaustively. They do not know at all the differentiation of the elements that are not clung-to (anupādiṇṇaka-dhātu). However, it is only for the Omniscient Buddhas [that this is known], such as:
"Because of the predominance of this particular element, the trunk of this tree is white; that of this one is black."
This one has thick bark; this one has thin bark; this one’s leaf is of such a kind in terms of color, shape, and so forth;
this one’s flower is blue, yellow, red, or white, fragrant or foul-smelling;
its fruit is small or large, long or round, well-shaped or rough, smooth or coarse, fragrant, sweet, bitter, sour, or pungent.
“Pungent, astringent, a sharp thorn, a blunt thorn, straight, crooked, red, and white”—thus knowledge proceeds in dependence upon the diversity of elements (*dhātu*). “In what exist?

means in the objects such as visible forms and so forth. “In various dependent originations” means according to the distinction between internal and external, and according to the distinction of the continuity (*santāna*) [of existence].

And [it refers] to the various classifications of the factors of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*). For each individual factor, beginning with ignorance (*avijjā*), is designated as "dependent origination.
Therefore, it is said in the *Saṅkhāra Piṭaka*: "Twelve conditions, twelve dependent originations.

"In various forms of emptiness and non-apprehension" means in those things of various natures which, being devoid of permanence, essence, and so forth, are empty by nature; and for that very reason, [they are empty] in terms of woman, man, self, what belongs to a self, and so on.

"Among non-apprehendable entities. Here, the letter *ma* serves as a euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*). "Among various meanings" refers to the various meanings such as the dependently arisen, which are the objects of the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*).
"Among phenomena" refers to the various phenomena such as conditions, which are the objects of the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*).
"Among etymologies" refers to the various etymological explanations consisting of definitive expressions for those very same meanings and phenomena. "Among insights" refers to...

Here, regarding the knowledges that have become the objects of the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) such as the analysis of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā), and which have received the name "analytical insight" (paṭibhāna) because they manifest in various ways with the thought, "These [words] illuminate this meaning," the multiplicity and diversity of virtue (sīla) in the passage beginning "in the various aggregates of virtue" has already been explained.
As for the others, however, they are self-evident, since they are easy to understand by following the method already stated.
However, since Nibbāna is non-differentiated and one alone, its diversity must be understood there by way of metaphorical designation; thus he said:
“Having transcended the various phenomena common to diverse people. By this, its diversity is illustrated through such expressions as “the crushing of intoxication” and so forth.
Having thus shown the greatness and diversity of wisdom by way of its objects, he now says, "What is laughing wisdom (*hāsapaññā*)?

and so forth, in order to show its state of laughter by way of associated states, its state of impulsion (*javana*) by way of its mode of occurrence, and its sharpness and other qualities by way of its function.
In this context, "abounding in laughter" means abounding in joy (*pīti*). The remaining terms refer to that same [joy].
Synonyms: "He fulfills virtue" means that, being joyful and elated, he does so by means of wisdom accompanied by rapture (*pīti*).
For wisdom accompanied by rapture and mental joy proceeds as if blooming and fully blossomed upon its object through the power of delight;
it does not proceed when accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*). Thus, setting aside the Pātimokkha virtue, he fulfills the other threefold virtue which is to be cultivated with laughter.

This is the meaning. Because it was mentioned separately, he speaks of the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) again. The same method applies to the "aggregate of concentration" (samādhikkhandha) and so forth.

It "swiftly and rapidly moves toward form as impermanent" means that by quickly and forcefully proceeding with the realization of the aggregate of form as impermanent—due to the extreme intensity of prior volitional formations and the distancing of opposing factors—one penetrates the characteristic [of impermanence] like a thunderbolt released by Indra.
Not becoming blind to the aggregate of form, one penetrates its characteristic of impermanence with speed;
therefore, the meaning is that it is called "swift wisdom" (*javanapaññā*). The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.

Having thus shown swift wisdom by way of insight (*vipassanā*) having the characteristics as its object, the words beginning with "form" are spoken in order to show it by way of powerful insight. Therein, "in the sense of destruction" means:
Because it has the nature of destruction, in that it breaks up right where it arises.

"In the sense of fear" means because of its terrifying nature. "In the sense of being pithless" means because it is devoid of a self as its core, and because it is devoid of a permanent core and so forth.

"Having weighed" means having weighed with the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*), which serves as a scale. "Having scrutinized" means having scrutinized with that very same [wisdom], which serves as a scrutiny.

"Having analyzed" means having revealed them as they truly are, having made the five aggregates manifest. "In the cessation of form" means by way of being inclined, sloping, and leaning toward Nibbāna, which is the cessation of the aggregate of form.

Now, in order to show impulsive wisdom (*javana-paññā*) by way of insight that has reached its culmination, the passage beginning with "form" is stated again. Some say it is by way of insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā*).
The sharpness of knowledge is to be understood specifically through the total eradication of its opposites;

thus, having stated, "Sharp wisdom is that which quickly cuts off the defilements," he spoke the passage beginning with "arisen sensual thought" in order to show those defilements by way of classification.
For one of sharp wisdom possesses swift direct knowledge, and his path does not waver.
He said: "The four noble paths are attained on a single seat," and so forth.

The penetration of the truths succeeds through seeing things as they truly are—namely, that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, suffering, subject to change, conditioned, dependently arisen, and of the nature to perish, decay, and cease"—and not otherwise.
In order to show penetrative wisdom by way of its causes, it is said: “He is full of urgency regarding all conditioned formations,” and so forth.
Therein, “full of urgency” means that, according to the method already stated, he frequently experiences a sense of spiritual agitation toward all conditioned formations.
“Full of trepidation” means that his mind is repeatedly terrified toward all conditioned formations by means of the dread born of knowledge. By this, he speaks of the contemplation of danger.
By the phrase "full of weariness," he refers to the contemplation of disenchantment (*nibbidānupassanā*);

by the phrase "full of aversion" and so forth, he describes its repeated arising. "Outward-turned" means having the face of knowledge directed toward *nibbāna*, which stands outside all conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra*);

or, it has the face of liberation as it has thus proceeded. "Penetration" (*nibbedha*) is the act of piercing through; that [penetration] belongs to this [contemplation], or it is that by which one pierces through.

Or, that wisdom which is piercing is "penetrative wisdom" (*nibbedhikā paññā*). As for what has not been analyzed here in terms of meaning, it is easily understood because it follows the method explained below.
It is called a "footstep" (*pada*) because insight and so forth proceed by means of it; thus, "step-by-step" (*anupada*) means "according to attainment" (*anusamāpatti*).
Alternatively, the phenomena that come under comprehension are "steps" (*pada*) because they serve as the basis for the occurrence of insight. Therefore, he said: "by way of attainment..."

"Or" (*vā*): "by way of the factors of jhāna" (*jhānaṅgavasena*) means "by way of the constituent parts of jhāna. However, in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), it is asked: "What is the meaning of the word *pada* here?
Therefore, he says "in successive order" (*anupaṭipāṭiyā*), explaining that the meaning here is "step by step" (*anupadaṃ*) or "in sequence" (*anukkamenā*).
"Insight into phenomena" (*dhammavipassanā*) refers to the insight into those phenomena included within each respective arising of consciousness associated with meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).

"Vipassati" means that, having grasped those various phenomena as they truly are by way of the doors of jhāna through the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), one comprehends them [with the thought], "In this way they are suffering," and so forth.

This is because the practice of comprehension for disciples who have reached the highest level occurs without exception within half a month, and because the knowledge of the disciple’s perfection (*sāvakapāramīñāṇa*) must be cultivated in such a manner. Thus...

"Even though"—that is to say, even if the Elder Mahāmoggallāna attained Arahantship not long ago, whereas the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) attained it much later—even so, because the Elder Moggallāna was also of great wisdom, the Elder Sāriputta is "even more greatly wise.
Now, in order to make this matter clearer, [the text says]: "The Elder Mahāmoggallāna," and so forth.

It has been said: "The range of comprehension" (*sammasanacāra*) means that which is the ground for insight (*vipassanā*), wherein one practices comprehension; it refers to that range of comprehension.

"Only a single portion" means that, being unable to fully comprehend and comprehend all the formations within his own personal existence, he comprehends and contemplates only a single portion, in accordance with the power of knowledge attained through his own specific application of effort. Is this not so?

And because of the statement: “Bhikkhus, without directly knowing, without fully understanding, without becoming dispassionate toward, and without abandoning everything, one is incapable of the destruction of suffering,” must one who desires to be liberated from the suffering of the round certainly fully understand everything that is to be fully understood? This is true;

however, this was said with reference to those phenomena that have entered the range of comprehension. Therefore, regarding all phenomena within one’s own continuum, as well as those within the continua of others—

And when one contemplates [the body] by way of its commonality as an external state, without making a distinction between their respective continua, this is the mode of contemplation for the disciples (*sāvaka*).
But the Elder, even regarding external phenomena, contemplated them by distinguishing their continua, extracting each one individually;
however, he did so merely by touching them with his knowledge. Therefore it was said: "As if pressing with the tip of a stick..."

"Pressing down with the tip of a stick, as it were, while comprehending only a single portion. In this context, regarding "by means of knowledge," it is said "as if pressing down with the tip of a stick," and so forth, because knowledge does not proceed in the same manner as the object to be known (neyya).
It is said "comprehending only a single portion" because there is no insight (vipassanā) into phenomena one by one in their successive order (anupada-dhamma-vipassanā).

They say that the range of the Buddhas’ comprehensive knowledge extends to the conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) contained within the mental continuums of beings in the ten-thousandfold world-system, as well as those not bound by the sense-faculties;
others say it extends to hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).

For likewise, having entered into the method of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) according to the three times, the great diamond-like wisdom (*mahāvajirañāṇa*) of the Buddhas proceeds through three hundred and sixty million modes.

[This is] the process [of insight]. Regarding the "process of comprehension" (*sammasanacāra*), some say it consists of the mental continua of beings dwelling in the Middle Country, together with those of the Paccekabuddhas, excluding those not bound by the sense faculties; others say it consists of the mental continua of beings dwelling in Jambudīpa.
Even for the Dhammasenāpati, the process of comprehension is simply the plane of insight (*vipassanābhūmi*) of the aforementioned disciples. In that regard:

The Elder understood it with exceptional excellence, without remainder, as phenomena following one after another (anupadadhamma). Therefore it was said: "You have comprehended, without omission, the range of comprehension for disciples.

In that context, regarding the phrase "the sphere of insight for disciples," this refers to ordinary disciples who are dry-insight practitioners (sukkha-vipassaka) and have attained mundane supernormal powers (lokika-abhiññā).

Among the six types of persons—the two Chief Disciples, the Paccekabuddhas, and the Sammāsambuddhas—because they have not attained the wisdom and skillfulness associated with the jhānas and higher knowledges (abhiññā) like those who practice bare insight (sukkha-vipassaka), they lack the ability to proceed toward their desired object during the time of insight meditation, just as blind people cannot reach a desired place.
They develop insight by remaining focused solely on the phenomena already grasped for analysis. Having attained mundane higher knowledges...
However, ordinary disciples are able to expand their insight (*vipassanā*) by means other than that through which they first began it, owing to their vast knowledge.
The Great Disciples (*mahāsāvaka*), because they were endowed with a resolute aspiration (*abhinīhāra*), were able to expand their insight even more extensively than that.
Among the Chief Disciples, the second [disciple] was distinguished by his excellence in resolute aspiration and concentration (*samādhi*).

Because it is preeminent, insight (vipassanā) makes it even more widespread than that. Furthermore, the first [type of person] makes it widespread through his great wisdom in a way not shared by the disciples.
A paccekabuddha, because of his even greater initial resolve (abhinīhāra), makes insight—which is already widespread—wider still, in accordance with his own resolve.
This is because, for Buddhas, there is the attainment of omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa) developed through the perfection of wisdom (paññāpāramī) being fulfilled in the most perfect manner.
"Suitable" means: just as an arrow shot by an archer like Sarabhaṅga, who is well-practiced in piercing the heart of a reed,
falls directly upon the target without being obstructed by trees, creepers, or other things along the way— neither sticking nor missing its mark— so too, insight (vipassanā),
without being obstructed or missing its mark in between, [penetrates] the phenomena to be comprehended through various methods according to their true nature.
It proceeds. The differentiation of the modes of its proceeding, which is called "great knowledge," has already been stated by way of enumeration.

Among these, the mode of practice of insight for those practicing dry-insight (sukkha-vipassaka) is like the light of a glowworm; that of ordinary disciples who have attained direct knowledge (abhiññā) is like the light of a lamp;
that of the great disciples (mahāsāvaka) is like the light of a firebrand; and that of the chief disciples (aggasāvaka) is like the light of the medicinal star (osadhitārakā).
To the Paccekabuddhas, it appeared like the radiance of the moon; to the Sammāsambuddhas, it appeared like the orb of the autumn sun adorned with a thousand rays.
Likewise, the practice of insight for those practicing dry-insight (sukkha-vipassaka) was like the movement of the blind by means of the tip of a staff;

for ordinary disciples who have attained mundane supernormal powers (lokīya-abhiññā), it was like traveling by way of a bridge of poles; and for the Great Disciples (mahāsāvaka), it was like traveling by way of a bridge of human legs.
It should be understood that for the Chief Disciples it is like traveling by a bridge of carts; for the Paccekabuddhas, it is like traveling on a great path for large oxen;
and for the Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas, it is like traveling on a great highway for large chariots.
Regarding the phrase "and having attained arahantship," the word *kira* is used here to indicate that this matter is one obtained through oral tradition (*anussava*).
Having reached [this realization], he understood it through observing that his own practice of insight (*vipassanā*) possessed a vast range and a state of sharpness, clarity, and courage.
But how did this Great Elder, while reaching *arahantship* more slowly than others who had attained it quickly, understand himself to be superior in wisdom?
To this he said: "Just as... and so forth. "A great tangle" (*mahājaṭa*) means a great web of branches.
The web was exceedingly well-woven. However, because he did not select [the best] when taking the bamboo, he obtained neither a strong nor a straight pole;

this was due to his failure to choose carefully when grasping the bamboo. "Accomplished in such a way" means that just as among those men one took the bamboo pole without selecting it while grasping the bamboo, and another took it after selecting it, so too it was effective.
"Exertion" (padhāna) refers to the application of oneself to spiritual cultivation (bhāvanā).

"Sixty-seven knowledges" refers to the sixty-seven knowledges among the seventy-three knowledges mentioned in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, excluding the six unique knowledges beginning with knowledge consisting in what has been heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*) and ending with the knowledge of the analytical power of ingenuity (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa*). For those [sixty-seven] are to be analyzed by disciples, but not the others.
"Wisdom of sixteen kinds" refers to the wisdom beginning with great wisdom (*mahāpaññā*) and the wisdom of the nine successive dwellings in attainment (*navānupubbavihārasamāpatti*).
This is sixteenfold wisdom. "Therein" means in that [wisdom].

"This occurs" means this sequential comprehension (*anupubbasammasana*) which is now being described occurs. "The section on insight" (*vipassanākoṭṭhāsa*) refers to the portion of insight analyzed according to the classification of the phenomena to be comprehended, such as applied thought (*vitakka*) and so forth.
"In the first jhāna" uses the locative case in a sense of proximity; therefore, "those phenomena in the first jhāna" refers to those things associated with the first jhāna.
The meaning is "phenomena" (*dhammā*). And in the phrase "within the attainment," the conventional designation "attainment" is applied to the mental states co-arising with that attainment.
"Determined" means having been determined; it is ascertained. "Delimited" means delimited by knowledge;
it is known by being distinguished according to its specific characteristic. "Surveying" means seeing directly with the eye of knowledge. "Directing" (*abhiniropanaṃ*)...
*Ārammaṇe cittassa āropanaṃ*: the directing of the mind toward the object. *Anumajjanaṃ*: the subsequent investigation of the mind within the object. *Pharaṇaṃ*:
the pervading of the body with sublime forms, or its state of expansion. *Sātaṃ*: pleasantness; sweetness. *Adhikkhepo*:
composure, which is the opposite of distraction (*vikkhepa*). *Phusanaṃ*: the touching [of the object] by the consciousness of the sense faculty after it has arisen from that [object].
It occurs in the manner of touching the object, as it were. Feeling (*vedayita*) is the experiencing of the object.

Perception (*sañjānana*) is the noting of the object by way of its blue color and so forth. Volition (*cetayita*) is the mental activity of the mind. Consciousness (*vijānana*) is the apprehension of the object.
Desire-to-act (*kattukamyatā*) is the mind’s need for the object. Resolution (*adhimokkha*) is the settling upon or the decision regarding that object.
Exertion (*paggāha*) is the uplifting of the mind, not allowing it to fall into the side of laziness; its meaning is "firm grasping" (*adhiggaha*).
Establishment (*upaṭṭhāna*) is the remaining [of the mind] having approached the object, or non-relinquishment [of the object].

Equanimity (*majjhattatā*) is the state of looking on with indifference toward the associated mental factors when they are performing their respective functions, just as a charioteer does toward horses proceeding evenly. [It is the state] of the associated phenomena toward the object...
*Anunaya* (concord) is the act of conciliating. "By way of intrinsic nature" means by way of their actual, true nature.
Here, only sixteen factors are included because they alone were defined by the Elder; they alone appeared to him at that time, and not the others, so they say.
Furthermore, by the inclusion of energy and mindfulness, faith and wisdom are also implied here due to their commonality as faculties (*indriya*).

By the inclusion of "truth" (*sacca*) alone, the six pairs beginning with tranquility (*passaddhi*), which share the common quality of being entirely blameless, as well as non-greed (*alobha*) and non-hatred (*adosa*), are included, because those states are comprised within the arising of the jhāna-consciousness. Furthermore, the Elder began by taking the states according to their commonality of definition (*vavatthāna*).
Others say that [the remaining factors] did not appear because they could not be formulated.
"Known as they arise" means that there is indeed understanding (*pajānana*) of these feelings even at the moment of their arising;

the same method applies to the other two phrases as well. "He knows that" means "knowledge of that" (*taṃ-ñāṇa*); the state of that is "the nature of knowing that" (*taṃ-ñāṇatā*), which means the self-awareness of knowledge.

It is associated with those mental states that are capable of being conjoined with it. "Abundance of knowledge" (*ñāṇa-bahutā*) is the multiplicity of knowledge within a single arising of consciousness.
The meaning is "the state of manifold knowledge. Now, in order to explain that very point, the passage beginning with "Just as" was stated.
It is not possible to know [them all together] because there is an absence of taking them as a simultaneous object. Furthermore, there is no unconfused comprehension for such a type of knowledge.
Only a single knowledge arises at that moment, because only a single adverting consciousness (āvajjana) arises; and without adverting, [knowledge does not arise].
There is the arising of consciousness. For this has been said:
"The gods who remain for eighty-four thousand aeons do not live even that long when they are conjoined with two [opposing] states of mind. And:
And regarding the statement, “There is no coupling grasped in consciousness”:

this is because the basis and the object have been grasped; that is to say, because the basis and the object upon which the factors of jhāna occur have already been delimited and grasped by knowledge beforehand.
It is just as, for example, [the coupling] of deer, pigs, and so forth.
Just as deer or pigs dwelling in a place surrounded by a trap are easy for a hunter to capture, whether from their point of emergence or their point of entry, so too is this case.
Therefore he said, "By the Elder," and so forth. "By that" means by the state of having encompassed the bases and objects.
"Of him" means of the Elder. "Of those states" refers to those states included within the arising of the jhāna-consciousness.

“Of phenomena. By the phrase “to one who adverts to their arising,” etc., it is shown that at whatever moment knowledge arises directed toward any particular thing—such as arising and so forth—it is precisely that very thing which becomes manifest at that moment. For knowledge does not arise without adverting.
“They come to be having not been” means that, having previously been non-existent, they come into existence; they were unarisen.

The meaning is "they arise. He sees the arising (*udaya*) of those phenomena because he perceives their state of possessing the moment of origination (*uppādakkhaṇa*), [seeing] that "having not been, they come to be.
For the acquisition of self-nature (*attalābha*) by phenomena, which makes known their prior non-existence, is their arising. "Having been" means having arisen.

"They pass away" means they perish moment by moment. He sees the passing away (*vaya*) because he perceives their state of possessing the moment of dissolution (*bhaṅgakkhaṇa*), [seeing] that "having been, they pass away."
For decay (*vaya*) is the awareness of the disintegrating nature of phenomena as they exist.
Since there is no approaching (*upāya*) toward those phenomena by way of passion (*rāga*), it is "without approach" (*anupāya*), meaning without attachment.
The construction is: "he dwells having been [thus]. Likewise, since there is no departing (*apāya*) from those phenomena by way of aversion (*paṭigha*), it is "without departure" (*anapāya*).
Non-opposition: because he lacks the adherence of craving and views, thinking “this is mine, this is my self,” he is independent of the bases for craving and views.
“Unbound”: because he does not depend on acquisitions, he is neither bound nor obstructed by desire and lust through the hindrance that opposes insight.
“Completely liberated”: for that very reason, by way of liberation through suppression, he is freed from sensual lust.
"Released. "Dissociated" means dissociated from opposing states by way of suppression.

[The phrase] "the boundary of defilements might be established by him" refers to the possibility that, having broken the course of insight (vipassanāvīthi) proceeding with reference to the sixteen states occurring within the attainment, lust and other defilements might arise; regarding that course of insight...
The boundary of defilements would be that which is produced by that mind, or by one possessing that mind.
"In those" means in those phenomena (*dhammas*). "His" refers to the Elder. "Even one" they say means even one among lust and the other [defilements].

If, according to the manner described, some [phenomena] do not come within range, then insight does not proceed uninterruptedly toward those phenomena; thus there would be a boundary of the object (*ārammaṇa-mariyādā*). Because the opposites have been suppressed...
It is said that because the states opposed to insight have already been suppressed, there are no defilements remaining to be suppressed even now.

"From this" means from the first jhāna. "The immediate" refers to the subsequent distinction of the higher jhānas and so forth. "Of that knowledge" means of the knowledge occurring in the form: "There is a further escape. "By way of repeated practice" means by way of its repeated production.

"In the sense of complete confidence" means through the removal of the turbidity of the defilements, or through the mind’s state of being truly serene due to the disappearance of the agitation caused by sustained thought (vicāra).
In the passages where it appears as "energy, mindfulness, and equanimity," it refers to the equanimity of purification (*pārisuddhi-upekkhā*);

in the passage "the feeling that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant," it refers to the equanimity of jhāna (*jhāna-upekkhā*); and it is stated that "at the place of pleasure, there is the equanimity of feeling (*vedanā-upekkhā*).

And by "at the place of pleasure" is meant the place where pleasure is mentioned in the first jhāna and so forth. "From the state of tranquility" means because of the state of being well-balanced in volition, due to the absence of diffusion or expansion toward the object.

That which was described as the "mental application" (ābhoga) of the mind—namely, the purity of mindfulness found in the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* and other texts—is, in its actual meaning, never separate from mindfulness;
thus he says, "it is simply purified mindfulness. This refers to the equanimity of purity (*pārisuddhupekkhā*), not the equanimity of the jhānas and so forth.
In such instances, there is never any absence of knowledge from mindfulness; therefore he says, "clearly comprehending through knowledge."
“Having offered. For likewise, in the third jhāna, when it is said, “mindful, dwelling in bliss,” the meaning of “clearly comprehending” (*sampajāno*) is already implied there.

Disciples do not possess insight into phenomena according to their successive occurrence (*anupadadhammavipassanā*), because the subtle manifestation of the remaining formations is difficult to discern and impossible to grasp by way of analytical separation. Therefore he said: “insight into the aggregates” (*kalāpavipassanaṃ*).
"Showing this, he spoke thus. 96.

Regarding the statement, "And having seen with wisdom, the taints (āsava) become exhausted": since the taints are being exhausted at the very moment of seeing, it is said that "having seen, they become exhausted. For even when referring to simultaneous time, such a linguistic usage is observed—as in:
"Dependent upon the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises."
“Having destroyed all darkness, arisen with intense radiance;
the sun, garlanded with rays, the maker of light for the eye of the world.

And so on in such passages. Or else, this word *disvā* has the sense of a cause (*hetu*), as in the case where it does not share the same agent [as the main verb], such as: “Having drunk ghee, strength...”

“Fear arises upon seeing a lion. For the destruction of the taints (*āsava*) is caused by vision, because when there is the realization through full understanding, realization through direct experience, and realization through development, the realization through abandonment is obtained.
“Having brought forth the pair” means that after entering the first jhāna and emerging from it, one develops serenity and insight in tandem while contemplating the factors of jhāna therein. Thus...

Up to the point where, having entered and emerged from the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he practiced contemplation there, yoking serenity and insight together, whereby the Elder attained Arahantship—it is with reference to this that it was said: "The stage of attaining Arahantship is what is taken here.
"Here" means in this sutta; for it was by means of the teaching of the *Dīghanakha Sutta* that the Elder [attained it].
He attained arahantship. At that time, since he was already an anāgāmī, there was no occasion for the statement "he enters into cessation";
therefore it was said: "The stage of attaining arahantship is what is intended here. If this is so, why was it stated:
"By completely transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling"? [The answer is: For the Elder...
Having demonstrated the qualities of a wise person in their entirety, he concludes the teaching by reaching the pinnacle of Arahantship.
Furthermore, entering the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) was a habitual practice for the Elder; therefore, he says, "But as for the attainment of cessation... they say.
By this, he shows that one indeed enters even the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) in between.

To explain how to open [the door], it is said: “*Tatthassā*” and so forth. In that context, for one who has brought together serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) in union through the mental application (*ābhoga*), “I shall attain cessation,” the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) becomes the head;
by virtue of that mental application, the turn for cessation arrives. The attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) is hidden; [one thinks], “The attainment of fruition...”

"Because there is an absence of mental application (*ābhoga*) [in the thought], 'I shall attain [it]'; the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) is the head"—here too, the meaning should be understood according to the method already stated.
By this, it should be understood that their arrival is dependent upon mental application.

"But as for the elders dwelling in Jambudvīpa," and so forth, is that statement exactly as recorded in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. "Within the attainment" means at the time of having entered cessation (*nirodha*).
"Material phenomena arisen from the three sources" refers to material phenomena arisen from temperature, kamma, and nutriment.
(97) "One who has attained mastery" means one who has well-cultivated mastery by way of distancing opposing states.
