"One who has reached perfection" means one who has reached the highest degree of perfection. "Born of the breast" (*orasa*) means born from the effort generated in the breast. "Produced" (*pabhāvita*) means brought forth. "By means of the Dhamma" (*dhammena*).
By means of the noble path-dhamma. For, because one is born and produced through the attainment of that [path], it is said: "born of the Dhamma, fashioned by the Dhamma.
"Of the gift of the Dhamma" refers to the ninefold supramundane gift of the Dhamma.
"From taking up" means from grasping; the sense is: from causing it to arise within one's own continuum. The rest is easily understood.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning of the Commentary on the *Anupada Sutta* is completed.
2. Commentary on the *Chabbisodhana Sutta* 98.
By one who declares, "Birth is exhausted," having professed the exhaustion of his own birth, the state of an *arahant* is thereby proclaimed.
"Because of the absence of that": by one who declares, "The holy life has been lived," meaning, "My dwelling in the holy life of the Path is completed.

"What was to be done has been done": by one who declares the state of having brought to completion by oneself all sixteen kinds of duties—namely, thorough knowledge and so forth—regarding the four truths through the four paths. "There is nothing further of this nature": [refers to the state of final liberation].

He said, "Even with a single word, the declaration of final knowledge (aññā) is indeed made," referring to one who professes the non-existence of future renewed existence (punabbhava) or the non-existence of further duties such as full understanding (pariññā) in the future. However, it is said that what is bound twice is as if well-bound;
here, the declaration of final knowledge is presented through four words, and therefore, this very point must be stated here.
The intended meaning is that it does not exist. Speaking of what has been seen through volition (*cetanā*) is called noble speech (*ariyavohāra*).

This word *dhamma* has the sense of "intrinsic nature" (*sabhāva*), as in such passages as "subject to birth, subject to aging," and so forth; therefore, "conformable to the Dhamma" (*anudhamma*) means an intrinsic nature that conforms to the state of the Noble Ones (*ariya*).
Because of their supreme fewness-of-wishes, the Noble Ones do not reveal their own virtues, yet [they uphold] the Teaching...

With the intention that [the relics] should be manifested even at the very moment of his final Nibbāna—in order to proclaim the state of leading to liberation and to generate enthusiasm for right practice among his fellow celibates—he said: “For one who has attained final Nibbāna... should be performed. 99.
*Dubbalam* means like softwood, easily broken, devoid of strength; the meaning is "without pith. *Virāgum*—
It has the nature of dissolving. It has the nature of vanishing, meaning it has the nature of going to destruction.
Because of its impermanence, suffering, and subject to change, and because even the slightest trace of gratification is absent, it is devoid of gratification.

They "approach" (upayā) in the sense that they reach or go toward [it] as appropriate, either by making it an object or by possessing it; thus they cling [to it], thinking, "This is mine, this is my self."
They are called *upādānas* because they grasp with a firm grip. It is the mental resolve (*cetaso adhiṭṭhāna*) because it is a state of mental approval that persists.
"By those" means by craving and views. "It" refers to the mind. "Adheres" means it settles down through attachment;
this is the meaning here: the mind adheres to the phenomena of personal identity (*sakkāya-dhamma*), clinging to them with the thought, "This is mine, this is my self."

It persists through these forms of adherence; likewise, because the mind underlies the phenomena of personal existence (*sakkāya*) by means of these, they are called "underlying tendencies" (*anusaya*), namely craving and views.
For in the same sense that lust and the other [defilements] underlie the phenomena of the three planes, the phenomena associated with them also underlie therein;
thus, it is said figuratively, "it underlies that. "Through their destruction and fading away" (*khayā virāgā*) is an ablative expression used in the sense of a cause.

“By destruction, by dispassion”: the meaning is stated here using the instrumental case in the sense of a cause (*hetu*). And in the phrase “by dispassion,” the word *iti* has the sense of “beginning with”;

by this, [terms] such as “by cessation” and so forth are included. These are indeed synonyms for one another, because they bring about the understanding of the very same thing—the complete cutting off (*samuccheda*)—through various means such as application (*upaya*), and so on.
100. It is called *patiṭṭhāna* because the remaining three primary elements (*bhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādārūpa*) are established therein;

it is called *dhātu* in the sense of being devoid of a living soul (*nijjīva*). Thus, it is the *patiṭṭhāna-dhātu*. It is called *ābandhana* because, like external water binding bath-powder, it binds the remaining three primary elements.
It is called *paripācana* because, like external heat ripening cooked food, it brings the remaining three primary elements to maturity. External wind...

It expands the remaining three elements, thus it is "expansion" (*vitthambhana*). The meaning of the word *dhātu* has already been stated. "Non-contacting element" (*asamphuṭṭhadhātu*) refers to the state of not being touched, because of their smooth and polished nature.
"Cognizing" (*vijānana*) is the apprehension of an object. "I, the self"—that is, "I";

[the thought] "material phenomena are my self" was not approached nor grasped as a portion of a self, that is, as a personal identity (*attabhāva*). Even those things supported by what is supported...
“Indeed, they are dependent,” he said, [explaining] “dependent on the earth element. Or, in another sense, they are dependent by way of themselves;

thus it is said, “by one method. Although derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) is also indeed dependent, nevertheless, because that [derived matter] is strictly dependent [upon the primary elements], it was not mentioned here.
Because it delimits space, it is stated as being “inseparable” from the delimiting space.
And because it is delimited in that manner, all primary and derived matter is said to be "supported by the space element.
Just as derived matter exists in dependence upon the primary elements, and just as the immaterial aggregates have the physical basis (vatthu-rūpa) as their support, so too—

according to the method stated as "the immaterial aggregates have as their basis the material phenomena supported by that"— the immaterial aggregates have as their basis the material phenomena such as the eye, which are supported by the space element.

By the word "thus" (*tathā*), he brings together this meaning: that the immaterial aggregates, beginning with feeling (*vedanā*), are called "name" (*nāma*) because they are dependent upon the space element (*ākāsadhātu*).
"In this case too" refers even to the phrase "dependent upon the space element," and not only to the phrases "dependent upon the earth element" and so forth.
"Both material and immaterial" means that all material and immaterial phenomena are indeed included; there is nothing excluded. "Co-nascent... dependent"—this [phrase applies to both].

This was stated by taking the support-condition (*nissayatta*) as established in its non-figurative sense (*nippariyāya*). However, if the support-condition were taken in the figurative sense (*pariyāya*) according to the method explained below—based on the statement:

"The 'postnascent condition' means that postnascent states of consciousness and mental factors are a condition for this prenascent body by way of the postnascent condition"—then all matter produced by the fourfold origination [would be included].

It should be said that it is "dependent on the consciousness-element. Likewise, because it proceeds with the immediately preceding consciousness-element as its condition, it should be said that it is "dependent on the consciousness-element. 101.
It is called "rūpa" (form) in the sense that, by undergoing a change in color and manifesting its state as being present within the heart, it is affected (*ruppati*). This is the meaning.
The visible-object base (rūpāyatana) is obtained in the primary sense (nippariyāyato) when it has come into the range of the eye-door, but not when it has not yet come into its range.

However, the state of being cognizable by eye-consciousness (cakkhuviññāṇa-viññātabbabhāva) is indeed obtainable even when that object has not come into the range, because it does not transcend its own intrinsic nature (tamsabhāvānativattanato).

Having thus divided the visible-object base into two ways, the Elder [Buddhaghosa] states that it is impossible to deny the status of "visible form" (rūpabhāva) even for a visible-object base that has not yet come into the range.
Not permitting a twofold division, he points out the "Channa-accusation" (channovāda), saying: "What will you do regarding the Channa-accusation above?
For therein it is stated: "Friend Channa, the eye, visual consciousness, and the phenomena cognizable by visual consciousness.
And herein, it is not only the visible object-base (rūpāyatana) that has come into the range of the eye-door which is referred to by the term "cognizable by visual consciousness."

It is not possible to discern that [the object] has been grasped but has not yet come into the range of perception, because the absence of the grasping of craving, conceit, and views by means of the form-base (*rūpāyatana*) in general is what is being illustrated.
Therefore he said, "This is not possible. "Form alone" means the form-base alone.
If this is so, how is the phrase "among things cognizable by eye-consciousness" to be interpreted? He says: "But those associated with eye-consciousness," and so forth. By eye-consciousness...
"Along with those things to be cognized" means: along with that mental consciousness by which the eye-consciousness is cognized as "impermanent," etc., [it refers to] those states associated with it;
this is the meaning. "Craving-desire" (*taṇhā-chanda*) means desire whose intrinsic nature is craving;
it is not the desire [defined as] the wish to act, but simply craving-desire. "By way of passioning" means: like dye upon a cloth.
By way of the mind’s coloring. "By way of delighting" means by way of taking pleasure in the object after having rejoiced in it;
for craving accompanied by rapture is called *nandī*. Craving is so called by way of the act of craving. 102.
*Ahaṅkāra* is the making of "I," such as "I am superior," and so forth. That by which one makes "mine" is *mamaṅkāra*.

"Sveva" refers to what was stated as "the conceit 'I am'. When the fourth jhāna has been thus demonstrated, why does [the author] ask, "Why was it stated without mentioning the two types of higher knowledge (vijjā)—namely, the recollection of past lives and the divine eye—when all mundane higher knowledges are being discussed?

The intention is that the two types of higher knowledge mentioned below ought to be stated here. The other [teacher] replies: "In all instances here, the inquiry concerning supramundane states is predominant."

Therefore, showing that the third true knowledge (*vijjā*) is explained by the passage beginning with “When he is thus concentrated,” he said, “The monks do not ask about worldly matters,” and so forth.
This sutta is called the *Ekavissajjita* (Single Response) precisely because it comes under the heading of the third true knowledge.

To show that it also has a designation by way of the noble qualities (*ariyadhamma*), he stated, “It is also named the ‘Six Purifications,’” and then [explained] the classification among those qualities.
To show this, the words beginning with "for here" (*ettha hi*) were spoken. "Purified" (*visuddhā*) means purified by way of cleansing that very objection.
"Making it into one" means making it a single section because it has come down in the Canon as a single unit in one recitation.
If this is so, how can there be "six purifications"? He says: "Together with the four nutriments. But how is it so here?
"Are the four nutriments to be included? Some say: "Having welcomed and rejoiced in what was said with 'Well said,' a further question may be asked";
thus, following the method already established below, the section on nutriment should be brought forward and recited.
Since the nutriments are also included under the phrase "all external signs," the nutriments are indeed present there in their actual sense.
Others, however, say that by the inclusion of the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha), edible food (kabaḷīkāra-āhāra) is included;

by the inclusion of the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), contact as nutriment (phassāhāra) is included; and by the inclusion of mental volition as nutriment (manosañcetanāhāra), consciousness as nutriment (viññāṇāhāra) is included even by way of its own nature.
Having shown the etymological correctness of the name of this sutta, "The Sixfold Purification" (Chabbisodhana), [the author] states that in the future as well, by such [a method]...
The passage beginning with “But these... was commenced for the purpose of showing the practice of the bhikkhus through this explanation.
“By way of the exposition of the Vinaya” means by the reason given in the exposition of the Vinaya;

or, it means according to the sequence of the exposition as it appears in the Vinaya. “Realization” (adhigama) is so called because it is to be attained; thus, there is a question concerning the realization of jhāna and so forth. Therefore he said: “In jhāna, liberation, and so on,” etc. “A question concerning the means” means a question concerning the means for realization. “How? means in what manner or by what method; such is the meaning.

Regarding the question, "Of which states are you a possessor?", this now demonstrates the manner of questioning after having specified those particular distinctions such as the jhānas and so forth, which were previously asked about in the form "What have you attained? without their specific divisions being defined.
"Therefore" means because the declaration of attainment must be verified by the aforementioned modes; "by this much" means by this extent.
One should not show honor based on mere explanation alone;
for an explanation may sometimes be incorrect, just as something that resembles gold appears like gold but must be purified by rubbing, heating, and cutting.
In the same way, one should place these [points] within the six positions just mentioned and purify them.

Regarding the phrase "should be told concerning the liberations, etc.," the word "etc. includes concentration, meditative attainments, knowledge and vision, the cultivation of the path, and the realization of the fruit.
It becomes "clear" because there is no lapse of mindfulness for one who has attained a distinction.

This same principle applies to the phrase "it becomes clear" in all the subsequent questions. "Skilled in learning and interrogation" means being proficient in recitation and the exposition of the Path. By which...
The practice by which the Noble Path arises is the preliminary practice; it is the "practice of arrival.
It is to be "cleansed" in the sense of being examined as to whether it is pure or impure. It is said that "it is not purified" because of the presence of negligent conduct in various instances.
It is to be "removed" by one's own admission. Having stated "it is purified," the passage beginning with "for a long time" is given to show the manner in which it is purified.
It has been said. Regarding the phrase "it is discerned" (*paññāyati*), the word "if" (*yadi*) is supplied; thus the connection is: "if that bhikkhu is discerned by means of that practice.
This practice is similar to the practice of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), because the defilements have been suppressed for a long time.

The river-mouth gate is the place where the river flows into the ocean. "Crushing" refers to [the fruit] being placed in a vessel with water and crushed, like a jujube or a *sālava* fruit. The rest is easily understood.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning of the Commentary on the *Chabbisodhana-sutta* is completed.
3. Commentary on the *Sappurisadhamma-sutta* 105.
"The quality of a true person" (*sappurisadhamma*) means the quality that produces the state of a true person. Furthermore, since that [quality] is the lineage of the true persons...
It is the Dhamma. Therefore he said, "the Dhamma of true persons"; this same method applies here to the phrase "the Dhamma of untrue persons" as well.

Having thus established the matrix (mātikā) by taking the Dhamma of true persons—which is both to be undertaken and practiced—as the beginning, he spoke the passage starting with, "And what, bhikkhus, is the Dhamma of untrue persons," while explaining it in a sequence that does not follow the initial order. Explaining it in that manner:
In order to show the reason by means of an illustration, the passage beginning with “Just as if... was spoken. By this, he shows the following meaning:
the practice of the method (ñāyapaṭipatti) consists in grasping what is to be taken up preceded by the relinquishing of what is to be abandoned;

therefore, the Teacher demonstrates that the qualities of a true person (sappurisadhammā) are to be accomplished, even though they are set forth out of sequence. Likewise, elsewhere it is said: “By non-association...”
“...and association with both fools and the wise. For it is these two types of families alone that are called “noble families” in the primary sense.
For it is precisely there that Bodhisattvas in their final existence take rebirth. “He” refers to the bhikkhu who practices with proper conduct.
“Making this the cause” means making that practice the reason; for such a way of practice is the cause for the honoring of the wise.
Nor is it high birth. "Great clans" (mahākula) means extensive clans, those lineages that have been acquired and are currently flourishing;
this is the meaning. 106. The word *yasas* denotes a retinue. Since the term *yasassin* refers to possessing an exceptional retinue, he says "endowed with a retinue.
Because they lack lordship (*ādhipateyya*), they do not rule over others; thus, their leader (*īsa*), the act of leading (*īsana*), is sovereignty (*issariya*).
“Of little account” (*akkhātabba*) means having few followers; therefore he said, “having a small retinue. For here the word *appa* has the sense of “absence. 107.

Regarding the statement “only nine ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) are mentioned”: herein, just as it is easy for one who is strict in the refuse-rag wearer’s practice (*paṃsukūlika*) to observe the three-robed practice (*tecīvarika*), so too is it easy for one who is strict in the alms-food eater’s practice (*piṇḍapātika*) to observe the practice of wandering for alms in regular order (*sapadānacārika*).

And for one who observes the single-session practice (*ekāsanika*), it is likewise easy to observe the practices of eating only from the bowl (*pattapiṇḍika*) and refusing food offered after the meal has begun (*khalupacchābhattika*).

“Easy indeed”—by the very statement beginning with “he is a wearer of rag-robes,” it should be understood that even those [practices] not explicitly mentioned in the Canon are included, because they too can be undertaken since they are easy to maintain.
Therefore he said, “there are thirteen. 108.

They are “made of that” (*tammaya*) because they are produced by that craving consisting of sensual thirst and so forth; they are ordinary persons (*puthujjana*) because they have returned to their natural state.
Their state is "being made of that" (*tammayatā*); by way of its opposite, it is "not being made of that" (*atammayatā*), which is the state of being free from craving.

"Making that very thing the cause" means making the very abandonment of craving the cause, even in the case of the first jhāna. "Having produced it in the mind" means having accomplished the states that are the opposites of craving, as described by the term "not being made of that.
"He does not conceive" means [he is free] from all conceiving (*maññanā*) by means of the Noble Path.

Because [the conceit] has been utterly cut off, one does not conceive of a person in relation to any object—whether it be a sphere such as sense-desire existence (*kāmabhava*), or a thing such as an elephant, a horse, a field, or a plot of land, or even a bowl, a robe, a monastery, or a courtyard. The remainder is easy to understand.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Obscure Meaning) for the commentary on the *Sappurisadhamma-sutta* is completed.
4. Commentary on the *Sevitabbāsevitabba-sutta* 109.
"Mutually" (*aññamañña*) means one thing and another. Therefore he said, "One thing is to be cultivated," and so forth. "By seven terms" (*sattahi padehi*) means by seven sentences.
A sentence (*pada*) is that by which the intended meaning is reached; it is a statement. This was to provide an opportunity for the Elder Sāriputta.
This should be understood according to the method already stated regarding the heirs of the Dhamma.

(113) "Acquisition of views" (*diṭṭhipaṭilābha*) refers to the acquisition [of views] by way of conditions; the same principle applies to the acquisition of perceptions (*saññā*). Wrong view and right view...
[omitted] ...are not included because they exist as mental conduct for those who have reached the path of action.
Because it has already been included. If this is so, why was wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*) not included in the section on the arising of consciousness (*cittuppāda-vāra*)?

Granted that the constituent parts of wrong view can be found there, nevertheless, at the moment of the arising of consciousness—whether mundane or supramundane—the category of the courses of action (*kamma-patha*) was not extracted. 115.

Regarding the phrase "perceptions of sensuality, etc.," here the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes the perceptions of ill will (*byāpāda*) and cruelty (*vihiṃsā*), just as [the perception of sensual desire] was included.

The perceptions of non-covetousness, non-ill will, and non-cruelty are included by the first word "ādi" (etc.), because the reading beginning with "perception accompanied by non-covetousness" is thereby included. 117.
Even for one who desires an end to the endlessness of sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) and so forth, there is indeed no end to such forms of existence.
There are four [types] by way of individuals. Therefore he said, “Even an ordinary person,” and so forth.
“Unwholesome states increase” means that they increase for one who does not practice for their abandonment; for that very reason, wholesome states decline.
Consequently, he produces a personal existence (*attabhāva*) that is truly suffering, both through the suffering of defilements and the suffering of karmic results.
How does the non-returner (anāgāmī), who is worthy of rebirth in the Pure Abodes after abandoning the fetters pertaining to the lower realm... [as before] ...increase?
To this he says, "The non-returner too," and so forth. He produces a personal existence (attabhāva) accompanied by suffering;

for it is by taking into account the increase of unwholesome states and the decline of wholesome states that is obtained thereby, that the production of a personal existence involving affliction (sabyābajjha) is stated even for the non-returner.

Thus, it should be understood that by taking the waning of the unwholesome and the increase of the wholesome as they are obtained, the production of an undefiled individual existence (abyābajjh’attabhāva) is said to occur even for an ordinary person (puthujjana) in their final existence (antimabhavika). Therefore he said, “Even an ordinary person,” and so forth.
Only the unwholesome diminishes; the wholesome does not, because it stands on the side of growth. Even there, it is specifically insight (vipassanā) [that increases].

He causes conception to take place; yet it is not a cyclic conception, because his aspiration is dependent upon *vivaṭṭa* (the turning away from the cycle) due to his being in his final existence, and because his knowledge has reached its fruition.
119. Regarding the term "ekaccassa" (of some), this genitive case should be construed as a nominative within the context of "abhinandati" (rejoices) and so forth.
The same applies to such terms as “becomes disenchanted” (*nibbindati*). In the phrase “even having learned it,” the particle *pi* is indicated by elision (*luttaniddiṭṭha*).

By saying “Even so,” and so forth, he points out the lack of certainty, challenging [the opponent] with the thought: “Let those who do not understand the meaning of what was spoken by the Blessed One remain excluded from benefit and happiness for a long time;
but even for those who do understand it, may it lead to the welfare and happiness of all for a long time.”
The other [type of person] indeed leads to the welfare and happiness of all for a long time; thus, by the words "without rebirth" (*appaṭisandhikā*), etc., he avoids the charge of inconsistency.
The rest is easy to understand.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Obscure Meaning) of the commentary on the *Sevitabbāsevitabba-sutta* is completed.
5. Commentary on the Bahudhātukasutta 124. "Fear" (*bhaya*) means the creeping of the mind;
thus he said, "terror of the mind" (*cittutrāsa*). "Calamity" (*upaddava*) means an obstacle.

Because it is a cause for distraction, it is called "the mode of non-one-pointedness" (*anekaggatākāra*). "Affliction" (*upasagga*) means an approaching [of suffering]. From that, there arises the occurrence of distress that cannot be remedied.
Because it is the cause of despondency for one who is being tormented by the absence of a remedy and is unable to do anything about it, it is therefore said:
"the manner of clinging here and there. When those who had been deceived failed to return on the day previously mentioned, [he] set fire to the door in order to prevent them from going outside.
“Covered with reeds” (*naḷehi*) means that after covering [the roof] above with a summary of reed-thatch, it is also covered on the sides according to the same method of roofing with wooden beams.
By the phrase “this is the same method,” he extends [the rule] to the state of being thatched with grass and the wooden nature of the remaining materials.

“The son of a widow” (*vidhavāputta*) is a characterization of those who have not subdued their own nature; for they are devoid of joy, undisciplined, unrestrained, and performers of what should not be done.
Why did the Blessed One act in this way, completing [the teaching] without even reaching the conclusion?
It was solely for the purpose of demonstrating the Elder Ānanda’s skill in questioning, and so that the assembled monks seated there might understand the teaching.

For it is said that they remained as if entered into darkness, not understanding the matter briefly stated; [the Buddha acted thus] thinking, "By means of the sequence of questions, they will grasp and come to know it."
125. The meaning is that only the apprehension of form has been explained, and nothing else.

Now, having extracted the truths from that [explanation], in order to show the meditation subject of the Four Truths, it is said: "All these," and so forth. As for the statement "there are the five aggregates":
the nine and a half elements constitute the aggregate of form; the seven and a half elements are, as appropriate, the four immaterial aggregates beginning with feeling.
Thus, the eighteen elements constitute the five aggregates. The five aggregates, excluding craving, are the truth of suffering.

"Cessation of occurrence" means the sign of non-occurrence. "Understanding of cessation" refers to the function of the Path by way of wisdom (*paññā*), for the Noble Path has right view as its foremost.
This has been stated having brought it to its culmination, both in terms of the plane of comprehension (*sammasana*) and its accomplishment.
Because it has been explained. By the phrase "he knows and sees," knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassana*) are stated;
since that is twofold—mundane and supramundane—he says, "The path is said to be together with insight (*vipassanā*)," showing both of these.

By the inclusion of the particle *pi* in the expression "even to this extent" (*ettāvatāpi kho*), [the author indicates] that by another method the Teacher intends to teach skill regarding the elements (*dhātukosalla*).
The Elder asks, “But how so, venerable sir? and thus the Blessed One clarifies expertise in the elements (*dhātukosalla*) by way of the earth element and the others as well.
In that context, while clarifying the reason for the teaching, he says, “The earth element... [and so on]... has been stated.
For those first six elements must be filled out by extracting them from the consciousness element (*viññāṇadhātu*). Having said this—
In response to the inquiry, "How are the form-elements (rūpadhātu) extracted?", the passage beginning with "the consciousness-element" (viññāṇadhātu) was stated in order to demonstrate that method.

While it is true that here the object of the body-consciousness-element (kāyaviññāṇadhātu) is already established in the teaching as the tangible-element (phoṭṭhabbadhātu), the earth-element (pathavīdhātu), and so forth;

nevertheless, since the body-element (kāyadhātu) itself must be extracted, [the author], demonstrating the method of extraction exclusively for one specific case, states: ... [The text continues with the extraction of the body-element] ... Thus, having shown the method of extraction for one side, he proceeds.

"This method applies everywhere," he said. Regarding the "mind-element" (*manodhātu*) in terms of the preceding and succeeding [moments], it should be understood as the functional mind-element (*kriyā-manodhātu*) from the perspective of its subsequent portion, because it exists in conformity with that.
But is it not the case here that this so-called mind-element is unmixed with the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*), and that this element is indeed distinct?
True, this is so in the teaching of the eighteen elements and in the exposition of the analysis of consciousness.
In the teaching concerning the body of tactile consciousness, however, it should be understood that this [tactile consciousness] is included within the body of mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇakāya*).

Whatever else needs to be said here should be understood according to the method explained in the *Visuddhimagga-saṃvaṇṇanā*. Alternatively, "by way of preceding and succeeding" means by way of antecedent and subsequent;
"mind-element" (*manodhātu*) should be taken as the resultant mind-element (*vipākamanodhātu*), because it precedes [the subsequent consciousness]. Afterward...
And because the mind-consciousness element does not arise immediately after the functional mind-element, nor does it arise immediately after the functional mind-consciousness element.

The Teacher’s teaching of the elements is solely for the purpose of demonstrating that phenomena are devoid of a sentient being and devoid of a life-principle; it is not intended for other purposes such as establishing their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
Even though these [other factors] are present here, this is the primary meaning; thus he said, "The method of search applies everywhere.
"By way of their opposites" means by way of their counterparts: pleasure has pain as its counterpart, pain has pleasure as its counterpart, and likewise joy and grief.
Just as the manifestation of pleasure and the others is prominent, but not that of equanimity, so too is the manifestation of lust and the others [prominent].
It is not manifest to delusion; therefore it is said, "by way of its non-manifest state. The body-consciousness element is indeed discerned because of its inseparable connection with that [delusion].
In the remaining elements, such as the joy-element and so forth, it is also discerned precisely because of that inseparable connection;
for joy and the others do not occur without the mind-element. Regarding the phrase "having extracted from the equanimity-element":
The four consciousness elements, beginning with the eye-consciousness element; the eight form elements, which are their respective bases and objects, beginning with the eye element;
the mind element; the mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity;
and the mental-object element accompanied by equanimity—thus these fifteen elements are to be extracted from the equanimity element. [The remaining elements include] the joy element, etc.
However, the four elements are included within the dhamma-element; thus, because the extraction of the body-element and the tangible-object element—
which serve as the basis and the object for the body-consciousness element from the pleasure-element— has already been shown by the method explained below,
it is simply stated that [the remaining factors] "should be filled in by extracting them from the equanimity-element."
"Thoughts of sensual desire and so forth are spoken of here by way of the 'sensual element' and so on;

therefore, it is said that 'the meaning of the sensual element and the others should be understood in the same manner as was stated for the thoughts of sensual desire and the rest among the two kinds of thoughts. For there it is said:
"A thought of sensual desire is a thought associated with sensual desire; a thought of ill will is a thought associated with ill will; a thought of cruelty is a thought associated with cruelty."
Applied thought (*vitakka*) associated with renunciation is "renunciation-applied-thought" (*nekkhamma-vitakka*); it extends as far as the first *jhāna*.
Applied thought associated with non-ill-will is "non-ill-will-applied-thought" (*abyāpāda-vitakka*); it extends from the preliminary stage of loving-kindness (*mettā*) up to the first *jhāna*.
Applied thought associated with non-cruelty is "non-cruelty-applied-thought" (*avihiṃsā-vitakka*); it [extends] with compassion...
It is said: "It applies from the preliminary stage up to the first jhāna.

To show that this matter has been explained in detail in the Abhidhamma, the words beginning with "In the Abhidhamma" were stated. Regarding the phrase "having extracted from the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu)":

here, by the mention of "sense-sphere," the six realms beginning with the fine-material realm (rūpadhātu) are included, as well as the seven consciousness-realms (viññāṇadhātu) whose objects are those [realms]. In that regard:
The eighteen [elements] consist of the five consciousness-elements and the five beginning with the eye-element.
However, the element of renunciation and the others are included within the mental-object-element (*dhammadhātu*) itself.
He states, "The five aggregates of the sense-sphere are the element of sensuality," meaning that phenomena which have become objects for sensual craving constitute the element of sensuality.

Likewise, those phenomena that have become the objects of craving for form are the form element (*rūpadhātu*), and those phenomena that have become the objects of craving for the formless are the formless element (*arūpadhātu*);

thus it is said: "the four formless-sphere aggregates," and so forth. Craving for sense-pleasures is "sense-sphere" (*kāma*) by means of eliding the latter member of the compound; similarly, craving for form and the formless is "form" and "formless.
Those spheres where these [cravings] range by way of taking them as objects are the sense-sphere and so forth; thus [are defined] the sense-sphere aggregates and the rest.
The state of sensual craving (*kāmataṇhā*) and so forth is to be understood.

By the phrase "by way of this method," he includes the canonical passage beginning with, "including the gods who wield power over the creations of others (*paranimmitavasavatti*), they range within this [realm].

The expression "ranging within this" is stated with reference to the objective sphere of sensual craving, which is delimited by the Avīci hell and the Paranimmita heaven; and the fact that craving has that as its location should be understood as being due to its inclination toward that [sphere].

The same method applies to the other two lines as well. Because sense-sphere phenomena possess all eighteen elements in their entirety, it is said that they "must be filled by extracting them from the sense-sphere element.
For the mind-consciousness element and the mental-object element consist only of a portion of form-sphere and formless-sphere phenomena.
"Having come together" means having become associated. For whatever number of conditioning phenomena are the cause for their own fruit, therein—
It is as if they have assembled for its production, because it is not produced when there is a deficiency.

Having been extracted from the conditioned element (*saṅkhata-dhātu*), it must be filled by the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*), because it constitutes a portion of the *dhamma*-element (*dhammadhātu*). 126.
With the intention, as it were, "While proceeding in this way, we shall reach the apprehension of 'self' (*attā*)," [one regards] the self...
Those that function by depending upon and for the sake of [the self] are internal; because they exist within them and are included therein, they are called "internal" (*ajjhattika*).

Those that are external to those are "external" (*bāhira*). The discussion on the sense bases (*āyatana*) and the discussion on dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) should be understood according to the method explained in the *Visuddhimagga*, and thus have not been elaborated here.
127. *Aṭṭhānaṃ* means a non-existent state (*avijjamānaṃ ṭhānaṃ*), or it is called *aṭṭhānaṃ* because there is no such state.

The same method applies here to the term *anavakāso*. For the concluding statement regarding that meaning is precisely the expression: “This possibility does not exist. Therefore, he said: “By both as well,” and so forth.
*Yaṃ* is the nominative singular used in the sense of a cause; since the sense of a cause is the sense of a reason, he said: “*Yaṃ* means by which reason.”
It is said here that the attainment of right view (*diṭṭhisampatti*) is to be understood by way of the highest description: "one who is endowed with the vision of the Path.
But from what source is this meaning obtained? From the indicative mark (*liṅga*). For this is the indicative mark, namely, the negation of approaching [existence] as permanent.
As for the phrase "in the four planes," this is because the formations belonging to the fourth plane have entered the sphere of the noble disciple’s range.
It has been stated [that they are conditioned], yet not with reference to those [unconditioned phenomena], because there is an approach to them by way of permanence. And he will say:

“But as for the formations of the fourth plane,” and so forth. Because the formations that are produced (*abhisaṅkhata-saṅkhāra*) and the formations that produce (*abhisaṅkharaṇaka-saṅkhāra*) are limited, the phrase “among conditioned formations” (*saṅkhata-saṅkhāresu*) was stated in order to include all formations without exception.
As for the reason for excluding supramundane formations, he himself [will explain].
He will say: "This reason does not apply because of the destruction of the bridge.
"Because of the preponderance of fire" means because of the excessive nature of the fire that dispels defilement. For it is thus that they are difficult to see due to their profound nature.

"They do not become objects for unwholesome states"—this is stated by way of the specific context [of the *Visuddhimagga*]. However, for beings who have not abandoned the perversions, even wholesome states do not become objects for them.
Showing that the perversion of taking what is not pleasant as “pleasant” is intended here as the basis for approaching [the object] as pleasant, it is said:
“One-sidedly... so it is stated. By the phrase “by way of the view of self,” he refers to the primary view.
Since the fact that Nibbāna is not an object of such a view was already stated below, it is said: “for the purpose of including the designations such as the kasiṇas. “Delimitation” means—
The delimitation of formations (*saṅkhārānaṃ paricchedo*) is the grasping of formations by way of their delimitation.
Showing that this must be done specifically according to those [formations] for which there is an adherence to them as permanent and so forth, he says: "In all instances," etc.

"In all instances" means in all instances such as permanence and so forth. "The worldling indeed" (*puthujjano hi*): the word "indeed" (*hi*) has the sense of a reason; because whatever formation [the worldling grasps] by way of permanence and so forth...

When one approaches [a view] during the stage of an ordinary person (puthujjana), by attaining the respective noble paths (ariyamagga) and grasping [those formations] as impermanent and so forth, one knows them as they truly are and thereby unties and releases that grasping and that view.
Therefore, the meaning is: "Where there is grasping, there is release"; thus, the formations belonging to the fourth plane are not included here under the term "formations" (saṅkhāra).

128. The designation "mother" and "father" is established through the relationship of children; furthermore, the conventional usage of the term "son" is seen in the world even by way of being given, being adopted, and so forth.

However, in order to show that [the primary sense] is established in its non-figurative (nippariyāya) sense as opposed to that figurative one (pariyāya), it is said: "Only she who gives birth is the mother; only he who procreates is the father.
Likewise, because an action of immediate retribution (ānantariya-kamma) is intended here, it is said: "Only one who has become a human being and is an Arahant whose taints are destroyed is intended."

It has been said: “This is impossible,” and so forth. Since this demonstrates that a noble disciple is incapable of depriving even his mother or others of life, one might think that it follows by implication that a noble disciple would never deprive anyone else of life. Anticipating this, he asks:
“But would a noble disciple deprive another of life? [The answer is: “Monks, this is impossible; there is no occasion for it.”
Because of the statement, "It is impossible that a person endowed with right view should intentionally deprive a living being of life," it is said, "This too is impossible.
Therefore he said, "Even if... and so forth. "For the purpose of illustrating strength" means for the purpose of illustrating the possession of such strengths as faith and the rest;
for by virtue of the power of faith and the other qualities acquired through the Noble Path, the noble disciple...
One does not commit such a blameworthy act.
Regarding the phrase "by five reasons": this is stated by taking together, under the commonality of being "reasons," those factors which accomplish the purpose and those which precede them;
it is not, however, because all five are capable of acting in conjunction. "By modes" means by reasons.

“By means of proclamation” (*anussāvanena*) means by means of a proclamation that is appropriate. It is the making known or the communication of one’s own words to the monks who are to be divided, in a manner suitable for causing division—that is, in such a way that a schism occurs.

Therefore he said, “Is it not you? and so forth. By the phrase “having made a verbal distinction in the ear,” he indicates that the expression refers to the manifestation of the grounds for schism in a public manner; therein, one’s own...
This shows that "proclamation" (*anussāvana*) is the making known of a matter that has been determined by way of secrecy.

It is stated that the formal act (*kamma*) itself, or the recitation (*uddesa*), is the criterion because the schism of the Saṅgha is established through them; however, the others are merely preliminary to those.
Therefore, he said "the transactions" (*vohārā*), and so forth. "Therein" refers to the transaction. The fruit immediately following death is called "immediate" (*anantara*); in that regard—

Those deeds are called *ānantariya* because they are connected with the immediate [rebirth] by way of producing that [result], having the nature of performing [the act] immediately, and having immediate purpose;
these very things are thus referred to as "deeds of immediate retribution" (*ānantariyakamma*).
As for "by way of deed," it means by way of the classification of deeds, such as: "In this way there is a deed of immediate retribution; in this way it is similar to a deed of immediate retribution."

"By way of doors" means by way of the doors of the body and so forth. "By way of stability for an eon" means by way of the distinction of what is an eon-stable resultant and what is not an eon-stable resultant.
"As results" means by way of the distinction of what ripens here and what does not ripen.
"By commonality and so forth" refers to the common and uncommon [kamma] of householders and those gone forth; by the word "and so forth," it includes distinctions such as feeling and the rest.

Because it is only while remaining in the human state that wholesome states attain a state of sharpness, clarity, and courage—as was the case for the three Bodhisattas at the time of the manifestation of their respective vehicles of enlightenment—so too do unwholesome states attain a state of sharpness, clarity, and courage only while remaining in the human state;
therefore, he said, "only when one has become a human being. And this applies even to the wholesome states of ordinary humans.
The attainment of distinction should be understood according to the method stated in the *Vimānavatthu-aṭṭhakathā*.
And as for the meaning already stated—that the kamma is weightier when one violates someone of the same class than when one violates someone of a different class—it was said:
"one's mother or father who has become human. Furthermore, even when the gender is changed, that very same continuum of the life-constituent (*bhavaṅga*) produced by that single kamma persists.

And because the continuity of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) is not something other [than the person], he said, "even one whose gender has changed. This same principle applies to an *arahant* as well.

The passage beginning with "its result" (*tassa vipākaṃ*) is a refutation of the claim that such an act constitutes an immediate offense (*ānantariya*); furthermore, a fourfold permutation (*catukoṭika*) is possible here.
Of these, the first permutation has already been shown; in order to demonstrate the distinctions among the others, the passage beginning with "but whoever" (*yo pana*) was stated.
Even if there is no conventional designation for it there, the action is nevertheless weightier and as grave as an ānantariya (immediate) offense;
thus he said, "It stands having reached the state of an ānantariya. This question refers to discourse arising from the desire for knowledge.
It touches upon an ānantariya because the basis for an ānantariya has been violated by the very intention to kill. An ānantariya...

It does not constitute an immediate offense (*ānantariya*) because the objective basis for such an offense is absent. For in all cases, the preceding volition of intention (*abhisandhicitta*) is the primary factor;

however, it should be understood that the murderous intent directed toward that object and the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) themselves are the criteria for determining whether an act is an immediate offense or not.
The fourfold classification regarding battle should be applied according to the circumstances present.
"By that very means" means by that same application. It is indeed the killing of an Arahant because an Arahant has been slain.

"It is given only to an ordinary person (puthujjana)" means that whereas the murderous intention proceeds by taking even a present object as its focus through the severing of the continuity [of life], the volition of generosity does not do so; for that [volition] takes the object to be given...
Having made it an object, there is merely the act of relinquishing; and that relinquishing consists in making it the property of another.
Therefore, it is given to whichever person it has been made the property of.

"The blood flows evenly" means it becomes accumulated as it is stirred up by the impact. "Larger" means heavier. "As in the case of attending to the body" means as in the case of attending to the Teacher’s physical body.
“Asannipatite” (when not assembled) is an indication of concord. “Bhedo ca hoti” (and there is a schism) means there is a schism in the Saṅgha.
“Vaṭṭati saññāya” (it is permissible by way of perception) means with the perception that such an act does not lead to a schism in the Saṅgha.
This should be construed as “tathā” (so it is) for one who acts in an assembly of fewer than nine; by the word “tathā,” the phrase “not an immediate offense” is drawn in, but not...
“‘There is a schism’—this refers to the following: at the very least, a schism in the Saṅgha occurs by means of nine [monks].
Those who speak according to the Dhamma are blameless because they abide in accordance with the Dhamma. A fracture in the Saṅgha is the preliminary stage to a schism.
They fulfill the door of the body alone, because it is to be characterized precisely as bodily action.”
The statement, “For when it is settled... [and] he is released,” does not accord with the *Kappaṭṭha-kathā* (Commentary on the Duration of an Aeon).

For it is said in the *Kappaṭṭha-kathā*: “Regarding the phrase ‘one bound for the states of misery,’ this sutta was spoken with reference to an ‘aeon of life’ (*āyukappa*), meaning that he would remain for a period of time equal to one-eightieth of an aeon. Furthermore, the phrase “only at the destruction of an aeon” means “only at the destruction of an aeon of life.”

When there is a purpose, there is no contradiction. And here, the phrase "while it is still standing" is stated by way of an unreal hypothetical assumption (abhūtaparikappa), as if to say, "it will perish tomorrow.

Because there is no contradiction—since one is cooked in hell for exactly one day, and beyond that, since there is no kappa, there is also no lifespan of a kappa—the application of the meaning should be understood in this way. "The rest" refers to [the offenses] other than schism in the Saṅgha.
There are other deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantariyakamma*).

[If it were the case that] "there are deeds that have been, ... [and so on] ... they are reckoned as such," then how could these be of immediate retribution, given that there is no giving of their result immediately after death?
Or, if there is the giving of a result, then the time for the result of these is only immediately after death, and not otherwise.
Certainty is determined by the restriction of the time of the fruit, not by the restriction of the giving of the fruit;

for if it were otherwise, even other [kamma] whose fruits are certain—namely, that which is to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*) and that which is to be experienced in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*)—would fall into the state of being certain [of yielding fruit].

Therefore, even when those things possessing the nature of ripening (*vipākadhammadhamma*) do not ripen due to the deficiency of other conditions and so forth, they remain [certain] by their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).

Just as the state of being subject to ripening (*vipākadhammatā*) remains fixed even when a powerful immediate offense (*ānantariya*) has already yielded its result, so too the process of those immediate offenses that have not yet ripened possesses a nature fixed for the yielding of their fruit and a nature that is immediate.

Thus, their "immediacy" (*ānantariyatā*) and their "fixedness" should be understood precisely through this necessity of yielding their fruit by way of their own intrinsic nature. And necessarily, because they possess the nature of immediate offenses, they possess that very same nature of fixedness.
And it must be accepted that these [karmas] proceed [to fruition], because in the absence of another powerful immediate (*ānantariya*) karma,
they invariably yield their fruit immediately after death.

But would it not follow that for other karmas to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*), in the absence of another giver of ripening, there would likewise be an invariable yielding of fruit immediately after death?
Does it follow that the process [of kamma] possesses a fixed nature regarding the giving of its fruit and a nature like that of an *ānantariya* (immediate) deed? It does not so follow.

This is because its result is to be turned back by a mental aspiration of a different class or by an obstructive factor; thus, there is an absence of the quality of being an absolute giver of fruit in the immediately following moment.
However, for those deeds that are *ānantariya*, there is no result of a different class that can turn back the fruit, unlike how the second jhāna and so forth turn back the first jhāna and so forth.

This is because all *ānantariya* (immediate) karmas have Avīci as their fruit. Furthermore, there is no mental aspiration capable of averting the fruit of an *ānantariya* karma—just as the mental aspiration of a virtuous person who desires rebirth in a lower realm can produce rebirth in a higher one—because one is cast into Avīci even against one's will;
nor is there any karma whatsoever that can destroy an *ānantariya* karma.
Therefore, immediately following those [deeds], their occurrence has the nature of producing exclusively kamma-result.

And although many deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantariya*) have been committed, because they possess a nature determined exclusively for result and because there is no confusion with a nature that would prevent ripening, they are ascertained by their very nature to be indeed determined.
Among those of identical nature, once the result has been given by one, the others [no longer ripen] by themselves.
Because the task that was to be done has already been accomplished by that [first act], they do not produce a second or third rebirth-linking.

It is not because of a lack of capacity; thus, there is no cessation of their status as "immediate" (*ānantariya*) kamma. However, since a greater weight is indeed found among them, it is said: "by which...
it ripens," in order to show that schism in the Saṅgha may possess a greater weight. For one person, however, the others serve as supporting factors.

These are to be understood as "they exist. By the statement "it ripens by way of rebirth-linking," it appears as if the giving of result during the course of existence (*pavatti*) for the others is likewise permitted.
The construction is: "Or she is not so virtuous" means that she is not virtuous in the same way as her father was virtuous.
If the mother is virtuous, then the matricide ripens by way of rebirth-linking; this is the construction.
"Of pure status" means one who has not been suspended. "Of the same communion" means one who has not committed a pārājika offense. "Within the same boundary" means within a single boundary.

"Unable to perform the Teacher's duties" means unable to perform those duties such as instruction that ought to be performed by the Teacher; it means having rejected the Blessed One. "Another founder of a sect" means another teacher. 129.
By the application [of effort] regarding noble birth and so forth, and by approaching deities and so on, one attains a state of security equal to that of the world-system of birth.
The birth-field (*jātikhetta*) is a place measuring ten thousand [yojanas]; the command-field (*āṇākhetta*) is the place where the exercise of authority occurs by means of one's own voice;

the object-field (*visayakhetta*) is a place that has become an object [of perception]. A "ten-thousandfold world-system" (*dasasahassī lokadhātu*) refers to a ten-thousandfold world-system situated surrounding this world-system together with its ten thousand worlds. Only those many possess the status of being a birth-field.
It is to be understood by way of natural law (*dhammatā*).
Some say it is "by way of inclusion. Others state that for all Buddhas, the birth-field is exactly that much, and the realization of the Dhamma belongs only to the deities residing therein.

The mention of only the six occasions beginning with the time of entering the mother’s womb is merely illustrative, since that trembling is also obtained at times such as the Great Resolve (*mahābhinīhāra*).
The "field of command" (āṇākhetta) is that which contracts and expands all at once. The command prevails by the inhabitants of that region receiving it upon their heads;
however, this occurs solely through the power of the Buddhas and not by virtue of their own intention.
Yet, according to the statement, "Or as far as he might wish," the command could prevail even beyond that limit if there were such an intention.
Regarding the statement "they do not arise," as for the claim that they exist, it was spoken by the Blessed One—who, while standing within this world-system, said such things as, "I have no teacher;

one equal to me is not found"—when he was asked: "But, friend Sāriputta, are there now any other recluses or brahmins who are exactly equal to the Blessed One in perfect enlightenment? To which I, venerable sir, replied: [they do not exist].
Having said, "One should not say so," the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta), in order to demonstrate the reason for that, presented this sutta:
"It is impossible, it is out of the question, that two Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, should arise simultaneously in a single world-system.
The intention is that by presenting this, he stated that there is no arising elsewhere except in this world-system, which serves as the Buddha-field.
“From one” means together; the meaning is “at one time. But how is that time delimited?
Showing that it extends from the moment of taking rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) in his final existence until his final nibbāna of the elements (dhātuparinibbāna), he said, “Therein,” and so forth.
He speaks in reverse order, beginning from the time he was seated [in the assembly]. “From the time of his final nibbāna” refers to the nibbāna without residue (anupādisesa).

"From the attainment of final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna": this refers to the interval between the Bodhisatta’s taking of rebirth-linking in his final existence and his Parinibbāna in the elements.
The arising of another Buddha is not precluded during this period; to show the reason for this, the passage beginning with "For three... was stated.
For when the practice disappears, the Dispensation (sāsana) declines, and thus an opportunity for the arising of another Buddha is obtained.
"Practice" (paṭipadā) refers to the preliminary practice that brings about penetration (paṭivedha).

Having stated that "the study of the scriptures (pariyatti) is the authority," he spoke the words beginning with "just as" in order to demonstrate that point by taking the Bodhisatta as an example; this [practice] has been made subordinate.
It should be seen thus. For, while demonstrating the stability of the Dhamma that leads to liberation, he points out the Dhamma that does not lead to liberation.
"When the *mātikā* has disappeared" means: the *mātikā* is the text of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) reached by the method beginning with "Whatever monk...

When that has disappeared—that is, when the recitation of the *Pātimokkha* known as the "Recitation of the Origin" (*nidānuddesa*), and the formal acts of going forth (*pabbajjā*) and full ordination (*upasampadā-kamma*) [are no longer performed]—then...
And the meaning is that the Dispensation (sāsana) stands. Alternatively, it is only while the Pātimokkha is being maintained that there is going-forth (pabbajjā) and full ordination (upasampadā).
This being so, both of these are included within the Pātimokkha, because in the absence of those two, there is an absence of the Pātimokkha.
Therefore, he said: "When the Pātimokkha, going-forth, and full ordination stand..."—meaning these are the causes for the standing of the Dispensation.

“The Dispensation stands. Alternatively, since the Pātimokkha depends upon full ordination (upasampadā), and full ordination depends upon going-forth (pabbajjā), therefore, when the Pātimokkha is established, and when going-forth and full ordination are established, the Dispensation stands.
For after the final penetration, the Dispensation of penetration is said to have perished; and after the final morality, the Dispensation of practice is said to have perished.
"Declined" means that when the last two types of breach of the virtue of penetration are combined as one, thereafter it is said to be "ruined. Thus,
while it is true that "the study of the scriptures is the measure for the endurance of the Dispensation," that study itself has practice as its cause.

In the absence of practice, there is no foundation; therefore, having shown that the disappearance of practice is the specific cause for the decline of the Dispensation, it was said, "There are three kinds of parinibbāna," in order to show that this decline of the Dispensation culminates in the parinibbāna of the relics (*dhātu-parinibbāna*).
"Piteousness" (*kāruñña*) refers to the piteousness of lamentation. [The relics] were scattered throughout Jambudīpa, other islands, and in the worlds of the devas, nāgas, and brahmās.

The gathering together of the elements of those who have attained stability upon the Great Enlightenment Seat (mahābodhipallaṅka), the emission of rays, the arising of the fire-element therefrom, and the becoming of a single mass of flame—all this is to be understood as occurring solely through the power of the Teacher’s resolution (adhiṭṭhāna).
"Anacchariyattā" means that there would be the fault of a lack of wonder (acchariyatta) even when two [Buddhas] were appearing simultaneously. "Buddhā nāma" [means...]
"Just as gold broken in the middle [remains] uniform, so too their teaching is of a single flavor"; thus he says, "and because there is no distinction in the teaching.
By this, he establishes precisely its lack of wonder. By the phrase "because of the absence of dispute," he shows that two [such teachings] do not arise together for the purpose of avoiding dispute.

*“Therein”* means in the *Milindapañha*. *“Bearing one Buddha”* (*ekabuddhadhāraṇī*) means that this world-system is of such a nature regarding these qualities of a Buddha that it is incapable of bearing the qualities of a second Buddha.
For it is impossible for this world-system to bear the weight of the distinction between those dhammas of quality produced by specific conditions; thus [it is said]: “No...”
Having said, "one should hold [it]," he spoke the words beginning with "it might move" (*caleyya*) in order to explain that very non-holding by means of another method of exposition.
Therein, "it might move" (*caleyya*) means it would quiver; "it might shake" (*kampeyya*) means it would tremble; "it might incline" (*nameyya*) means it would lean to one side;

"it might sink down" (*onameyya*) means it would subside; "it might bend in various ways" (*vinameyya*) means it would lean diversely hither and thither; "it might be scattered" (*vikireyya*) means by the wind...
It would be scattered like a heap of chaff. "Vidhameyya" means it would perish. "Viddhaṃseyya" means it would become completely shattered.
And being in such a state, it would not remain anywhere; thus he said, "it would not find a place of rest.
Now, showing an illustration for that, he said, "Just as, O Great King," and so forth. In that context, "samupādikā" means...
It is called *samupādikā* because it flows evenly upward; the meaning is that it moves level across the surface of the water.

"By color" means by shape. "By measure" means by height. "By thinness or thickness" means by the state of being thin or thick; the meaning is by circumference (*pariṇāha*). "Pleasing" means being desirable, producing a sense of liking.
"Becoming languid" means having become languid because of that food. "Having become like a drooping staff" means...
Because he was unable to bend down due to having eaten to his full satisfaction, his staff remained unbent.
"Having eaten once, he would vomit" means that having swallowed even a single mouthful, he would vomit it up.
"The earth shakes from the excessive burden of Dhamma" implies that the earth indeed stands by means of Dhamma; how then could it [shake] because of that very same thing?
He asks with the intention that [the cart] "moves" means it will perish. Again, the Elder said:

"In the world, a 'jewel' is seen to be that which supports a household and is esteemed by the world; yet, because of its heavy nature, it becomes the cause of the cart's breaking when it has become an excessive burden.
And so too is this Dhamma: while supporting those who possess it with various benefits and happiness, it is esteemed by the wise."
Showing that it becomes an excessive burden due to its weightiness and its state of being unfathomably profound, he said, "In this case, Great King, there are two carts," and so forth.

By this very passage, it should be understood that the cause for the trembling of the earth at the time of the Tathāgata’s descent into his mother’s womb and other such occasions has been described. From one cart, a jewel—from one, from a single [cart].
Or, it means "having taken from the cart" as if it were the treasure of a cart.
*Osāritaṃ* means uttered; the sense is that it was spoken. *Aggo* means the foremost among all sentient beings.
*Sabhāvapakati* means a nature that is innate and not artificial. *Kāraṇamahantatāya* means by virtue of the greatness of the qualities that constitute a Buddha.
What is meant is that the qualities of a Buddha are produced by means of the causes known as the perfections (pāramitā).

Earth and other such things are vast entities, and great states such as those of Sakka are each unique within their respective domains; likewise, the Perfectly Enlightened One is great and unique within his own domain.
And what is his domain? It is the plane of Buddhahood, or as much of the knowable (ñeyya) as there may be.
Thus, by saying, "The Blessed One alone is like space, having an infinite range," he demonstrates the absence of a second Buddha in other world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).
By this very phrase— namely, by the phrase "of a single world-system"— [it refers to] ten thousand world-systems.
They are included because they belong to the field of birth (*jātikhettattā*). By the phrase "in one world-system alone" (*ekacakkavāḷeneva*), it means precisely within one world-system.
Just as when it is said, "they arise in this very world-system," it is appropriate to delimit that it is in Jambudīpa within this world-system, and even there, specifically in the central region;
so too, when the field of birth is intended by the phrase "in a single world-sphere" (*ekissā lokadhātuyā*).
It is appropriate to delimit [the world] by this very world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).

Regarding "the cessation of disputes" (*vivādūpacchedato*): it refers to the cause for the cessation of disputes. When two [beings] have arisen, the non-arising of any dispute that might occur between them is precisely what is meant here by the "cessation of disputes.
By the phrase "on a single island," etc., it is shown that even on other islands, they do not arise together.
This shows that it is indeed like a single lamp. "He might fall away" means he would fall away because he must remain within the region of a world-system (*cakkavāḷa*). 130.
"Human state" (*manussatta*) refers to the human condition, because it is the basis for the attainment of qualities such as going forth (*pabbajjā*).

"Perfection of gender" (*liṅgasampatti*) refers to the male state. "Causes" (*hetu*) refers to the perfection of causes preceded by mental and verbal aspirations. "Seeing the Teacher" (*satthāradassana*)...
The presence of the Teacher. "Going forth" (pabbajjā) refers to the going forth among ascetics who maintain the doctrine of karmic action, or among the bhikkhus.

"Perfection of qualities" (guṇasampatti) refers to the attainment of qualities such as the higher knowledges (abhiññā). "Veneration" (adhikāra) refers to exceptional honor paid for the sake of the Buddha.
"Zeal" (chandata) refers to an especially intense desire to act with skillful intent directed toward perfect enlightenment. "The convergence of eight factors" (aṭṭhadhammasamodhāna):
By the conjunction of these eight factors. "The directing of the aspiration" (*abhinīhāra*) means the resolve of the body.

"It succeeds" (*samijjhati*) means it is accomplished; this is the summary here. The detailed explanation, however, should be understood according to the method already stated in the *Paramatthadīpanī* commentary on the *Cariyāpiṭaka*.

“Perfectly complete in all aspects” means that, by virtue of having the full complement of characteristics, it is endowed with every aspect, such as the protuberance on the head (*sattussada*) and so forth.
For it is not possible for a woman to have the private parts concealed by a sheath (*kosohitavatthaguyhatā*), and indeed, the second nature is inferior to the first nature.
Therefore, he says in the immediately following section, “Because,” and so forth.
"Because a man is reborn there" means: because one who has been a man in this human world is reborn there in the Brahma-world with a Brahma-body.
By this, he shows that although the male sex organs are absent, the Brahmas possess the appearance of men.
It is precisely with reference to that male appearance that it was said: "If a man were to exercise the status of a Brahma."

For this very reason, he said, "Even though they are equal," and so forth. If that is so, [one might ask] why women do not arise in the Brahma-world; therefore, he said, "The state of being a Brahmā," and so forth.

(131) By the Pāḷi passage beginning with "Of bodily misconduct," etc., what is called the "determination of kamma" is explained. *Samañjanaṃ* is *samaṅga*; one who has that is *samaṅgī*, meaning "endowed with.
Alternatively, *samaṅgī* means "one whose nature is to associate. It refers to the state of being endowed with the accumulation [of kamma] during the prior phase.
Possession of volition (*cetanā-samaṅgitā*) occurs by way of the volition that brings about a decision;
or, possession of exertion (*āyūhana-samaṅgitā*) occurs by way of the continuity of volition, or possession of volition occurs by way of the specific moment of each respective volition.

Possession of karma (*kamma-samaṅgitā*) occurs by way of an accumulated karma whose result has not yet matured; whereas possession of result (*vipāka-samaṅgitā*) occurs by way of the manifestation of the result once the karma has begun to ripen.
The state of being possessed of manifestation refers to the time when karma and so forth manifest.

"At the moment of accumulating wholesome and unwholesome karma" means at the moment of striving toward both wholesome and unwholesome karma. By the word "tathā" (thus), the phrase "wholesome and unwholesome karma" is drawn forward.
Just as the karma performed becomes capable of yielding its fruit, so too is it performed and accumulated. It is "capable of ripening."
The construction is as follows: "When [beings] are arising, the sign of rebirth (upapattinimitta) appears, being capable of ripening in the second existence and so forth.

It "moves" means it turns over. For when a particular sign has been presented by one karma, the presentation of a different sign by another karma due to a specific condition constitutes that turning over.

"Dog-livelihood" (*sunakhajīvikā*) means one whose way of life is sustained by dogs. "Offering of a carpet on the ground" (*tala-santharaṇa-pūjā*) means an offering consisting of covering the surface of the earth with flowers.

"By way of possessing the karma of the volition of accumulation" (*āyūhana-cetanā-kamma-samaṅgitā-vasena*) means: through the repeated accumulation of bodily misconduct, and because it is not overturned by the knowledge that brings about the destruction of karma when that very [misconduct] is being formulated by the volition of final determination (*sanniṭṭhāpaka-cetanā*), [the being is reborn] according to the karma thus accumulated.
And by way of being possessed of [these qualities]. 132.

Thus, having made it "splendid" (sassirikaṃ) by means of its beauty in both meaning and phrasing—through its manifold variety of diverse methods such as the analysis of the various elements (dhātu) as previously described, and through its supreme subtlety and profundity—he says, "Hold it.
Here, "it" (naṃ) is merely a particle. They are called "turnings" (parivaṭṭī) because meanings are turned around by means of these, such as the elements (dhātu) and so forth.
Reversals and divisions of the teaching. It is called "fourfold" (*catuparivaṭṭa*) because it has four reversals or occurs in four ways; it is a discourse on the Dhamma (*dhammapariyāya*).
It is the "Mirror of the Dhamma" (*dhammādāsa*) because it is the Dhamma itself, acting as a mirror in the sense already explained due to its nature as the teaching (*pariyatti*).

Alternatively, it is the "Mirror of the Dhamma" because it is a mirror for the various phenomena (*dhamma*) in the sense of their manifestation. For just as by means of a mirror the removal of impurities and blemishes from the faces of beings is accomplished, [so too is this].
Thus, by this sutta as well, the removal of the stain of impurities from the mouths of yogis is shown.

Therefore, because yogis have attained victory by crushing the defilements through the attainment of serenity (*samatha*) by means of this sutta, it is the "Great War Drum" (*mahāberī*) and the "Ambrosial Drum" (*amatadundubhi*) for the proclamation of entering the city of the Deathless (*amatapura*).
"Stated here" means stated in this sutta. "Unsurpassed victory in battle" is so called because of its unsurpassed nature.
“Victory in the battle against the defilements,” this being understood as “one conquers by means of this. The remainder is indeed easy to understand.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning of the Commentary on the *Bahudhātuka-sutta* is completed.
6. Commentary on the *Isigili-sutta*.
133. It is called *samaññā* because one is designated (*samāññāyati*) by means of it; the meaning is "name. By means of this, they designate [something] as "this is such-and-such a name";
or rather, *paññatti* is the mere act of designating in that way—it is simply a name. Therefore he said: "It is a synonym for the first term.
"In the remaining cases as well" refers to the three sections beginning with "of the Paṇḍava mountain," and so forth.
Having first explained the origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) of the sutta, the following was said—beginning with “*Tadā kirā*” (It is said that then)—in order to provide a commentary on its meaning.
“*Na pabbatehi attho*” means there is no purpose for the Blessed One’s speaking about mountains.
“*Isigilibhāvo*” means the state of being named Isigili. “*Itī*” means by this reason; the sense is: considering this introductory occasion (*aṭṭhuppatti*).
"In the shrine chamber" (*cetiyagabbha*) means in the shrine house (*cetiyaghara*), inside the shrine (*cetiya*).

"The great double door" (*yamakamahādvāra*) refers to a large door fitted with twin panels (*yamakakavāṭa*). "Having made it twofold" means that after constructing a cave in the interior of the mountain in the form of a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), they divided it into two parts;
at that time, they dwelt there.
In explaining the time of mastery (*vasitakāla*), the passage beginning with "In the past, it is said... was spoken in order to show the origin of their mother starting from her third existence.
"She desired" means that, while she was parching rice in a field hut, about five hundred large, charming grains of parched rice, the size of *mahākarañja* flowers, sprouted there; she took them...
She placed them upon large lotus leaves. At that time, a Paccekabuddha was walking near a field boundary for the sake of favoring her.

Seeing him, her mind filled with serene faith, she took a single large, fully blossomed lotus flower, placed fried grains (*lāja*) upon it, and approached the Paccekabuddha while prostrating herself on her five limbs.
Having paid homage, she made this aspiration: "Venerable sir, by the power of this merit, may I obtain five hundred sons endowed with great majesty.

At that very moment—precisely when she had made the aforementioned aspiration—five hundred deer-hunters, who had gathered their provisions and whose knowledge of individual enlightenment (paccekabodhi) was fully matured, [arrived].
Having given sweet meat to that very Paccekabuddha, they made this aspiration: "May we become her sons.
They say that because they had come to be her sons through many past births, it happened for them accordingly. Regarding the phrase *pāduddhāre*, it means at every step.
And here, by the term *pāduddhāra* (the lifting of the foot), the act of setting [the foot] down is expressed.
"Depending on the womb-impurity" means: having made the womb-impurity that has emerged outside their support, they are produced by way of moisture-born birth (*saṃsedaja*).
Some say "by way of spontaneous birth" (*opapātika*). "Having established the destruction and fall" means: having commenced insight (*vipassanā*).

Insight is preceded by the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) and preceded by the seeing of name-and-form together with its conditions; it [contemplates] conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).
When one who is reflecting has seen the characteristic of impermanence, the remaining characteristics— namely, "that which is impermanent is suffering,
and that which is suffering is non-self"— become very easy to understand. They brought forth the knowledge of *paccekabodhi* (solitary enlightenment) because,
having fulfilled the perfections for solitary enlightenment over two incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons, their knowledge had reached full maturity.
Having themselves practiced insight (vipassanā) according to the method already described and brought it to its culmination, they attained the knowledge of Pacceka-bodhi.
It is said that they all recited that very same verse; thus it is stated: "This was their verse of explanation.
*Saroruha* means born in a lake. *Padumapalāsapattaja* means produced together with the small and large petals of the lotus.
"Padumapalāsapatta" refers to a lotus thicket where there are lotus petals known as small and large lotus leaves.
"Born therein" means born in that lotus thicket. "Well-flowered" means beautifully blossomed, fully opened.
"Frequented by swarms of bees" means both followed by and hovered around by swarms of bees.
"Subject to impermanence" means having arrived at impermanence by way of the change in color and so forth from moment to moment.
"Having known" means having understood through the wisdom of the Path accompanied by the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*). "One should wander alone" means:
