therefore, another who wishes to be like me should practice in this way and wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.

135. They are "substantial among beings" because they are endowed with mindfulness as their essence, the essence of virtue, and so forth. They are "free from suffering" because the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*) has entirely vanished for them. They are "free from craving" because craving has been utterly cut off. "The cutter of conceit" is a term of praise.
"They indeed have the same name" means that other Paccekabuddhas, not mentioned in the Canon (*pāḷi*) among those who have appeared here, likewise share the same names as these.
The phrase beginning with "For among these... is stated in order to clarify this very point already mentioned. [End of] separate section.
"Without stating separately" means without stating each one individually by its own form. "And others" was said because they are not common [to all]. The remainder is indeed easy to understand.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Isigili-sutta* is completed.
7. Commentary on the *Mahācattārīsaka-sutta*.

136. It is noble (*ariya*) because it is far removed (*āraka*) from faults; hence he said, "faultless" (*niddosa*). Furthermore, that faultlessness is distinguished by its supramundane nature (*lokuttara*), which is why he said, "supramundane.
Right, beautiful, praised, and leading-out concentration is "right concentration" (*sammāsamādhi*); thus he said, "right concentration means path-concentration.
The fruit is seated (*upanisīdati*) therein because its existence is bound up with that [concentration].
He said, "With its proximate cause" (*saupanisaṃ*) means "with its condition" (*sappaccayaṃ*). He said, "With its equipment" (*saparikkhāraṃ*) means "with its retinue" (*saparivāraṃ*);

it is called "equipped" because it is surrounded, as if by attendants, by way of being a co-nascent and other types of conditions. "Preceding" (*purecārikā*) refers to the development leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī bhāvanā*).
They are "preceded" because they function as conditions by way of such conditions as co-nascence (*sahajāta-paccaya*) and others. Therefore it was said:
"and right view of insight" (*vipassanā-sammādiṭṭhi*). Now, in order to show these [factors] according to their functions, the passage beginning with "right view of insight" was stated.

Therein, the inclusion of the term "investigation" (*parivīmaṃsa*) is for the purpose of showing that right view is the precursor because it proceeds in each arising of consciousness as dominated by investigation (*vīmaṃsādhipateyya*).

This demonstrates that the various moments of path-concentration serve as the forerunner. "At the conclusion of investigation" means at the end of the knowledge of conformity (anuloma-ñāṇa) that has proceeded in such a manner.

"Uprooting the cycle of existence acquired on the plane" means they sever the cycle of defilements (kilesa-vatta) that has lain latent within their own continuum for a long time. "Calming it down" is a synonym for the same thing.
"Calming" means that they calm even what remains of the round (*vaṭṭa*) by way of making it no longer proceed;
for this very reason it is said: "Right view of the path... arises. "That" refers to right view.
"Both kinds" refers to both kinds as previously stated, because here the function of path-wisdom accompanied by insight-wisdom is being shown.

When the characteristic is penetrated, the state characterized by that (the dhamma possessing the characteristic) is also penetrated; thus it is said: “He understands wrong view... [and so on]... by way of its object.
This same method applies to insight-right-view as well. “By way of function” means by way of the function of development.
In the case of right-view, one understands through non-delusion, owing to the absence of delusion attained therein. “By way of function” means by way of the function of penetration.

But that is indeed non-delusion in every respect; thus he said, "from non-delusion" (*asammohato*). "Knowing thus" (*evaṃ pajānanto*) is the awakening to things as they truly are, [namely] that "wrong view is wrong view.
"His" (*assa*) refers to the person possessing that [knowledge].
The word *dvāyaṃ* is spoken with a long vowel; therefore he said, "I speak of a dyad. It is that which has two parts (*dve avayavā etassa*).
It is a dyad. Therefore he said, "I speak of two divisions. One portion of merit is itself "merit-portioned" (*puññabhāgika*);

by changing the letter *k* to *y* and applying the feminine gender, it is stated as "merit-portioned" (*puññabhāgiyā*). "Of that which is reckoned as a substrate" means of that which is reckoned as the continuity of the aggregates (*khandha*).
"The door to the Deathless" refers to the Noble Path. "He makes known" means he makes it known by way of its leading forth and other characteristics;

thus he said, "he shows it by analyzing it. Therein, he shows it through non-delusion by means of the destruction of delusion. "In that meaning" refers to the meaning of making known the door to the Deathless.
"Attained to the factors of enlightenment" means having attained the state of being a factor of enlightenment. This is because it proceeds by way of the path and by way of leading forth.

Because path-wisdom is common to all eight factors, and because a part is considered a "limb" (aṅga) of the whole aggregate, he said, "a limb of the noble path," showing the remaining factors by way of their being limbs.
"That monk" refers to a monk who knows wrong view as "wrong view" and right view as "right view. "For the purpose of abandoning" means for the sake of abandoning by way of complete eradication.

"For the sake of attainment" means for the realization of right view of the path (*maggasammādiṭṭhi*). "Wholesome effort" (*kusalavāyāmo*) refers specifically to the effort associated with insight (*vipassanā*), which arises from skillfulness.
"He remembers" thus he is "mindful" (*sato*); since that mindfulness of his consists in being endowed with mindfulness, it is said:
"endowed with mindfulness. And here, although the right view of insight, as well as right effort and mindfulness, [are present]—
They surround [it] by being both co-nascent and pre-nascent; for it is said: "Thus these three states run alongside and revolve around right view.
Furthermore, by the words "In this case... and so forth, the surrounding of the remaining factors by way of their appropriate concomitance with the right view of the path is applied.
By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "right intention, etcetera,"...
The inclusion of right speech, right action, and right livelihood is because they are taken as the retinue for the others;
for it is not possible to speak of them as both the retinue and the possessor of the retinue simultaneously, due to the confusion that would arise from such a commingling.
The word "three" refers to right view, right effort, and right mindfulness, which are indeed co-nascent retinues, since those [factors] existing at the moment of the Path are intended here.
Because [such states] are impossible during the moments of insight (vipassanā) or in the abstinences (virati).
137. The intention is that it is "by way of reasoning established in the world.
"Reasoning" (vitakka) is the drawing toward the object—like water in a well—in various ways by means of conjecture, thinking, "It must be thus and so. By way of intending (saṅkappana):

It is by way of conceptualizing (kappanā) that it grasps each respective object. It should be understood that "reasoning" (takkana) and "conceptualizing" (kappanā) apply only to those [mental factors] that are not co-nascent with themselves.

By the term "one-pointedness" (ekagga), he shows that the designation "absorption" (appanā) applies specifically to that very applied thought (vitakka) which has received assistance from this concentration (samādhi).
Or rather, through the distinction of absorption, the mind places itself upon the object by means of applied thought.

Since there is no initial application of thought (*vitakka*), he asks, "How then? and says, "But when there is initial application of thought," and so forth. By this he shows that the mind mounts upon the object by its own inherent nature (*dhammatā*);
thus, the grasping of the objective phenomena is established by their own intrinsic nature and does not depend on another factor.
However, when initial application of thought occurs, it functions specifically by way of directing the mind toward the object. Even though this is so...

Since the specific manner in which a thought with applied thought (*savitakka*) grasps its object arises from a thought of the same nature that is free from applied thought (*avitakka*), it is evident that applied thought is a specific condition for the mind’s grasping of an object.
However, others say: just as someone, by relying on a royal favorite or a friend connected to him, gains access to the royal palace...

It mounts and enters; thus, depending on applied thought (*vitakka*), the mind mounts the object because applied thought has the nature of directing the mind toward the object, while other mental factors lack that specific nature.
Therefore, the Blessed One said: "The directing of the mind.
If this is so, how does a thought devoid of applied thought mount its object? It is solely by the power of applied thought. Just as he...

Just as a man, through familiarity, enters the royal palace without apprehension even in the absence of [an escort], so too, through familiarity, the mind mounts its object without applied thought (vitakka), even in the absence of applied thought.
"Through familiarity" means by way of the cultivation of applied thought occurring repeatedly within the mental continuum (santāna).
For it is by virtue of applied thought occurring frequently in the continuum that the mind mounts its object.

It has been long practiced; therefore, it sometimes proceeds even without that particular thought, just as a consciousness accompanied by knowledge, having been long practiced through the mode of comprehension (*sammasana*), sometimes proceeds through the mode of comprehension even when devoid of knowledge;

or just as that which proceeded while accompanied by defilements, by virtue of long practice, proceeds even when entirely free from defilements due to the latent tendency (*vāsanā*) of those defilements.
This should be understood in the same way.
"He constructs speech" means he produces speech; the meaning is that it serves as a specific condition for the arising of vocal sound.

Mundane thought (*vitakka*), accompanied by thirty-two types of consciousness, constructs speech because it generates vocal intimation (*vacī-viññatti*). It is precisely called "verbal formation" (*vacī-saṅkhāra*)...
Its name is *ruḷhita* (conventional); however, it is called *saṅkhāra* because of its capacity for that [activity] or because of its arising from cessation.
Having stated, “They surround supramundane right intention,” one might ask: among the three kinds of right intention, which one do they surround at times?
Addressing this objection, he says, “In this case,” and so forth. They are found in various states of consciousness because they have various modes of attention as their cause.
And they arise even in the preliminary stage. It receives three names because it performs all three functions with particular excellence through the total eradication of the threefold opposite.
This same method applies to right speech and the others as well. 138.
That by which one abstains is called *veramaṇī* or *virati*. Because it serves as the cause for abstaining from false speech, it is so designated.

Because it involves the reflection upon and the destruction of enmity, volition (*cetanā*) is also called "joy in abstinence" (*viratipīti*); thus it is said: "Both abstinence and volition are appropriate.
"It delights far away" means that when [enmity] has been cut off, it drives it far away. "It delights without them" means that it exists absolutely without them.
"From this and that" refers to false speech (*musāvāda*), such as speaking of what was not seen regarding what was seen. Because it is by nature non-arising, it has turned back in a specific sense.
140. "By means of the threefold basis for hypocrisy" (*kuhanavatthu*) refers to the threefold basis for hypocrisy produced by evil desire (*pāpicchatā*), namely:
the consumption of requisites (*paccayapaṭisevana*), indirect hinting (*sāmantajappana*), and the maintenance of deportment (*iriyāpathapavattanasaṅkhāta*).

The construction is: "those who have as their sign (*nimitta*) and virtue (*sīla*) the production of requisites by means of this hypocrisy acting as the instrument. For the sake of gain within one's own sphere, [this occurs] by way of reviling, censuring, and disparaging others.
Grinding, rubbing, harassing, and extortion. Having received something from one person, one gives it to another;

thus, by means of gain, one seeks to win further gain—this is "seeking gain through gain. This constitutes wrong livelihood (micchā-ājīva) as described in the Canon by way of hypocrisy (kuhanā) and so forth.
To the question "Who, then, is this? he says: "For the sake of livelihood," and so on. The restriction "of those very [women]" is used because "when the livelihood is disturbed..."
It was stated thus, taking it that [the defilement] "rages only through the doors of body and speech. 141.
One who possesses right, praised, beautiful, and liberating view is a "right-viewed person" (*sammādiṭṭhi*).
Since right view is the support for the clear realization of the truths and the actualization of Nibbāna, it is therefore said:
“‘For one established in right view of the path’ means: it is capable, it exists, and it arises and proceeds together with that [view].
‘Right knowledge’ (sammāñāṇa) is intended here in the sense of knowing things as they truly are, which is reflective knowledge (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa).

And since this occurs only when one is established in the concentration of the path, he said—beginning with ‘For one established in right concentration of the path... right knowledge is capable’—in order to show this meaning.”

What does this show? It shows that just as a person established in the right view of the path is called "one of right view," so too one established in the knowledge of reviewing the path and fruit is called "one of right knowledge.

Furthermore, it shows that through the occurrence of the right concentration of the path and fruit, there arises right knowledge, and from right knowledge, right liberation arises. First, regarding the concentration of the fruit:

Let it proceed; but how is the concentration of the path (maggasamādhi) so called? That too deserves to be described as "proceeding" because, by virtue of its state of being unshakable, it constitutes absolute concentration, and because it proceeds through the accomplishment of its function. Regarding the phrase "excluding the eight factors of fruition":

this refers to the eight factors consisting of right view and the rest which constitute the fruit, since they are taken separately in such passages as, "In one of right view, right intention arises," and so forth.
"Setting aside. "Having performed the review of right knowledge" means having made the reviewing-knowledge (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa) into right knowledge (sammāñāṇa).

Regarding the phrase "to make the fruit": it is stated that it is fitting to make right liberation (sammāvimutti) into the states associated with the fruit, which have received the name "fruit" because they coexist with the dhamma of the fruit and because their intrinsic nature is that of fruition (vipāka). And so it is said in the commentary on the Sallekha Sutta:

“However, with the exception of the eight factors beginning with right view that are associated with the fruit, the remaining phenomena should be understood as right liberation. (142) “Wasted away” (*nijjiṇṇa*) means worn out; the sense is that they are shattered and destroyed.

Regarding the statement “the fruit has been explained,” they say that by this section—“Monks, for one of right view, wrong view is wasted away”—the fruit of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*) has been explained.

The intention is that "wearing away" (*nijjīraṇa*) means "subsiding" (*paṭippassambhana*). However, the Majjhimabhāṇakas, taking "wearing away" to mean "complete eradication," state that the Path is what is spoken of [in this context].

"In the sense of seeing" means in the sense of directly seeing the four truths by way of the clear realization of full understanding (*pariññā-abhisamaya*), and so forth. "In the sense of making known" means by way of direct perception of those things as they have been seen.
In the sense of making the paths and fruits manifest. "In the sense of being intent upon that" means by way of the state of resolute confidence (*adhimuccana*) toward Nibbāna as it has been realized.

"Wholesome factors" refers to blameless categories. "By giving a great result" means by the granting of a great, abundant supramundane result of happiness, as well as a result of bodily and other forms of suffering.
Just as it is called the "Great Forty" because it gives a great result, so too it is shown to be the "Great Forty" even by virtue of its many components.

It has been said: “In this sutta, moreover, five kinds of right view are taught,” and so forth. For the word *mahā* (great) possesses many meanings, as in such terms as *mahājana* (the great multitude).
And here, by way of the distinction of objects (*vatthu*), ten factors of wrong view are taught through the phrases beginning with “there is no giving”;
and likewise, by way of the distinction of objects, ten factors of right view are taught through the phrases beginning with “there is giving. Thus, there are twenty [factors].

Just as there are ten factors of rightness (*sammattadhamma*) by way of the path—such as "Bhikkhus, for one of right view, right intention arises"—and ten factors of wrongness (*micchattadhamma*) by way of their opposites—such as "for one of wrong view, wrong intention arises"—making twenty in total;
likewise, there are twenty in the case of the fruits. How, then, are there ten factors such as right view even in the summary?
Twenty? Thus, these two sets of forty, together with the previous [set], should be understood as three sets of forty that have been analyzed.
143. That which is censurable is the direct opposite of that which is praiseworthy; even one who praises what is censurable is, in fact, censuring what is praiseworthy.
For the praise of what is censurable proceeds precisely by way of the disparagement of the qualities of what is praiseworthy.
He said: “Even one who says, ‘This wrong view is beautiful,’ is indeed censuring right view,” and so forth.
By the word “and so forth” (*ādi*), he includes such statements as, “There is no cause, there is no condition for the defilement of beings.
Therefore, “those who speak thus” means those who speak thus in rejecting the cause. “Those who have entered the fixed course” (*okkantaniyāma*)—
"Plunged into the fixed course of wrongness. Regarding such statements as "having adopted such a tenet," whatever is to be said has already been stated in the commentary on the *Cūḷapuṇṇama Sutta*;
therefore, it should be understood according to the method explained there. For this [statement], "incurable even for Buddhas," and so forth, is similar to what was said there.
"Out of fear of self-reproach" means out of fear of the reproach that others might speak later on, such as, "They even revile right view," and so forth.

"Out of fear of collision" means likewise out of fear of offending others. "Obstruction" (upārambha) is the restraint to be exercised by another in accordance with the Dhamma against oneself; the fear of such obstruction is the dread of being censured.
Since this, in its actual meaning, is the fear of reproach, he said, "out of fear of reproach. The rest is easily understood.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Mahācattārīsakasutta* is completed.
8. Commentary on the *Ānāpānassatisutta* 144.

In the phrase "pubbenā" (by means of the former), the instrumental case is used in the sense of the ablative. Since it is stated [in the text] as "another distinction," the word *pubba* (former) refers to a specific distinction; thus he says: "from the former distinction, beginning with the fulfillment of virtue (*sīla*)," and so forth.
145. "Accomplished" means accomplished through practice according to the instruction.

That which was intended here as "not yet attained"—namely, the purpose for which one goes forth in the Dispensation and the attainment of distinction—is the sign of jhāna and insight; thus he said, "of the arahantship not yet attained.
*Komudī* means "possessing white water-lilies" (*kumuda*). It is said that at that time the white water-lilies were in full bloom; therefore he said [that].
“Because of the presence of *kumuda* [white water lilies], it is called *komudī*. A collection of *kumudas*, or the *kumudas* themselves, are *komudas*;

because they exist there, it is called *komudī*. “The inclusion of the invitation” (*pavāraṇasaṅgaha*) refers to the gathering for the purpose of coming together without performing the Great Invitation (*mahāpavāraṇa*).
“Of one who has begun insight” (*āraddhavipassakassa*) means of one who has commenced insight; that is, one who has developed and intensified insight.

“Bhikkhus will come here,” meaning those who have completed the rains retreat and performed the *pavāraṇā* ceremony, with the intention: “We shall pay homage to the Blessed One, we shall purify our meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*), and we shall report whatever special attainments we have gained.
“These bhikkhus” refers to these bhikkhus who are newly established in calm (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
They will not be able to produce special attainments due to their lack of suitable lodgings and other necessities.
"Unobstructed" (*apalibuddha*) means not being harassed by others. Because it was within the rainy season, they were not permitted to take up lodgings.
Even if [lodging] is given to one person, it is as if it has been given to all; therefore, having stayed for one month in each place where they had heard [of the Dhamma], they departed. 146.

"Alam" means suitable, that is to say, appropriate—just as in such expressions as "it is enough to become disenchanted" (*alam eva nibbinditum*). Having carried it bound in a bundle, they ate what was in the bundle; this is how the *o*-sound is substituted for the *a*-sound. Thus he said: "provisions for the journey" (*pātheyya*).
147. "Vipassanā has been explained" means that the cultivation of insight (vipassanā-bhāvanā) has been explained by way of the perception of impermanence alone.
For the function of insight is not accomplished by the mere contemplation of impermanence. The intention is that there are many monks who take delight in detailed exposition.
Therefore he said, "Therefore," and so forth.

149. "In all instances" means in all sections. Since even in such passages as, "Therefore, bhikkhus, one should contemplate feelings," the contemplation of feelings is stated by way of the experiencing of rapture and so forth, he says:
"This was said with reference to pleasant feeling. It is stated as "careful attention" because it is the state of attention in the development of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).
Wisdom is spoken of by the name "perception" because it is the application of those [mental factors]. By the name "attention" (*manasikāra*)...
Feeling has been mentioned because it is made the object of attention due to its being cultivated through meditation.
"Setting aside applied thought and sustained thought" is said because they are verbal formations.
Even though this is so—that is, even though it is called "attention" because it is included within the category of attention—nevertheless...
The state of contemplation of feelings (*vedanānupassanā*) would not be tenable [for the former], for his object (*ārammaṇa*) is the inhalations and exhalations.
However, by taking as an object the "basis" (*vatthu*)—the physical basis that serves as the locus for the occurrence of feelings such as pleasure—the feeling itself experiences;
thus, by showing the absolute nature of feeling, he demonstrates this point: that the state of contemplation of feelings is indeed tenable for him. This refers to the application of this practice.
Regarding the phrase "in two ways," he says "by way of the object and by way of non-delusion" in order to show those [two ways] with reference to which it was stated.
"The two jhānas accompanied by rapture" refers to the first and second jhānas associated with rapture, which one enters in succession. "At the moment of attainment" means at the moment of entering.
"By the acquisition of jhāna" means by being endowed with jhāna. "By way of the object" means by way of the door of the object.
Then, the rapture included within that jhāna having that as its object becomes clearly discerned because the object itself has been clearly discerned.
Just as when someone wandering in search of a snake has discerned its lair, the snake itself is also discerned, since it is easy to capture it by the power of spells and charms;
so too, when the object—which serves as the abode for rapture—has been clearly discerned, [the rapture is also discerned].
That rapture is indeed clearly experienced both through its specific characteristic (*salakkhaṇa*) and its general characteristic (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*), because it is easy to grasp.
"At the moment of insight" (*vipassanākkhaṇe*) means specifically at the moment of seeing by means of path-wisdom (*magga-paññā*) preceded by insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*).
"Through the penetration of characteristics" (*lakkhaṇapaṭivedhā*) means by way of penetrating the specific and general characteristics of rapture. For that which...
This is the characteristic of rapture both specifically and generally; when that [characteristic] is known, it is known as it truly is.
Therefore he said: "Rapture is clearly experienced through non-delusion.
Now, in order to clarify this matter by means of the scripture, he said: "And this has also been stated," and so forth. Therein, "by way of long inhalation" means:

"By way of the long inhalation as its object": this refers to one who understands the one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind—that is, the one-pointedness of the mind which has acquired the name "non-distraction" included within the jhāna—by means of the wisdom associated with it.
For just as rapture is experienced by way of the object, so too are the states associated with it.

They are indeed clearly discerned by way of the object. "Mindfulness is established" means that mindfulness associated with jhāna, through long inhalation, when that object is present, is said to be established in the jhāna as well by way of the object.
"By that mindfulness"—that is, by that mindfulness thus established, together with that aforementioned knowledge—
Because that object is well-penetrated, by means of it, that joy is fully experienced as having that as its object.
The remaining phrases—namely, the phrases beginning with "by means of long out-breaths"—are also included.
Thus, the words beginning with "iti" were spoken in order to show how the meaning stated in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* is applied to this sutta.
It is called "attainment" because it is to be attained by this yogin through attention; thus it is said:
"by the attainment of attention consisting of feeling associated with jhāna.
"The sign of the in-breath and out-breath" refers to the object, which is the counterpart sign obtained by depending upon the in-breath and out-breath.

Even though he performs [various actions], because he proceeds having established mindfulness and clear comprehension, and because the object of that [consciousness] is fully understood by way of its objective support, he is indeed called "one who contemplates mind in the mind. Thus, contemplation of the mind also occurs solely through the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension;

therefore, he said "not indeed," and so forth. It is called *pahāna* (abandoning) because one abandons by means of it, or because it itself abandons; [it is] knowledge (*ñāṇa*). By way of mental distress (*domanassa*)...
The hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpāda-nīvaraṇa*) is shown because it is associated with that [state]. "Of that" refers to the section on the hindrances.
"Knowledge that effects abandonment" means the knowledge of abandoning. "Succession of insight" refers to insight in its progressive order.

"One who has entered into serenity" means he looks upon the mind that has entered into the sign of intermediate serenity with equanimity. "Arising together" means through the departure of the opposing factors.
It is an appearance as a single state. Regarding the phrase "there is equanimity toward co-nascent states":
because it does not engage in the functions of exertion, suppression, or encouragement, there is equanimity toward objects;

thus, the equanimity described in the passage, "He abandons what exists, what has come to be, and attains equanimity," occurs for one who has entered upon the practice. It is solely toward phenomena such as the hindrances.

Having seen that the states such as the hindrances have indeed been abandoned, he then becomes one who looks on with equanimity after having seen, through wisdom, even the knowledge of their abandonment as it truly is.
For this was said by the Blessed One: "Bhikkhus, even states (*dhamma*) are to be abandoned, how much more so non-states (*adhamma*).

(150) "He investigates by way of impermanence, etc. means he investigates and sees them through the various modes such as impermanence. "Unworldly" (*nirāmisa*) means free from the bait of the defilements (*kilesa*).
"By the subsiding of bodily and mental distress" means by the suppression [of such distress] through the attainment of a state of well-being in body and mind.
It is "regarded with equanimity" because it proceeds with a single nature toward co-nascent states by means of co-nascent equanimity.

The mindfulness that occurs in relation to that body and has the body as its object is the mindfulness-enlightenment-factor belonging to the preliminary stage. This same method applies to the others as well.
This "descending" (*okkamana*) or "slowing down" (*oliyana*) by way of a mental state accompanied by joy is laziness (*kosajja*);

"overstepping" (*ativattana*) or "rushing on" (*atidhāvana*) from that is agitation (*uddhacca*). That which is free from both of these—the state of neutrality (*majjhattākāratā*) consisting in neither sinking nor overstepping—is the equanimity (*upekkhā*) of the enlightenment factors (*bojjhaṅga*).
Now, with the words "Just as," etc., he clarifies that very state of neutrality by means of a simile.
Whether by striking with a goad or pulling with a rein—there is nothing that should not be done; there is [something to be done].

"Momentary" (*ekacittakkhaṇika*) means those that arise together with each individual consciousness by way of insight (*vipassanā*). "Having various flavors and characteristics" (*nānārasalakkhaṇa*) means having both various functions and various intrinsic natures.
152. All these have already been explained in the commentary on the *Sabbāsavasutta* regarding the successive occurrences of mindfulness (*sati*) having inhalation and exhalation as its object.
By way of the object, the states that have that as their object are included; however, because they are associated with mundane consciousness within a single continuum, they are mundane (*lokiya*).
As these increase, they fulfill the fourfold mundane foundation of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).

"The fruit of clear knowledge and liberation, which is Nibbāna" means that the extinction of defilements (*kilesa-nibbāna*), which is the fruit of the liberations, is to be understood through those very [liberations]; it is indeed the great Nibbāna of the Deathless for clear knowledge and liberation.
It was stated thus because it is to be realized through realization. And its fulfillment consists precisely in the experiencing of the Deathless by making that [object] the mental support.
Here, in this sutta, both mundane and supramundane factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) are mentioned;

taking this much as the basis, it was stated in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) by way of explaining the meaning: "Thus, in the place where the mundane occurs, the mundane is spoken of. "The Elder" (Thero):...
The Elder Mahādhammarakkhita. Elsewhere it is said, "it occurs thus":

in other suttas where mundane and supramundane states appear mixed together in various places, it must be explained that in such cases the mundane has appeared there, whereas here the supramundane has appeared.
The supramundane appears above [in the sense of] "fulfilling clear knowledge and liberation"—thus the supramundane.

This has come down in the teaching above; therefore, only the mundane factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) that fulfill true knowledge and liberation (vijjāvimutti) should be explained here, because the supramundane factors of enlightenment are already included by the mention of "true knowledge" (vijjā). Consequently, one should accept the meaning as stated by the Elder.
The rest is easily understood because it follows the method already described.
The Elucidation of the Meaning of the Commentary on the Ānāpānassati Sutta is completed.
9. Commentary on the Kāyagatāsati Sutta, §§153–154:
Sensual pleasures are "dwellings" in the sense of being a refuge for those sense-sphere beings who rely upon them; they are "clinging to the dwelling."
“Attached to what pertains to the household” means they are connected with active involvement in worldly affairs. “They run” means they proceed with impetuosity;

for proceeding with impetuosity is called “running. “Intentions” refers to whatever wrong intentions there may be, including intentions of ill-will, cruelty, and so forth—all of which are likewise attached to the strands of sensual pleasure.
“Only within the range of their own resort” means they operate only within the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) that has been taken up as their domain.
For it is called "the internal object" (*gocarajjhatta*) because it serves as the objective range for the meditation established by means of the Dhamma.
It is "body-centered" (*kāyagatā*) because it proceeds and occurs within the body of inhalation and exhalation; thus, it is "mindfulness directed to the body" (*kāyagatāsati*).

By using the term "mindfulness," he refers to the states of meditation associated with it—namely, the body of inhalation and exhalation and so forth—having discerned each respective part as a basis for serenity (*samatha*).

Because it is encompassed by mindfulness; or rather, having spoken of mindfulness with the body as its object—which occurs by way of attention to impermanence and so forth directed toward that which is thus encompassed—the text says "encompassing the body" and so on, showing them together as a single unit.
In the *Satipaṭṭhāna* [Sutta], specifically the *Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta*, body-contemplation is taught in fourteen ways, consisting of broken-down particles.
Contemplation of the body was explained by concluding with bones; here, however,

because the subsequent teaching is expanded by way of the four jhānas produced through the color-kasinas of the head-hairs and so forth, there is the development of mindfulness directed to the body in eighteen modes.
156. "Of that bhikkhu": of that bhikkhu who has attained mastery in the cultivation of mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati-bhāvanā*).

"They partake of true knowledge (*vijjā*) by way of association" means they partake of true knowledge by way of the co-nascent, mutuality, dependence, association, presence, and non-disappearance conditions;
the meaning is that they reach a state of virtual unity with it. "In the portion of true knowledge" means in the section concerning true knowledge.

"They occur" means that, by virtue of sharing the nature of true knowledge (*vijjā*), they occur within a portion of that [knowledge], namely the section of true knowledge. The states associated with them are contact and so forth.
Is it not the case here that it is impossible for true knowledges themselves to be "portions of true knowledge"? It is not impossible.

For that true knowledge by which those states associated with true knowledge possess the quality of being portions of true knowledge is itself metaphorically designated as such, on account of its being the cause thereof.

"One true knowledge is true knowledge; the rest are factors conducive to true knowledge. Among the eight types of true knowledge, one is taken as "true knowledge" itself, while the others should be understood as "factors conducive to true knowledge" because they share a portion of that [knowledge].

Since there is no restrictive rule stating that among those things which have the nature of occurring together, this alone must be called "true knowledge," it should be said that the factors conducive to true knowledge occur in exactly the same way as the portion of true knowledge.
"Water-pervasion" (āpopharaṇa) means the complete pervading of the great ocean by the water-kasina, which has become the counterpart sign;

this is what is called "water-pervasion. Alternatively, considering it as the function of the knowledge of the divine eye, or for the sake of the divine eye, the pervading of light should be understood as "divine-eye-pervasion.
In both cases, [it refers to the filling] of the small rivers flowing toward the ocean.
Their being pervaded by the mind should be understood as their state of being submerged within the ocean.

Here, the mention of "small streams" refers to the fact that after a certain period of time, their water comes to be included within the ocean; it does not mean that they exist for only a short duration, like the great rivers outside.

They enter upon an opportunity for the arising of defilements; that opening is also called a "gap" (*chidda*). "Object" (*ārammaṇa*) means the support for the arising of defilements. "As far as the end" means as far as the limit of the heap of clay.

(158) "By direct knowledge" (*abhiññāya*) means by the direct knowledges such as the various supernormal powers (*iddhividha*). "Of what is to be realized" (*sacchikātabbassa*) means of the phenomena such as resolve and transformation which are to be made manifest through direct perception.
He says, "direct knowledge itself is the cause," because there is a dependence upon realization (*sacchikiriyā*).
"But for the accomplishment of the cause of direct knowledge, they are manifest. "Bound by boundaries" means made at the mouth of a water-channel.
Because they can be easily reviewed at whatever time one desires, as if they were a properly harnessed vehicle.
"Made into a foundation" means having been brought to the state of being a foundation for attainments. "Not set in motion" means not set in motion through the frequent practice of meditation.
"By way of familiarity" means by way of the firmness of repetition, that is, through long-term cultivation.
"Well-mastered" means brought to the highest excellence in every respect. "Well-initiated" means produced in an exceedingly correct manner. The rest is easily understood.
The elucidation of the hidden meaning in the commentary on the *Kāyagatāsati-sutta* is completed.
10. Commentary on the Saṅkhārupapatti Sutta (Sutta 160).
"Arising of formations" (*saṅkhārupapatti*) means the arising of those formations designated as resultant aggregates;
the sense is "their production. Since a restriction is intended in this phrase, it should be understood as "the arising of formations alone."
Having said this, he spoke the words "not of a being" to show that [the self] has been turned back by that [teaching]. By this, he rejects the false doctrine that a being or a soul (*jīva*) arises.

Having thus shown arising by way of the phenomena that arise, he now says "by a meritorious formation (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*)" and so forth, in order to show it also by way of the phenomena that produce arising.
In that context, even by a meritorious formation regarding sense-pleasures...

Rebirth occurs; however, that [rebirth] is what is included in this sutta. In the phrase "by the formation of merit" (*puññābhisaṅkhārena*), the word *vā* has the sense of an alternative (*vikappa*) that refers to an unstated meaning.

Regarding this reference to an unstated meaning, the phrase "by the formation of the imperturbable" (*āneñjābhisaṅkhārena*) has not been mentioned. Alternatively, while rebirth has been mentioned and likewise the task (*kicca*) has been mentioned, the formation of the imperturbable, although not mentioned here in its own form, is nevertheless included by the very mention of the formation of merit.
"It is grasped" (gahito) is how it should be understood. Some, however, read "by means of meritorious and imperturbable volitional formations" (puññāneñjābhisaṅkhārehi).
"Of the aggregates leading to existence" (bhavūpagakkhandhānaṃ) means of the aggregates of clinging that lead to existence in a happy destination. 161.
They are mundane because they include the cycle of kamma (kammavaṭṭa). It is faith that is to be relied upon which serves as the cause for rebirth in existence.

The fourfold purification of virtue, such extensive knowledge of the Buddha’s word, the relinquishing of material things, the knowledge of the ownership of kamma, and the view of the fruit of kamma—these are to be understood as faith and the other [faculties].
"He establishes" means he establishes by way of directing his aspiration; for here the meaning is "he aspires. "He settles" means he establishes it so that it is well-settled therein.
“Together with aspiration” means together with the aspiration that occurs in this way: “O, may I... [etc. ...be reborn.
“Faith and the rest” means that those very five factors beginning with faith, as previously described, are called *saṅkhāra* in the sense of forming (*saṅkharaṇa*) rebirth;
for that very reason, they are called *vihāra* in the sense of bringing about a distinguished state of existence (*bhava*). “In that place” means in that place of rebirth.
The "path" (*magga*) is so called because a person endowed with those [five] factors seeks and searches for rebirth by means of them.

The "way of practice" (*paṭipadā*) is that by which one proceeds. Here, however, volition (*cetanā*)—being merely a conditioned formation—is already included by the mention of faith and the other [factors];
therefore, the restriction is made. By the very inclusion of "aspiration" (*patthanā*), which occurs through the fashioning of rebirth, [volition is likewise encompassed].
Some say it is "grasping" (*gahaṇa*), because it performs the function of determining [rebirth] by way of producing the mental factors associated with the act of doing.
For volition (*cetanā*) is indeed karma; there is nothing further to be said regarding its production of rebirth.

However, because of its performance of that function, these states—faith and so forth, as well as aspiration (*patthanā*)—act as the determinants for rebirth in a particular state; thus, it is for the sake of rebirth therein...
By stating that they "occur," their status as the Path and so forth is expressed. Therefore he says, "For one who...
and so on. By this, he shows that both these factors—faith and aspiration—when combined, distinguish the karma and determine the destination (*gati*);

the underlying intention is that the taking of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is not determined by karma alone. Although it is said here, "having performed the karma," [the result is determined by these two].
Furthermore, it is indeed permissible to establish a resolution even before the accumulation of kamma.

Regarding the phrase "having performed the kamma," there is no restriction of time—as in the expressions "he eats after heating [the food]" or "he lies down after eating"—and thus it is said that one may make a resolution at any time whatsoever after performing the kamma;
this is stated as a demonstration of proper conduct (*cāritta*). For just as the aspiration for existence (*bhava-patthanā*)...
As long as it is not completely cut off by the Path, it remains a condition for new, accumulated karma that has not yet arisen.
Furthermore, it serves as a specific condition in the same way that [kamma] is produced when determined. Therefore it was said:
“For one who possesses five qualities, there is no fixed destination for their aspiration.”
165. *Sabbaso va* means it becomes manifest in every respect, as in: "This is black, yellow, white, green, circular, non-circular, square, complete, small, large," and so forth.

167. *Sundaro* means beautiful due to being free from defects such as blackness and the like. *Ākarasampanno* means possessed of an excellent source due to its arising from a perfect mine. *Dhovanādīhi* means by means of washing, heating, polishing, and so forth. 168.
It is called *satasahasso* because it brings a hundred thousand world-systems under its own control. Furthermore, regarding that [world-system] therein...
Because making light means making it manifest, it is said: “the Brahmā who pervades with light. This same method applies to the passages below, such as “the thousandfold Brahmā,” and so forth.
“Made of *nikkha* gold” means made of Jambūnada gold measured by the *nikkha*.
Some say that a *nikkha* is twenty pieces of gold; others say it is twenty-five pieces of gold. “Gold” means four *dharaṇas*.
They say: because of its limited nature, it is not capable of withstanding striking or submerging.

"By more than" means by more than five measures of gold, yet not reaching the measure of a *nikkha*. Furthermore, it is not beautiful because, due to its lack of breadth, it does not appear magnificent;
precisely because of its lack of beauty, it appears to consist of coarse elements. "In them" means in those grounds where the branch has grown.

“Fixed. “Tet” means golden sprouts. “Having heated” means having warmed. Regarding “sampahaṭṭhaṃ,” he said “washed, rubbed, and polished,” meaning that after applying a coating of copper-colored clay, it was washed, rubbed with a stone or similar object, and polished with sheep’s wool or similar material.
"Having increased that very light": here, it is the pervasion by light itself. Alternatively, whatever is the pervasion of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*), that is also the pervasion of light.
For to whatever extent the yogi pervades a place with the light of the kasiṇa, to that same extent the knowledge of the divine eye touches that place.
Thus, when the pervasion of the divine eye is demonstrated, the pervasion of light is demonstrated as well.
The meaning is as follows. "In all places" means in every instance where the word "having pervaded" (*pharitvā*) occurs. "Without destroying" means without causing it to be mixed or blurred.
"Like the pervading of a *kasiṇa*" means it appears or manifests like the pervasion by the light of a *kasiṇa*;

the intention is that this is because the pervasion by the [pure] elements in the Brahma-world is shown to be like the pervasion of the radiance of a gem. However, the radiance of the body is similar to the radiance of a precious jewel (*nikkha*).

It is said: “The filling of the body is seen like [the scattering of] grains. Regarding the statement that there is no commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), it must be understood that this refers to a commentary on the meaning of the canonical text (*pāḷipada*) that has been definitively determined;
however, when it is not so determined, its non-existence is as if it were absent.

Having thus rejected the claim that the non-recitation of such a work constitutes the absence of a commentary, he explains how it should indeed be stated: [The text continues: ...as it ought to be stated, so...
The intention is: what is the purpose of the word "pervading" (*viyā*) if [the light] has not descended?

Just as the fathom-wide radiance (*byāmappabhā*) of the Buddhas is resolved (*adhiṭṭhāti*) to remain at all times within the space of a fathom, so too the pervading of that Brahmā’s body—the spreading of the bodily light—is constant for all time.
These other four types of pervading should be explained without destroying one another and without mutual contradiction.
“By means of resolve alone there is suffusion” is a synonym for the term *pharaṇa* (suffusion).
“It spreads” means it spreads by way of the aforementioned suffusion. “It knows” means it knows by way of resolve. 169. “And so forth”:
by the word “and so forth,” one includes the *subha* (the beautiful) [meditation subjects]. “The Radiant Ones” (*Ābhā*) refers to the deities belonging to the plane of the second jhāna collectively.

This was stated by way of a general rule. Then, regarding "Subhā" (the Radiant), this refers to those belonging to the plane of the third jhāna. Therefore he said: "There are no separate deities," and so forth.
Even when the aspiration is made generally, if the jhāna factor cultivated is limited (*paritta*), rebirth occurs among the Parittābha deities;
if it is middling (*majjhima*), among the Appamāṇābha deities; and if it is sublime (*paṇīta*), rebirth occurs among the Ābhassara deities.
"It occurs" is how it should be understood. The same method applies here for "subha" (the beautiful) as well. Since it is easily understood through the very method explained below, he said:
"The sections on the Vehapphala deities and so forth are indeed evident.

By the passage beginning with "May one be reborn among the sense-sphere deities," etc., [it is shown] how faith and the other [faculties], when combined with jhāna and insight, have that [rebirth] as their basis.

"He fears that it might happen. The other, showing that although faith and the rest have the nature of absorption (*jhāna*), they bring about rebirth in the Brahma-world and even Nibbāna because they possess conditions—such as being the basis and support-condition for *jhāna* and insight (*vipassanā*)—said, "These five qualities," and so forth.
Therein, "virtue" (*sīla*) refers to the virtue of equipment (*sambhāra-sīla*). The non-returner (*anāgāmī*) has completely severed the lower fetters (*orambhāgiya-saṃyojana*).
If, being similar [to those in the lower stages], he is unable to transcend rebirths entirely, he is reborn in the planes of the noble ones (ariyabhūmi) according to his accumulated kamma of jhāna;
thus it is said: “The non-returner... is reborn. “Having developed the higher path” means having developed the supreme path (aggamagga).
“The destruction of the taints” means he attains the total exhaustion and abandonment of all taints (āsava). The rest is easily understood.
The Elucidation of the Meaning Obscured in the Commentary on the *Saṅkhārupapatti-sutta* is completed.
And the commentary on the *Anupada-vagga* is finished.
3. The *Suññata-vagga*.
1. Commentary on the Cūḷasuññata Sutta 176.
"Having fixed a time limit" means that those who enter [meditative attainment] must indeed fix a time limit.
However, the Elder fixes a time limit for the purpose of performing his duties toward the Blessed One, thinking: "When this much time has passed, [I shall do] this..."
“[The attainment] of the Blessed One must be performed. Having entered that very attainment right there and emerged from it, it was said with reference to this:

“having fixed a time limit. By the phrase “having entered the emptiness attainment of fruition,” he refutes the claim made by others that “neither stream-enterers nor once-returners enter the attainment of fruition.”
"Emptiness": because of the emptiness of self and the emptiness of permanence, conditioned phenomena appeared [to him].

For the penetration of emptiness by those in training (sekkha) is precarious, because the perceptions of beauty and pleasure have not yet been abandoned; therefore, that elder became desirous of hearing a discourse on emptiness.
"As if striking yoke against yoke" means as if acting by striking one chariot-yoke with another chariot-yoke.
The construction is: "Directly, emptiness... [etc. ...is not able to find a footing. "A single phrase" means a single phrase on emptiness.
By saying "Previously, indeed... and so forth, the Blessed One reveals that even during his first awakening he was frequently established in the dwelling of emptiness;
thus, he said, "even during the first awakening. "One," and so forth, is for the purpose of showing that the Elder is a fit vessel for the discourse on emptiness.
"To hear" means to hear by making it an object, attending to it, and applying one's whole mind.

"To grasp" means to take up the Dhamma as it truly is within the heart—by means of memorization, interrogation, and mastery—so that it does not perish, like lion’s fat placed in a golden vessel. "To expound" means to demonstrate it to others in detail.
It is possible. "Therein" means in the Palace of Migāra’s Mother. "Made" refers to those constructed by way of wooden figures, cloth figures, and painted figures:
namely, the wooden figures made by carving them onto pillars and the like; the cloth figures fashioned as statues on balconies and the like;
and the painted figures designed through mural work on the walls. [The phrase] "of Vessavaṇa, Mandhātā, and others... [is used].
[This refers to] those things made in the form of statues, such as Vessavaṇa, Mandhātu, Sakka, and so forth. "By way of painting" means by way of paintings on monasteries and the like.
"Even though it stands fixed" means even though it remains standing, having been established with its constituent parts.
"For the purpose of repairing what is worn out" means for the sake of restoring worn-out parts such as porticos, gabled roofs, and palaces, in their respective locations.
It was established by means of a secret sign. "To be used" means it should be utilized by way of assigning it to this or that task with the thought, "I shall make use of it.
"This has been said" refers to what was stated, such as, "This Migāra’s Mother’s Palace is empty," and so forth.
"Constantly" means at all times, both by night and by day. "A single state" (*ekabhāvam*)—the accusative case is used here in the sense of the nominative—refers to a single non-emptiness.
“Unity” (*ekatta*) means being alone, not empty. “A village” (*gāma*) is [defined] by way of its occurrence:
it is called a “village” by way of worldly convention, taking into account houses, settlements, streets, crossroads, junctions, and so forth.

“By way of defilements” (*kilesavasena*) means by way of attraction and aversion toward those things. By the phrase “the same method applies,” this meaning is indicated: “the perception of humans that has arisen either by way of occurrence or by way of defilement.”
It extends by analogy. And here, just as the mention of "village" includes the perception of houses and so forth, so too the mention of "human being" includes the perception of women, men, and so on.

Since the perception of "forest" depends upon trees and the like—and since mountains, groves, thickets, and so forth are included therein—one does not take those existing subdivisions into account there, but rather [speaks] depending on the forest as a single unit.
He attends to the perception of the forest. "Enters" means he penetrates it. "Resolves" means he decides upon it.
"Agitations due to occurrence" refers to the agitations established by the occurrence of gross phenomena, owing to the absence of such tranquility.

"Agitations due to defilements" refers to the agitations arising from attachment and aversion. Regarding the second phrase: "Whatever agitations there might be regarding the perception of human beings..."

In this phrase, "dependent upon," [it means]: because of the continuity of attention, there is the subtlety and ease of the perception of formations—that "this occurrence of phenomena is not as gross as before"—which constitutes the meaning of "carita" (conduct/behavior). Thus he said, "there is merely the distress of occurrence.
The construction is: that which is the mass of defilement-distress does not exist in this perception of distress. [This refers to] the mere distress of occurrence.
The construction is: "When something remains, one understands that what exists is indeed present.

"Emptiness as arising" (*suññatā nibbatti*) means the process of occurrence (*pavatti*) is emptiness. For that which is associated with emptiness is itself empty; here, however, it is referred to as "emptiness" (*suññatā*). 177.
*Assā* means that the Blessed One’s mental activity occurred in the manner now being described. "Absolute emptiness" (*accantasuññataṃ*).
“I shall teach the state of Arahantship which is called ‘supreme and unsurpassed. Regarding the phrase “because of not attaining a distinction through the perception of forest”:
this is because by attending to [the object] as “forest, forest,” there is no attainment of a distinction such as jhāna, whereas by attending to it as “earth,” a distinction is attained.
Now, in order to clarify that very meaning by means of a simile, the passage beginning with “Just as” was spoken. Thus...
When sown in this way, rice and other crops come to fruition. "Constant practice" means regular practice; it refers to the meditation subject that is to be mastered.
Regarding the word "dependent," since the term "arisen" (*sambhūta*) is intended as the ellipsis here, he says "arisen dependent upon.
For perception has arisen dependent upon the earth.
In the earth-kasiṇa, he perceives earth, not the natural earth. "Of that" means of the earth-kasiṇa.
"By those" means by the boils and so forth. "Well-beaten" means beaten properly so that not even a trace of a wrinkle remains.
The bank of a river, lake, or the like is called a *kūla* (bank) in the sense of being the source of water; it is "elevated" (*uggata*) because of its high state.
*Viyāti* means *ukkūla*, a high place on the ground. *Vigataṃ kūlaṃ* is *vikkūla*, a low place. Therefore he said, "high and low.
"*Ekaṃ saññaṃ*" means the single perception of "earth" alone. 182.
Even though there is an absence of the signs of formations (*saṅkhāranimitta*), it is called "signless" (*animitta*) due to the absence of such signs as these.
To demonstrate these, it is said: "devoid of the sign of permanence and so forth. "Consisting of the four great elements" means dependent upon the four great elements.
"Associated with the six sense bases" means accompanied by the six sense bases, beginning with the eye base. 183.
"Insight into insight" (paṭivipassanā) refers to the further insight into phenomena. "Here" refers to the path and fruit as they have been personally realized and directly experienced.
He says, "On the noble path and in the noble fruit," in order to show the distress remaining with the substrate of clinging (*upādisesa*).

Since the substrate of defilements (*kilesūpadhi*) has been entirely abandoned, the substrate of the aggregates (*khandhūpadhi*) remains undifferentiated; the distress conditioned by that is the "distress remaining with the substrate of clinging.

For this purpose [he speaks]. Because the perception of a village is gross from the perspective of its object, while the perception of a human being is subtle, therefore, by means of the perception of a human being...

Having turned back the perception of a village. Furthermore, since even the perception of people is coarse compared to the perception of a forest—which is subtle in relation to a common object—therefore, one turns back the perception of people by means of the perception of a forest.
The reason for turning back the perception of earth and so forth has already been stated below and in other suttas. "Successively" means according to the sequence of the path.
It is called "absolute emptiness" (*accanta-suññatā*) because it is absolutely empty due to the total absence of any basis for the permanent core (*nicca-sāra*) and so forth.

(184) It is called the "fruition attainment of emptiness" (*suññatā-phala-samāpatti*) because it is the fruition of the emptiness liberation and because it is to be entered by means of the contemplation of emptiness;
thus, it is the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship that has received this name.

Because there were paccekabuddhas in the past and there will be them in the future, but at present—due to the continued existence of the Buddha’s dispensation (buddhasāsana)—paccekabuddhas do not appear;

therefore, without mentioning paccekabuddhas, it is said: "Even now, those known as Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddha. For indeed, while the Buddha’s dispensation endures, paccekabuddhas do not arise.
[They] come to be. The remainder is indeed easy to understand.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning (*Līnatthappakāsanā*) for the Commentary on the Cūḷasuññata-sutta is completed.
2. Commentary on the Mahāsuññata-sutta.

185. He is black by complexion, not by name. Regarding the phrase "a layer of straw," etc., the word "etc. includes items such as a mattress (*koccha*), a woolen rug (*cimilika*), and a wooden frame (*kaṭasāra*). "Of the monks in a group" means of those monks who are bound together in a group.
If there is no such thing as doubt, why [does the Buddha] say, "Are they many? To this he says: "Preceded by applied thought," and so forth.
In that context, "that which has applied thought as its prior part" is *vitakkapubbabhāgā*; it refers to the question. That [question] is: "Are we many here..."

The word "bhikkhū viharanti" [is a statement], whereas "vitakko" (reflection) refers to the mental intention that arose in the Blessed One at that time in the form: "Are there many bhikkhus living here?
He said—"And this particle 'nu' occurs prior to the reflection"—showing that this particle 'nu' was uttered to indicate the state of that very reflection. Even though...
While walking, having seen [the monks], he asked, "Many bhikkhus are dwelling here," and thus it was spoken by the Blessed One by way of inquiry.

Then, as the subsequent instruction beginning with, "Indeed, Ānanda, a bhikkhu does not shine who delights in company," proceeds to its conclusion, it is not called 'undetermined'; rather, it is indeed determined separately.
Having seen this and having determined it for himself, he asks in that manner for the purpose of initiating a discussion. For it has been said:
"The Tathāgatas ask even though they already know. Therefore he said, "It is said that from this... and so forth.
Just as water that has flowed out of a river plunges according to its downward slope, so too do beings converge according to their elements (dhātu).
Therefore it was said: “Living in a group is like water crossed by a river. Now, in order to demonstrate this matter in detail, it was said:

“The hells, the animal womb,” and so forth. Because the powder for rubbing with *kuruvinda* stones remains without any gaps when placed in a tube due to its fine and subtle nature, he said: “Like a tube filled with powder. Seventy-five...
"Five hundred thousand families" means exactly five hundred and seventy thousand families;
however, by way of individuals, seven crores of people lived there at that time.
Then he thought: "How so? Granted, this is the nature of the world, but it is indeed unsuitable for my teaching. Thus he spoke.
“By me,” and so forth. *Dhamma* means that which is established by its own nature. *Saṃvega* is said to be the knowledge accompanied by moral dread (*ottappa*).
However, this is not possible, because one must desire to meet [others] through such means as attending to the sick, giving exhortation, and instruction.
*Gaṇabhedana* means the separating from the company of a group.
186. *Kataparibhaṇḍan* means the mending, in the manner described, of a robe for which prior arrangements had been made. *No* means "to us. *Anattamano* means one whose mind is not satisfied.
Because it involves being together with one's own group, he says "the gathering of one's own assembly" (*sakaparisasamodhāna*).

However, here "group" (*gaṇa*) is said to mean a collection of people, as expressed by "the gathering of various people" (*nānājanasamodhāna*). It shines because of practicing according to the instructions given.

It is called *nikkhama* because it emerges from sensual desire (*kāma*); thus, it is the happiness arisen by way of such emergence. Seclusion (*paviveka*) is the withdrawal from the company of crowds and the company of defilements;
it is the happiness arisen by way of such seclusion. The happiness that brings about the subsiding of lust and the other [defilements] is the happiness of subsiding (*upasama-sukha*).
The happiness that brings about the full awakening of the Path is the happiness of full awakening (*sambodhi-sukha*). That which is to be desired is *nikāma*.
Or, one who obtains [it] is one who obtains it at will. Because one obtains it without suffering and with ease, one is called "one who obtains it without difficulty" (*adukkhalābhī*).
"Scanty" (*kasira*) means "little"; thus he said, "One who obtains it without scarcity (*akasiralābhī*) is one who obtains it abundantly.
"Occasional" (*sāmāyika*) means that liberation from defilements occurs at a specific time; because it is absolutely so, it is *sāmāyika*, where the letter *ma* has been lengthened to *ā*.
Having done so, he said: "At the moment of absorption, it is liberated from the defilements.
"Delightful" means desirable and charming due to the continuity of its factors and the continuity of its object. "Non-temporary" means absolutely liberated.

By the words "to this extent," etc., [the author] shows, through both positive and negative concomitance (anvaya and vyatireka), that for one who delights in company, this constitutes an obstacle to the attainment of distinction.

And he shows this together with an illustration. Therein, that state of being an obstacle is twofold: having as its cause the non-arising of factors conducive to purification, and having as its cause the arising of factors conducive to defilement.

Having first clarified the former by means of the passage beginning with “delighting in company,” he now clarifies the latter in order to explain the arising of hatred: “Now, the arising of hatred...”

The passage beginning with "dassento" and so forth has been stated. Just as in such passages as, "Dependent upon bone and dependent upon sinew, dependent upon skin and dependent upon flesh, the enclosed space comes to be designated simply as 'form' (rūpa)," the word *rūpa* here is a synonym for the physical body composed of the four primary elements;
thus he said, "‘Rūpa’ means the body. [And it is said: "I do not, Ānanda... [suffering, grief, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair]."

Why was this said? Is it not the case that even for those who have begun insight meditation (*vipassanā*) and whose minds are indifferent toward both body and life, there is still the maintenance of the body by way of avoiding what is unsuitable and cultivating what is suitable?
True; however, that [maintenance] is only for one who, depending on a healthy body, desires to apply himself to the accomplishment of the Dhamma—it is only by way of the accomplishment of the Dhamma.
For it is with regard to the state of being an instrument for the Dhamma that [this was said].
The maintenance of the body consists in avoiding what is unwholesome and cultivating what is wholesome, thereby engaging in practice more effectively;
such a person is not called "delighting in the body," because that [delight] must be dispelled through reflection, as it depends upon [wrong] consideration.
Regarding the phrase "Upāli the householder," here too the words "by way of attaining discipleship under the One of Ten Powers" should be supplied and connected.

187. Although seated in the midst of an assembly surrounded by a retinue through the power of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), he was nonetheless alone because of his exclusive inclination toward seclusion (*ekāntaviveka*).
By this, the Teacher demonstrates the state of being secluded through his own seclusion.

To exclude the signs corresponding to the material and immaterial [realms], it is said: "of the conditioned signs of form and so forth. Because of its exceedingly peaceful, sublime, and most profound nature...
Specifically, it is called an *ārammaṇa* (object) because it binds or fetters; that very object is "internal" (*ajjhatta*) by virtue of being included within one's own continuity (*sasantati*).
What, then, is it? He says: "Emptiness (*suññatā*) means the attainment of the fruit of emptiness.

Because it is a state of seclusion from the substrates of existence (*upadhiviveka*), the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*) is intended here as "seclusion"; thus he says, "with a mind inclined toward seclusion," and so forth. Without leaving even a mere trace of dissolution...
Because the states conducive to the taints (*āsava*) have been removed from there, it is "by means of that which has become free" (*vigatantena*);
thus, having reached their complete exhaustion, it is stated in the Canon as "by that which has become exhausted" (*byantibhūtena*). *Uyyojana* means relinquishing;
that which possesses this is *uyyojanika*, or that which urges forth or relinquishes. For not all discourse proceeds solely by way of urging forth.
It proceeds; therefore it is said, "connected with incitement.

"Like one taking oil for cooking" means that just as when cooking oil one must not let the allotted time pass, so too one should not let the duration of one's own attainment lapse. For just as a skilled physician, while cooking oil, [attends to] this and that...
Just as one who intends to prepare oil considers whether it should be cooked until firm,
or moderately cooked, or until harsh, and cooks it after observing the proper time for each, so too the Blessed One, while teaching the Dhamma,
observes the ripening of the knowledge of those to be trained; and having taught the Dhamma at the appropriate time without overstepping it, he dismisses the assembly.

And he urges [the practitioner] on with a mind inclined toward seclusion alone. Even the two types of fivefold sensory consciousness are indeed inclined toward Nibbāna by virtue of the mental consciousness being directed toward it.

For, because the Buddhas have thoroughly understood all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), even when sublime forms and so forth come into the range of their perception, the repulsiveness of other [objects] becomes manifest and stands out all the more; therefore, for one scorched by the heat of summer...
Just as water naturally flows toward a cool place, the mind flows only toward Nibbāna, because of its exceedingly peaceful and sublime nature.
(188) "Internally only" (*ajjhattameva*): here, the object of the jhāna is intended; thus he says, "only internally as a range" (*gocarajjhattameva*).
Here, "internally as one's own" (*niyakajjhatta*) refers to emptiness (*suññata*). For it is the unmastered foundational jhāna that is intended here by the term "internally as one's own."

Because specific insight is intended here, "internal" (ajjhatta) refers to one's own [body] as being devoid of life and devoid of a sentient being; the meaning is "the principle of non-self" (anattatā).
"By knowing the state of non-attainment" means by knowing: "Now my meditation subject has not entered the proper path;
it is proceeding only along a wrong track."
But why did the Blessed One, in this context, include the foundational jhāna rather than specifying only the jhānas that serve as the basis for insight?
He said: "Because of a foundational jhāna that is not well-mastered," and so forth. It does not leap forward because it is not properly concentrated.
However, he [thinks]: "Internal phenomena do not appear to me as free from tangles and free from thickets; well then, let me [attend] to external phenomena..."
“If I attend to certain formations that have appeared, the others will surely appear as well”—thus he attends to another... [and so on].
Just as by means of the foundational jhāna, so too by means of the jhāna of comprehension, one is liberated in both ways;
thus he said: “How then does he attend to the imperturbable in the formless attainments? It is not so.
"My mind does not leap forward" means that my insight-consciousness (*vipassanā-citta*), having entered the path, does not proceed.
"Only the foundational jhāna" refers to the jhāna that serves as the foundation for insight.

"It should be brought to mind again and again" means it should be repeatedly attained in order to produce sharpness and clarity in the insight. Because of its lack of subtlety when it does not proceed...
When the act of cutting no longer proceeds [in the mind], one enters into insight (vipassanā) and performs the work of sharpening it;
thus he said, "attention flows toward the meditation subject" by way of abiding in both serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā).
(189) "It succeeds for me": because there is no difference between what precedes and what follows in the course of practice, he says, "the meditation subject succeeds for me."

"By knowing. "Without losing the postures" means: having passed the time according to one's own strength so that fatigue does not arise, one maintains the postures by proceeding with the proper measure; thus, one does not lose the postures. "In all instances" refers to the instances of standing, sitting, and lying down.
Regarding the instances of conversation, however, they state specific distinctions here and there. "This was said" refers to the statement beginning with, "By this dwelling," and so forth.
190. Since sensual thoughts and the like share the same nature as gross sensual lust and ill will, it is said: “Having explained two paths by means of the abandoning of thought.
In the phrase “among the strands of sensual pleasure,” the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*).

The expression “on account of some cause for the arising of defilements” is stated with reference to the specific cause for the arising of defilements in that particular individual; otherwise, all five strands of sensual pleasure are indeed causes for the arising of defilements.

"It occurs" means "occurrence"; thus he says, "from occurrence. Furthermore, because that [occurrence] belongs to the mind (*citta*) and not to a sentient being (*satta*), it is stated in the Pāḷi as "of the mind" (*cetaso*).
The letter *m* is for the purpose of euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*), and the vowel *e* has been changed to *a*;
thus he says, "this being so, this..."

191. "Latent tendencies" (anusaya) refers to the threefold latent tendency—namely, the latent tendency of conceit, the latent tendency of attachment to existence, and the latent tendency of ignorance—which are all abandoned by the path of Arahantship.

"In the manner already stated" means according to the method described thus: "Immediately after that path, there is the fruit; emerging from the fruit, one who reviews it knows the state of their abandonment, and through that knowing, he is possessed of clear comprehension."

It comes from the wholesome, thus it is "conducive to the wholesome" (kusala-āyatika); those [states] which have this quality are "conducive to the wholesome. Therefore he said, "come from the wholesome.
Furthermore, that quality of theirs being conducive to the wholesome occurs both by way of decisive support (upanissaya) and by way of co-nascence (sahajāta);
to show both of these, he said, "namely as follows," and so forth.
But since among the aforementioned states some are mundane (*lokiya*) and some are supramundane (*lokuttara*), he asks: "Why then are they specifically called 'supramundane'?
He replies: "They are superior (*uttara*) and distinguished (*visiṭṭha*) in the world.

By this he shows that the jhānas and so forth are called supramundane because of their preeminence among mundane states, not because of crossing over the world. Whatever exalted consciousness (*mahaggata-citta*) there may be belongs to Māra.

It is not its object because it does not belong to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*), let alone being a basis for insight (*vipassanā*) with its defilements thoroughly washed away; thus he said, "it is not possible to know it.
There is one benefit to devotion to meditation: the acquisition of discourses on the Dhamma that are conducive [to it].
Why was it said, "for the sake of this"? It means: for the sake of the entire Sutta. Why was it stated, "by way of what is conducive and what is not conducive"?
Is it not the case that the ten bases of discourse were presented by way of what is suitable (*sappāya*)? True, this is so;

however, because they were presented by way of discourse on what is suitable preceded by the mental advertence (*āvajjana*) to what is unsuitable (*asappāya*), it is said: "They were presented by way of both the suitable and the unsuitable.

As for the phrase "by way of the learning of what has been heard" (*sutapariyatti*): although those ten bases of discourse do not appear there in their own form, they are included within the *Sutta*, *Geyya*, and so forth; therefore, it is said: "By way of the learning of what has been heard."
It is said, "They have arrived. Because they have arrived in their own forms by way of fulfillment, they should be explained while remaining in this place.
"Meaning" (attha) refers to the general meaning.
193. "Anuāvattanti" means they turn toward [the teacher] again and again, facing him, and act in accordance with him through such acts as paying homage.
“Craving for infatuation” means the mode of infatuation with the conditions. Since craving proceeds by way of that mode as a longing, he says:
“it longs for; it sets [the mind] in motion. “By the calamity of the defilements” means by the calamity known as the defilements.
For defilements are called “calamities” because they cause great harm to sentient beings. By that which has arisen within oneself...
"Affliction by defilements" means an affliction caused by a pupil is "pupil-affliction," and an affliction of the holy life is "affliction of the practitioner.

By the phrase "the same method applies to the other afflictions as well," he extends this principle [to all cases]. What has been described is death in terms of qualities (*guṇamaraṇa*), not death in terms of physical life.
"One who gains little" means one who obtains only a small measure of distinguished attainments. "Thus it was said" refers to the aforementioned affliction of the practitioner.
It is said to be "more productive of painful results and more productive of bitter results" in this way.

For the calamity of teacher and pupil is mentioned by way of non-Buddhist systems, whereas the calamity of those living the holy life is mentioned by way of the Dispensation. Indeed, in a poorly proclaimed Dhamma and Vinaya, wrong practice is not a great offense because of the laxity of effort in one's adherence to what is false; but in a well-proclaimed [Dhamma and Vinaya]...

Misconduct regarding the Dhamma and Vinaya is a great reproach, because it causes one to fall outside of the great benefit. Therefore he said, "But in the Dispensation," and so forth. (196) "Therefore" (*tasmā*) refers back to what precedes;
