it is a reference to the preceding matter by way of its being the cause for that meaning.

Thus he said, "Because," and so forth. One who possesses a friend is "one who has friends" (*mittavā*); the state of being such is "friendliness" (*mittavatā*), and [the following is] by means of that. By way of friendship...
He said, "by means of the practice toward friends" (*mittapaṭipattiyā*). The same method applies here as well to the phrase "by being an enemy.
By the words "even a mere misdeed or a slight transgression," he shows that one who violates other [precepts] does so all the more easily.
He said, "I shall not practice in such a way," referring to the exertion for the welfare of disciples through exhortation and instruction.
"Raw" (*āmaka*) refers to an unbaked clay vessel. "I will not deal with you in that way" means:
like a potter with raw vessels, I will not deal with you merely by making you known [to others]. "Having expelled" (*niggaṇhitvā*) means having driven out.
Even mundane qualities (*lokiyaguṇa*) are intended here as the very "essence" (*sāra*), because they serve as the foundation for supramundane qualities (*lokuttaraguṇa*).
The remainder is indeed easy to understand.
The Elucidation of the Obscure Points in the Commentary on the Mahāsuññata Sutta is completed.
3. Commentary on the Acchariyabbhuta Sutta.
197. Since particles (*nipāta*) are substitutes for case-endings (*vibhattipatirūpaka*), they illuminate the respective meanings of those particular endings as appropriate.
Here, the word *yattha* functions as the nominative case; the word *hi* has the sense of cause (*hetuattha*); and the word *nāma* has the sense of wonder (*acchariyattha*).
Because these three words indicate the sense of wonder, it is stated that "it is a particle in the sense of wonder. However, this is [only] from one perspective.
The three terms [are explained as follows]. For he will say: “*Yatra* is a word for the future by way of being a particle.
The word *papañca* has been explained above. Regarding the phrase *chinnavaṭume*:

because the cycle of all defilements (*kilesavaṭṭa*) and the cycle of unwholesome kamma have been cut off, and because the cycle of result (*vipākavaṭṭa*) will be discussed below, he says: “*Vaṭu* refers to the cycle of wholesome and unwholesome kamma.”
“By way of a particle (*nipāta*)” means by connection with the word *yattha*. “A term for the future” is said because it resembles a term for the future;
for a term for the future is that which expresses a future meaning, and here the meaning is past.
“He recollected” is said with reference to the state of having recollected—because the verbal construction “he will not recollect” has the future as its object. But when, by them...
Even after the discourse had been delivered by the bhikkhus, the Blessed One continued to recollect those Buddhas.
"Of khattiya birth" and so forth refers to those born into an unadulterated khattiya lineage that has flourished from generation to generation. "Brahma-birth" means brahmin birth.
The same method applies to their clans (*gotra*). "By mundane and supramundane virtue" means by virtue produced through the perfections (*pāramitā*).
Because of the Buddha’s unique qualities, by means of his mundane and supramundane virtue which is not shared with others;
thus, by performing a separate reflection on each of the virtues without exception, he will recollect them as “one of such virtue. This same method applies to the remaining [qualities].

Just as the factors conducive to true knowledge are the states associated with true knowledge, so too are the factors belonging to concentration—the states associated with concentration—such as mindfulness, energy, and the rest.
He said: "Because the factors belonging to the side of concentration were already included below, the 'dwelling' (vihāra) was also included.
Therefore, it is stated that "this" and so forth refers to the dwelling intended here as being distinct from the factors belonging to the side of concentration.
Or, just as mundane and supramundane concentration and wisdom are comprised within the eight attainments, insight, the path, and the fruit.
Although the phrases "of such nature" (*evaṃdhammā*) and "of such wisdom" (*evaṃpaññā*) were already mentioned below,
they are mentioned again here as "thus liberated" (*evaṃvimuttā*) by way of the specific mode of activity consisting in liberation from their respective opposites. Likewise,

although the qualities belonging to the side of concentration (*samādhipakkhadhammā*) were mentioned under the phrase "of such nature," [they are mentioned again] by way of their own specific mode of activity known as the divine abidings (*dibbavihāra*), the brahma-abidings (*brahmavihāra*), the imperturbable abidings (*āneñjavihāra*), and the noble abidings (*ariyavihāra*).
If it were said that [the term] "dwelling thus" is taken again here [in the phrase] "having depended," there would be no contradiction.

Even at the time when the states of fruition (phala-dhamma) are occurring, the subsiding of the defilements (kilesa) is not produced by the power of those [fruition-states] themselves; rather, it is because the defilements have been eradicated by the Noble Path (ariyamagga).
Thus he said: "Because they have arisen with the defilements subsided through the power of the Path."
That which abandons is called the "abandoner" and "liberated from what is to be abandoned" because of its state of being dissociated.
When speaking in terms of the analysis of abandonment, how can Nibbāna—which is not an abandoner—be said to be liberated? Precisely because it is dissociated.
For Nibbāna is by its very nature entirely dissociated and detached from all defilements, standing at a vast distance from them; therefore, its liberation...
Because it has emerged from that [suffering], it is called "emancipation," "liberation," and "abandonment"; thus he said, "Nibbāna," and so forth.
(199) These are the marvelous and wonderful qualities of the Tathāgata, not within the domain of disciples; however, you have heard my teaching.
Thus, placing the responsibility solely upon the Elder, he said, "May this appear even more extensively to you."
Regarding the phrase "mindful and clearly comprehending" (*sato sampajāno*):

although the state of clear comprehension (*sampajañña*) is obtained here according to the distinction of time, it is stated as "two kinds of clear comprehension," etc., in order to show it by way of its classification into modes of movement. As for the expression "taking eight boons":
how does a deity give a boon, and how is that which is being given to another successfully acquired by that other? It is solely through the power of kamma.

For if that karma has already gained its opportunity such that its fruit ripens by means of that [devata], then there arises the conventional expression that "the boon was given by the devata" and "it was obtained by the other.
Furthermore, the boons wished for by another should be understood as a specific application (payoga) that serves as a condition for the ripening of the karma.
Even though those [boons] are not invariably [determinative] in the process of ripening, [they still function as conditions].
The deities of little power do not know whether this aspiration of his will be fulfilled or not; however, Sakka, being wise, knows some of them.
Therefore it is said: “While receiving the eight boons granted by Sakka out of confidence,” and so forth.
In the phrase “in the first impulsion-moment” (paṭhamajavanavāre), it refers to the very first impulsion-moment that has arisen; for that [moment] is proximate to the rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi).
He is unaware because he does not know [the process] due to his attachment to the state of a deva, since he is arising [therein].
There is a cognition uncommon to other deities because it proceeds from the second impulsion-moment onwards.
By the words "other deities" and so forth, the Bodhisatta’s state of being established in clear comprehension (*sampajañña*) therein is shown by way of contrast.
He contemplates it. "They pass away by cutting off their food"—this is said with reference to those corrupted by play (*khiḍḍāpadosika*).
Even for others who have fallen into infatuation with divine enjoyments, there is indeed a lack of clear comprehension while they remain.
Is there no such object? [No,] for those gods, depending upon an object that is so sublime and exquisite...

They even go so far as to cut off their own food when they are fainting; why then, does he raise this objection to suggest that such a sublime and excellent object of perception does not exist for the Bodhisatta?
It is to reveal the power of the Bodhisatta’s clear comprehension (*sampajañña*).
For wherever the Bodhisatta is reborn, there he surpasses other beings by ten distinctions.
Not only was he a deity there, but even so, it is this quality of being "mindful and clearly comprehending" that is stated here as the marvelous phenomenon.

200. Longevity in a state of rebirth comes about through the power of wisdom; and since the Bodhisatta possesses great wisdom, it is with the intention that he must possess such longevity in each and every existence that [the question is asked]: "In his other existences, what..."
He challenges him, saying, "He does not remain for the full span of his life. The other admits, "Yes, he does not remain," and states the reason for this with the words, "For at another time...
Death by resolution occurs through the power of resolving, "I shall not exist here.
Indeed, through the perfection of the qualities of the perfections (*pāramitā*), in various successive existences, by means of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*)...

Because their mental continuum has been distinguished by the attenuation of self-attachment and the loftiness of great compassion toward sentient beings, and because their resolve has attained a state of sharpness and clarity, the intentions of Bodhisattvas are fulfilled;
they possess mastery over both their minds and their actions. Therefore, wherever they are reborn, the perfections (pāramīs) flourish perfectly within them.
Having passed away according to the manner described, they are reborn there.
For indeed, this Great Being, having passed away in various births within this very eon without losing his meditative absorption (jhāna), was reborn in the Brahma-world;
after remaining there for only a short time, he passed away from there and was reborn here. Therefore it is said: "This passing away does not happen to others."
By the phrase "because all the perfections have been fulfilled," he shows that there is no such thing as passing away while remaining fixed in a particular state due to a lack of further purpose.
Furthermore, just as in his final existence there was the manifestation of great prosperity— resembling divine fortune and preceded by the emergence of the four great treasures—
so too, for one who has become a Buddha, there arises an attainment unique to him and not shared by others, by way of incomparable giving and other virtues.

And it should be understood that, after this, there is no further experience of divine excellence for the Great Being other than by virtue of the accumulation of merit undertaken with such resolve as to remain for the full extent of his lifespan. For this is the natural law (dhammatā) here:
it is according to the reckoning of human years, not the reckoning of celestial years. "Portents" refers to the portents preceding his passing away.

Regarding the phrase "without fading" (*amilāyitvā*): it should be understood that by the very mention of "unfading," the excellence of color, the excellence of fragrance, and the excellence of beauty of those garlands are also demonstrated.
Because there is not even a trace of external or internal dust or grime, the garments on the bodies of the devas remain at all times perfectly pure and radiant.

He said: "The same principle applies to clothing as well. That which is neither cold nor hot is such that, by way of counteracting the cold, it does not produce excessive heat that must be endured, nor does it—having itself become harsher—overpower [the body] and cause perspiration;
such is what is neither cold nor hot. At that time means at the aforementioned time near death.
"By way of drops and drops" means that sweat is released drop by drop, like pellets of urine.

"Brokenness of the teeth" (*khaṇḍicca*) is the state of the teeth being broken. "Graying of the hair" (*pālicca*) is the state of the hair becoming white. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), one includes the wrinkling of the skin.
The meaning is that the person's physical form becomes exhausted, but not specifically through broken teeth, graying hair, and so forth. "Disgusted" (*ukkaṇṭhita*) means a lack of delight.
This is because she stands before him providing, in particular, exceedingly magnificent and especially desirable riches that arise one after another.

"Only the wise" means only those deities endowed with intelligence. Just as deities, having reflected, "By what kind of meritorious deed was this person born here who has just been reborn?", come to know, "By such-and-such a meritorious deed was he reborn here," so too...
He said, "Those of great merit," and so forth, because they indeed know some other merit performed by themselves in past existences; thus they are called "of great merit.

They are not perceived because of the extreme length of time, due to the limit of the supreme lifespan. It is "not leading out" (*aniyyānika*) because it does not bring about the transcendence [of suffering] for beings, owing to their lack of being fit vessels.
Beings are said not to possess the supreme lifespan because of the prevalence of evil; thus he said: "For at that time, beings..."
“They are those whose defilements have become excessive. Here it may be asked: “Why do the Fully Enlightened Ones arise only in the human world, and not in the worlds of the gods or the Brahmās?
First of all, they do not arise in the world of the gods because there is no opportunity for living the holy life (brahmacariya) there, and likewise because [the conditions] are not extraordinary.
For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, possess extraordinary qualities; such is their nature of possessing extraordinary qualities.
It is not manifest to those remaining in a divine state as it is to those who have become human.
For when the Perfectly Enlightened One is seen in his state as a deva, the world perceives the Buddha’s majesty only as the majesty of a deva, and not as the majesty of a Buddha;
such being the case, one does not resolve upon the Perfectly Enlightened One, does not gain confidence in him, and does not relinquish the grasping at the notion that he is a mere lord or a creation.

And because the divine state of existence persists for a long time, one is not released from the doctrine of partial eternalism (*ekaccasassatavāda*). The same principle applies here to the statement, "They do not arise in the Brahma-world.
For the Blessed Buddhas arise only in the happy destination of humans, and not in the happy destination of devas, in order to liberate beings from such misconceptions;
even when arising in the happy destination of humans, [they do so for that purpose].
They are not of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*), because if they were of spontaneous birth, they could not avoid the faults already mentioned.

Furthermore, just as it is desirable to establish a framework of the Dhamma for the sake of those to be guided by the Dhamma, so too it is desirable to establish the bodily relics (*dhātu*) for the sake of those to be guided by the relics.
For the bodily relics of those of spontaneous birth do not remain after their final Nibbāna.

Therefore, they are not of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*). And in their final existence, the Great Bodhisattvas, in order to manifest the human condition, even take wives and remain in the midst of the household until they see the face of a son.
Even though the perfections (*pāramitā*) of virtue, renunciation, wisdom, and so forth have reached full maturity, they do not go forth [into homelessness].
What is the use of such inquiry into the reasons? For this is the practice consistently followed by all Buddhas, namely:
That full awakening occurs only for those who have become human beings and not for those who have become gods—this is the natural law (*dhammatā*) in this regard.
For likewise, even the Great Resolve (*mahābhinīhāra*) directed toward that goal succeeds only for those who have become human beings, and not for others.
But why is it that Perfectly Enlightened Ones arise only in Jambudvīpa and not in the other continents? On this point, some say:

—“Because the ground of the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), which is not overcome by the earth, which is endowed with the majesty of the Buddhas, and which is an immovable place, arises only in Jambudīpa, therefore [the Buddhas] arise only in Jambudīpa”; and likewise, because for others as well, those places that are not abandoned are found only there.
This, however, is our own preference in this matter: because for the Great Bodhisattvas of previous Buddhas...

The aspiration for the enlightenment of a disciple (*sāvakabodhi*) by those who are disciples of enlightenment (*sāvakabodhisatta*), as well as the accumulation and maturation of the perfections of a disciple (*sāvakapāramī*), succeed only here in Jambudvīpa within this world-system (*cakkavāḷa*)—which serves as the Buddha-field for Paccekabuddhas—and not elsewhere.

Furthermore, the appearance of a Buddha is for the purpose of training those to be trained (*veneyya*); thus, it depends upon specific individuals to be trained, such as the chief disciples and others.
Buddhas arise only in one Jambudīpa, not in the other continents. And this principle is the established custom of all Buddhas;
thus, the arising of those Supreme Beings occurs in that very place, and it should be understood that they proceed from one to another through mutual dependence, like the wheels of prosperity.
Therefore he said: "Buddhas do not arise in the three [other] continents; only in Jambudīpa."
"He sees the island as it is being produced. By this method, the reason for the restriction of the teaching should also be stated.
Now, the khattiya clan is honored by the world because it is worthy of worship even by the brahmins.
He saw the clan [thinking], "A king shall be my father," because the clan must be designated by way of the father. "For ten months and seven days more"—this refers to the duration.
By this he knew his own absence of obstacles and her experience of divine excellence in the Tusita realm.

"Those deities" refers to the deities of the ten-thousandfold world-system (*dasasahassicakkavāḷa*). But how did they know the Bodhisatta’s fulfillment of the perfections (*pārami*) and his future state as a Perfectly Enlightened One (*sambuddha*)?
It was by virtue of the deities of great power; for the most part, [they know it]...

And those deities are partakers of the realization [of the Dhamma]. For indeed, on many occasions during the Blessed One’s distribution of the gift of the Dhamma, there was an assembly of deities residing in ten thousand world-systems.
"I am passing away" he knows, because through the mental processes associated with knowledge that are proximate to death, the state of being present at the moment of death is clearly understood.

The death-consciousness does not know [the rebirth-linking consciousness] because of the brevity of the moment of the death-consciousness. For that reason, it is indeed outside the range even of the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cutūpapātañāṇa*).
The same principle applies to the rebirth-linking consciousness as well. "The sequence of adverting" (*āvajjanapariyāya*) means the order of adverting.
Since it is not possible to determine the object by merely adverting to it once, therefore that same object [must be adverted to] a second time.
And having adverted for the third time, it is determined; and here, by the heading of "adverting," the entire course of impulsion is included.

Therefore he said: “He will know during the second and third courses of consciousness alone. Because he knows from several mental moments prior to the moment of death, “Death is near for me,” it is said:
“At the very moment of death, he understands: ‘I am passing away. Regarding rebirth-linking:
However, because it has not occurred previously, the rebirth-linking consciousness does not know [the details]. From the moment of the arising of attachment, one understands:
"In such-and-such a place, rebirth was taken by me. This same meaning has already been stated: that one knows from the second impulsion onwards.
"At that time" means at the time of taking rebirth-linking. Regarding the statement "the ten-thousandfold world-system shakes," the cause for the shaking is explained below.

This has already been stated. Since the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who possess great compassion, are for the most part filled with joy because they are intent on providing welfare and happiness to sentient beings, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that their rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) occurs through the first great resultant consciousness (*mahāvipākacitta*).

However, the Elder Mahāsīva [argues] that although the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who possess great compassion, are intent on providing welfare and happiness to sentient beings, [the rebirth-linking does not occur through a resultant consciousness].
But because they have a disposition for seclusion, are inclined toward the cessation of formations (*visaṅkhāra*), and are frequently characterized by equanimity toward all formations,
rebirth-linking is said to be taken by means of the fifth great resultant consciousness.
"From the seventh day prior to the full moon" means from the seventh day before the full moon.
"From the ninth day of the bright fortnight" is the meaning. "On the seventh day" refers to the full moon of Āsāḷhī.
"This dream" refers to the dream of the form that is now being described. "Their queens" means the queens of the Great Kings.
And furthermore, it was a male embryo, not a female embryo; "a son shall be born to you"—this much only did those brahmins [say].

They spoke according to the method of the science of dreams. However, regarding the passage beginning with "If he shall dwell in a household," they proclaimed the future matter exactly as it was, through the intervention of deities.
Regarding the phrase "descent into the womb" (*gabbhāvakkanti*): here, "womb" (*gabbha*) refers to the mother's belly; "descent" (*avakkanti*) is the arising therein. Thus far.
The descent into the womb lasts until he emerges. He emerges while still remaining [in the womb], like a preacher descending from his Dhamma-seat.
(201) Since it is said that "he enters" (*okkamati*) using a term for the present as if it were occurring in the immediate vicinity of the present, he says:
"the meaning is 'he has entered' (*okkanto hoti*). "It is thus": there is his clear comprehension in the manner just described. It is not [present] while he is entering.
Because the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) is difficult to discern. Thus it has been said: "The mind of rebirth-linking does not know.
Or, it is immeasurable because it extends over ten thousand world-systems (cakkavāḷa). It is sublime because of its exceedingly radiant nature.
"Devānubhāva" means the power and radiance of the devas; for the radiance and light of the devas prevails, but not their sovereignty.
Therefore he said, “of the devas,” and so forth.
It is *agha* because it cannot be struck by anything such as trees or shrubs; it is *abādhā* (unobstructed). Therefore he said, “perpetually open.
It is *asaṃvutā* (uncovered) because it is not closed off by anything below or above. Therefore he said, “without support even below. Therein, by the word *pi* (even),...

Just as the intermediate spaces between worlds (lokantarika) are unconfined because there is no earth below to cover the water, so too, above, they are shown to be unconfined and without support due to the absence of celestial mansions (devavimāna), as in the case of the world-systems (cakkavāḷa).

They are called "darknesses" (andhakāra) because darkness exists therein. Visual consciousness (cakkhuviññāṇa) does not arise there due to the absence of light, not because of a defect in the eye. Likewise...
For it is said: “By that radiance, they recognize one another.
At the time of midday for those dwelling in Jambudīpa, half of the solar disk appears as setting to the inhabitants of Pubbavideha, and as rising to the inhabitants of Aparagoyāna;
the same applies to the remaining continents. Thus he said: “They appear simultaneously in the three continents.”
Otherwise, however, it appears simultaneously over only two continents.
By this same method, the dispelling of darkness for nine hundred thousand yojanas in each direction should also be understood.
"They do not suffice by their own light" means they are unable to illuminate by means of their own radiance. In the space reaching up to the summit of Mount Yugandhara...
Regarding "from wandering," it is said: "They wander through the middle of the Cakkavāḷa mountain.
"Vāvaṭā" means those who are attempting to seize [them] for the purpose of eating. "Viparivattitvā" means having turned over.
"Chijjitvā" means having been released from the place where they were stuck due to fainting, or having been cut off by way of the severing of limbs and members. "Accantakhāre" means...
It may be said that "extreme saltiness" is mentioned with reference to the state of extreme cold resulting from the absence of the heat of sunlight.

For that water which remains for the duration of an eon (*kappa*), poured down by great clouds that bring about prosperity and supports the earth, cannot possibly be as salty as the water that destroys the eon;
if it were so, even the earth would dissolve. Or else, by the power of their evil karma, [the water] for those *petas* becomes like natural water.
It is said, “in water that is extremely alkaline,” because at that time that water undergoes a transformation into an alkaline state, just as saliva undergoes a transformation into a state of phlegm.
“On all sides” means from every part, in all six directions.
“By way of the four Great Kings” means by virtue of their common status as the four Great Kings, beginning with Vessavaṇa.
203. "By her very nature" means that, without having to take [the vow] in the presence of another, she was endowed with virtue by her own nature alone, having resolved it spontaneously.
"Among humans" is said with reference to the ordinary conduct [of beings]: "In a human woman, a mind characterized by the desire for a male may arise toward human males.
However, even among the devas, such a thought did not arise at all in the mother of the Bodhisatta.

Just as, through the power of the Bodhisatta, no thought of sexual desire arose in the mind of the Bodhisatta’s mother, so too, by his very power, she could not be approached by any man; thus it was said: "Her feet did not move;
she was bound as if by a divine chain."

Previously it was stated that "a mind associated with the strands of sensual pleasure does not arise," yet later it is stated that "she sports, provided and endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure.
How is this not mutually contradictory? To this he says, "Previously," and so forth.
"The negation of the basis" means the prohibition of the basis for unchaste conduct. Therefore he said, "by way of the man's intention."
“Acquisition of an object” means the acquisition of the objects of the fivefold sensual pleasures, such as visible forms and so forth.
204. “Fatigue” means exhaustion. For at that time, even the heaviness and rigidity of the body do not exist for her.
It was said, “She sees what has entered within her womb”; from what point onward does she see it? He says: “From the stage of the *kalala* and so forth.”
"Having passed beyond," and so forth. He himself states the purpose for seeing; because that [purpose] is absent, he does not see during the stages of the *kalala* and so on.
"By the son" means by one who is young, weak, and lying on his back. The passage beginning with "That which belongs to the mother" is stated according to the natural course of events.
For even compared to the womb of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*), the womb of a Bodhisattva receives special protection due to its accumulation of merit.
Because of its preeminence, the Bodhisatta’s mother, having become one whose diet and conduct were exceedingly suitable, carefully tended him.
"Facing east" means facing the mother's front. Now, in order to show both the internal and external causes for the [Bodhisatta] being visible while remaining within the womb, it is said:
"Karma performed in the past," and so forth. "Of her" refers to the queen. "The place" (vatthu) means...

Regarding the womb: because there is no obstruction of light—due to the womb of the Bodhisatta’s mother being like a layer of crystal or a mass of clouds—the Bodhisatta’s mother can see the Bodhisatta within her womb.
But does the Bodhisatta likewise see his mother and other forms before him? No, he says: "But the Bodhisatta," and so forth. Why?
But since one does not see even when the eye and light are present, he said: "For visual consciousness does not arise within the womb.
Just like inhalation and exhalation, visual consciousness also does not arise there due to the absence of the corresponding attention (*tajjā-samannāhāra*).
205. Just as other women, having given birth, die while being overcome by such a disease, [so too does this woman].
Furthermore, while the Bodhisatta was in the womb, no disease arose in the Bodhisatta’s mother;

she passed away solely through the exhaustion of her lifespan, as this matter has already been explained above. He states the reason for this with the words beginning "the place inhabited by the Bodhisatta.
"Having removed" means having led her away from the position of chief queen. "Is not able to protect" means...
If she does not properly attend to the care of her womb, the fetus becomes subject to many afflictions.

"The physical basis is pure" means that the seat of the womb is thoroughly cleansed. The descent of the Bodhisatta into the womb during the third stage of the mother's middle age is also included within the contemplation of the limit of her lifespan, because it avoids the physical changes that arise with the onset of old age.
However, the transformation arising from the nature of a woman is pacified by the very power of the Bodhisatta.
"Born seven months" means born in the seventh month from the moment of conception; because of his extreme delicacy, he was not able to endure cold or heat.
One born eight months is certainly more developed in limb than one born seven months, yet certain parts of the skin—
Those attaining consciousness cannot endure the impact; therefore, that [embryo] does not live. However, they say that for one born seven months, those [consciousnesses] have not yet arisen.
"Remaining indeed" means remaining precisely in a state free from suffering; for because of the intensity of suffering, that [suffering]—
Other women, unable to endure [the labor], give birth while sitting or lying down. "Upavijaññā" means those who have reached the time of delivery.
"All the inhabitants of the city" refers to those living in the six cities, such as Devadaha and others, which surround Kapilavatthu.
"The deities receive him first" means: "We ourselves shall be the first to receive this Great Man, the Lord of the World."
The Suddhāvāsa Brahmas, whose taints are exhausted, receive [the text] from the beginning, manifesting their own joy as they have conceived profound reverence and esteem.
"Sūtivessantī" means wearing the guise of a midwife. "Some" refers to the residents of the Uttaravihāra monastery. "Like the eye of a fish" is said by way of its appearance. 206.
"By means of a leather thong" means a thong made by sewing together deerskins. "Of great majesty" means of great power. "Of great renown" means having a large retinue and a wide-spread reputation.
"Bhaggavibhaggā" means that by emerging from the narrow passage, they have become as if broken and shattered;
by this, he shows their lack of solidity. "Being unattached" means being unclinging and unbound anywhere in the womb or the birth canal.
"By water" means he emerges unsmeared by the water contained within the womb.
Because for such a being smeared [with impurities], there is an absence therein of water, mud, and so forth.
Indeed, through the power of the Bodhisatta’s merit, from the moment of taking rebirth-linking, that place remains pure, like a most fragrant perfumed chamber, wafting the scent of sandalwood.
"Water-whirlpools" refers to masses of water.

207. "Muhuttajāto" means having been born for a moment, being only a mere moment old. "Anudhāriyamāne" means being led along in accordance with [the mother's] inclination. "Āgatāneva" means having already arrived at that place. "Anekasākha" refers to a diamond set with hundreds of facets made of jewels.
"Sahassamaṇḍala" refers to a diamond with many thousands of facets established upon those [lower ones]. "Marū" refers to the gods.
"But it should not be viewed thus" is said because the surveying of the directions was performed even before the seven steps were taken. Therefore he said:
“‘The Great Being’ and so forth. ‘Like a single courtyard’: by virtue of being open, they became like a single courtyard, similar to the courtyards of monasteries and the courtyards of cells.
‘There is no one even equal to you’: they said this because there is no one here even equal to you in order to see what is distinguished;
how much less anyone superior? ‘Foremost of all’: most excellent. This is a synonym for ‘exertion’ (padhāna).”
For here, the word "first" (paṭhama) refers to this. Therefore he said, "the others," and so forth. And in this context, while the highly influential deities speak thus, how do the others speak?

Simply by seeing the majesty of the Great Being. For to the highly influential deities, just as the majesty of the Great Being was manifest, the majesty of those similar to him was also directly perceived. As for the others, however—
Having heard their words, those who believed and inferred accordingly spoke thus.
Demonstrating that the very acts of the Bodhisatta immediately after birth were the precursors to specific attainments, he said, "And herein," and so forth.
Therein, "establishing" refers to the acquisition of the four bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*).
The preliminary sign [of his birth] was due to the successful establishment in the supramundane states by way of the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*).

His facing toward the north was a preliminary sign of the world’s crossing over. His walking seven steps was a preliminary sign of proceeding toward the seven factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) and so forth.
His holding up of the pure white umbrella was a preliminary sign of holding up the perfectly pure umbrella of liberation (*vimutti*).
The five insignia of royalty are a premonitory sign of being surrounded by the qualities of the fivefold liberation;

the surveying of the unobstructed quarters is a premonitory sign of unobstructed knowledge; the statement beginning with “I am the foremost” is a premonitory sign of setting in motion the irreversible Wheel of Dhamma;
and the proclamation that “this is my last birth,” expressing the absence of future birth, is a premonitory sign of the state of non-attachment... [and so forth].
It should be understood that for each specific distinction to be attained in the future, its respective sign is to be regarded as an "infallible sign" (*avyabhicārī-nimitta*).
The phrase "not yet come" (*na āgato*) is stated with reference to the state of not having arrived according to the sequence (*anupubbī*) that will be explained in this sutta and elsewhere.
"Having brought forward" (*āharitvā*) means it should be illustrated by bringing it forward according to the method found in various suttas and commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
The statement "the ten-thousandfold world-system shook" was spoken here, even though it is not included in the Pāḷi text, in order to show that it is the root of the wonders that will be described;
other similar cases should be understood in this same way. "That" refers to the lute bound with strings and the drum bound with leather;
this is merely an illustration of the fivefold musical ensemble, or else the word "and" (ca) should be understood as including the others as well.
"Broke" means they broke precisely at the places where they were fastened to the feet. "Vanished" means they subsided.

"Illuminated by their own splendor" means they became exceedingly radiant, lit up by their own light. "Did not flow" means they did not stream. "The wind did not blow" means a harsh wind did not blow;
however, a gentle and pleasant wind blew, bringing happiness to sentient beings. Those things situated on the earth...
They were unable to remain in their high positions. "Endowed with a favorable season" means endowed with a season characterized by being neither too hot nor too cold.
Placing the left hand upon the chest and making a sound by clapping the broad right palm is "apphoṭana.
Releasing a sound from the mouth by whistling is "seḷana. "There was a single row of banners"—here, the word *iti* has the sense of "and so forth" (*ādi*).
Because of that, the gods rained down a rain of various flowers and fragrant blossoms; while the sun was shining, the stars shone;
clear and serene water welled up from the earth; creatures dwelling in holes and burrows emerged from their lairs;
even greed, hatred, and delusion became diminished; dust on the earth subsided; and unpleasant odors [vanished].

The summary of these events should be understood as follows: darkness vanished, a divine fragrance wafted through the air, the gods possessing form appeared before humans in their own visible forms, and there was no longer any passing away or rebirth among sentient beings.
Furthermore, all thirty-two omens that had arisen at the time of the Great Resolve occurred then in their entirety.

"In that case too" means that this state of being a prior sign (pubbanimitta) should be understood as applying to those very events such as the earthquake and so forth, and not only to the standing and other postures of one newly born;

this is the intended meaning. It is a prior sign for the attainment of omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa) because it shakes all that is to be known, including the doctrines of the founders of other sects.
Even without being prompted by anyone else, [these signs occurred] in this very single world-system (cakkavāḷa).
The gathering together of those who were not even prompted by anyone, having assembled all at once, is a premonitory sign of receiving the Dhamma;
the first reception by the deities is a premonitory sign of attaining the divine abodes (*dibbavihāra*);
and the subsequent reception by humans is a premonitory sign of attaining the imperturbable abode (*āneñjavihāra*), due to the quality of remaining unshakable in that very place.
The sounding of lutes without instruction from another, but by oneself alone, is the omen for the attainment of the successive meditative abidings.

The sounding of drums is the omen for the proclamation of the Dhamma-drum, which is capable of making itself heard to an assembly extending to the limits of the world-system, and for the sound of the drum of the Deathless.
The severing of fetters and the like is the omen for the severing of the bonds of conceit.

The "foretoken" (*pubbanimitta*): reaching a good port is a foretoken for the attainment of the differentiation of knowledge regarding meanings and so forth, corresponding to those very meanings and so forth.

"By the flavor of Nibbāna" means by the flavor of the extinguishing of the defilements (*kilesa*). "Of the state of having a single flavor" refers to the Teaching (*sāsana*) which possesses a single flavor everywhere.
To the question, "What is the foretoken for the non-blowing of the wind? he says: "For the shattering of the sixty-two types of views."

The departure of birds from their unstable and shifting perches in the sky and elsewhere for the sake of reaching the earth is a precursor to sentient beings abandoning such false attachments and taking refuge in the Triple Gem with their very lives. The playful frolicking of deities through clapping and other gestures,
as well as their manifestation of joy, arises from the attainment of bliss and the awakening to the true nature of phenomena (dhamma-sabhāva) through the realization of the state of existence.
It is a premonitory sign. Regarding "the raining down of the force of the Dhamma": it is a premonitory sign for the raining down of the nectar of the Dhamma by the force of the knowledge of teaching.

The experience of the bliss of the path and fruit produced by taking as a basis the jhāna obtained through mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*) is the acquisition of the nectar of mindfulness directed to the body;
and because that body brings about bliss that is free from distress, the absence of oppression by hunger and thirst is called its premonitory sign.

“Garlanded with the wreaths of the noble banners” means this is a premonitory sign of being garlanded by the wreaths of the noble path and enlightenment factors for the world including the devas. As for what has not been explicitly mentioned here, that is easily understood.
“Here” refers to this place where it occurs in the passage beginning with “Just born. It has already been answered; therefore, [we shall not discuss it] here.
The intention is that there is nothing new to be said. At that time, even though the Great Being was walking upon the earth, he appeared to the great multitude as if he were walking through the sky;

this is the fixed order of things, the natural law of Bodhisattvas—this is stated according to the doctrine of determinism (*niyativāda*). "In former births, such a kamma consisting of the accumulation of merit..."
“Because it was performed and accumulated by the great multitude, it appeared in such a manner”—this is spoken from the standpoint of the doctrine of past deeds (*pubbekata-kamma-vāda*).
Because of their tendency to lean upon these beings, their own respective karma alone is called the "lord" (*issara*);
its "creation" (*nimmāna*) is the production of its own fruit. Even a Great Being, though capable of overwhelming the world together with its devas—
"He was born through exalted meritorious karma; therefore, he is called 'created by a Lord' (issara-nimmita). And this is his specific quality of being created: namely, his great majesty.
By means of which he appeared thus to the great multitude"—this is a statement made according to the doctrine of creation by a Lord (Issara-nimmāna-vāda).
Having spoken much in this way about various matters, [the author asks]: "What is the use of this figurative discourse? and at the conclusion, [he speaks] directly.
He explained it thus: "How could one just born go upon the earth on foot? One of such great majesty must surely go through the air.
By virtue of this supposition, he appeared as if going through the air.
However, because he had already taken seven strides so rapidly, although his form was visible, he seemed as if invisible to the multitude. As for his state of being naked:
It should be understood that his small stature was not unsuitable for such a mode of deportment;
rather, by virtue of the marvel produced through the power of his karma, he appeared as if adorned with ornaments, and stood before the great multitude as if sixteen years of age.

Because the actual majesty of the Bodhisatta—befitting his state as a Buddha—was proclaimed exactly as it is, [the assembly] was as delighted as if by the Buddha himself... [and so on] ...they were filled with joy.

"Having become manifest" means having become clear. Whatever formations the Buddhas wish to define appear to them—whether at the moment of their arising or otherwise—as perfectly well-known and thoroughly manifest, as clear as an amala fruit on the palm of the hand.
Therefore he said, "Just as," and so forth. "When there is no opportunity" refers to the time when the investigation is not proceeding.
“Without remainder” (*nippadesa*) means entirely. “When they have reached the opportunity” (*okāsappatta*) means when they arise at times such as walking or standing;
the intention is that they have reached the opportunity because they arise at a time suitable for comprehension (*sammasana*).
“Within seven days” is stated with reference to the ordinary mode of comprehension of Buddhas; however, if they so desire, they comprehend the formations that have arisen at any time whatsoever.
The remainder is indeed easy to understand.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning (*Līnatthappakāsanā*) for the Commentary on the *Acchariyabbhuta-sutta* is completed.
4. Commentary on the *Bākula-sutta*.

209. Just as when it ought to be said "dvattiṃsa," the word *dvi* is replaced by *bā* and thus it is called "bāttiṃsa," so too here, by applying the substitution of the letter *bā*, the conventional designation "Bākula" arose.
To show that this is an etymological name (*anvatthasaññā*) for him, the passage beginning with "For his...
was stated. "Having bathed his head" means having bathed his head in the Great Ganges for the sake of auspiciousness.
Having bathed him. "By way of submerging" means by way of submerging only slightly in water reaching the height of the knees.
Having abandoned [the child], they fled, driven by the fear of death. They die while being struck, not merely by being bound with a net.
"By the power of the boy" means by the power of the boy’s merit. He died as soon as he was pulled out; there was no further effort for the sake of his death.
What was done? By whatever means there might have been harm to the child. "That" refers to the fish. "Entirely" means with all its limbs intact.
"Does not cherish" means he does not treat it as his own, nor does he conceive of it as anything at all. She was cutting it open behind him by the power of the child’s merit.
"He obtains the child" means that after having the drum beaten with a proclamation, he announced the news and declared his own sonhood.
He explained: "Because she was carried in her womb, it is impossible for one who is not one's mother to act as such, owing to the state of being a progenitor.
'Even those catching fish' means even those who catch them after buying them. And since those catching them in that manner take everything included therein, he said:
'There are none who take them while leaving the kidneys and so forth outside. This person, too, cannot act as a mother."
[He was called] "Sakka" because of his status as a master. [The boy] was to be an heir to both families because he was the son of two.

"Eighty" means eighty years from birth. Since the defilements were not completely eradicated merely by going forth, the question must indeed be asked whether the perception of sensual desire had previously arisen [in him] so that he might transgress; therefore he said: "And thus, friend..."
“Kassapa, you should ask. 210.

“Having determined” means having determined this or that section by means of the remaining sections. “One who divides the courses of action” (kamma-patha-bhedaka) is one who effects a distinction among the courses of action.
In this context, sensual thought (*kāma-vitakka*) is called a course of action when it has reached the point of application through the doors of body and speech.
At the mind-door, it is accompanied by covetousness (*abhijjhā*) that arises through the act of appropriating another’s property for oneself;

thus, the Elder [Buddhaghosa] stated that there are likewise perceptions of sensual desire (*kāmasaññā*), as well as perceptions of ill-will (*byāpāda*) and cruelty (*vihiṃsā*) thoughts. He said, "Both of these are indeed a breach of the courses of kamma.

This was said with reference to a perception that has not yet reached the level of a full course of kamma; for if one were to say, "perception is merely what has arisen," then even the mere thinking (*vitakka*) would [be included].
The Elder’s intention is that the scriptural passage occurs by way of both [types of action], even though they have not yet reached the level of a full course of action (*kamma-patha*). 211.
"Accumulating action" (*āyūhana-kamma*) means action to be accumulated by oneself. "Foul-furred" (*loma-kiliṭṭhāni*) means having foul fur; the sense is "having foul hair. Why is it so?
Because, like the gods who wield power over the creations of others (*paranimmita-vasavatti*) in the realm of sense-pleasures, there is no accumulation of action whatsoever.
He said, "And this is not surprising," because it has never been seen or heard of before that even another renunciant should receive such requisites.
This is the duty of elders who maintain families (*kulūpaka*), yet the Elder had never at any time been one who maintained a family.

To show that here the entire period of milking a cow is intended, he said, "a cow... even for as long as it takes. "He bound [him]" means he established him as one to whom [requisites] were to be given regularly.
Defilement (saṃkileso) is so called because it is similar to strife (raṇa), in that it causes a person who possesses defilements to be subject to strife.
When he says, "Another knowledge arose," he shows that he did not claim to have attained Arahatship. [An objection: "Does such a statement not amount to a claim?
To this he replies with the words, "Moreover," and so forth.

212. It is called *avāpuraṇa* because one closes (*avāpurati*) the door with it. Because it was taught after the first collection, it is included in the second collection. The rest is easily understood.
The explanation of the hidden meaning of the commentary on the Bākula Sutta is completed.
5. Commentary on the Dantabhūmi Sutta.
213. "Should touch" (*phusayya*) means that what is intended is the touching by knowledge; therefore, "should obtain" (*labheyya*) means he should attain it.
"Practicing in this way" means practicing in the manner described as "diligent, ardent, and resolute.
By the restrictive particle "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "only in the portion not known," he excludes the attribution of fault to himself.

214. Regarding *appanā-upacāra*: they explain the meaning as having spoken after reaching both absorption (*appanā*) and access (*upacāra*). Alternatively, access accompanied by absorption is "absorption-access" (*appanā-upacāra*);

the meaning is that he spoke after reaching that. It "goes out" (*nikkhamati*), thus it is "going out" (*nikkhama*); going out from the desire for grasping is "renunciation" (*nekkhamma*), namely the first jhāna and so forth.
He said this because, when there are sensual defilements, one brings them near to oneself, relishes them, and partakes of them; thus he said: "In both kinds... [and so on].
“While enjoying sensual pleasures. Regarding the phrase “of two kinds”: it is of two kinds by way of being inferior or superior, and so forth. 215. *Kūṭākāra* means deep deceit;

it refers to such acts as causing a person to fall from a high place when in an unsuitable situation. *Dantagamana* means proceeding with the teeth, that is, entering the realm of the Gandhabbas. *Pattabbā bhūmi* means the prosperity to be attained through right action. 216. *Laṅghakaṃ vilaṅghakaṃ* refers to leaping back and forth by way of mutual exchange;
it is the grasping of each other’s hands. Therefore he said: “Having taken hand in hand.”
217. "Capable of seizing" means capable of seizing a wild elephant by means of words after having enticed it with courtesans and female elephants.
"Having looked too far" means having looked from an excessive distance. "Lust for this place" refers to the lust arising in this forest, the elephant grove.
"It leads to happiness" (*sukhāyati*) means it brings about or causes happiness to proceed; alternatively, the reading is "it carries away happiness" (*sukhaṃ harati*).
*Ḍiṇḍima* is a drum (*ānaka*). "With all crooked faults laid aside" means with all faults of deceit removed. "With impurities cast out" means with the impurity of contentiousness departed.

(219) "Of virtues dependent on the five strands of sensual pleasure" refers to unwholesome virtues; or alternatively, "of virtues based in the household" refers to virtues dependent on the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
(222) "This method applies everywhere" refers to the series of similes introduced as "the middle-aged," "the youth," and so forth, [and] by means of [the terms] "the elder" and so on.
Regarding the sections on the similes that follow: it should be understood that this same method applies to the five sections concerning the side of defilement.
The rest is easy to understand.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning (*Līnatthappakāsanā*) for the commentary on the *Dantabhūmi Sutta* is completed.
6. Commentary on the Bhūmija Sutta 223.

"Even if they should make an aspiration" means: even if they practice while making a wish such as, "By this holy life, may I become a god or some other kind of deity, or may I be liberated from suffering," they are incapable of attaining the fruit.
The intention is that [the mind] is defiled by craving for the holy life (*brahmacariya*). "Even if one makes no aspiration" means not forming a wish according to the method already stated.
They are incapable of attaining the fruit because their state is undetermined.

For it is through the power of aspiration (*paṇidhāna*) that the fruit of merit becomes "determined"; since that is absent, the merit performed does not attain [its result]. This is the intention regarding the third alternative.
It is stated by way of both positions; the fourfold question, beginning with "the fourth alternative is the right application," is brought forward by way of a net.
In that context, "hope" (*āsā*) means aspiration. When there is a wrong grasp, it does not ripen; when there is a right grasp, it ripens.
In both cases, there is what is called "expectation of both. This refers to one who, placing false states (*micchattadhamma*) foremost, [practices] the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
It cannot be said that for one who practices the holy life (brahmacariya) improperly, the fruit according to their intention succeeds,

because they have practiced the holy life in a way that is not based on right method (ayoniso). However, it cannot be said that for one who practices the holy life placing rightness (sammatta) at the forefront,
the fruit of the holy life does not succeed according to their intention, because they have practiced the holy life in a way that is based on right method (yoniso).
Therefore it was said: “Even if one makes an aspiration and leads the holy life unmethodically,” and so forth. The remainder is easy to understand.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Obscure Meaning) for the commentary on the *Bhūmija-sutta* is completed.
7. Commentary on the *Anuruddha-sutta*
230. Regarding the statement, "Having approached, they spoke thus," in order to show the reason for their approach, he said, "It was a time of discomfort for that lay follower.
*Avirādhitam* means "not causing failure" or "not disagreeable. The construction is as follows:
whether those teachings have different meanings or the same meaning, let whatever among them is not disagreeable be what occurs to you. *Jhānameva* means "only jhāna."

The lay follower’s intention is that this refers only to the immeasurable absorption (*appamāṇajjhāna*); however, because it is called "liberation of mind" (*cetovimutti*), it is said to be simply one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*). 231.
To the extent that the shadow spreads at midday, or to the extent that leaves fall in a windless place—that much is "the foot of a tree" (*rukkhamūla*).
"It is said" refers to the area measured by the root of a single tree as thus described.

"Having been overspread by the kasiṇa-sign" means that one who enters the jhāna having the kasiṇa as its object dwells in that kasiṇa... [as stated]. There is no mental application (*ābhoga*) at the moment of jhāna.
Granted there is no mental application at the moment of attainment, yet prior to that, such mental application may exist; it is with reference to that [prior state] [that this is said].

Some say it is "lofty" (*mahaggata*). Now, in order to show the distinctions found in those liberations of mind (*cetovimutti*)—despite their lack of difference in terms of any specific quality—with respect to their objects and so forth, the passage beginning with "In this case" (*ettha*) was stated. The sign (*nimitta*) does not expand because there is no sign to be expanded.
Unlike the earth-kasina and others, no "breaking open" (*ugghāṭana*) occurs through the meditation on space.

"These jhānas" refers to the jhānas of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*). Because they lack the fourteenfold subduing [of the defilements], they do not serve as bases for the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*).
Because there is no eradication of the signs [of form], and because the immaterial jhānas lack the power of resolve, they do not serve as bases for cessation (*nirodha*).

By way of being the round of kamma, they [are the basis] for the three rounds: the round of defilements (*kilesavaṭṭa*), the round of formations (*kammavaṭṭa*), and the round of results (*vipākavaṭṭa*).

The state of being a condition is the act of providing a basis for the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*). They are called "transitions into existence" (*bhavokkamanāni*) because by means of them one enters various states of existence (*bhava*) precisely through the process of rebirth.

The meaning of the second method should be understood as the reverse of what was stated [previously]. Because it is obtained by breaking open [the confinement], there is a transcendence beyond the formless jhānas;
this alone is the distinction. "In this way" means by the aforementioned modes, such as the non-increase of the sign and the increase of the sign.

"Various" (*nānā*) means having various intrinsic natures (*sabhāva*). "Thus" (*evaṃ*) means they have various phonemes (*byañjana*) because they are expressible by the terms "immeasurable" and "lofty.

Although it would indeed be possible here to extract [the term] even from the immeasurable attainments (*appamāṇa-samāpatti*) in order to show the cause for rebirth in existence (*bhava-upapatti*) which will be explained later, the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) has nevertheless made its application by extracting it only from the kasiṇa-jhānas;
therefore, it was stated thus. Alternatively, by the inclusion of the term "lofty" (*mahaggata*) here...
It should be understood that this includes the divine abodes (brahmavihāra) mentioned as "immeasurable" (*appamāṇa*), because that designation applies equally to both. 232.

"Thus it is said": even in the absence of such a specific mental application (*ābhoga*), it is said, "He dwells having pervaded [the world] with the perception of limited light (*parittābhā*) and having resolved upon it.
This is because for one who increases the *kasiṇa* by making it immeasurable, there arises the practice of cultivation (*bahulīkāra*) by way of increasing the *kasiṇa*.
There may be greater strength in jhāna and weakness in its absence; however, when mastery has been cultivated, there is no need to speak of the failure to properly purify opposing states.
Thus, demonstrating the lack of proficiency in jhāna through five modes, he said, "or even as much as a drop on the tip of a finger," and so forth.
It is precisely because of the jhāna's lack of power that the radiance resulting from it is also less.
"It is indeed impure," he said: "The color... is defiled. The second method should be understood as the reverse of what was stated.
There too, the limited nature of the color is due to the limited nature of the kasiṇa;
or rather, because it conforms to a limited object, the sign—even the circle of light—would also be limited. This is the intended meaning. "Extensive preliminary work" means:

The preliminary work (*parikamma*) is by means of a vast state (*vipulabhāva*). The remainder to be said regarding the third and fourth methods is exactly the same as what was stated for the first and second methods.
"Difference in color" (*vaṇṇanānatta*) refers to the difference in the body's color, whether it be yellow, red, or white.

"Difference in radiance" (*ābhānānatta*) refers to the difference in light according to its limited or vast extent. "Difference in flame" (*accinānatta*) refers to the difference in the fire element according to its length and so forth.
“Diversity. “They settle down” means they settle, sit, or remain by way of attachment and delight; therefore he said, “they dwell. 234. “They shine and blaze” means they radiate light;
thus he said, “endowed with radiance. Or, “by that factor” refers to the cause of radiance, which consists in its limitedness and its immeasurability;
and since that, in actual fact, is simply the cause for rebirth in a particular state of existence, he said: “of that...”
“By way of a factor for rebirth. The state of bodily lassitude is the body’s distension, which serves as the cause for languor (*tandī*) and other such states.
235. “The perfections”: fulfilling the perfections of a disciple (*sāvakapāramiyo*), which lead to the status of a great disciple (*mahāsāvaka*).

“In the Brahma-world”: he obtained rebirth either in the personal form of a Brahmā (*brahmattabhāve*) or in the Brahma-world (*brahmaloke*); and this has also been stated in the *Theragāthā*. “Unmixed”: not [mixed] with others...
"Unmixed" is the meaning. "Formerly wandering" means my wandering by way of birth in past existences;
"that wandering was mine"—this is the meaning. The rest is easy to understand.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Anuruddha-sutta* is completed.
8. Commentary on the Upakkilesa Sutta 236.
He spoke thus because he desired their welfare, not out of disregard for the Blessed One’s words.
As for those who did not accept the Teacher’s words at that time, they stood silent and abashed, having said nothing; therefore—
Neither group showed a lack of respect toward the Teacher.
"By whom he was not seen" means by whichever of the two groups he was not seen due to being preoccupied with other matters or because of being separated by walls, doors, and so forth.
"For the sake of taming" refers to those monks who had been brought to a state of humility by those lay followers.
"For the sake of subduing. "They established" means: they declared that for whoever gives to these monks, there shall be a fine of a hundred [pieces] and a thousand [pieces].

237. Because there is a variety of sounds due to their being in factions, it is called "diverse sound" (*puthusadda*). "A crowd of people" (*samajana*) refers to a group of people whose intentions are focused on quarreling.
Even though he stands among the characteristics of a fool, he does not think, "I am a fool. And "furthermore" refers to his own state of foolishness.
Furthermore, even though they were unaware, they did not perceive—nor did they know—that the very cause of a schism in the Saṅgha was arising within themselves, like a blister upon a wound.
Having become "those whose range is speech" (vācāgocarā), meaning their domain consisted solely of words set in motion by quarreling; [the phrase] *mukhāyāmaṃ* refers to the extent of their dispute.
"Stretching out their faces as they speak": they do not know that; they do not know that quarrel. Indeed, there is no one who, while making a quarrel, does not know it.
However, to show how they do not know it, he said: "In this way, this is full of danger.
This so-called quarrel, because it fails to bring about the welfare of oneself and others and because it produces harm, even in this very life...
"In the present life and in the future life" means it is fraught with danger; "with fault" is the meaning.
"They nurse a grudge" means they persist in pursuit by way of resentment. "Ancient" means old, due to having been practiced and repeatedly practiced by former ones such as the Buddhas.
"They do not know" means they do not establish the perception of impermanence.
"Of those who have long-standing enmity" means of those whose enmity has persisted for a long time due to the severing of bones and so forth, by way of bringing it about.

This was spoken for the purpose of illustrating the praise and blame of one with wise companions and one with foolish companions, [showing] that "these bhikkhus are prone to quarreling because of their association with fools;
however, this would not happen for those with wise companions. [It refers to] manifest dangers such as lions and tigers, and [internal dangers] such as lust and hatred.
And having overcome concealed dangers.
In the phrase "Mātaṅga in the forest of Mātaṅgas" (*mātaṅgo araññe mātaṅgaraññe*), the compound is formed by the elision of the *sar* vowel.
Since the state of being an elephant is already expressed by the word *mātaṅga* itself, he says, "‘Nāga’ is a designation for greatness," in order to clarify his vastness.
For the word *nāga* also has the meaning of "great," as in such passages as: "Thus [the Buddha spoke] to the Nāga, the elephant with tusks like chariot-poles.
The particle *kira* is a grammatical particle (*nipāta*) used to indicate tradition (*anussava*). By it, he shows that this is a succession of what has been heard.
Indeed, that danger was already fully understood (*pariññāta*) by the Blessed One long ago; the Teacher did not become disenchanted because of it, but rather—
During the rainy season, there were some who were not yet ready to be converted by the Buddha; therefore, going elsewhere was the means for taming those bhikkhus.

While traveling toward Pālileyyaka, he went to encourage the Venerable Bhagu, who was living alone, as well as the Elder Anuruddha and others who were living in harmony, and [he spoke] this "Admonition on Defilements" to the Elder Anuruddha.
"He went there to give it; therefore, they say he was a quarrelsome person"—here too, the same principle applies to the inclusion of the word *kira*.
This has been explained in exactly the same manner in the Gosiṅgasāla Sutta.
Regarding the phrase "But how so?"—because it is the final among the questions stated, [it is referred to as] "But is there, indeed? for the final question.
It was already stated; it is not asked again with "But do you have... because its existence has already been established.
Furthermore, that is the supramundane dhamma. "Of the elders" means of the elder Anuruddha and others; they do not [lack it].

He asks about the preliminary light because, having performed the necessary preparation for the knowledge of the divine eye, he asks about the preliminary light for the sake of its arising. "Preliminary light" (parikammobhāsaṃ) means...
The meaning is: "the light produced by preparatory concentration" (*parikamma-samādhi-nibbatta-obhāsa*), that is, the light generated by access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*).

For one who has attained the fourth jhāna, having developed the light-kasina for the purpose of preparing the divine eye, the concentration established in access is called "preparatory concentration" (*parikamma-samādhi*);
the light therein is called "preparatory light" (*parikamma-obhāsa*). Referring to this, he said: "I perceive the light" means the preparatory light.

“We perceive,” he said. For as far as he wishes to see forms with the divine eye, he stands having pervaded that extent of space with the light-kasina (obhāsakasiṇa). He sees that light and the forms therein by means of the knowledge of the divine eye;
and the elders practiced in this manner. Therefore it was said: “We perceive both the light and the vision of forms.”
However, because the stage of preliminary work (parikamma) passed away for those who were seeing the visible form, the radiance vanished;

when that had vanished, even the visible form was no longer perceived. For "preliminary work" refers to access concentration (upacāra-jhāna) having the aforementioned kasiṇa as its object; "seeing the visible form" for those who see it occurs by way of the kasiṇa-radiance; [and] the kasiṇa-radiance...
And as for the phrase "by way of preliminary work" (*parikamma*): neither of those two occurred because of the non-occurrence of preliminary work.
The Elders did not consider this to be due to being beginners; therefore it was said, "We did not penetrate.
"The sign is to be penetrated" means that after showing the cause through direct perception, [one penetrates] with the knowledge of the perfectly purified divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).
The Teacher speaks because he wishes to establish the Elder [in the truth]. "Will they not cause him to stumble?

means "Will they not cause him to be deluded? They will indeed cause him to be deluded"—this is the meaning. "Doubt arose" because, regarding the forms appearing before his divine eye, since they were unprecedented, the thought "What indeed is this form?
What indeed is this? had not yet been severed by the Path.
Doubt and uncertainty arose. "Concentration has lapsed": because doubt had arisen, the preliminary concentration (*parikamma-samādhi*) vanished;
for that very reason, even the preliminary light (*parikamma-obhāsa*) disappeared, and he did not see forms even with the divine eye (*dibba-cakkhu*).
"I will not attend to them"—it was through the power of such attention (*manasikāra*) that forms appeared to him; while he was seeing forms, doubt arose.
"Something arises; therefore, now I shall not attend to anything," he thought, and became silent.
It was with reference to this attainment of silence that it is said, "non-attention arose.
Due to the absence of such non-attention, a surge of energy arose. Thus, his vigor was firmly exerted.
In order to pacify sloth, torpor, and agitation, his energy became over-exerted; consequently, a powerful joy rooted in the household life arose, which corrupted the concentration of his mind.
Therefore, he said: "An elation has arisen. "From that" means from the state of slackened energy.
"He would fall" means he would become excessively exhausted. "That is mine" refers to the mind being overcome by aspiration.
"Jappeti" means "abhijappā," which is craving (taṇhā). Perception that is manifold, having various natures, is "nānattasaññā.
"Atinijjhāyitattaṃ" is the state of gazing with excessive contemplation.
"Parikammobhāsameva" means precisely the light arisen from preliminary work (parikamma). "And I do not see forms" means...
Because of being intent upon the attention to illumination, I do not see forms with the divine eye.
Thinking "it is only the form of the object," I attend only to that which has become the objective range of the divine eye in the place pervaded by it.
He said, "illumination in a limited place," because here the illumination is limited by way of the kasiṇa-forms. Limited...
“Forms” refers to only a few; and since their limitedness is due solely to their location, he says, “forms in a limited place.
The second section, beginning with “and immeasurable,” has already been stated. With reference to the limitedness of the light, preliminary concentration is called “limited”;
and because that very light is immeasurable, it is called “immeasurable concentration. In that...

"At that time" means at the moment when that limited concentration has arisen. The divine eye is also "limited" because it sees limited forms. 245. Regarding "concentration of the two or three jhānas":

in the fourfold system, this refers to the concentration of the second and third jhānas; in the fivefold system, it refers to the concentration of the second, third, and fourth jhānas—this is how the construction should be understood.
"Concentration of the two jhānas" in the fourfold system refers to the concentration of the second and third jhānas.
In the fivefold system, it is the concentration of the second jhāna by way of the fourth and fifth [factors]. Regarding "the concentration of the threefold and fourfold jhānas":
the construction is that in the fourfold system it is the concentration of the third jhāna, and in the fivefold system it is the concentration of the fourth jhāna.

"Threefold" means concentration of three kinds by way of being accompanied by rapture (*sappītika*). "Included therein" means having the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of being accompanied by rapture and so forth.

Granted that the Blessed One might have developed these knowledges even while producing the knowledge of recollecting past lives in the first watch and the knowledge of the divine eye in the last watch;
however, it is with reference to those knowledges that serve as the basis for insight (vipassanā) that he said, "in the last watch.
Therefore, he said, "For the Blessed One," and so forth. "Of the fifth jhāna" means by way of that which possesses the five jhāna factors.
There is no path consisting of the first jhāna alone. That [path] was the fivefold method belonging to the mundane sphere of the Blessed One.
"This" refers to the statement beginning with, "I develop concentration that is accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought.
This was said with reference to a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane, not as being either exclusively mundane or exclusively supramundane. The rest is easily understood.
The elucidation of the hidden meaning in the commentary on the *Upakkilesa Sutta* is completed.
9. Commentary on the *Bālapaṇḍita Sutta*. 246.

“By these” means by such things as ill-considered thoughts. By this, he indicates that the word *lakkhaṇa* (characteristic) has the sense of the instrumental case. “Those very ones” refers to the characteristics.
Thus. "Of him" means of the fool. "Foolish signs" (bālanimittāni) are those by which one is marked or recognized as "this is a fool.

"Apadāna" refers to a well-known deed. Since ill-considered thoughts and so forth are well known in the case of a fool—or rather, in the sense of defining his character—they are therefore called "the fool’s apadānas" (bālāpadānāni).
One who thinks with a mind corrupted and defiled by covetousness and other such states is "one who thinks ill-thought thoughts" (ducintitacintī).
One who speaks what is ill-spoken is called a "speaker of ill-spoken words" because he utters false speech and the like, which are corrupted by greed and other defilements.

One who performs a blameworthy deed is called a "doer of blameworthy deeds" because he commits acts such as the taking of life, which must be done according to those very same [defilements]. Therefore, he said, "Reflecting," and so forth.

That which is born depending upon those [defilements] is "arising from that" (*tajja*). For that very reason, that which is suitable or appropriate for them is "fitting for that" (*tassāruppa*). Therefore, he said:
“Of that same nature,” and so forth. “While being told” means while it is being spoken. 248.

Because for beings, the karmas accumulated according to their own tendencies provide the opportunity, and the signs of karma and the signs of the destination (gatinimitta) presented by those [karmas] come into the range of the mind at the time near death; at that time, they seem to hang down and overwhelm [the mind].
They appear as if hanging down or as if completely covering [the mind]; therefore it was said: "For they appear in the manner of hanging down and so forth.
Since it is the very mode of appearance that at that time becomes the object-sphere of the mind, he said:
"When that mode of appearance has come into the range of perception."
249. Regarding the phrase "he does not say 'it is not possible,'" this expresses the meaning that both negations constitute the natural sense [of the statement].
By the phrase "it is not easy," however, the state of being difficult is indicated; and showing that even what is difficult can be accomplished by means of a skillful method, he says:
"But it is not easy," and so forth. "By that" refers to their mutual meeting through passing straight through one another.
“Assa” means for the thief. “Even more than this” means during the midday period and the evening period [he was struck] with a hundred spears.

“It does not even approach a fraction” (saṅkhaṃ pi na upeti): by this it is shown that there is not even a mere measure to be reckoned; thus he said, “it does not even reach the state of being a number.
The same method applies here to the phrase “even a mere deposit” (upanikkhepanamattam pi). “A part of a fraction” (kalabhāgaṃ) refers to parts.
The section on enumeration. Therefore he said, "the hundredth part," and so forth.

"Even the mere looking" means even the mere looking by way of setting it down. "That penalty for labor" means that fivefold penalty for labor they indeed inflict by turning it over according to all four sides;
however, it is recorded in the Pāḷi by way of a single side. "Of the house..."
Of a great house. "In every way" means from all its constituent parts. "Blazing up" means having become a single mass of flame. "Well-boiled" means thoroughly cooked.

"Divided" means it has arisen as if divided by the common karma of the beings produced therein. "Surrounded on all sides by an iron enclosure" means encompassed and enclosed by an iron wall. "Pairs of balls" refers to pairs of playthings for children.

"Suffering in this way too" means that it is suffering in the manner already described—both by way of the aforementioned burning hells and by way of being the objective domain of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
251. "Having licked with the teeth" means having scraped with the upper teeth. "Savoring" (*assāda*) refers to the relish based on taste; it is the craving for flavor. Therefore he said:

"One who has consumed the flavor through greed for flavor. 252. "Ugly" (*durūpa*) means misshapen. "Hard to look upon" (*duddasa*) means that because of that very deformity, one is unpleasant to behold. "Lakuṇṭhaka" means short.
"With a neck tucked in" (*paviṭṭhagīva*) means one whose neck is drawn into the space between the shoulders. "Large-bellied" (*mahodara*) means having a protruding belly. For the most part...

For beings with a hunchback are those who have short necks and broad bellies; thus it was said. "One-eyed" means one whose vision is impaired, as it is stated: "either one-eyed in one eye or one-eyed in both eyes.
"Lame" refers to one who is deficient in a hand, so he said: "either lame in one hand or lame in both hands.
Here, "crippled in a wing" (pakkhahata) refers to one whose body or side has been damaged by wind-disorder (*vāta*) or other such causes.
It is intended [here] as one who is not paralyzed; thus he said: “A *pakkhahata* is a cripple (*pīṭhasappī*).
It is for the purpose of showing the continuity of suffering—that is, for the purpose of showing how it proceeds by way of the continuity of resultant suffering throughout successive births.
A *kali* is that by which the Teaching is defeated, ruined, or lost; it is a defeat of splendor. That very thing, because of its similarity to a die (*gaha*), [is called *kali*].
"Seizure by calamity" (*kaliggaha*) is what is said. They bind themselves to the root of their own household, which they have inhabited.
