Therefore he said, "One would come to be bound by oneself. The culmination of foolishness on the plane of folly is the performance of karma leading to rebirth in hell;
thus it is simply said, "one is reborn in hell. By that very mention, however, from there...
The plane of the fool is elucidated by way of successive rebirths in the remaining states of misery through the performance of very soft and softer kamma, and so forth. 253.

"In accordance with what was stated" means according to the sequence of the explanatory statements such as "this one is a fool," which are characterized by [the opposite] such as "this one is a wise person.
"By way of mental good conduct, etc. refers to non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view while reflecting.
These [verses] should be applied by way of the three good conduct practices of the mind, beginning with "one thinks only what is well thought.
256. Commentary on the Wheel-Treasure:
*Uposatha* refers to the virtue endowed with eight factors that should be observed by householders on all days.
One who has the *uposatha* by virtue of its undertaking—that is, one for whom it exists—is an *uposathika*. Therefore, he said: "of one who has undertaken the *uposatha* factors.

"At that time" means at that moment; at which time, having perfected the accumulation of merit consisting of giving, morality, and so forth conducive to the state of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*), and having fulfilled the duties of a wheel-turner, [he attains] rebirth in a specific location such as Kāsi, as well as the excellence of qualities such as noble birth, physical form, wealth, and sovereignty.
And at that time, he stands in a physical form corresponding to that [status].

For at such a time, the supreme person destined to be a Wheel-turning Monarch—endowed with the aforementioned qualities—having become an anointed Kṣatriya king, being pure in virtue, practices right conduct by bestowing hundreds of thousands [of coins] and so forth on every Uposatha day; it is not when the Wheel-treasure has arisen.

It was at that very time. Therefore he said: “In the morning... [and so on] ...this is the natural law. (In this context, *dama* is the restraint of the sense faculties; *saṃyama* is the restraint of virtue.

“Conditioned by merit consisting of the aforementioned kind of kamma” means having as its cause meritorious kamma such as giving, self-control (*dama*), and restraint (*saṃyama*), which brings about the status of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*).
“Resembling a cluster of blue sapphires” means equal to a collection of sapphire gems (*indanīlamaṇi*). “Because it is endowed with divine power” refers to its beauty.

Because it is endowed with divine-like powers such as having a pleasant sound, traveling through the air, emitting light, being non-obstructive, and being the cause for accomplishing whatever the king desires;
"in all ways" means in all beautiful modes. "They fulfill" means they make it complete. And that fulfillment of it will now be explained in detail.
*Panāḷī* means a hole. The intended meaning is that the rows of teeth are pure, glossy, and without gaps.
*Nābhipanāḷiparikkhepapaṭṭesu* refers both to the band encircling the navel and to the bands encircling the holes of the navel.
*Suvibhattāvā* means well-proportioned because they do not overlap one another. The gems are well-proportioned within the intervals between the boundary lines.
They say that these [marks] become manifest after [the body] has been offered as a sacrifice.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "boundary lines, etc.," it includes such things as floral designs (*mālākamma*). In the passage beginning with "well-colored" (*suratta*), by the mention of "well-colored," he excludes the complexion of Mahānāma;
by the mention of "pure" (*suddha*), he excludes impurity; and by the mention of "glossy" (*siniddha*), [he excludes roughness].

Regarding its roughness: although the rim-circle of that Wheel-Treasure (cakkaratana) was produced as if without joints, it would not have been beautiful if it were entirely and exclusively the color of coral;
therefore, at the places where the natural wheel has joints, it was fashioned from red Jambunada gold.
It is with reference to this that it is said: "But at its joints," and so forth.
"On the back of the wheel-rim" means on the surface area of the wheel-rim.
"In the spaces between ten spokes each" means in the areas near the intervals between ten spokes each. "Variegated with circular holes" means variegated by holes shaped like circles.
"Well-struck by a skilled craftsman" means well-beaten by a highly skilled artisan; the meaning is that it was played. "Charming" (vaggū) means...
“Delightful” (*manoramo*) means “arousing passion” for those who hear it as “charming” (*rajanīyo*). “Desirable” (*kamanīyo*) means “lovely.

“Garlands of flowers hanging down” means garlands of fragrant flowers suspended [there]. Regarding “the circumference of the rim” (*nemiparikkhepassa*), it refers to the circumference at the edge of the rim.
It is stated as “of both naves and shafts” (*nābhipanāḷīnaṃ*) by way of the two sides of the single nave-shaft; for that shaft is indeed one.
"By which two" refers to the two lion-faces. Again, "by which" refers to the clusters of pearls.
"Causing them to listen" means making them attentive to hear. "The moon in front, the wheel-treasure behind"—thus, by way of sequence, in the order of before and after.
"At the end of the inner palace" means near the northern lion-window of the king’s inner palace (antepura) in Anurādhapura at that time.
It is stated thus because a lion-window (sīhapañjara) exists on the northern side of such a palace.
"Easily able" means that one is able to worship easily by scattering handfuls of flowers with the hand while remaining exactly as one is— neither having to climb up nor having to stretch the body.

It is radiant with the splendor of gems of various colors; it is brilliant with the radiance of the precious hues of diverse kinds of cloth. It extends upward into the sky; having come forth, it proceeds by rising high into the space above the place where it stands.

"Fit for settlement" means suitable for the layout of enclosures and ramparts. "Having easily obtainable food and requisites" means that its provisions—such as grain, milk products, firewood, grass, and other foodstuffs—are readily available. "Enemy army" refers to the military force or the command of another king.
*Āgatanandano*: having come, he is one who causes joy to arise; or, *āgataṃ* means "arrival," and because he rejoices by means of that, he is *āgatanandano*.
*Gamanasocano*: he sorrows because of departure. *Upakappetha*: arrange, prepare, or provide for each other in succession;

the meaning is "bring near. *Upaparikkhitvā*: having investigated, having examined from the perspective of cause, nature, result, and the disadvantages pertaining to both the present life and the future life.
They are called *vibhāvino* because they clarify the meaning through wisdom (*paññā*), making it manifest; thus, they are the wise. *Anuyantā* means followers. *Ogacchamānaṃ* means sinking down.
*Yojanamattaṃ* refers to an area measuring one league (*yojana*) in breadth.
However, due to its depth, it sinks down just as the ground appears [level]. Therefore, he said, "the surface of the great ocean," and so forth. At the end is the Wheel-Treasure (*cakkaratanaṃ*).
For the purpose of not being overwhelmed by water during an army's march. 257.

"Having the eastern ocean as its limit" means having the eastern ocean as its boundary; that is, making the eastern ocean the limit. "Of the four-cornered [world]" means of that which has the four oceans as its limits—the four divisions beginning with Pubbavideha.
The Description of the Elephant Treasure.
258. Regarding the phrase "with yellow sandalwood, etc.," the word "etc. includes the four types of fragrant substances and so forth.
They say, "one should contemplate its arrival" because it has been well-cultivated through the fulfillment of the duties of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*).
It is called "sevenfold-supported" (*sattapatiṭṭha*) because it stands upon seven parts: the tail, the excellent limb (the trunk), and the hand—these three—and the four feet.
It does not come to others, such as ministers and so forth, who are merely thinking about it. "Having removed" means having removed it by means of his own power;
for other elephants cannot endure its scent alone.
Commentary on the Horse-Treasure (Assaratana)
"From a Sindha horse-breed" means from a breed of horses originating in Sindha.
The description of the jewel-treasure:
"Equal in size to the hub of a cartwheel" means it is equal in circumference to the hub of a large cart. "At both ends" means...
"At the two ends" means at the lower and upper extremities. "From the edge of the pericarp" means from the boundary of the pericarp of the two golden lotuses.
"Having placed them in a net of pearls" means having established them upon a perfectly pure net made of pearls. The Description of the Woman-Treasure (*itthiratana*).
Having stated, "The jewel of a woman (itthiratana) appears," in order to show the manner of its appearance, it was said:
"From the Madda royal family," and so forth. It is said that the Madda country is the source of the birth of beautiful women.

By "perfection of configuration" (saṇṭhānapāripūri) is meant the well-proportioned arrangement of the limbs of the body, such as the hands and feet; for the perfection of the whole is established through the perfection of its parts.
"Form" (*rūpa*) means the body. "Worthy of being seen" (*dassanīya*) means fit to be beheld because of its beautiful appearance.
It gladdens the mind through joy for those who reflect wisely, by way of faith in the result of kamma.

By the statement of the cause—"bringing about confidence"—just as the perfection of complexion and beauty was stated [to arise] from loveliness (*pāsādikatā*), so too the perfection of loveliness is stated [to arise] from being worthy of being seen (*dassanīyatā*).
He shows the method by which the accomplishment of beauty and loveliness must be stated.

Alternatively, in reverse order, the accomplishment of attractiveness through the possession of fine color and complexion, the accomplishment of loveliness through attractiveness, and the accomplishment of beauty through loveliness should be applied.
Having thus shown beauty and the other qualities by way of the excellence of the body, he now [shows them] also by way of the absence of defects in the body.

To demonstrate these, it is said: “or handsome,” and so forth. Therein, just as they are possessed of the proper proportions, so too, by virtue of their height and girth, they are pleasing, being neither too tall nor [too short], and so on.
Thus, because humans possess the excellence of a divine form, it is said: “not having attained a divine complexion.
“Physical defects” refers to flaws of the body. “Absence” means being utterly and completely removed from them.
"Of that which has been split a hundred times" means of that which has been split a hundred times.
This expression "split a hundred times" is stated with reference to a tuft of cotton; however, there is no such thing as splitting a tuft of down (*tūla*).
According to some, the four types are saffron, *tagara*, pine resin, and *yavanapuppha*; others say they are *tamāla*, *tagara*, pine resin, and *yavanapuppha*.
"Like one burnt by fire" means like one burnt by the fire that has reached the seat.

"At the very outset" means before any other duty, at the very moment of seeing; this is the meaning. She is called *kiṅkārapaṭissāvinī* because she responds with "What shall I do? when asked, "What task must I perform for you, O King?
regarding each specific duty she ought to carry out for him.
"Women, for the most part, are of a deceitful nature," but to show that this is not the case for the Woman-Jewel (itthiratanassa), it is said, "She would be...
and so forth. "Virtues" (guṇā) refers both to physical beauty and to virtues of conduct.
"By the power of her former deeds" means by the power of her own former deeds; that is, by the power of those former deeds conducive to the state of being a Woman-Jewel.
Even for a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavattin*), meritorious karma conducive to a retinue is indeed a decisive support (*upanissaya*) for such a specific fruit.

Therefore, he said: "relying upon the merit of a wheel-turning monarch. By this, it should be understood that the status of those [other] specific qualities as being supported by that [merit] is likewise clarified in the case of the remaining treasures.
This refers to the fulfillment obtained previously by way of partial attainment.
From the moment he attained the status of a Wheel-turning Monarch (cakkavatti), [the other treasures] became perfected in every respect.
Regarding the description of the Householder-treasure (gahapatiratana):
"By nature" means by its very essence, even prior to the manifestation of the Wheel-treasure (cakkaratana).
The commentary on the Counsellor-treasure (*pariṇāyakaratana*):
"Depending upon" (*nissāya*) means relying upon.

260. "Seizing the opportunity" (*kaṭaggaha*) is said to be seizing victory; it is the grasping of one's own people by way of their being the "cutting edge" (*kaṭa*), through the accomplishment of their welfare.
Having done so, he said, "by way of victory. The construction is: "by a single stroke" means that by a single application of effort (*ekappayogena*), one would attain hundreds of thousands.
The rest is easily understood because it follows the method already explained.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Bālapaṇḍita-sutta* is completed.
10. Commentary on the *Devadūtasutta* 261.
Regarding the phrase "two houses," etc.: by the word "etc.," the passage beginning with "the six doors... even as they wander about" is included.
Indeed, it should be understood that this much alone is explained in detail in the *Assapura Sutta*. However, the passage beginning with "with the divine eye," etc., [is not].

Although it has been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*, because it is considered to be a commentary on the Suttas, it is stated here: "It has already been explained in detail in the *Assapura Sutta*.

(262) He concludes the teaching with the world of the devas, starting from hell, thereby instilling a sense of urgency regarding the phenomena of defilement (*saṃkilesadhamma*) and bringing it to a conclusion through the phenomena of purification (*vodānadhamma*).
The second [section], however, should be understood as the reverse of what was stated; this is distinguished by the specific inclinations of those to be trained (*veneyya*).
It should be understood. Now, in order to explain the meaning stated in brief, the words beginning with "If" are spoken. "He" refers to the Blessed One.
"Some elders" is said with reference to the Andhakas and others, as well as the proponents of consciousness (Viññāṇavādins).

They are called "hell-wardens" (nirayapālā) because they guard those in hell—that is, they protect them by not allowing them to escape from it. [They do so] for those in hell who are enveloped by the suffering of the infernal realm...
Or, they are called *nirayapālā* because they are capable (*alaṃ samatthā*) [of inflicting punishment]. "That" refers to the statement, "There are no hell-guardians.
"It has indeed been refuted" means it has been refuted in the Abhidhamma by such methods as: "In hell there are hell-guardians, and there are also those who inflict punishment.
For if there were no such beings as hell-guardians, there would be no infliction of punishment; for when there is one who inflicts punishment, there can be the act of punishing.
The intended meaning is that they must exist. Therefore he said, "For just as," and so forth. Here it is asked:
"But are these hell-wardens beings belonging to hell (*nerayika*), or are they not beings belonging to hell? What follows from this?

If, first of all, they were beings belonging to hell, then since they would be produced by karma leading to hell, they themselves would experience the suffering of hell; and if that were the case, for other beings belonging to hell...
They would be incapable of inflicting torture, and there would be no distinction such that "these are the denizens of hell" and "these are the hell-wardens.

Furthermore, if those who inflict torture were identical in appearance, strength, and stature to the others, there would be no fear or terror for the latter. If, on the other hand, they are not denizens of hell, how could their existence there be possible?
It is said: the hell-wardens are not denizens of hell; they are produced by karma conducive to rebirth in states other than the hell-realm itself.
For they are reborn there by means of a different karma altogether from the karma that leads to birth in hell, because they belong to the class of *rakkhasas*.
Thus say the Sabbatthivādins:
"They are prone to anger, performers of cruel deeds, and always delighting in evil."
“They rejoice among those who suffer; they are born as Yama’s rākṣasas.

Regarding this, as for what some say—that they might experience the suffering of torment, or that they might torture one another, and so forth—this is without substance, because the wardens of hell lack the very status of being hell-beings themselves.
Even if the wardens of hell were not hell-beings, [the argument remains untenable].
But how is it that those wandering upon the hellish ground—which is made of iron, blazing, aflame, and glowing—do not experience the suffering of burning?

It is due to the power of their karma. For just as the possessors of psychic power, such as Mahāmoggallāna and others who have attained mastery over the mind, when they approach the hellish ground through the power of their *iddhi* out of compassion for the denizens of hell, do not suffer from the pain of burning...
They are not afflicted; this should be understood in the same way.
If it is argued that this is because the scope of supernormal power (*iddhi*) is inconceivable, then this too is similar: because the ripening of karma (*kamma-vipāka*) is inconceivable.
For they were produced by such a kind of karma that, while remaining entirely unafflicted by the suffering of hell, they [appear] as hell-beings.

They go forth; yet it is not tenable that external objects cease to exist merely by that [act], because the quality of being desirable or undesirable is distributed individually among the gatekeepers and the men at the gates.

For what is desirable for one gatekeeper or man may be undesirable for another, and what is undesirable for one may be desirable for another. And having established this, as for what some say: "There is no..."
[The objection] beginning with, "By means of their karma, they burn others with fire," is refuted by this.
As for what they say—"How can there be the birth of those who are hell-beings (nirayika) there?"—it is because of the presence of tortures for the hell-beings in hell.
For karma that produces a personal existence (attabhāva) suitable for the torture of a hell-being is produced in the very place of hell, having been directed toward such a desirable [rebirth].
And these [beings] have greater strength, height, and girth than the denizens of hell; they are exceedingly terrifying in appearance and even more cruel in their methods.
By this very fact, it should be understood that the birth of the "tormenting" crows, dogs, and so forth, who afflict the denizens of hell, is also described there.
Nor should it be said that beings in one destiny can torment those in another destiny, for such a thing is seen elsewhere as well.
As for what some say—that the guardians of hell, the hell-dogs, and so forth, are indeed devoid of a sentient nature—that too is merely their own opinion, because such a thing is not seen elsewhere.

For there is no such occurrence of a phenomenon that is devoid of a sentient nature and yet, without being prompted by actual sentient beings, accomplishes the functions of a sentient being; such a thing has never been seen before.
There is no distinguishing factor between those who prevent the thirsty from drinking and men with sticks and weapons in their hands, whether they possess actual existence (*sattabhāva*) or lack it.
There is indeed an impairment by means of a dream, yet the capacity for efficacy is not the measure, because the purpose is accomplished even by mere seeing and so forth.
For instance, in a dream, there is no accomplishment of a purpose through the enjoyment of food and such; rather, it is the form created by supernormal power (*iddhinimmānarūpa*).

But here, an answer has already been obtained because the range of supernormal power (*iddhi*) is inconceivable. If it is argued that here too the ripening of karma (*kamma-vipāka*) is inconceivable, that is not so, because it is unproven.
That the hell-guardians (*niraya-pāla*) exist as the ripening of karma for those in hell is unproven;

rather, according to the method already stated and from the Pāḷi itself, their status as actual beings (*satta*) is established. For it can indeed be said: "Those designated as hell-guardians, who are reckoned as beings..."

“The occurrence of phenomena (*dhamma*) is destructive of others with intentional purpose, because of the existence of its function, like the continuity of a *rākṣasa* that feeds on vital essence (*ojā*) and so forth.
And here, it is impossible to deny that this is preceded by intention, because it is tormented in such and such ways according to the intention;

for that very reason, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) due to [the case of] massed rocks and the like. As for those who say: “It is a particularity of the primary elements (*bhūta-viśeṣa*)...”
"Thus, these beings, possessing specific qualities such as color and shape and having a terrifying appearance, receive the designation 'hell-wardens'.
This [argument] is unproven, because it was established directly in the Pāḷi that "there are hell-wardens in the hells.

Furthermore, just as in the Noble Discipline (ariyavinaya) the actual existence of hell-wardens is not proven, so too it is for one who maintains the doctrine that they are mere conceptual designations (paññatti).
Their claim that there is "mere primary matter" (bhūtamatta) is entirely unproven, because they do not admit the actual existence of material phenomena (rūpadhamma) whatsoever.

For those so-called "primary elements" (bhūtāni) do not exist in the ultimate sense (paramatthato). If he speaks while grasping at the ultimate sense, then why does he reject the eye, visible forms, and so forth?
Let this [objection] rest; it concerns those whose reasoning is unstable and who have not abandoned delusion and perversion.
In this investigation of the debate, one must reach the conclusion: "Indeed, there are wardens in hell.
And if they exist, even in the absence of external objects, the claim that there is a restriction of place and so forth—as if in a hell—is not established;
rather, it should be understood that the restriction of place and so forth exists only when external objects do indeed exist.
Because he leads and restrains beings according to their accumulated meritorious deeds by means of the arrival of the divine messengers (*devadūta*), he is called *Yama*.
Because he is the king of the *vemānika* ghosts (*peta*), he is the "King" (*rājā*). Thus it is said: "The one named Yamarāja is the king of the *vemānika* ghosts.
"Karmic ripening" (*kammavipāka*) refers to the ripening of unwholesome karma. "Vemānika ghosts" refers to those [resulting from] mixed karma, by way of both dark and bright [actions].
Having done so, they take rebirth through wholesome karma, like the deities of the woeful states (vinipātika-devatā). For they are indeed partakers of the paths and fruits;
however, during the course of existence, they experience sometimes the fruit of merit and sometimes the fruit of demerit according to their karma.
But for those in whom the Noble Path arises, from the moment of attaining that path onwards, only the fruit of merit arises.
It is to be seen. The fruit of demerit is not as bitter as before; others say that for those remaining in the human state, it is only mild.

Regarding the phrase "a righteous king" (*dhammiko rājā*), his righteousness should be understood here by way of the very same principle of arising determined at birth, just like that of a son of a righteous deity (*dhammadevaputta*).
"At the gates" means at the four gates of the great hell of Avīci.

“Subject to birth” (*jātidhammo*) means having birth as one’s inherent nature due to the influence of karma and defilements. Therefore, he said, “the very essence of birth” (*jātisabhāvo*). And since this essential nature never departs—just as heat is the nature of the fire element—he said, “not yet liberated from birth,” and so forth.
263. Now, in order to demonstrate that birth itself is a messenger from the gods, the passage beginning with “a young boy” was spoken.
This means that even if one does not speak these words verbally, by the force of the facts (*atthāpatti*), it is as if one were speaking them.
The meaning is "to the wise. "In this way, birth will come to you" means that birth—in the form of a youthful state that is defiled, loathsome, and incapable—will come to you.
Granted, this [birth] has already arrived; however, regarding the future, one should desire the application for its further arrival, but not for that which has not yet come.
Thus he said, "birth will come. For this very reason he said:
"Thus for her... [as before] ...do so. "By that" means by that reason, namely, by way of being an object of knowledge for the wise.
"Thigh-strength" (*ūrubala*) refers to one who possesses thigh-strength; by this, he shows the capacity for traveling long distances, coming and going, leaping, and so forth.

By "arm-strength" (*bāhubala*), however, he shows the capacity for performing tasks to be done with the hands. By the mention of "swiftness" (*java*), he shows the capacity for the manifestation of speed.
They have vanished and perished. The rest is exactly as described in the first discourse on the divine messengers (*devadūta*).

It is called *byādhi* because it brings about various sufferings; or rather, it is called *byādhi* because one is afflicted (*ādhīyati*) by it specifically—thus, "by that disease. "Stricken" (*abhihata*) means oppressed or afflicted. 265.

"Torture" (*kāraṇā*) refers to a form of torment such as the cutting off of hands and so forth, so called because "by this, excessive pain is inflicted. That very thing, in the sense of being something to be performed by those who inflict punishment, is "punishment-torture" (*kammakāraṇā*), meaning torture as a judicial penalty.
266. "Bahuṃ pāpaṃ kataṃ" means evil has been committed many times; by this, he expresses the frequent repetition of that evil.
Alternatively, "bahu" means great. For the word *bahu* is also seen in the sense of "great," as in "bahu vata kataṃ assa" and so forth;
thus it is said to mean "heavy. He who stands having committed such heavy or frequent evil is reborn in hell itself, and not otherwise.
He is led into the presence of Yama by the messengers of Yama.
"Paritta" (limited) means limited either by its extent or by its duration; in the former sense, it means "not much," and in the latter, "not frequent.
To clarify the aforementioned point through a simile, the passage beginning with "Just as... was stated. "That which must be done" refers specifically to the punishment. Having investigated...
"Having investigated. "A place of adjudication" means a place for legal proceedings. "Those with slight evil kamma" means those with weak evil kamma.

Because their evil kamma is weak, and because the wholesome kamma they have performed and accumulated is strong enough to provide an opportunity [for its result], they remember by their own natural disposition as well.
The Ākāsa Cetiya is a shrine constructed on an open plateau atop a mountain peak. Regarding the phrase "the sound of the flames of fire":
having heard the sound of the fire's flames as they crackled, "paṭapaṭā," he recollected the robe he had offered, thinking, "It was like the red robe I once offered at the Ākāsa Cetiya.
"He does not remember even five" means that he was utterly deluded by a powerful evil kamma.
He does not accept the five signs. He remains silent, for he sees no remedy there for one who is liable for the legal act.
267. They say that the great hell, Avīci, is exactly one hundred yojanas in height. It is nine times nine yojanas in breadth.
Because of the vastness of the Great Hell, its wall is likewise one thousand yojanas; such is the measurement of its height.
Because it encompasses everything, it is said to be "ten thousand yojanas.

(268) *Jhāyati* means it returns to its original state. *Tādisameva* is said because it is similar to what preceded it; thus it is expressed as "the raised [portion] is exactly the same. Alternatively, *bahusampatto* means that having passed through many places, he has arrived at the eastern gate.
*Channaṃ jālānaṃ* refers to the six nets raised from the four directions, as well as from below and above. *Sattānaṃ*...

Regarding the term "uninterruptedness" (*nirantaratā*): let it be that the Avīci hell is so called because of the uninterrupted state of both the flames and the beings there, due to the abundance of kamma leading to rebirth in hell.
But how is there uninterruptedness of suffering? To demonstrate this, he says: “At the door of the body...

[omission] ...one consciousness accompanied by pain,” and so forth. In that context, there is adverting (*āvajjana*), receiving (*sampaṭicchana*), investigating (*santīraṇa*), and determining (*voṭṭhabbana*).
There are two types of resultant consciousness with that as their object; thus, there are six accompanied by equanimity.

Even so, although there do occur there states of consciousness accompanied by equanimity and the feeling of equanimity finds its opportunity, nevertheless, the feeling of pain is more powerful, bringing about suffering as if cutting the body incessantly with a sharp, keen blade. These feelings...
It arises as if it were continuous, overwhelming and suffusing [the mind]. Therefore he said, “by the power of its consuming nature,” and so forth.
Or rather, because it has an extremely undesirable result there, equanimous feeling with an undesirable object is called “suffering”;
whereas in the states included within the jhānas and in the existence of happy destinations, because of the abundance of desirable results, [feeling] with a desirable object [is called happiness].
And because even equanimous feeling is called "pleasure," it should be understood that this state is called *Avīci* (the Uninterrupted) due to the absence of any interval of suffering.

269. One foot is in the Great Hell (*Mahāniraya*), while the other falls into the Feces Hell (*Gūthaniraya*); being hurled there by the force of karma, one places a step in between because of the remaining momentum of the action. It is as wide as the neck of an elephant in circumference.
It is as long as a ship carrying a single *doṇa* measure in length. "Lotus leaves" refers to iron spikes with sharp points like razor blades, appearing exactly like lotus petals.
“Below, razor-edges” means they are placed upon the ground below; and the rattan creepers have sharp-edged thorns made of iron itself.
Therefore he said: “There he suffers,” and so forth. “Kusa-grass” is so called because it belongs to the species of *kusa* grass.
“Harsh sand” is sand that is rough, with sharp points, and shaped like a crossroads (*siṅghāṭaka*).
270. "He polishes the lower teeth" means he makes them so smooth that nothing can be placed inside the mouth.
"Starting from the drinking of molten copper"—by this stated reason, he also describes the causes of the tortures in reverse order.
"By the second" means by being scraped with axes. "By the third" means by being scraped with adzes. It remains exactly as it was.
Because it serves as a cause for spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and leads to the great welfare of the world.

271. "Those who have entered an inferior body" means those who have entered an inferior selfhood (*attabhāva*). Regarding "clinging" (*upādāna*), although there are four kinds of clinging, since its meaning consists in the grasping of craving and views, he says "in the grasping of craving and views.
It is called "origination" (*sambhava*) because aging and death originate through it.
"Grasping" (upādāna) is said to mean "that which serves as the cause for birth and death. "Without grasping" (anupādā) means not having grasped. Therefore, he said "without having grasped.

"Those who have transcended all suffering" means they have indeed transcended the entire suffering of the round of existence (vaṭṭadukkha), because with the cessation of the final consciousness, even a trace of the suffering of the round is no longer possible.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Obscure Meaning) of the commentary on the *Devadūtasutta* is complete.
The commentary on the Chapter on Emptiness is completed.
4. The Chapter on Analysis (Vibhaṅgavagga). 1. Commentary on the Discourse on One Fortunate Night (Bhaddekarattasutta).
272. *Ekā ratti* means a single night. One for whom this single night is auspicious (*bhadda*) is a *bhaddekaratta*, namely, a person who is cultivating insight (*vipassanā*).

Therefore, it is said: “Because of being endowed with the practice of insight. However, because it proceeds with reference to that [insight], one is a *bhaddekaratta* by virtue of associating with the *bhaddekaratta* [state].
Therefore, the Blessed One said: “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the summary and the exposition of the *bhaddekaratta*...”
"I shall teach. It is called *uddesa* because by means of it one points out (*uddisati*) the matter that is to be taught; it is simply a brief teaching.
However, since it stands at the place of origin for the words of the detailed exposition (*niddesa*), it is called a *mātikā* (matrix) because it is like a mother;

therefore he says, "The *uddesa* is the *mātikā*. It is called *vibhaṅga* because by means of it one analyzes (*vibhajati*) the matter already pointed out; it is a detailed teaching. Thus he says, "the analysis in detail."
“Because it analyzes and classifies the matter as it was taught in detail.

Having reached and passed beyond the three moments beginning with arising, it is past (*atīta*). As for its meaning, it is said to be “the five aggregates that have vanished,” which is why he says, “in the five past aggregates.
“One would not follow after with craving and views” means by way of delighting in craving and views.
The meaning is: one should not experience it, one should not delight in it.

Just as "misapprehension" (parāmāsa) is the false adherence to past forms and so forth by way of a perverted grasp such as "permanent," so too "view" (diṭṭhi), "undertaking of action" (kammasamādāna), and "longing for views" (diṭṭhipatthanā) are the false adherence to future forms and so forth by way of a perverted grasp such as "permanent."
Rejecting that [view], he said: “One should not long for it through craving or views. In the phrase “what is past,” the word *iti* has the sense of “beginning”;
by this, it includes the term “unattained. For that too is a statement of reason. Therefore he said, “and because. Herein, this is the intended meaning:
“The past should not be delighted in by way of craving and so forth, because it is entirely non-existent.”
“Like a rabbit’s horn, so too the future should not be longed for. Herein, it might be argued:
“The past need not be rejoiced in because rejoicing in it serves no purpose; however, longing for the future may yet bear fruit, so it should not be rejected in its entirety.
This is not so, for that too must be rejected because it is accompanied by affliction. Therefore he said, “Because,” and so forth. Therein, “abandoned” means:
"Devoid of intrinsic nature" (*nissaṭṭhasabhāva*): "ceased" means broken; "passed away" means destruction;
"unattained" means not having reached its own nature, such as arising and so forth; "unborn" means not born; "unproduced" is a synonym for that same term.
"In whatever [place]" means at whichever moment, or in whichever collection of phenomena it has arisen—all of that.
"Without neglecting. In the phrase "in the forest, etc.," the word *vā* has the sense of indefiniteness.

By this, because there is no restriction as to place—whether in the forest, at the foot of a tree, or in mountain caves and so forth—it shows that the practice of contemplation (*anupassanā*) must be performed with constant application.

He says, "unshakable, unagitated," because insight (*vipassanā*), when being cultivated through the method of pairs and so on, becomes truly unassailable by opposing factors, just like the Twin Marvels and other such powers. Thus he says: "unshakable, unagitated. This...
"It was said for the purpose of showing insight and further-insight. Since this meaning in the verse is appropriate by way of insight (*vipassanā*), he says, "For insight," and so forth.

To show that it is indeed unshakable and immovable in its absolute sense, rather than through figurative discourse (*pariyāya-kathā*), he says, "Or else," and so forth. But how can there be a cultivation (*anubrūhanā*) of Nibbāna, which is eternal?

He says "again and again" (punappunaṃ) and so forth. By this, he shows that while those phenomena which are the objects [of concentration] are developed, their object also is, in a sense, developed by means of frequent attention (bahula-manasikāra).

Heating from the beginning is *ātāpana*; by this, he refers to the element of exertion (*ārambha-dhātu*). Heating all around is *paritāpana*; by this, he refers to the elements of striving (*nikkama-dhātu*) and perseverance (*parakkama-dhātu*).
And so on. His "army" (*senā*) is like an army in the sense of being his companion (*sahakaraṇa*).

In the phrases beginning with "oath" (*saṅgara*), he refers to the employment of conciliation by mentioning the making of friends. By mentioning "bribery," he refers to the giving of bribes, and thereby the employment of gifts. "A mass of force" (*balarāsī*) refers to a troop of elephants, horses, and so forth.
By this, he speaks of the divisions of punishment. For even dissension (*bheda*) belongs only to one who possesses power.

It succeeds; and this fourfold [effort] proceeds by means of the application of skillful methods (*upāya*). It is called "binding" (*saṅgara*) because it gives rise to attachment, clinging, and aversion in various places—either in its preliminary stage, or by way of binding, or by way of its manifestation through formal undertaking.

It is "exerting" (*uṭṭhāhaka*), meaning endowed with the energy of exertion. It is "peaceful" (*santa*) because it has the characteristic of sewing together the welfare of oneself and others, or because it moves away from states of unwholesomeness.
273. "In this way he was of such a form" refers to the past by means of agreeable forms, because of the retrospective recollection (*anvāgamana*) of delight therein.

The same method applies to feeling and the other aggregates as well. Regarding the phrase "by way of wholesome, pleasant, and joyful feeling," the word *vedanā* (feeling) should be applied individually to each: by way of wholesome feeling, by way of pleasant feeling, and by way of joyful feeling.
When there is delight in craving (*taṇhā*), there is delight in views (*diṭṭhi*).
They are indeed established—thus it is said: "he is possessed of craving. [The phrase] "inferior form, etc."... he does not conceive;

for although the object is unattractive, conceiving proceeds by way of the very state of being attracted. He does not cause it to recur because, through suppression, delight has been removed from afar.

274. Since the conceptualization of craving and views regarding future forms and so forth proceeds by way of their being exalted and beautiful, he said: “One should understand: ‘Such was my form... and so on. 275.
It might be said that, in order to establish by way of contrast the illumination of Nandi’s lack of retrospective reflection, [the Buddha] stated the summary:
“Would one not go back to the past? and then explained it with the words: “And how, bhikkhus, does one go back to the past? and so forth.

The analysis has been stated; thus, when the analysis of the summary beginning with "And whatever state is present" is being explained by way of contrast, it was said: "And how... pe... should it be stated?
This objection was raised without considering the Teacher’s method of instruction, which is supremely profound, because [the text says]: "And whatever is present... and so forth.
The detailed exposition (vibhaṅga) beginning with “And how, bhikkhus, regarding present phenomena...

proceeds by way of negating insight (vipassanā) through the method of contrast (byatireka) with respect to the summary (uddesa) beginning with “Whoever [sees] phenomena...”. Therefore he said, “But because...,” and so forth.
In that context, “of that very” means of insight itself. Having extracted the heading (mātikā) in order to show its absence, he says: “It is withdrawn.”
Having extracted the words by way of the matrix (mātikā) out of a desire to explain, the detailed exposition was stated beginning with: "Here, monks, the one who has not heard [the Dhamma]...

the one who has heard... and so forth. "Due to the absence of insight" means that because of the non-cultivation and non-suppression of insight, one is dragged here and there among various objects by craving and views, as if by enemies, being established in this or that state.
For that very reason, one is brought into the ocean of the lower realms and the ocean of saṃsāra. The bright side (the path of purification) is to be understood by reversing what has been stated.
The rest is easy to understand.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Obscure Meaning) of the commentary on the *Bhaddekaratta-sutta* is completed.
2. Commentary on the Ānanda-Bhaddekaratta Sutta 276.

Turning the mind away from external, manifold objects, its perfect settling upon a single object—whether it be access (appanā) or seclusion (paṭisallāna)—is any state of meditative attainment (samāpatti-vihāra). However, in this context, the noble dwelling (ariya-vihāra) is intended.
He said: “Having emerged from seclusion,” and so forth. Although the Blessed One already knew [the answer], he asked for the purpose of initiating a discourse.
For it has been said: “Tathāgatas ask even though they know; Tathāgatas do not ask even though they know,” and so on.
He gave his approval means that he uttered the sound “well done. Furthermore, since that is praise, the word “well done” (sādhu) has the sense of praising.
Therefore he said, "praising the teaching. Encouragement (*sampahaṃsana*) is the act of making those possessing virtues joyful by means of existing qualities;
mere extolling by way of recounting virtues is praise (*pasaṃsā*). This is the distinction between them.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Explanation of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Ānanda-bhaddekaratta-sutta* is completed.
3. Commentary on the Mahākaccāna-Bhaddekaratta Sutta 279.
It is called *tapodā* because it is a pool (*rahada*) whose water is heated (*tapaṃ*) due to its hot nature. Thus he said, "of the pool of boiling water.
To show in detail the meaning that was stated in brief, [the text] says, "of Vebhāra Mountain," and so forth.

It has been said. "From that lake" means depending upon that lake. For even though that lake is located within the realm of the nāgas, it is connected above it to a body of water in the human world. Therefore it was said: "The river named Tapodā flows.
"Such as this" means heated and warm; and by way of a name corresponding to its nature, it is called Tapodā.
The meaning is as follows: "The world of the departed" (*petaloka*) refers to the individual hells (*paccekaniraya*), which are the dwelling places of the departed.

"Of this park" (*imassa ārāmassa*) refers to the Tapodā Park. "From there" (*tato*) means from the river known as the Tapodā. "A great pool of water" (*mahāudakarahado*) refers to a large pond filled with water.

(280) "Abundant" (*samiddho*) means excellent; the sense is that it is indeed complete. "The beginning of his holy life" (*ādibrahmacariya*) means that for him, this was the commencement of the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
Thus, he is one who practices the fundamental holy life (*ādibrahmacariyaka*). Therefore, it is said:

"consisting of the practice belonging to the prior stage. The statement "the past, the future, and the present" is an expression for the awakening to conditioned phenomena by way of their division into the three periods of time.
Although analysis by way of the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth is common [to all suttas], in the first, second, and fourth suttas, however...

Having analyzed by way of the aggregates (*khandha*), the Teacher here does not do so, but establishes the teaching in this manner for the purpose of analyzing by way of the bases (*āyatana*) in a different way.
For in this way, all phenomena suitable for comprehension, both in brief and in detail, are shown after having been analyzed;
this, it is said, was the Blessed One’s intention here, which the Elder [Buddhaghosa] has followed according to the method.
In order to show that [the subject] has been grasped, it was said: “In this [sutta], it is said,” and so forth.
Therein, he established the matrix (mātikā) by way of the twelve bases alone; that is, he established the matrix with reference only to the twelve mundane bases.
Just as [the teaching] was analyzed by way of the aggregates (khandha) in three suttas, if the Blessed One had intended an analysis here as well, it would have been done in that manner.

He might have analyzed it; however, since he entered the fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭī) without having analyzed it in that manner, the Elder analyzed it by standing on the principle that the analysis intended here by the Blessed One is precisely by way of the twelve bases (dvādasāyatana). Therefore he said: "Having grasped the underlying method (naya), he spoke thus.
"Made heavy" means made difficult to perform. "A footing shown where there is no footing" means [a footing shown] in the sky.
The term *pada* (foot/step) is used because it demonstrates that the common meaning [of the word] has a specific scope.
*Nikantivijñāna* means consciousness associated with the craving of attachment (*nikanti-taṇhā*), according to the statement: "It is bound by desire and lust" (*chandarāgappaṭibaddhaṃ hoti*).
*Mano* refers to the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*), which serves as the door for the impulsion moments (*javana*) occurring through the mind-door.
283. “He established by way of aspiration” means he set the mind in motion by way of aspiration.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Obscure Meaning) of the commentary on the *Mahākaccāna-bhaddekaratta-sutta* is completed.
4. Commentary on the Lomasakaṅgiya Bhaddakaratta Sutta 286.
One whose body hair is thick and dense is called *lomaso*. However, because his hair is sparse, he is called *lomasako*; thus it is said: "Because of having the appearance of slightly sparse hair.
*Lomasaka-aṅgiya* means one who possesses limbs (*aṅgiya*) that are *lomasaka*. The first *ka*-kāra is meaningless; the second is merely for the purpose of extending the verse.
"On the Red-Blanket Stone" means on a stone the color of red woolen cloth. "Having descended" means having come down from the sky.
Because they do not accept gains or honors given after witnessing a miracle, they do not dwell on the main thoroughfares.
"From ten thousand world-systems" implies that they have come [from there], as it is used in the ablative sense. "By the deities who had assembled."

This is an expression of the instrument [of speech]. He spoke... for the purpose of inspiring urgency and for the sake of inciting the knowledge of those gods who, due to the dullness of their application of wisdom, were unable to penetrate [the truth], by bringing about a state of sharpness and clarity in that knowledge.

"Therein" means in that assembly of gods, or in this teaching. "Of godhood" (devattassa) means of the state of being a god; the meaning is "of divine prosperity. Of "Bhaddekaratta" (the One Fortunate Night)...
“Of this sutta” means of the *Bhaddekaratta*.
“Learning” (*uggahaṇa*) is the grasping [of the teaching] by way of hearing, both in terms of the phrasing and the meaning; thus he said:
“Sitting in silence and listening, one is said to ‘learn’. “Mastery” (*pariyāpuṇana*) is making [the text] familiar through speech; thus he said: “Reciting it aloud...”
“By doing so, one is said to master it. The mastery of a text consists in its retention; however, since establishing it in others is more manifest, he says:
“By teaching it to others, one is said to retain it. The rest is exactly as explained below.
This concludes the *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Obscure Meaning) for the commentary on the *Lomasakangiya* and *Bhaddekaratta* Suttas.
Complete.
5. Commentary on the Cūḷakammavibhaṅga Sutta. 289.
"By the beauty of the limbs" means by the loveliness of the limbs—the parts of the body such as the hands, feet, and so forth. Whatever offspring...

It is the head that is considered base; in the world, this is the common usage for a "young man" (*māṇava*), as it is said that for the most part beings possess pure elements during their early years;
thus it is stated, "they spoke [of them] in their youth. "From the state of being a lord" means from the condition of sovereignty.
"Accumulation" means a hoard. "A wise man dwells at home" because even when expenditures are small, wealth is exhausted.
Even when accumulated in small amounts, they increase; therefore, he speaks of the purpose instigated by greed, namely:
"A person of discernment, without incurring any expense, might continue to live the household life simply by generating this [wealth].
Through greed for wealth... [and so on] ...is reborn. For the destination of one who is subject to greed is either hell or the animal realm. Indeed, it has been said:

—“Bhikkhus, consciousness that persists, persisting while attached to the gratification of signs or attached to the gratification of secondary characteristics, if one were to die at that time, I declare that one will go to one of two destinations:
either hell or the animal realm. One will be reborn in hell because it is impossible to obstruct karma for which the opportunity has already been made.
The phrase "having bent down" is said with reference to the state of having the head and shoulders cast downwards.
The statement "reborn in the Brahma-world" is said with reference to the cultivation of the conduct of a brahmin. He asked about that occurrence, saying:
"I have heard this: 'My father was reborn as a dog'; was this spoken by the venerable Gotama? He asked about this occurrence, asking, "What was this that was said?"
"Having spoken in that same way" means having spoken exactly as it was said to the dog.
"For the sake of non-deception" means for the sake of not deceiving his own statement, namely, "The brahmin Todeyya was born as a dog";
the intention is to demonstrate the absence of deception. "I am known by him" means: "By this son of mine, I was known as his father in a previous birth."
"Having known 'we are'": it is said that the dog displayed itself in such a way through the power of the Buddha, not by virtue of remembering its past births.
However, its barking upon seeing the Blessed One was due to the latent impression (*vāsanā*) established in a previous birth.

"Concealed by existence" means concealed by the state of another existence. The word *nāma* is used here in the sense of "it is indeed so. "The interval between rebirths" refers to the taking up of the rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in another birth.

He was born into a lowly state. It is said that he was a student of the science of bodily marks (*aṅgavijjā*); therefore, he formulated fourteen questions concerning short lifespans, long lifespans, and so forth.
It occurred to him thus: "The specific differences among these beings, such as short lifespans and the like, are observed by way of their major and minor limbs.
But it is not fitting to say that 'the major and minor limbs [are the cause] up to those respective [results].'"
“Therefore, there must be some other reason for this. The ascetic Gotama will explain that reason in detail, and then my conviction that he is omniscient will become an unshakable certainty.

Others, however, say: “The fulfillment of one’s desired aims occurs by means of great spells and secret sciences (*mahā-manta-vijjā*) after having entered into an animal or a human being; therefore, [this is not so].”
"To this extent, the omniscience of the ascetic Gotama has been thoroughly ascertained.
Suppose now I were to ask him a question concerning the fruit of kamma; if he answers that question while satisfying my mind, then I shall have the conviction:
'Truly, he is omniscient. Thinking thus, he asks those questions."
“Bhaṇḍakaṃ” means property; the meaning is “that which belongs to one. They take what is to be given by karma, thus they are “heirs to karma”;
the meaning is that they partake in the fruit of the karma they themselves have performed and accumulated.
Speaking of that inheritance of karma by way of a metaphorical designation for its cause, he said: “Karma is their inheritance, property,” as in: “Monks, of wholesome states... [and so forth].
“Through the cause of undertaking [the vow], merit increases in this way.
Since the fruit, though distinct by its own nature, appears as if undivided and mixed, it is called a *yoni* (source) because of this; thus he says: “Kamma is their *yoni*, their cause.
One is bound (*bandhati*) or closely bound (*saṃbandhati*) through the sense of “mine-ness” (*mamatta*), hence a *bandhu* is a kinsman or blood relation. But kamma is an absolute bond indeed.
He said: "Kamma is their kinsman. It stands as a support. For there is no support for beings equal to kamma;
no other, such as an Īśvara or a Brahmā, can act [for them], because they lack the capacity to perform or prepare such [a role].
Whatever else needs to be said here should be understood according to the method explained in the *Visuddhimagga-saṃvaṇṇanā*. It is kamma alone.
Why was this determined? Is it not the case that the defilements (*kilesa*) are also a cause for the inferior or superior state of beings, and not merely [kamma]? This is true;
however, it was stated with the understanding that the cycle of rebirth (*vipākavaṭṭa*) produced through the application of defilements is indeed set in motion by kamma.

Having said in brief, "You do not understand the meaning of what has been said," [the opponent asks: "Is it not the case that the Blessed One, being of great compassion, speaks solely for the purpose of making others understand?"
He says, "He teaches the Dhamma," beginning with the words, "It is said that this [person] relies on conceit," and so forth.
"By what is complete" (samattena) means by what is sufficient; the meaning is: by that which has been performed and accumulated in such a way that it is capable of yielding the fruit.
Furthermore, such a state is called "not deficient" in one's own duty; therefore, he says, "by what is perfect" (paripuṇṇena).

Regarding the phrase "by undertaking" (*samādānena*): here, "undertaking" (*samādāna*) means grasping or misapprehending by means of craving and views; thus it is said, "by what is grasped and misapprehended.
One proceeds to good or bad destinations by means of this, hence it is a "way of practice" (*paṭipadā*), namely, kamma.
For that reason, it is called a "path of action" (*kammapatha*).
“This is the way. To show the domain of the obstructing (upapīḷaka) kamma—that it may be both weak and harmful—it is said:

“by powerful kamma,” and so forth. “By powerful kamma” means by meritorious kamma. “It is as if it speaks” means it acts as if it were speaking. Why is it said, “it might cause [rebirth] to arise”? Is it not the case that kamma which has the nature of an obstructor does not have the nature of a producer? All of this—

Some say that this is a figurative expression (*parikappanavacana*): just as certain people, though unable to actually do anything against an enemy or opponent, present themselves as if they were capable by means of some pretext, so too is it here.
Others, however, say: "If the ripening of this karma oppresses [the being], it would [otherwise] ripen of its own accord in that very place."
If it were to find an opportunity, it would cause that person endowed with it to be reborn in the states of misery;

however, because that karma has become powerful and has begun to ripen through the convergence of remaining conditions, it therefore becomes known as "upapīḷaka" (obstructive), as it obstructs its other result.
It is for this very purpose that the term "powerful" is included in the phrase "reborn by powerful karma."

This has been said. For these designations—namely, "oppressive" (*upapīḷaka*), "interrupting" (*upacchedaka*), "productive" (*janaka*), and "supportive" (*upatthambhaka*)—are applied to these kamma-formations according to their function;
they do not act as supports for the sake of production in the same way that wholesome states do.
"Having oppressed" means having afflicted by way of resistance and so forth, just as one who presses sugarcane and the like afflicts the sugarcane juice and so forth.
“Nirojanti” means devoid of vitality (*nitteja*). “Niyūsanti” means devoid of flavor (*nirasa*). “Kasaṭanti” means devoid of essence (*nissāra*). “Parissayanti” means calamity (*upaddava*).

Now, having stated “of the child,” etc., in order to show the manner of bringing about calamity, and in order to demonstrate the manner in which wealth is destroyed, it was said again, “of the child,” etc. “Kumbhadohanā” means those who yield a jarful of milk.
“*Gomaṇḍale*” means in a herd of cattle.
“Having made it the range of eight *usabhas*” means that the archer, having followed after his pursuer, aimed at the enemy with a distance of eight *usabhas*.
“*Taṃ*” refers to the arrow. “*Añño*” refers to the enemy. “*Tattheva pāteyya*” means he would cause it to fall right there, having aimed very closely.
Because the water is disturbed. "Water containing predatory fish" means water inhabited by predatory fish such as makaras and the like.
"Productive karma" (janaka-kamma) is so called because it produces rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), owing to its capacity to yield a full maturation;

it does not merely produce the maturation of the course of existence (pavatti-vipāka). By the word "etc. in "abundance of wealth, etc.," one includes abundance of health, abundance of retinue, and so forth. It does not include long life and the like.

For these [states] have been produced by karma conducive to short life; another [kamma] is able to support them by means of producing long life, but not one that is extremely ugly, of little influence, of low birth, or lacking wisdom, by way of possessing beauty and so forth.
For he will say accordingly: "In this answer to the question," and so on; and that [is said] by way of illustration.
It should be understood that it is so stated.

"The former" refers to the obstructive and interruptive [kamma]. With the intention that the obstructive and injurious [kammas] are those which ward off the arising of wholesome resultant [consciousness], it is said:
"only two are unwholesome. Regarding the statement "the supportive is only wholesome," here, just as with the productive [kamma]...
It possesses the nature of both; likewise, there is no contradiction in stating that the others also possess this dual nature.

For indeed, it is not impossible for Devadatta and others, for those reborn as nāgas and so forth, and for ghosts (petas) who have not yet descended from here, to experience the support, suppression, or destruction of the result of unwholesome karma in the hells and other realms.
And having established this, [the following applies] to one who has taken rebirth through even a single among many acts of immediate retribution (*ānantariya*).
The assistance rendered to others by that [kamma] has been stated; that too is capable.
For when a deed is performed, it supports the wholesome or unwholesome fruit produced by the generative [kamma], such as the symptoms of disease or the equilibrium of the elements.
However, when a deed is performed, it [supports] the resultant and the kamma-produced matter of one who is capable of birth, both at the moment of rebirth-linking and during the course of existence.
That which, when performed, brings about the arising of a result— whether desirable or undesirable— that has been produced by another [cause], and which,

through the non-arising of conditions that would obstruct or interrupt it and through the arising of conditions that nourish it, causes the continuity of that result to persist for a long time in accordance with the capacity of the producer,
is the *upatthambhaka* (supportive). Likewise, that which, when performed, [affects] what has been produced by the producer...
When a wholesome or unwholesome fruit is obstructed by a sign such as the equilibrium of the elements of disease, that is "oppressive" (*upapīḷaka*).

However, when a fruit—which, by virtue of its generative capacity, would otherwise continue for a long duration—is cut short due to the arising of a condition that interrupts it once a certain action has been performed, that is "destructive" (*upaghātaka*).
This is the essential point here.
"In those" means among those kamma-formations. "By the interrupting kamma" means by the kamma that injures the life-span.
To show that this state of being injurious must be understood in two ways, it is said: "by one who takes life," and so forth.

[The life-span] cannot [be interrupted] by the kamma of taking life because the mental continuum (santāna) has been conditioned (*abhisaṅkhata*) in such a way. For the continuum in which [the kamma] arises is conditioned by that very [kamma].
It must necessarily be so desired, because the ripening of that [kamma] is bound precisely there.
By this, he shows that at the very moment of the accumulation of wholesome kamma, the taking of life causes such an impairment of its capacity;

consequently, the kamma becomes of little fruit. Through the phrase "long-lived" and so forth, it is shown that by the power of this impairment, it is like a crop grown in a field [that has been damaged].

This shows that these are states that determine rebirth. For it is only when wholesome kamma provides the opportunity for a specific, determined rebirth to ripen that the act of killing—which draws along a rebirth-linking consciousness—determines that rebirth for the sake of a short lifespan;
thus he says, "or, having determined the rebirth itself, it makes one short-lived. This is because the volition of killing has an extremely bitter result.
One is reborn in hell through the volition of final determination because that purpose has not been exhausted;

however, the others are not so heavy, as it is said: "The former... [etc. ...is [lighter]. But here, that which is similar to what was stated below should be understood according to the method already explained.
"Human and non-human dangers" refers to calamities caused by humans and non-humans. "From the front" means from the eastern gate; "from behind" means from the western side.
"Spreading forth" means spreading among one's attendants or in the region of the deities.
"By others" means by those who came before. "Presence" means being directly manifest through the state of mastery. Having brought [this] forward.
"Debtors" refers to creditors. "Occupations" refers to trades such as commerce and so forth. "Action consisting of non-killing" is action that is the opposite of killing;
the meaning is action performed by way of abstaining from killing. It conduces to long life because the result corresponds to the nature of the action.
"By this method" refers to [the method] regarding those actions that conduce to short life and those that conduce to long life.
Regarding actions, it is by the method of analyzing their leading-on as previously described.
By the word "also" (*pi*) in the phrase "actions such as harming," he includes those actions that proceed by way of anger, envy, malice, stinginess, stubbornness, and ignorance.
"In the same way" means that one speaks of the action of killing in its actual sense (*atthato*).

It is said, "by name," as if they were speaking in that very way. From the statement, "Whatever they aspire to, all that is obtained by this," it follows that just as every wholesome state is the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for all success, so too every unwholesome state is the decisive support for all failure;
thus it is said, "having brought about the loss of enjoyment through oppression," and so forth.
For this method is also shown by way of the kamma of taking life.
Regarding the phrase "non-harming and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes actions proceeding from non-anger, non-envy, generosity, lack of pride, and the state of being wise. 293.
One whose mind possesses envy is called "envy-minded"; thus he says, "a mind associated with envy. "Abusing" means [abusing] by means of grounds for abuse.
"Abusing. "He binds with envy" means he follows after envy; he causes the mind to proceed accompanied by envy itself.
"Of little power" means of little influence and little renown. Therefore he said, "he is not renowned.
Furthermore, that lack of influence of his becomes manifest through the absence of a retinue; thus he said, "having few followers."

294. "One does not become a giver by way of stinginess" means that one does not fail to be a giver solely due to the absence of anything to be given. For a person who is not stingy gives as is appropriate whenever there is something to be given.
295. In order to show the ultimate limit regarding the field worthy of salutation, it is said, "the Buddha, or...

Although there are others—such as mother, father, elder brothers, and so forth—who are worthy of salutation and the like, the performance [of such acts] toward them may be characterized by stubbornness and other such faults.
It leads only to birth in a low family. The connection is that it is not possible to do so during the course of existence (*pavatta*).
By this, he shows that this is the domain of karma that yields its result during the course of existence. Therefore, he said: "But as for rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) alone," and so forth. 296.
"By mere non-inquiry" means that one is not reborn in hell by the mere act of not inquiring; however, because of the cause of non-inquiry...

Showing that the statement in the Pāḷi, “She was not one who questioned thoroughly,” etc., implies that rebirth in hell might occur due to failing to do what ought to be done and so forth, he said, “But one who does not question thoroughly,” and so on.
He brought [the discourse] to its proper conclusion means that he brought the teaching to its completion according to the sequence of the connection.
The remainder is easily understood because it follows the method already explained.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning of the Commentary on the Cūḷakammavibhaṅga Sutta is completed.
6. Commentary on the Mahākammavibhaṅga Sutta 298.
Regarding "the fruitlessness of kamma": this refers to its worthlessness by way of its fruit, that is, the absence of fruit. Thus he said: "Fruitless means worthless."
"Without fruit"—this states the meaning of the word *sacca* (truth) as it actually is. However, the wanderer says by the word "truth" that very same thing is "with fruit.
For the Teacher’s intended "mental action" (*manokamma*) is indeed fruitful; this is the underlying intention.
And this refers to the statement beginning with "vain bodily action" and so forth. "Having taken that up" means having taken it up through tradition. "This" refers to...
The wanderer Potaliputta speaks with reference to the discourse on the cessation of perception (*abhisaññānirodha*).

For that [doctrine] had also become well-known among the followers of other sects. "The Elder" refers to the Elder Samiddhi. The intention is that the wanderer [speaks thus] thinking: "The Elder protects the Blessed One by adopting what was spoken by the Blessed One, yet taking it in a way that is actually different from that, out of fear of being accused of fault."
He said, “...he will think it should be protected,” meaning: “It should be protected by being freed from blame.
It is called *sañcetanika* because it possesses volition (*sañcetanā*). The word “kamma” was spoken by the wanderer because he desired even volitional action for himself at that time.
Because it is conditioned by formations, even form itself is said to be "a formation as small as a sesame seed. Therefore he said:
"He sees it with the fleshly eye alone. This refers to seeing [the meeting]—that is, referring to seeing it in some particular instance—and not to seeing it through full understanding (*pariññā*).
Therefore the Blessed One said: "But whence could there be such talk and discussion?"

299. "The suffering of the round" (*vaṭṭadukkha*) refers to the suffering of *saṃsāra*. "The suffering of defilements" (*kilesadukkha*) refers to the suffering arising from the fever of passion born of the defilements.
"The suffering of formations" (*saṅkhāradukkha*) refers to the suffering spoken of thus: "Whatever is impermanent, that is suffering.
If it were spoken [in this way], would the Blessed One have spoken thus with reference to such suffering as this, as was spoken by the Venerable Samiddhi, without making a distinction?
The intention is that the explanation is indeed appropriate.
300. *Ummaṅga* means emerging; for one who has become confused in discourse, a question concerning an object of ignorance in the interim is an *ummanga*.
Therefore he said: "A question-impasse (*pañhāummaṅga*). Why was it not stated as "even with the divine eye"? For that is not an improper emergence.
"Is it within the range of the divine eye? Granted, this is not within the range of the divine eye itself, but it may be within the range of the peripheral vision of the divine eye;
thus it was so stated. "By the very intention" means that by taking it according to the intention of the Elder Udāyī, he recognized that emergence as being improper.
"To sit down properly" means he was unable to sit down in the manner one sits when first seated.

Because the Elder Samiddhi spoke of the matter exactly as it was, without fabrication, it was said: "He will speak only of what is not real. Therefore he said: "He will emerge in a way that is not based on reason" (*ayoniso*).
Three feelings were asked about because the state of being felt is common to one who feels them without distinction when it is asked, "What does he feel?
That which is beneficial for a pleasant feeling is "to be experienced as pleasant" (*sukhavedaniya*). Therefore he said:
—“That which has become a condition for pleasant feeling. Regarding the phrase “in the others,” this refers to [the categories] such as “to be experienced as painful” (*dukkhavedaniya*).

“Below the volition of the three jhānas” means that, since the context is “from the wholesome,” it refers to the volition of the three jhānas below the wholesome of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*).
“In these” refers to these kamma-s of the sense-sphere and fine-material sphere that are to be experienced as pleasant.
By the word "also" (*pi*) in the phrase "neither-painful-nor-pleasant also," he includes this meaning: "and pleasant [feeling] when the object is desirable.

If it is asked, "If it produces neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling elsewhere than where it occurs at the body-door, then why is it said, 'because it produces only pain'?", he says: "But that feeling... and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "volition of the fourth jhāna," one should also say "wholesome volition of the formless sphere" (*arūpāvacara-kusala-cetanā*). For just as [it is said], "by the body... [so too here].

Regarding the phrase "by speech and by mind," here, by way of taking whatever is available, the sense that "it is to be experienced as pleasant or as neither-painful-nor-pleasant by the mind" applies even to wholesome states of the formless realm (*arūpāvacara*).
This is because such a state produces pleasure, since the sixteen resultant consciousnesses are produced from the superior wholesome consciousness associated with knowledge (*ñāṇasampayutta-kusala*).
And this same principle applies below, in the passage "it is also neither-painful-nor-pleasant."
It should be stated as follows: previously, painful feeling was explained by way of a figurative method (*pariyāyato*), for this is an exegesis of the Suttas;

however, in order to show it again now by way of the non-figurative method (*nippariyāyato*), the passage beginning with "Furthermore" (*apicā*) was spoken. Therefore, in this context, that which is to be experienced as painful (*dukkhavedaniya*) is appropriate only by way of its actual occurrence (*pavattivasena*).

Because this [painful feeling] is applicable only by way of its occurrence, by means of this, all that is to be experienced as pleasant (*sukhavedaniya*)— [...is to be understood].* *(Note: The original text appears to be an excerpt from a commentary on the Abhidhamma or a related Pali work. The ellipsis indicates the sentence continues beyond the provided fragment.)*
And it is appropriate to speak of that which is to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant only in terms of its occurrence (*pavatti*).

"Attachment" (*ālaya*) means delight. "Knowledge of the Great Exposition of Kamma" (*mahākammavibhaṅgañāṇa*) means knowledge in the great analysis of kamma, or the great knowledge of the analysis of kamma.
Since "exposition" (*bhājana*) refers to a detailed description (*niddesa*), whereas this is a mere summary (*uddesa*), he said: "Which..."
“Four... [as before] ...the laying down of the matrix. 301.

This is a separate connection because the Great Analysis of Kamma (Mahākammavibhaṅga) as it was recited is not a suitable vessel for this knowledge, and because it is not included within the connections of question or intention. Therefore he said, “For this,” and so forth. This...

"Making it the object" means here, with reference to the *Kammavibhaṅga* (Analysis of Kamma) stated by way of a person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*), such as "one who takes life," "one who takes what is not given," and so forth.
"Having obtained this condition" is a synonym for that same phrase. "They grasp this view" refers to:
"There indeed are, sirs, evil kamma-results; there indeed are not, sirs, evil kamma-results."
And these [faculties], like the blind men who saw the elephant, remain at the mere sight of it and grasp at a vision devoid of thought.
Energy (*vīriya*) is "ardor" (*ātappa*) by way of burning up the defilements; that same energy is "exertion" (*padhāna*) by way of striving;

it is "application" (*anuyoga*) by way of repeated engagement; likewise, it is "heedfulness" (*appamāda*) because one does not neglect through its cultivation, and it is "right" (*sammā*) by way of thoroughness (*yoniso*).
It is called "right attention" (sammāmanasikāra) in the sense that one attends by means of this; with this intention, he said, "These five are merely names for energy.

Alternatively, heedfulness (appamāda) is the non-neglect of mindfulness. The meaning here should be understood as follows: "Right attention" refers to that specific act of attention through which, when present, the knowledge of the divine eye (dibbacakkhuñāṇa) succeeds. "Concentration of mind" (cetosamādhi) refers to that which is accompanied by the knowledge of the divine eye.
“Concentration of mind. Therefore he said, “the divine-eye concentration (*dibbacakkhu-samādhi*). “In another way” means in a way other than performing unwholesome deeds;
that is, it is the performance of wholesome deeds. Thus he said: “Because of having fulfilled the ten wholesome courses of action (*kusalānaṃ kammapathānaṃ*).
“By the exertion of view” means by means of view, by the power of view. “By the misapprehension of view” means by means of view [regarding] the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*).
"Having transcended by means of misapprehension. "Having resolved" means having resolved and adhered [to the view], thinking:
"Only this is true; all else is false. "Having taken up" means having grasped it with a firm hold. "He speaks" means he speaks while demonstrating to others the position he himself has adopted.
302. Regarding the phrase "In this regard, Ānanda": here the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning" (or "etcetera"). "This too" refers to this statement. "In this regard, Ānanda."

The meaning is: "and such statements as these. It is not a vessel for the knowledge of the Great Exposition of Kamma (*mahākammavibhaṅgañāṇa*), because that [knowledge] is not explicitly described here.

"Of it" (*assa*) refers to the Great Exposition of Kamma; for its matrix (*mātikā*) has been laid down by way of what should be permitted for recluses and brahmins possessing the divine eye, and because it exists as a mere enumeration (*uddesa*) by way of vision. Therefore he said, "But here," and so forth. In that regard:
Regarding the phrase "here, moreover" (*ettha pana*): it refers to the passage beginning with "In that regard, Ānanda" (*tatrānandā*).

"Of those possessing the divine eye" (*etesam dibbacakkhukānam*) means of those possessing the divine eye who have appeared in each of the four preceding sections. "So many" (*ettakā*) is said by some whose speech is truthful.
"Authorized" (*anuññātā*) means permitted; "not authorized" (*ananuññātā*) means prohibited. Here, the mere state of being unauthorized is illustrated by way of what was not authorized.
In the passage beginning with "Therein, Ānanda," the word *tatra* (therein) indicates the locative case used for specification; thus he said, "among those four recluses and brahmins.
This statement—"It seems, sir... there is a result"—was spoken in this manner. *Assa* refers to that recluse or brahmin who speaks in such a way.
*Aññenākārena* means by another reason than the one stated in the phrase "It seems, sir... and so forth.
"In two places" refers to these two textual passages: "There is indeed, sirs... [resultant] ripening," and "He has been reborn in a state of deprivation... [down to] hell.
They are permitted because the existence of that meaning is established therein. "In three places" refers to: "He who indeed, sirs...
is reborn in hell"; "And what he... perceives those [sensations]"; and "And whatever he... [perceives]."
Regarding these three textual passages beginning with "vain knowledge" (*moghamaññan*), [the view] is not authorized because its object is inconclusive and because it involves a wrong adherence.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "For otherwise, Ānanda, is the Tathāgata’s great knowledge of the analysis of kamma.
From that [perspective], those recluses and brahmins who have not abandoned their distortions perceive the analysis of kamma through their partial knowledge. Thus...
