The meaning is that the Great Knowledge of the Analysis of Kamma (mahākammavibhaṅgañāṇa) belongs to the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Enlightened One (sammāsambuddha), because he has come in such a way—namely, by having entirely abandoned all perversions (vipallāsa)—and for other reasons as well. 303.
The construction is: "prior to that [kamma] which was seen while performing it by means of this divine eye (dibbacakkhu). From "therefore" (tato)... [the rest of the sentence follows].
Prior to the performance of that karma: *khaṇḍo* refers to the youth; *sivo* refers to Īśvara; *pitāmaho* refers to Brahmā. By *issarādīhi*:
by Īśvara, Brahmā, Pajāpati, and so forth. *Visaṭṭho*: created. By *micchādassanena*: by way of wrong view. *Yaṃ*: whatever karma. *Tattha*:
among those karmas proceeding by way of killing living beings and so forth. *Diṭṭheva dhamme*: in this very life.
The construction is: "one experiences the result in that very same personal existence. "Having been reborn" means having arisen in a second existence.
"In another turn" means in some other existence whatsoever.
"One mass of kamma" refers to a single collection of kamma distinguished by such types as killing living beings and so forth. "One mass of result" refers to the result of that very same [kamma].
By means of a factor, one [sees] a single collection of kamma-result. "By this" means by the aforementioned divine eye; "not seen" means not seen by such a recluse or brahmin.
"Three" refers to the three stated in the passage beginning, "Or else that was done by him in the past. "Two groups of kamma-results" refers to the two groups of kamma-results:

those to be experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*) and those to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparāpariyāyavedanīya*). As for those to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*), however...
That has been seen; therefore, it is said, "two. One has been seen and three have not been seen;
thus, there are four groups of kamma regarding both what is seen and what is unseen. Likewise, one has been seen and two have not been seen; thus, there are three groups of result (vipāka).
These seven points are the seven bases for the operation of knowledge as previously stated. "Of this specific kamma, this..."
Because neither the action nor its fruit had been seen, it was said, "In the second instance, nothing was seen by means of the divine eye.
According to the method stated previously, the three heaps of karma should be understood;
here, because of the absence of anything seen by the divine eye, it is said, "their respective locations."

That by which one becomes or increases is "capable" (*bhabba*), meaning a cause for growth. That which is not capable is "incapable" (*abhabba*); thus he said, "devoid of existence" (*bhūtavirahita*).
"Shining forth" (*ābhāsana*) in its own fruit is "manifestation" (*ābhāsa*); thus he said, "it shines forth, overcomes, and obstructs.

"Powerful karma" (*balavakamma*) refers to highly blameworthy karma, categorized as that which is practiced with intensity and so forth. "Near" (*āsanna*) means at the time of death; "frequently" (*abhiṇhaṃ*).
"By attendance" means by being near to that death-consciousness.
"Powerful karma" refers to wholesome karma that is powerful due to factors such as its being weighty or frequently practiced. "Of weak karma" means of one's own weak [karma].
"Wholesome [karma] performed nearby"—here too, "nearness" should be understood in the same manner as previously explained.
"By way of manifestation" means by way of the manifestation of karma at the time near to death. "Of that" refers to that person.
The construction is: "Unwholesome [karma] manifests, having become the cause for rebirth.

The followers of other sects (titthiyā) grasp any kind of unwholesome karma as the cause for any kind of result, amidst the intervals between different karmas and their results, just as the blind men who saw the elephant did.
"Adhering to what is merely seen as if it were real," thus it is said: "The followers of other sects... [and so on]... appears. Regarding "the other two":
this refers to this pair consisting of those who are capable and those who appear to be capable, and those who are incapable and yet appear to be capable.

This same method applies to the application of the first two types of karma according to the first and second persons, by way of the manner in which they appear. This very same method applies according to the third and fourth persons.
The method of application for the latter two karmas is as follows:
Because the third karma is wholesome and because he was reborn there in heaven, it appears as the wholesome factor that served as the cause for his birth there.
Likewise, because the fourth karma is also wholesome, yet because he was reborn in hell, [it appears] as the cause for his birth there among the followers of other sects.
"It appears having been unwholesome. Furthermore, whatever is not analyzed here in terms of its meaning is indeed easy to understand.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Obscure Meaning) for the commentary on the *Mahākammavibhaṅgasutta* is completed.
7. Commentary on the *Saḷāyatanavibhaṅgasutta*.

304. Regarding the phrase "they should be known": here, it is intended that feeling (*vedanā*) is what should be understood in such a way that the six internal sense bases (*ajjhattikāni āyatanāni*), once known, lead to the transcendence of the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*). Thus he says: "They are to be known by means of the path together with insight (*vipassanā*).

In this context, knowing by means of the path should be seen as knowing through non-delusion, while knowing through insight is knowing by way of the object. This applies to the remaining terms as well.

The same method applies here. They are called "mental explorations" (*manopavicāra*) because by means of them the mind explores with distinction—that is, it proceeds toward an object—namely, applied thought and sustained thought (*vitakka-vicāra*).

For the mind proceeds together with applied and sustained thought, which respectively cause the mind to direct itself toward and to examine the object; it does not proceed devoid of them. Therefore he said, "applied and sustained thought," and so forth.
Beings proceed by means of these, according to their respective capacity, toward either the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) or its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*).

The seven steps are those based on the household, which are the steps of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭapada*). A trainer of those to be trained is a *yoggācariya*. Therefore, he said, "of those to be tamed and the tamers.
The word "the rest" refers to the remaining seventy-one types of consciousness, since only consciousness together with contact and form is intended here.

"Here" means in this teaching on the group of sixfold consciousness. It should be understood that the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) is indeed distinct from the triad of mind-elements (*manodhātu*).
“Contact in the eye” means contact arisen in dependence upon the eye. Therefore he said: “This is a designation for contact associated with eye-consciousness.
Just as there is no seeing of forms by consciousness alone, so too there is none by the eye-sensitivity alone; thus it was said, “by eye-consciousness.
By this, in the Pāli, the function of that which depends [on the eye] is stated by way of the support, namely, “by the eye.”
...it shows. "By way of object" means by way of being an object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*). Why is it stated simply as "he explores"?
Is it not the case that there is also the operation of applied thought (*vitakka*) therein? True, there is; however, since that [operation] belongs to the same category here, he says:
"and applied thought associated with it. Here, the exploration of the associated states is [attributed] only to applied thought and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
"Function" (*kicca*) is stated as "mental explorations consisting of applied thought and sustained thought.

"Exploration associated with joy" (*somanassūpavicāra*) means an exploration conjoined with joy; it is like saying "a chariot drawn by thoroughbreds," which is why he says "together with joy," and so forth.
(306) Because they are the dwelling place of the mental explorations, they are like a house; thus he says "house-based" (*gehassitāni*), referring to visible forms and the rest.
"Dependent on the strands of sensual pleasure. Because it is an emergence from the perception of permanence and so forth, "renunciation" (nekkhamma) is insight (vipassanā);

thus it is said, "dependent on renunciation," meaning "dependent on insight. Regarding "of things desired" (iṭṭhānaṃ), he says "of things sought after" (pariyesitānaṃ) in the sense of being sought through such means as farming or trade.
However, the state of being dear is already expressed by the word "lovely" (kanta); therefore, [the phrase] "it delights the mind of those things to be longed for" (kāmitabbānaṃ mano rameti) is used.

"Of delightful things. "Worldly bait" (*lokāmisa*) means that which is grasped by the world; it is craving (*taṇhā*). It refers to those things associated with it through being made desirable by way of being graspable and through being conditioned (*paṭisaṅkhata*).
The intention is that what was done in the past arises [as a result], because the experience of an objective referent (*ārammaṇika-anubhavana*) is impossible [otherwise].
To show that such recollection occurs through the recollection of the grasping of views (*diṭṭhaggahaṇa*), [the text says]:...
“‘As it was said’ and so forth is what was stated.
‘The aspect of impermanence’ means the aspect of non-existence after having existed.

‘Transformation, fading away, and cessation’ refers to that which is to be transformed in two ways—by means of aging and by means of death—and is therefore disintegrated and broken up. However, in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), because...”
In order to show this distinction— that arisen form does not remain in that very same mode, but rather abandons its natural state known as the stage of arising,
and having abandoned it, departs from it toward the stage of aging, and while departing, ceases through the occurrence of dissolution—
the phrase beginning with "by the abandoning of its natural state" was stated. And here, [it should be understood] "as it really is with correct wisdom."
Although it is said, “seeing,” what is intended is the knowledge of realization (*anubodha-ñāṇa*) by way of insight (*vipassanā*) that has entered the path;
thus it is said, “by means of the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*),” because this is a description of the process of mental application (*upavicāra*). For he will say:
“When a desirable object has come into the range of the six sense doors,” and so forth. “Seeing the dissolution of formations (*saṅkhārānaṃ bhedaṃ passanto*)” refers to all formations.
He sees that which has the nature of breaking up moment by moment with insight-knowledge proceeding along its course.
Therefore he said, "In the sharp state of formations," and so forth. Therein, "in the state of formations" means in the state of formations that have become the object.
"Sharp" means keen due to the power of meditation and the balance of the faculties. "Clever" means not being overcome by opposing states, and possessing the capacity to overcome them.
They proceed clearly and keenly.

Because the mind is tranquil through the suppression of the defilements, because he perceives the fear in saṃsāra, and because it is based on superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma), the delight of a bhikkhu is non-human;
thus, it is the delight of seclusion, the delight of renunciation.
"From whatever" means in whatever manner, such as through the modes of comprehension in insight (vipassanā) and so forth; this is the meaning.
"The arising and passing away of the aggregates" refers to the origination and dissolution of the five aggregates of clinging.
For the wise who understand—that is, for those who have initiated insight—this joy and gladness should be understood as "deathless" because it is the cause for attaining the deathless (nibbāna).

"At the six doors" means when desirable objects have come into range; that is, when the sixfold desirable objects—consisting of visible forms and so forth—have respectively entered the range of the six doors. This use of the locative case (*bhummavacana*) refers to the object (*visaya*).

"Present" (*paccuppanna*) here refers to the present by way of continuity (*santatipaccuppanna*). By way of the highest description, what is intended here by "supreme liberation" (*anuttaravimokkha*) is Arahantship.
But how does one establish longing for that? For Arahantship has not yet been attained.
Is it the case that there is an object, yet no longing arises directed toward it? Or who says this: "One establishes longing by making arahantship the object"?

Rather, one sets up an aspiration directed toward arahantship attained through hearsay or established by mere hypothesis, and fixes the mind upon it. Therefore the Blessed One said: "When indeed shall I [attain] that sphere..."

"I shall enter upon and abide in [it]. "The base" (*āyatana*) refers specifically to Arahantship, because it possesses the state of being the cause for the endowment with the six factors and so forth, and because it consists of the mind-base (*manāyatana*) and the mental-object-base (*dhammāyatana*); thus it is so described.

Furthermore, this sorrow arises for one who establishes an aspiration, because it occurs simultaneously with that aspiration. For there is no co-existence of greed and hatred. It is said to be "rooted in aspiration."
By this, he explains that the word *upaṭṭhāpayato* (of one who establishes) expresses the sense of a cause. *Evaṃ* means in the manner stated by the words beginning with “When indeed might I...
(*kudāssunāmā*). *Ussukkāpetuṃ* means to exert oneself so as to bring about [the result] through the path. 308.
*Aññāṇupekkhā* means equanimity accompanied by ignorance, which proceeds without clear observation. By each respective factor of the path...

Because he has conquered, without remainder, the defilements that lead to those various states of deprivation (apāya), the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) is, in the primary sense, called a "conqueror of the flood" (oghajina);

because of the absence of those [defilements], the worldling (puthujjana) is, in the primary sense, called a "non-conqueror of the flood" (anoghajina); however, a trainee (sekha) may be called a "conqueror of the flood" in a figurative sense.
Preventing even that [figurative application], he said, "the meaning is 'one whose taints are not destroyed'. In the future...

"Having conquered fruition" means that because he stands having completely conquered fruition for the future by way of making it not recur, only one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) is, in the primary sense, called a "conqueror of fruition";
because of the absence of that [conquest], an ordinary person (puthujjana) is, in the primary sense, called a "non-conqueror of fruition";
however, a trainee (sekha) may be a conqueror of fruition in a secondary sense. Preventing even that [secondary application], he says: "The meaning is 'only for one whose taints are not destroyed.'"
He said: The phrase "not seeing form" (*rūpa*) should be brought from the text and connected [to the preceding].

Although the word "of the worldling" (*puthujjana*) was already stated previously in the text, the subsequent statement "of the uninstructed worldling" (*assutavato puthujjanassa*) is for the purpose of showing that this equanimity belongs to the blind worldling, not to the noble worldling. For the equanimity based on the household life [arises] toward whatever object-base there may be...
"Of one who has regard, not of one who is without regard" means that it may occur toward a desirable object or an object that is neither-desirable-nor-undesirable;

therefore, it is said: "when a desirable object has come into range. However, through ignorance, there occurs the manifestation of the mode of equanimity toward that [object]. Hence he says: "toward a lump of sugar," and so forth.
"Not being attached to the desirable and not being averse to the undesirable" refers to the fact that, for the most part, sentient beings are attached to what is desirable.
It is stated [in the text] with the intention that there is aversion toward what is undesirable.

For improper attention (ayoniso-manasikāra), by way of various objects, does not establish a fixed rule for the impulsion (javana) in any instance; thus, attachment and aversion can arise even toward an object contrary to what was previously mentioned.

Nevertheless, it should be understood that, in actual meaning, his attachment and aversion are indeed rejected. Regarding "non-equanimity" (asamapekkhana), it refers to viewing things unequally or improperly.
[This occurs] in the apprehension of an object preceded by non-systematic attention and delusion.
(309) "By way of occurrence" means both by way of production and by way of repeated cultivation.

"Depending upon" and "having come to" mean having treated [the factors] as the basis for arrival and as the supporting condition (*nissaya-paccaya*). They are said to be "transcended" by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana*).
"Ussārentā samussārentā" means:
having grasped the commonality of the state of joy, it is said, "having caused the similar to abandon the similar.
Here too, that which abandons is indeed powerful because of its capacity to abandon; it is especially so because of the powerful nature of the defiled phenomena.
However, with reference to its state of strength, it was said, "Now, by one who is strong," and so forth.
Because the attainment of the factors of purification is intended here due to their state of strength, the abandoning of even the grief based on renunciation is illuminated herein.
Since equanimity is intended as the factor that abandons [the remaining defilements], it was said, "The discourse on equanimity is to be understood. Of the jhāna...

This refers to the contemplation of miscellaneous formations (*pakiṇṇakasaṅkhārasammasana*) for both those who have not yet attained and those who have attained, as indicated by the phrase, “having made pure formations the basis.
It is accompanied by equanimity because, through the proficiency gained in meditation, contemplation sometimes occurs by way of direct equanimous observation (*ajjhupekkhanavasena*).
This is due either to the jhāna serving as the basis or to the states being contemplated. This is insight that has arrived [at its goal].
It is stated with the restriction that "insight leading to emergence is accompanied by joy" because it is predominantly accompanied by joy.
The same method applies here to the phrase "it is accompanied by equanimity.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in "the fourth jhāna, etc.," the formless jhānas (*arūpajjhāna*) are included. "Similar to the preceding" means exactly similar to the preceding; [namely,] it is accompanied by equanimity.
"Or it is accompanied by joy" means that it is accompanied by mental pleasure (*somanassa*).

"With reference to this" means with reference to the abandoning of insight accompanied by joy by means of the insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā*) which is itself accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā-sahagata*), starting from the basis of the fourth jhāna and so forth.
And here, "abandoning" should be understood as having the characteristic of transcending (*samatikkama-lakkhaṇa*).

This is the distinction regarding the stage of adverting for insight (*vipassanā*). For the insight leading to emergence, the "insight into the jhāna entered" and the "insight into the foundational jhāna" are proximate;
the "phenomena comprehended" refers to the aggregates (*khandhā*) that have become the object of insight.
"The inclination of the person" refers to the practitioner when there is a difference between the foundational jhāna and the comprehended jhāna: "Oh!"... [the rest of the passage continues].
"May I possess five-factored jhāna [rather than] four-factored jhāna"—such was his former inclination (*ajjhāsaya*). He causes them to recite this as well;

here, in the first Elder’s exposition, it is precisely this... [which] restricts the desire not to attain factors that transcend the foundational jhāna for the knowledge of equanimity toward formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa*) that has arisen from each respective foundational jhāna, such as the second and so forth.

Because of the cultivation of the development of dispassion (*virāga-bhāvanā*) and because the other [factors] lack that quality. For by this very principle, in the first Elder’s statement, paths based on the first jhāna without a basis are themselves of the first jhāna;
and other paths, such as those of the second jhāna and so forth, are of their respective jhānas according to the constraints of the jhāna and insight that serve as their bases.
In the same way, the constraint of insight should be applied to the remaining statements as far as possible. Therefore he said:
“In their doctrine as well, it is this very insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanā*) in the prior stage that determines [the result]”—this has already been stated;
therefore, the intention is that it need not be discussed here.

(310) It is "of various kinds" (*nānattādi*) because it is divided into categories such as those belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), and so forth, or wholesome (*kusala*), and so forth. Hence he said, "of many types" (*anekappakārā*).

“Based on diversity” means having various objects such as visible forms, sounds, and so forth as their support. “Uniform” means being of a single nature due to the absence of distinctions such as class, plane, and so on.
“Dependent on a single object” means occurring with respect to an object in only one way. Below, “ignorance-equanimity” was mentioned in the passage beginning with “of the fool, the deluded.
Above, he will speak of “six-factored equanimity” in the passage beginning with “he dwells equanimous. Two.
Equanimity (upekkhā) is included because it is one for both [types of objects], because it must be grasped as a single category, and because it is manifested by equanimity based on diversity.
Ignorance-equanimity (aññāṇupekkhā) exists right there in each respective instance regarding sounds and so forth.

By the phrase "regarding forms" (rūpesu), not only specific objects of the form-sphere (rūpāyatana) are grasped, but rather the kasiṇa-forms as well; thus he says: "and the state of equanimity regarding forms."

“‘Other’,” and so forth. To show that here even the state of being supported by unity is intended only by way of association with the object of unity, and not by way of the object itself, it was said, “But because...,” and so forth.
For this very reason, he said, “Therein...,” and so forth. “By way of association” means by way of conjunction (*sampayoga*).
“Supported by the base of infinite space” (*ākāsānañcāyatananissitā*) means supported by the aggregates of the base of infinite space.
"In the remaining ones as well" means in those based on the base of infinite consciousness and so forth.

"Insight-equanimity regarding the formless sphere" means insight-equanimity having formless-sphere phenomena as its object. The same method applies here for "insight-equanimity regarding the fine-material sphere.
"Consisting of that" (*tammaya*) means produced by craving, which is divided into the categories of sense-sphere, fine-material, and formless. [This refers to] the phenomena of the three planes.
The state of those [things] is "being made of that" (*tammayatā*). It is craving (*taṇhā*) by virtue of which quality the application of the word occurs to a given object;
it is the designation for that. Thus he said: "Being made of that is called craving. "Not being made of that" (*atammayatā*) is so called because it is the opposite of "being made of that.

"Equanimity of insight" (*vipassanupekkhā*) refers to that which has come down in the passage on the investigation of formations: "Whatever exists, whatever has come to be, that one abandons and attains equanimity."
“Equanimity that has become neutral.
(311) Regarding the phrase *yadariyo*, he shows that the letter *da* is used for euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*) and that the word *ya* is in the accusative plural;
thus he says, “those noble ones who [practice] the foundations of mindfulness. Granted, the word “noble one” (*ariyo*) applies to all those who have penetrated the Truths.
This is common; however, because the specific quality about to be described belongs exclusively to the Buddhas, it is said: "The Noble One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
For this majesty does not belong to Paccekabuddhas and others. Regarding the three instances:
either "they do not wish to listen," or "some do not wish to listen while others do wish to listen," or "they wish to listen"—referring to those who have practiced and those who have not.
Regarding the three foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) characterized as the practice of the disciples:
"establishing mindfulness" means establishing mindfulness at all times because of being untainted by aversion or attachment, and because of turning away from both of those.

This constant establishment of mindfulness belongs only to Buddhas, not to others, because it is an exclusive quality (āveṇika-dhamma). Here, "desire to hear" (sussūsā) refers to the wish to listen with earnestness.
Showing the absence of that [faith], he said, “they do not wish to hear after having believed.

Regarding “na aññāya,” since it should have been stated as “na aññāyā,” he explained it as “for the purpose of not knowing,” with the elision of the letter *ya*. He said, “having transgressed... they imagine,” because the very non-acceptance of the Teacher’s instruction constitutes the deviation.
"By way of grief based on lust"—this should be understood here as a statement merely intended to exclude [that specific case].

Since even grief based on renunciation is expressed by the negation of being "pleased" (*attamano*)—as in the Teacher’s use of the phrase "he is not pleased" (*na ceva attamano hoti*)—which implies displeasure (*anattamanatā*) by way of context, he refutes that [misinterpretation] by saying: "It should not be understood that 'he is not pleased' means [only] this."
For the destruction of the bridge belongs to the Tathāgatas. If this is so, why is there a rejection of mental elation? He says:

"But this was said because, among those who have not entered [the path], there is an absence of any cause for mental displeasure. By "outflowing of resentment" (paṭigha-avassavena) is meant the streaming forth of resentment through the six sense-doors;
the meaning is the occurrence of resentment. It should not be understood that the word "uppilāvito" has such a meaning.
Because the state of being elated was abandoned at the very foot of the Bodhi tree. The phrase "among those practicing" is stated by way of topical context;
however, even among those not practicing, there is no cause for the Tathāgata’s displeasure. This has been said:
this statement beginning with “he is pleased” was spoken because it is possible for the Teacher’s blameless mind to be delighted by the right practice of his disciples.
312. "Thus he is trained" means he is instructed by being brought to a state free from unruliness.

Since what is intended here is the running toward one direction alone without turning back—by way of not changing one's posture—the running even of tamed elephants and the like toward a single direction is appropriate only in the sense of not turning back;
thus it is said: "Running without turning back, he runs toward only one direction."
“Without turning back with the body” means without even turning the body around. He ranges through the eight directions by way of liberation, not by way of the eastern direction and so forth.
“All at once” means in a single stroke, or on a single day in one part;
for a “stroke” (pahāra) is said to be a third part of a day. And here, “ranging” is by way of entering the meditative attainments (jhāna-samāpatti).
Because it proceeds with a swift consciousness that is stainless and free from remorse, he said, "He indeed attains [it]. The rest is easy to understand.
The explanation of the hidden meaning in the *Saḷāyatanavibhaṅgasutta-vaṇṇanā* is completed.
8. Explanation of the *Uddesavibhaṅgasutta*.
313. “The pointing out of a meaning that is to be pointed out is the *uddesa* (summary), and the analysis of it is the *vibhaṅga* (analysis,” thus he said:
“the matrix and the analysis”). The four phrases beginning with “one should weigh” (*tuleyya*) are synonyms for wisdom (*paññā*).

Alternatively, “one should weigh” means one should thoroughly weigh that Dhamma by means of wisdom consisting in weighing, according to the method of exertion and so forth. “One should examine” (*tīreyya*) means by means of wisdom consisting in examination...
One should cross over by means of wisdom through the attainment of knowledge and activity therein.

"One should grasp" means that, having thus attained, one should investigate the benefits, the gratification, and the danger. "One should delimit" means that, having delimited the meaning by means of delimiting knowledge, one should know it.
"In regard to objects" means in regard to various objects such as forms and so forth. "By way of attachment" means by way of longing and by way of dependence.
“Remaining” means occurring. “Within the range of the field of activity” (gocarajjhatte) means within that which has become the object of meditation.
For when it is grasped by the mind of development (bhāvanācitta), having been mastered and not relinquished, it becomes as if internal; thus it is called the “range of the field of activity.
If, for a bhikkhu who has begun the development, an attachment should arise toward the object of development, then by means of that attachment, further—
Having abandoned cultivation, it is said to be "stuck" by way of mental contraction; in the absence of that, it is said to be "not stuck.
Showing this when it is stated as "not stuck internally," he says: "not stuck by way of attachment to the internal objective field.
For he will say later: "For that which does not persist by way of attachment is partaking of decline."
"It does not exist; it is exclusively conducive to distinction. "Without grasping" means without grasping anything among form and so forth by way of craving and the like.
For by not grasping in that manner, one would not be distressed through craving, fear, and so forth.
"And of the remaining suffering" refers to the suffering of sorrow and so on. Or, "and of the remaining suffering" refers [to the rest] by way of the headings of birth, aging, and death.
Because the suffering of ripening (vipākadukkha) has been included, the meaning is that it refers to both the suffering of defilements (kilesadukkha) and the suffering of saṃsāra.

316. Form itself is the "sign of form" (rūpanimitta) because it serves as the cause for the arising of defilements. One who runs after it by way of lust and so forth is "one who pursues the sign of form" (rūpanimittānusārī). 318.

"Not fixed by way of attachment" means that while it might be fixed by way of expectation, it proceeds having abandoned attachment; thus, it brings about higher distinction. Therefore he said, "By way of attachment," and so forth.
320. "Grasping and non-distress" refers to the five aggregates of clinging.
Having grasped them by way of the grasp of craving and so forth, thinking "this is mine," etc., there is distress through the influence of craving and fear;
conversely, by not grasping them, non-distress is to be understood. To reveal the intention of the Great Elder as to how this becomes non-distress through non-clinging:
Why does he raise this objection? The statement "because there is nothing to be grasped" is a declaration of the reason for the absence of agitation due to non-grasping on his part.
The passage beginning with "If indeed... is its justification. Agitation due to grasping would exist for him because that which is to be grasped is grasped in such a manner.
"In such a way" means by way of being permanent and so forth. "Even though grasped" means even though taken up and adhered to; [yet it remains] as if ungrasped.

They exist because they are grasped through improper attention (*ayoniso*) and because they must be understood by relying on those who are wise. "By way of views" means by way of the mode of grasping through wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*);
for that [grasping] is not in accordance with reality and is non-existent in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*). "In meaning" means in the ultimate sense.
It is called "agitation due to non-clinging" precisely because, owing to the absence of any mode of being clung to, one does not cling to it.
Having thus established [the term] as "agitation" (paritassanā).
"It changes" (parivattati) means that it is not that very same form which changes by occurring otherwise;

rather, it perishes and breaks up through the abandoning of its natural state and the departure of its own-being. "Transformed" (vipariṇataṃ) means having reached a state of alteration, being ruined. "Kamma-consciousness" (kammaviññāṇaṃ):

Regarding *abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇa*: because of the false grasp such as “form is self,” consciousness—which has been described according to the various divisions of form—undergoes a corresponding transformation.
It is called *vipariṇāmānuparivatta* because it occurs by following after and revolving around change.
Demonstrating that the agitation arising from that is the agitation born of transformation, he said: [the agitation born of transformation].

“Of change... [and so on] ...of agitation. And “the arising of unwholesome states” refers to the phenomena of unwholesome mental arisings that occur in such ways as, “Alas, what I once had is now no more for me,” and so forth.

“Having dispelled” means having dispelled by way of not providing an opportunity for them to arise, because they are rendered incapable of occurring. “By way of fearfulness” means both by way of being afraid and by way of mental terror.
"By the thirsting for it" means by the longing for it. "With vexation" means with the vexation of mental distress;
for that very reason, it is "with suffering" due to mental pain. "By the perception of a jewel-casket" means by the perception arisen [in one] that a casket which is actually empty is full of jewels.
"Agitation because of not having taken it" means that, since there is nothing to be taken, even the act of taking belongs to the side of what is non-existent.
Grasping leads to what is called agitation.

(321) By showing the absence of kamma-viññāṇa through the demonstration that if there were kamma-viññāṇa, there would be a following along with the differentiation of form, [the text] shows the total absence of defilements for one whose taints are destroyed. The rest is easy to understand.
The elucidation of the hidden meaning in the commentary on the Uddesavibhaṅga Sutta is completed.
9. Commentary on the Araṇavibhaṅgasutta 323.
"By way of what pertains to the household" means by way of dependence on the defilements, that is, by way of partiality (*anurodha*). "One should neither lift up" means one should not favor.
"Nor cast down" means one should not suppress by way of hostility, that is, by way of what pertains to the household. [Rather,] without partiality, by way of encouragement (*sampahaṃsana*):

Speaking of qualities as they truly are is not "exaltation" (ussādanā) because there is no fault [in such speech]; likewise, speaking of faults as they truly are by way of discernment, without contradiction, is not "depreciation" (apasādanā).

"The very nature itself" means one should speak of the very nature of a person as it truly is, without making it known to anyone, just as the Venerable Subhūti Thera did. This is called "well-determined happiness."
It is for one who has specifically discerned happiness through such [phrases] as “blameless within” (ajjhattaṃ anavajjaṃ).

As for the phrase “disparagement in his absence,” this refers here to secret speech that proceeds by way of inciting malicious talebearing; thus he says, “the meaning is ‘malicious speech’ (pisuṇavācā).
It is called *khīṇa* because it is exhausted (*khīṇa*); for it harms and afflicts both the one who speaks it and the one on whose account it is spoken.
This is the meaning; it refers to that which is called "exhausted" (khīṇa). Since this speech is crowded with and defiled by the mental corruptions (kilesas), it is therefore said:
"crowded and defiled speech. By this, he includes the remaining threefold misconduct of speech (vacīduccarita).
"Having resolved" means having adhered [to it] with the thought, "This alone is the truth. "Having taken up" means having grasped it. "One would speak" means one would engage in such conduct.
“Worldly convention” (lokasamaññā) means worldly designation (lokasaṅketa). 324.

It is called “relinking with sense-desires” (kāmapaṭisandhi) because it is associated with sense-desires by way of its object and its mental concomitants; it is the pleasure of sense-desires. Therefore he said: “by means of pleasure associated with sense-desires.
“Accompanied by suffering” (sadukkha) means accompanied by the suffering of result (vipākadukkha) and the suffering of defilement (saṃkilesadukkha).
Likewise, "with fever" means it is with fever both by way of the fever of kamma-result (vipāka-pariḷāha) and the fever of defilements (kilesa-pariḷāha).

It is called a "fetter" (saṃyojana) because, by being a wrong practice, it binds beings to that very place, not allowing them to escape from the round of existence (vaṭṭa) but causing them to sink right there;
specifically, craving (taṇhā) is the fetter of existence. Therefore he says, "this is the name for craving. It is not craving alone [that is meant].
Pride and the others also establish their status as fetters (*saṃyojana*) by way of binding thoroughly and completely through all fetters.
Therefore it was said: “Bhikkhus, for beings hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving. This tetrad:
“Those who are devoted to the pursuit of pleasure connected with sensual desire and accompanied by joy, and those who are devoted to the pursuit of self-mortification...”

“...devoted,” having stated this based on the aforementioned tetrad, he said, “He was placed in this foremost position,” and in order to demonstrate in detail how he was so placed, he spoke the words beginning with “Of the Blessed One.
Elevation and disparagement are recognized because the Tathāgata must exercise the teaching of the Dhamma in accordance with the types of persons to be trained. This...
A person... [as before] ...is not said to be "perfect in conduct" because there is no teaching of the Dhamma on behalf of others by way of acting as their advocate.
329. "Disparaging behind one's back" means censuring the faults of one who is worthy of censure. For one who is worthy of censure never becomes worthy of praise;
however, it should be spoken only after knowing the proper time for it—thus he says, "or having known the appropriate and fitting time. Even in the case of one whose speech is exhausted...
The same principle applies to his use of a private dialect, as it possesses the same functional capacity (*yogakkhema*).

330. *Ghātīyati* means it is struck down. A sound is broken or lost; the meaning is that there is a disruption. *Gelaññappatto* means having reached exhaustion or fatigue. *Apalibuddhaṃ* means not afflicted by defects. 331. *Abhinivissa voharati* means:
having adhered to that regional dialect, thinking, "It is exactly thus, and not otherwise."
He practices [this]. "Transcending" (*atidhāvana*) is a mere conventional designation; it is a description established by worldly convention.
Not remaining at the level of mere designation, but instead grasping firmly as if it were ultimate reality, is what is meant by "discourse.
"Not grasping" means not adhering [to such views], but discoursing merely on the basis of conventional designations.
333. *Mariyādabhājanīya* means the demarcation of the mutual non-confusion between the aforementioned right practice and wrong practice.
*Raṇa*: beings cry out because of these, or even those who do not cry out [are so called] because they are the cause for crying out; thus they are *raṇā*.
These are lust, hatred, and delusion, or the ten defilements, or all exclusively unwholesome states, which produce various kinds of suffering.
Beings cry out when overcome; thus, it is "with conflict" (*saraṇa*). Alternatively, the word *raṇa* (conflict) is conventionally established for the dust of passion and so forth.

Therefore, he said: "With dust, with defilement. However, because it is stated in the Canon as "this state is accompanied by suffering," etc., the pursuit of sensual pleasure and so forth are also called "with conflict";
thus, the nature of suffering and the rest is "conflict," while the unwholesome states that produce them possess the quality of being "with conflict."
And they should be understood. The meaning of the terms beginning with "without conflict" (*araṇa*) should be understood as the opposite of what was stated [previously].

"He purifies the basis" means that by entering the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and thereby making himself of great fruitfulness, he purifies himself as a worthy recipient of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya-vatthu*); this purification of the basis for the attainment of cessation occurs for those who have emerged after having entered the attainment of cessation.
The purification of the offering given to Paccekabuddhas, such as the Elder Mahākassapa and others, should be illustrated. Therefore he said, “For thus,” and so forth.
By the phrase “just so,” he concludes the section beginning with “while wandering for alms.
Regarding the statement, “Subhūti the Elder purifies the offering,” it means that they give preceded by a mind made supple through the cultivation of loving-kindness (mettā) and by great respect.
By this, he shows the purification of the gift from the perspective of the donor. However, the purification of the object [of the gift] is shown by way of its counterpart.

[The Buddha asks: "Is it possible to act in this way?"—that is, he asks whether such mastery over the resolve for a swift rising is possible even among ordinary disciples. The other [responds]: "What need is there to speak of the Chief Disciples and the Great Disciples? Even among ordinary disciples..."
Showing that [this state] is obtainable among those who have attained mastery (*vasitā*), he said, “Yes, it is possible,” and so forth. The remainder is easy to understand.
The elucidation of the hidden meaning of the commentary on the *Araṇavibhaṅga-sutta* is completed.
10. Commentary on the *Dhātuvibhaṅga-sutta*.
342. It is said that he undertook a journey with haste because he intended to go specifically for the sake of the clansman Pukkusāti, whose life-span was not yet exhausted.
"If there is no discomfort or displeasure in your mind caused by my going away," [he said]. "He" refers to one who has already arrived previously.
"'What has been given is indeed given' means that what has been given once is sufficient; it is proper, and there is no need to give again"—this is the intended meaning.
"Only what was done is done": the intention is that what was done for the sake of inclusion—namely, the appropriate deed—is indeed done; it is not to be reversed again.
Regarding Pukkusāti, he said, "both as one born of noble birth and as one of noble conduct," because in both respects his status as a son of good family was complete.
"Therein" means at that time of his arrival from Takkasilā. He gladdens people and brings them satisfaction, like a child lying on one's lap.
He causes [them] to obtain. Jewels arise because the border region is dependent upon mountains, the ocean, and so forth.

"Pleasant to behold" means that it brings happiness through the very act of seeing. "Of such a kind" means both pleasant to behold and pleasant to hear. "Invaluable blankets" means expensive woolen cloths.

"In a solid casket" means in a casket made of the essence of sandalwood and other precious materials. "Having had them engraved" means having had them carved. "Having had them coated with lac" means having closed the opening and applied a coating of lac.

He knew that there was a bundle of fine cloth within because it did not appear to be very heavy. "They were priceless" means they were of great value due to their excellence of color, excellence of texture, great measure, and the difficulty of imitating them;
the intention is that the king, being of great merit, certainly possessed such things.
If this is so, why did he fall into the deliberation, "What indeed shall I send? To this he says: "But furthermore," and so forth.
This refers to King Bimbisāra. He began to search because jewels are of many kinds and possess progressively higher and more excellent qualities.
"Gold, silver, and so forth" means gold, silver, coral, gems, pearls, beryl, and the like. "Bound to the sense faculties" means connected to the visual and other sense organs.
"A portion" means he did not attain even a single part [of such a jewel] by way of its qualities.
Because of the commonality of having fully awakened to the truths by oneself (*sāmaṃ*), it is said that "the Jewel of the Buddha is also twofold.
There is no jewel equal to the Jewel of the Buddha, for there is no one like the Buddha to be found in this world or the next.
It is stated as "even the sound," and so forth, considering that [this quality] occurs at the very first enlightenment (*paṭhamabodhi*).
The king, being pleased, thought, “It is as if I have been granted permission to send someone there even though they do not exist.
Therefore—because there was not even for a single full day the demarcation of a dwelling place for Buddhas in that region—for that reason.
“Facing the eastern direction” means a lion-window facing the eastern direction; by this, he shows its well-distributed illumination.
Thus, in order to show that such was the realization (samudāgama) of the Blessed One, which is not shared by others, it was said: "Having thus fulfilled the ten perfections," and so forth.
And in order to show that for one who has thus achieved such a realization, this is the corresponding perfection of the fruit (phalasampadā), it was said:
"From the Tusita abode," and so forth.
The "Noble Dhamma" (ariyadhamma) has the Noble Path as its primary component, and the Noble Path is comprised of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya).
Since these have been included by way of mere enumeration, he said: "having written down a portion of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.

The Minor Precepts (cūḷasīla), etc., are to be understood according to the method set forth in the Brahmajāla Sutta. "Restraint of the six doors" refers to mindfulness and clear comprehension (satisampajañña).
Mindfulness and clear comprehension in seven aspects by way of restraining the six doors beginning with the mind; contentment with the four requisites such as robes in twelve modes;
lodgings conducive to meditation, including the analysis of forest dwellings, the foot of trees, and so forth;

the abandoning of the hindrances as stated in the passage beginning, “Having abandoned covetousness for the world”; and the preliminary work, which consists of the preliminary exercises for the *kasiṇas* and other objects.
There are thirty-eight meditation subjects according to the method handed down in the Pāḷi.
I have written this practice in brief, following the sequence of purification up to the destruction of the taints (āsava-kkhaya).
"Sixteenfold" refers to the application of sixteen kinds of meditation. "Made of palm-leaf" means in a palm-leaf box that is divided by various walls and sewn together with fine, delicate cloth.

"Having wrapped it with a cloth outside" means: first having wrapped it with fine woolen cloth, then having placed it sequentially into thirty-three caskets, and then having wrapped and covered it with a fine cloth on the outside.

Let it be merely cleansed by the removal of grass and shrubs, sweeping, and so forth; [let it not be adorned] with the decoration of placing jars full of plantains, raising banners and flags, and the like.
"Do not finish it"—this is the meaning. "Prepare by the majesty of the king"—the meaning is: "arrange it in a manner befitting my king; adorn it.
"Of the *antarabhogikas*"—of the royal ministers (*mahāmatta*) who are devoted to the inner court. "Swift messengers" (*javanadūta*)—male messengers who travel quickly.
"Those who move together with cymbals" (*tāḷāvacara*)—those who perform while accompanied by cymbals.
Because he had heard from the minister that the King had performed acts of worship and honor specifically for the sake of the gift,
he placed the gift in a high position and sat himself on a low seat. "This will not be [a gift] for another jewel" means that this will not be for another jewel—
such as those consisting of gems, pearls, and so forth— because it is fashioned from gems, pearls, and the like.

A powerful joy arose because, due to having cultivated meditative development and being permeated by its latent tendencies within the Buddha’s teaching for a long time, the cause of his matured nature shone intensely from within, like a lamp inside a jar.
"I maintain" means I desire; it means I take up. "Doubtful speech" refers to a state of indecision. "He makes an interval" means...
He makes that mark between two footprints; the meaning is that he stepped over with one foot.
"By the path she had gone" means by the path taken by that queen as she was departing and being sent away. "That mark," however, refers to the mark made by Pukkusāti.
"A leaf-parasol" refers to a handful of palm leaves.
"Out of reverence for the Teacher" means arising from the great affection and profound respect born of the confidence inspired toward the Teacher.

At that time, as he was traveling while keeping the Teacher alone in mind and leaning toward him, he did not even give rise to the thought, "I shall ask," because there was no such reflection as, "Where does the Teacher dwell now?
However, upon reaching Rājagaha, by virtue of the message sent to the King...
There, because there were many monasteries, he asked, "Where does the Teacher dwell?
It should be understood that the Teacher’s departure alone and his journey on foot for forty-five *yojanas* were performed as an act of homage to the Dhamma (*dhammapūjā*).

Furthermore, the fact that it is customary for Buddhas to perform such homage to the Dhamma has already been explained in detail below. However, concealing his Buddha-majesty and appearing in the guise of a stranger—
In this context, his going there was for the purpose of allaying the fatigue of the journey through the confidence of that clansman.
For one whose fatigue from the journey has not been allayed is not a fit vessel for the teaching of the Dhamma; thus he will say later:
"But did not the Blessed One," and so forth.

"Uruddhanti visālanti keci" means some [interpret it as] "vast and wide. By means of the phrases beginning with "more than three hundred yojanas," etc., he shows, through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya* and *vyatireka*), the giving of exhortation to fellow celibates (*sabrahmacārī*) for the purpose of subduing stinginess (*macchera*).

By the phrase beginning with "accantasukhumālo," he demonstrates that the noble son’s reverence for the Dhamma coincides with and accords with the Teacher’s reverence for the Dhamma. By that, [he shows] what was done by the Blessed One...
By clarifying that he went out to meet him, he shows that one should likewise provide appropriate support for other sons of noble family who are worthy of it.
"As large as the Brahma-world" refers to its height.
"By power" means by the power of his supernormal abilities (*iddhi*), such that he [could come] within the range of hearing.
It does not approach; thus, it is unable to bring about pacification. "Avibbhanta" means free from wandering, devoid of greed.
Having stated, "But this is a gerundive neuter," for the purpose of explaining it, he said, "by means of a pleasing posture.
This instrumental case should be understood as expressing a characteristic of the state (itthambhūtalakkhaṇe). Therefore, he said, "according to how one conducts oneself," and so forth.
It is unpleasant for those who look upon it. For even when lying in the lion’s posture, some parts of the body appear as if scattered and strewn about.
The four-jointed couch consists of the two hip joints and the two knee joints. "It does not stand" means it does not proceed;
there is no occurrence of speech at all when one is not asked, "Who are you? and so forth.

"Because no discourse arises for one who does not establish a discourse": thus, because a discourse has not proceeded by way of such a question, no further discourse on the Dhamma arises or originates. "Therefore" (*iti*):
for that reason, he asked for the purpose of establishing a discourse, for the purpose of setting a discourse in motion, or for the purpose of initiating a discourse.
"He speaks only of his own nature" means that because he has never before seen the Blessed One himself, he thinks, "How could I know [the Buddha]?

and thus speaks only of his own nature—that is, merely his own inclination—and not of the nature of the Buddha’s form-body (*rūpakāya*), which is well-known to the world including the devas and established by its very nature. Alternatively, "he speaks only of his own nature" means:
“Even though he knows ‘this is precisely it,’ at that time he speaks of the very nature of the form-body (rūpakāya) as it occurs through the Blessed One’s own inclination;
the intention is that [the path] does not suppress [it]. Therefore he says, ‘For thus not... and so forth; the intention is that the characteristic of insight itself is the way (paṭipadā).”

343. Having stated, “Without explaining the preliminary practice,” in order to show the reason for not explaining the preliminary practice and to demonstrate the preliminary practice itself in its true form, it was said, “For one who...,” and so forth.
Even with an impure preliminary practice, insight does not function in that way; how much less so when it is entirely absent. Thus: “For one who... [the text continues].
For it is said: “… [and so on] … it is not completely pure. And as for what is called the "preliminary practice," it consists briefly of the fifteen factors of conduct;

thus he says: “He explains this preliminary practice, beginning with the restraint of virtue…” It accomplishes the function of a vehicle because it effects a state of being untiring through the journeying upon the path.
Having been cultivated over a long period and having reached full maturity—
The novice’s virtue (sāmaṇerasīla), established through the perfection of its causes, is also complete, having attained the state of being unbroken and so forth;
because it is rooted in past causes, it is called "virtue" (sīla).
The elements (dhātuyo) exist in the ultimate sense (paramatthato), whereas the person (purisa), which is a conceptual designation (paññatti), does not exist. Then why did the Blessed One...
When explaining insight (vipassanā), which is the proximate cause for Arahantship, he began the teaching by way of what is non-existent as its primary factor, saying:

"The Blessed One," and so forth. In some instances—such as in the phrases "possessing the three knowledges" (tevijjo) or "possessing the six direct knowledges" (chaḷabhiñño)—he shows the non-existent by means of the existent. In other instances—"Monks, the form of a woman, having seized the mind of a man... [the Blessed One spoke].

In such passages as "it remains," one shows the existent by means of the non-existent. In some instances, such as "eye-consciousness" or "ear-consciousness," one shows the existent by means of the existent.

In other instances—such as "the kshatriya youth enters into union with the brahmin maiden"—one shows the non-existent by means of the non-existent. But here, however, [one shows it] by means of the existent.
It shows what is non-existent. For the compound meaning of “consisting of six elements” (*cha-dhāturo*) is non-existent because it refers to a person (*puggala*);

however, the meaning of its constituent parts (*avayava*) does exist, though it is a subordinate meaning. Since that [subordinate] meaning, although subordinate according to the sequence of words (*sadda-krama*), is primary according to the sequence of meanings (*attha-krama*), he said:
“showing the non-existent by means of the existent. This is because the teaching here is based upon the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*).
To show the reason, it was said, "If indeed," and so forth. "He would establish" means:
he would direct the mind of a clansman toward the elements alone; he would perceive them thus; he would teach the Dhamma in this way—this is the meaning.
"He would cause doubt" means: in the absence of a person, who performs [the action]? Who experiences it? Is this merely the elements? What indeed is this, and how?

"Would he give rise to doubt, thinking 'Is this so?'? Would he fall into confusion?"—this means that while the meaning is being taught, he would fall into confusion as if existing in a darkness endowed with four factors.
Being in such a state, because he has become an unfit vessel for the teaching, he would not be able to receive the teaching. "He spoke thus" means he spoke thus: "It consists of six elements."

"As for that which you perceive as 'a person'": that collection of material and immaterial phenomena which occurs as a continuous stream and is distinguished by specific designations—such as "person," "being," or "woman"—that which you perceive in this way is composed of six elements (*ṣaḍdhātu*).
Although other elements distinct from these six exist, it is stated thus for the purpose of easy comprehension; for by grasping those [six], one grasps them all.
And because these must be grasped by them, this matter has already been shown below. "In the remaining phrases" refers to such phrases as "possessing six bases of contact" (*cha-phassāyatana*).
"Having four foundations" (*catur-adhiṭṭhāna*) means that which has four supports (*patiṭṭhā*);

it is a "foundation" (*adhiṭṭhāna*) because one stands firm (*adhitiṭṭhati*) or establishes oneself (*patiṭṭhahati*) by means of it. It refers to those qualities, such as wisdom (*paññā*), etc., by standing upon which one attains the supreme goal, Arahantship.

This is a synonym. Therefore he said, "He is indeed a bhikkhu," and so forth. "From this" means from the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*). "Having turned away" means having turned back and having retreated.
Or, "from this" means from these six elements and so forth; for in one who is settled and dependent upon these, the highest attainment is impossible.
"Well-established" means well-established by way of the attainment of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*). For it is thus...
By completely severing all opposing factors, he becomes established therein.

"The influxes of conceiving do not flow" means that because the stream proceeding through all six doors has been purified by the Path, has entirely disappeared, and has reached total cessation, they no longer flow.
Therefore he said, "they do not flow. Since conceit has been completely severed, that which was not yet severed—

There is no such thing as a defilement that is not pacified; therefore it is said: “The sage is called ‘the peaceful’,” because he has attained extinction (*nibbuta*) through the extinction of the fires of lust and the other defilements.

“One should not neglect wisdom” means that one should not neglect the wisdom of concentration and insight by means of the practice of heedfulness, which proceeds in the manner described in such passages as: “By walking and sitting during the day, he purifies his mind of obstructive states.”
By this, he refers to the development of serenity and insight in the prior stage (*pubbabhāgiya*). "One should guard truth" (*saccamanurakkheyya*):

by way of this expression for guarding truth, he refers to the purification of virtue (*sīla-visodhana*); for one established in truth, fulfilling the undertaken virtue without violating it, makes it conducive to concentration (*samādhi*).

Therefore, he said: "One should guard verbal truth. "One should expand the abandonment of defilements" (*kilesapariccāgaṃ brūheyya*): by way of the "overcoming by substitution of opposites" (*tadaṅga*) and so forth.
One should increase the method for abandoning the defilements. "One should train in the subsiding of the defilements" means that one should train in the method for the subsiding of the defilements—

namely, the foundations of wisdom and so forth pertaining to the supramundane— so that those defilements, having been abandoned by way of their respective factors and so on, do not produce a feverish burning in the continuum through their habitual manifestation.
"For the purpose of attainment" means for the purpose of acquisition.
347. "As previously stated" means as stated previously thus: "Having four foundations, where, being established, the influxes of conceiving do not flow.
348. "It would have to be stated" means it would have to be stated by way of exposition. "By such [terms]" means by such [terms] as these. Duty.
"There is none" because there is no function [to perform]. "A disorderly sequence of elements" means not following the proper order.

"Precisely according to the nature of the Dhamma" means according to the actual character of the qualities to be taught. "An ascetic practice suitable for oneself" means an ascetic practice capable of suppressing one's own defilements.
"To one's own liking" means that which should be approved by teachers according to the disposition of one's own mind; "conducive to one's temperament."
The meaning is as follows. By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "in the *Hatthipadopama-sutta* and so forth," one includes such texts as the *Visuddhimagga* and the *Dhātuvibhaṅga*.
(354) The particle "also" (*pi*) in the phrase "this too is here" has the sense of inclusion; by it, one includes the subsequent teaching: "Then, nothing but equanimity remains.
For that too is a separate connection (*anusandhi*). [Objection: But is this not [already] included in what was previously enumerated?
Is there a method of sequential connection [in the text] such that "there will also be an exposition of the consciousness element"? No;

because the teaching does not proceed according to the method of the exposition of the consciousness element, he said "from below," and so forth. However, by the words "Or else" (*yaṃ vā pana*), he clarifies that the teaching possesses a sequential connection.
For the Blessed Buddhas do not deliver a teaching that lacks a sequential connection. [The phrase] "by way of insight leading to the path" (*āgamanīyavipassanāvasena*)...

By virtue of that [insight] which, having previously occurred, was established in the place of arrival; "consciousness as the agent of action" refers to consciousness accompanied by insight that performs the function of insight, [thinking]:
"This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
"By way of the element of consciousness" means by way of the receptacle for the element of consciousness as it was previously mentioned. Of the Teacher...
"For the purpose of explaining" means for the purpose of explaining by way of a detailed exposition (*niddesa*), since it was established by the Teacher merely as a summary (*uddesa*).
For its state of not having been explained is precisely what remains to be explained and what remains to be penetrated.
He said "untainted" (*nirupakkilesa*) because that mind is purified through the removal of its opposites; however, this is due to the fact that the defilements (*upakkilesa*) have been abandoned.
It is purified. It is for the purpose of seeing arising by way of its origin, and for the purpose of seeing subsiding by way of the cessation of conditions.
Because it is beneficial to pleasant feeling by way of being its cause, it is "to-be-experienced-as-pleasant" (*sukhavedaniya*). Therefore he said: "it has become a condition for pleasant feeling.

(360) Both the material meditation subject (*rūpakammaṭṭhāna*) by way of the analysis of the four elements, and the immaterial meditation subject (*arūpakammaṭṭhāna*) by way of the gateway of pleasant and painful feelings, have become proficient.
The phrase “it will remain only for the purpose of the Teacher’s discourse” negates the very meaning stated as “for the purpose of the clansman’s penetration.
Therefore, in order to support that stated meaning, it is said: “For in this case,” and so forth.
“In the fine-material-sphere jhāna of the clansman” means in the fine-material-sphere jhāna attained by the clansman. Thus he said: “A bhikkhu who is proficient…”
“This is for you, the fourth jhāna of the form realm. Whatever charcoal vessel is fit for heating gold is intended here by the word “torch,” thus he says “a charcoal pan.
“Should prepare” means one should arrange it so that the gold placed therein is heated.
“With flaws removed” means with the blackness vanished. “With dross removed” means with the fine blackness eliminated.

The objection beginning with “But why? was raised with the intention that the Dhamma should be taught for the purpose of dispassion toward all mundane phenomena by one who wishes to establish others on the Noble Path. [In response:

By the Blessed One, who is skilled in training those to be trained, the praise of equanimity of the fourth jhāna was first spoken according to the disposition of those to be trained. Regarding that...
Speaking by way of reply, he said, “Of a clansman,” and so forth. 361.
*Tadanudhammaṃ* means a state conforming to that wholesome state of the formless realm;
the meaning is the preliminary practice (*pubbabhāga-paṭipadā*) by which its attainment occurs. Therefore, he said, “the jhāna of the fine-material sphere.”
"By grasping that" means by one who practices that way of practice through the grasping of it.
"Beyond this" refers to [the stages] such as the "base of infinite consciousness" (*viññāṇañcāyatana*). 362. "Of that very" refers to the immaterial-sphere absorption (*arūpāvacara-jhāna*).

Furthermore, this immaterial-sphere absorption with its result is "conditioned" (*saṅkhata*) because it is produced by conditions coming together and meeting. "Fashioned" (*pakappita*) means established by way of conditions. "Accumulated" (*āyūhita*)...
It is condensed. "By one who acts, it is acted upon" means it is practiced by one who practices;
it is conditioned. Like Nibbāna, it is neither permanent nor eternal; rather, because its nature is to break up moment by moment, it is temporary.

For that very reason, it has the nature of passing away and so forth—all this is an analysis of the disadvantage in phenomena belonging to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*). Regarding suffering:
"Established" means established in the suffering of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra-dukkha*). "Without refuge" (*atāṇa*) means devoid of protection due to its nature of passing away.
"Without shelter" (*aleṇa*) means devoid of a place of rest because it provides no defense against that [passing away]. "Without resort" (*asaraṇa*) means having no recourse.
"Become without resort" (*asaraṇībhūta*) means being without recourse at all times.
If only a portion of the aggregate and so forth were taken, it might be difficult to cure; therefore, it is said: "without allowing him to seize either the trunk or the head.
Regarding the phrase "just so," this is the application of the simile: the Perfectly Enlightened One is like the skilled physician;
the persistence of the suffering of defilements is like the effect of the poison; and the physician’s removal of the poison from its place and applying it above [is the parallel].

Just as by the power of the Blessed One’s teaching, the noble son’s attachment to the realm of sense-desire (*kāmabhava*) is exhausted and he develops the formless meditative absorptions (*arūpajjhāna*), so too is the removal of the suffering of the lower-tier defilements (*orambhāgiyakilesa*) for the noble son, like a physician administering an emetic to cause poison to fall to the ground.
"Not having attained" means not having reached the form-sphere meditative absorptions (*arūpāvacarajjhāna*). "Not yet acquired" is a synonym for that same state.
"All this" refers to all that has been explained in detail as "impermanent," "unstable," and so forth—namely, this entire danger.
He spoke of it with the single phrase "this is conditioned" (*saṅkhata*), because the meaning of that [danger] is completely exhausted by the term "conditioned" alone.
"Does not strive" means he does not exert effort or gather together activity by way of the volition that causes existence. Therefore he said: "Not..."
"He makes a heap. Since "volitional formation" (abhisaṅkhāra) is the activity of volition (cetanā), he says, "he does not will.
Furthermore, since that [activity] is a mental construction (kappa) by way of its capacity to produce a fruit, he says, "he does not construct.
If the volition of formation is sublime, there is growth consisting in the greatness of the fruit; if it is not sublime, there is no growth. Thus he says, "for growth..."

"Or [to] decline. By saying "standing within the domain of a Buddha," the Blessed One—by virtue of his own perfect Buddhahood and his lion-like manner of conduct—speaks thus in order to exhaustively include the specific distinctions attainable by disciples, even while elevating the teaching;
he does not speak by transcending the domain of disciples to teach solely from within his own domain as a Buddha. Therefore he said: "He grasped the pinnacle of Arahantship."
If the son of good family had thus penetrated his own [nature]... then why did the Blessed One reach the pinnacle of Arahantship in his teaching?

To this he said, "Just as if," and so forth. "Prior to this" means prior to the attainment of the fruit of Non-returning mentioned above. "His" refers to the son of good family. "While speaking... [refers to the Buddha].
There was neither doubt nor perplexity regarding the Dhamma of the Blessed One, because doubt had already been completely eradicated by the first path itself.
"In certain places" means in those instances where [beings] were to be disciplined accordingly. For this noble son, too, having attained the fruit of non-returning, recognized the Blessed One.
Therefore it is said: "From which time by him... and so forth.
363. Regarding the phrase *anajjhositā* (not clung to), the meaning is "that which is not to be clung to. Thus he said: "It is not fit to be grasped by swallowing and digesting.

364. Latency (*anusaya*) is indeed passion; thus it is "passion-latency" (*rāgānusaya*). And since that [latency] is capable of arising when the conditions assemble, it receives the designation [of being able to arise];
hence it was said: "Taking a pleasant feeling as its object, passion-latency might arise. But it is not [the case that] for that...

There is no arising [of feeling] because of the impossibility of its conjunction with the three moments. This same method applies to the remaining cases as well. "The other" refers to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
"Dissociated" means dissociated by necessity due to being unbound by any fetter (*saṃyojana*).
"Body-limit" (*kāyakoṭika*) means that which has the body's ultimate end as its limit. "In the second phrase" refers to this phrase: "ending with life."
“Of clinging” means of *upādāna*. Regarding the phrase “they will become cool,” the meaning stated is “they will cease.

However, in response to the objection—“How can the cessation of feelings within the twelve sense-bases (*āyatana*) constitute the attainment of coolness?”—he says, “For the defilements...,” and so forth.
“By the question on origination” refers to the question on the cessation of the truth of origination in the *Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta*.
Is it not the case that when the fever of all defilements has entirely vanished, what is called "coolness" is intended merely as the cessation of feeling?

Therefore, it might be argued that here "feelings" (vedayita) are mentioned, and not defilements; yet even this coolness, which consists in the absolute cessation of feelings, occurs only through the total eradication of defilements.
To address this, he says: "Feelings also," and so forth.
365. "This is the correlation by way of simile": herein, the fetters are like the flame of the lamp;
the four aggregates, which serve as the support for feeling, are like the bowl that holds the lamp; the defilements are like the oil; the round of kamma is like the wick;
the worldling who goes on the round is like the man who carries the lamp; and the path of Arahantship is like the man who cuts off his head.

Because it effects the total cutting off of the continuum, there is the extinguishing of feeling through the condition of non-nutriment—just as a lamp flame is extinguished by the lack of fuel—and this occurs by way of *nibbāna* without residue (*anupādisesa*) for the kamma and defilements that serve as the immediate condition.

At the beginning, [it is said] "by means of concentration, insight, and wisdom"; thus, from a concentration well-practiced through the preliminary path consisting of those three, [one attains] Arahantship.

And from the wisdom of insight (vipassanā-paññā) which serves as its proximate cause. "Superior" means more distinguished. Regarding the phrase "endowed with this," the word "this" (evaṃ) expresses the meaning of the word "this" (idaṃ);
thus he says: "by means of this supreme foundation of wisdom consisting of the fruit of arahantship.

It exhausts all the suffering of the round of existence; thus it is the "destruction of all suffering" (sabbadukkhakkhayo), namely, the supreme path (aggamaggo). Because it is included therein [within that path], it is said: "therein..."
He says, "Knowledge" means "knowledge of the destruction of all suffering," which refers to the knowledge of the path of Arahantship.

Knowledge of the fruit of Arahantship is intended here, because when there is the destruction of all suffering according to the method already stated, the knowledge that has arisen is considered to have that [destruction] as its cause. Regarding the word "his":
"A bhikkhu endowed thus is endowed with this supreme foundation of wisdom..."
Regarding the statement, “It occurs for the bhikkhu”: 366.

*Hi* means because. *Vimutti* refers to the liberation of the fruit of arahantship; therefore, by “knowledge of the destruction of all suffering,” the knowledge of the fruit of arahantship is intended.
*Sacca* refers to the ultimate truth, Nibbāna, and not the truth of the path.
Granted that the liberation of the fruit of arahantship is unshakable because it cannot be disturbed by its opposites;
however, because of the statement, "They are established in truth," he said, "It is called unshakable by way of making the object unshakable. "Vitatha" means destroyed;
the meaning is that it is something different from how it was produced in the state of its arising, due to being subject to transformation through aging and death.

For it is said to be "false" (musā) because its nature is such that it is shaken by aging and death. Therefore he said: "Of a deceptive nature (mosadhamma) means having the characteristic of perishing.
That which is "not otherwise" (avitatha) is so called according to the method already stated; for that is its true nature, since it is obtained at all times precisely as such.
By way of serenity and insight (samatha-vipassanā), it is the "truth of speech" (vacīsacca); that which [is attained] by way of serenity and insight—
Purity alone is verbal truth; beyond that are the truths of suffering and its origin, which consist of the actual, the deceptive, and the real nature [of phenomena].

Thus, since these [latter] are non-false by virtue of their own respective intrinsic natures and possess the quality of being non-deceptive, Nibbāna alone—the ultimate truth—is even more supreme because it is more exalted than them.
Therefore, "because of the more exalted state of Nibbāna itself."

367. *Upadhi* means that "suffering is laid down (*upadhīyati*) here"; thus, the aggregates and the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) are *upadhi*. Alternatively, they are *upadhi* because they "lay down suffering" (*upadahanti dukkhaṃ*);

thus, the defilements and volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) are *upadhi*. "Fully grasped and adhered to" means that, by way of their state of being fully acquired, they are grasped by craving and adhered to by views.
[The phrase] "through the abandoning of defilements by means of serenity and insight" refers to their abandonment by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana*).

And because of the abandoning of the defilements by means of the relinquishing of their constituent parts. It is "superior" because there exists no other mode of abandonment that is more distinguished.
368. "By way of causing resentment" means by way of the arising of mental resentment. "By way of malice" means by way of the state of mental corruption.
"By way of corrupting completely" means by way of being corrupted in every respect. If [these] three terms...

It shows that the relinquishing of the defilements by means of the path of arahantship is the foundation of relinquishment (*cāgādhiṭṭhāna*), and their pacification by that same path of arahantship is the foundation of peace (*upasamādhiṭṭhāna*).
Herein, specifically, "relinquishing" (*sampajahana*) is the giving away (*cāga*) that brings about the state of non-arising;
whereas, conversely, that which is the absence of those [defilements] at that time due to their being pacified through such relinquishing is "peace" (*upasama*). This is the distinction between them.
369. *Maññitaṃ* means conceiving (*maññanā*); the meaning is the conceptual construction (*kappanā*) such as "this is mine" and so forth.
Because it is common to the obstruction of ignorance, the grasping of craving, and so on, the phrase "I am this" here demonstrates the conceiving of views regarding "I.

However, since that view arises through the grasping of what belongs to the self (*attaniya-gāha*) by way of the conceiving of conceit (*māna-maññanā*), that very [conceiving] is included by the term "this"; thus he said: "‘I am this’ is one and the same conceiving of craving."
"It is appropriate. "In the sense of being an affliction" means in the sense of oppression; for it is through the power of conceptualization (*maññanā*) that beings experience things as such.

"In the sense of being internally corrupt" means by way of its state of being defiled within. For because it is corrupted by conceptualization, the personal existence (*attabhāva*) of beings is subject to the root of suffering;
and because it drips with the impurity of the defilements, it is repeatedly shattered and split apart by arising, cessation, and dissolution.
