The intention is that by means of this, all such struggling will cease to exist.
The word *kappa* can also be used as a synonym for time in general, rather than denoting a specific period of time; thus he says, "For all time (*niccakappa*) means at all times (*niccakāla*)."

Just as a person who has not abandoned craving and views is dependent upon and clings to them, so too [the mind] is dependent upon those [aggregates] because it is non-material; thus he said, "of one dependent on craving and views. As for "wavering":
since wavering—in the sense of the disadvantage of right practice that has not been undertaken—is called a "disgraceful wavering" in the discipline of the Noble One, therefore...

He said: "There is agitation. However, when there is no wavering of the mind due to the suppression of such conceptual proliferation (papañca), there is indeed the subsiding of the defilements because the meditation has entered its proper course; thus he said: "When there is no wavering, there is tranquility.
By this it is stated: "What is called the subsiding of the defilements occurs."

In the sense of inclining toward another existence, there is "inclination" (*nati*). Therefore he said: "When inclination is absent means when there is an absence of attachment to a dwelling place and the obsession with craving for existence.
"Coming by way of rebirth-linking" means the arrival right here from another existence by means of seizing rebirth-linking;
there is no going to another existence from here by way of death or passing away, because of the absence of coming and going.
Because there is no occurrence of even karma accumulated through volitional effort by way of a conceptualization of its arising.
"By way of passing away" means that there is no death (cuti) by way of passing away from the state of rebirth, nor is there any reappearance (upapāta) by way of being born in the future.
Since there is no going, no coming, no passing away, and no reappearance, for that very reason, it is neither here, nor yonder, nor in between the two.
Because there is an absolute absence of the going and coming of the body, there is no passing away and rebirth at all;

therefore, it cannot be said that he stands in this world. Nor can it be said that he stands in the other world, nor can it be said that he stands between the two. Thus he said, "Neither in this world," and so forth.
In this context, it is because there is no locus for wandering that is distinct from both this world and the other world.
By saying "not between both," he rejects the idea that [the state] is included within both; thus, he says, "it does not exist in either place.
This very thing is the "end": the non-existence, the non-occurrence, and the non-arising in both this world and the next;
this indeed is the end, the final conclusion, of the entire root of suffering.
394. "Cut the windpipe! he said, and began to cut the pipe. At the very moment he started to cut it, the cutting proceeded, yet because he was not free from lust, the fear of death overcame him;
consequently, the sign of his future rebirth appeared. With a mind filled with agitation, he thought:
"Even that fellow, after declaring himself blameless among his companions in the holy life, will die with lust still within him."
While comprehending formations by way of their impermanence and so forth, he attained Arahantship.
Having previously frequently reached the knowledge of rise and fall through insight, he attained Arahantship at that very moment;

immediately after reviewing the fruit of Arahantship, he attained Parinibbāna as one who "cuts the neck" (samasisi), due to the cessation of life resulting from the severing of the windpipe. For it is not possible for one in his final existence—
A danger to life arose before he had attained arahantship. "Of the elder" means of the Venerable Elder Channa. "By the declaration":

this is the instrumental case used in the sense of a cause, meaning "by the cause that is the declaration. For it was by that cause that the elder, exerting energy, intensified his insight (*vipassanā*).
"By this" refers to the words beginning with, "There is, Bhante. "The elder" refers to the Venerable Elder Sāriputta.
"He asks," venerable sir, "is one who was formerly addicted to socializing with families; he asks how such a person will attain final nibbāna.

By the Blessed One’s statement, "In the past, he lived in association with families," even though he was known among his fellow celibates as one who had associated with families, his state of non-association became evident at this point in the discourse where the Blessed One said, "These are they, Sāriputta," and so forth. He was mature and wise.
Even when practicing correctly, some remain unrestrained. The rest is easy to understand.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Explanation of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Channovāda-sutta* is completed.
3. Commentary on the *Puṇṇovāda-sutta*.
In the *Anantara Sutta*, it is stated: “Seclusion means the attainment of fruition. There, however, the noble dwelling of the General of the Dhamma was intended;
here, on the other hand, seclusion for one who has not yet accomplished his task is called physical seclusion, thus he says:
“‘Seclusion’ means being alone. Furthermore, in the phrase “forms cognizable by the eye,” this refers to the form that is to be cognized.

"The eye is the gateway for one who cognizes"—thus, both the internal and external bases are referred to together by the word "that" (*taṃ*) through their commonality in being objects of delight and so forth. Therefore, he said: "And that—that is, both the eye and visible forms.
Furthermore, the consciousness indicated here by the word "to be cognized" refers to the associated mental states.

Both of these are already expressed by the phrase "mental phenomena cognizable by the mind" (*manoviññeyyā dhammā*), and thus they are not included here. This same method applies to the remaining cases as well.

"By way of conjunction" (*samodhānena*) means by way of co-existence; the meaning is that it occurs together with the mind, that is, through its arising simultaneously with the mind, such as delight and craving.
Therefore he said: "Delight arises. "The conjunction of the suffering of the five aggregates" refers to that which is comprised of the five aggregates.
It occurs simultaneously with the manifestation of the truth of suffering.
Since suffering arises only by way of the six doors, and likewise its origin (samudaya), he said: "Thus, in the six doors," and so forth.
Because the cycle of defilements (kilesavaṭṭa), the cycle of kamma (kammavaṭṭa), and the cycle of result (vipākavaṭṭa) have been explained, he said: "The cycle has reached its peak."
"Having brought [them] together, he shows [it]. Regarding "the second method": this refers to the second mode of teaching stated by the words beginning with "And yet there are...
The intention is that there is neither a sequential connection (*anusandhi*) as such, nor a connection based on underlying intention (*ajjhāsayānusandhi*);
rather, the very possibility of a connection based on a question does not exist here. "In seven instances" refers to: reviling, abusing, striking with the hand, and so forth.
Regarding "blows with clods, blows with sticks, blows with weapons, and depriving of life"—in these seven instances [the Buddha spoke] the words beginning with "How fortunate indeed are they!
in order to cause them to roar the lion's roar connected with patience.
(396) "Fierce" means wrathful; because their minds are defiled by that, they are said to be "corrupt. "Sinful" means evil. "Harsh" means...
They are *luddā* (cruel) because they lack even a slight degree of confidence or affection;
or they are *pharusā* (harsh) due to their harsh speech, and being such, they are called *luddā*. Therefore it is said, "they are *kakkhaḷā* (hard-hearted).
And with this—thinking, "We shall inflict upon them such undesirable things as the cutting off of hands, the cutting off of noses," and so forth—they will threaten them by showing them fear.
Regarding "the jar-headed mallet" (*ghaṭikamuggara*): it is said that they show the shape of a jar at the upper end of the handles;
therefore, it is called a "jar-headed mallet. Regarding "with a weapon such as a single-edged blade" (*ekatodhārādi*), this refers to weapons such as a sword or a scimitar.

Having stated, "This is the name for restraint of the sense faculties (*indriyasaṃvara*) and so forth," he shows the textual passages where restraint of the sense faculties and the like are described as "taming" (*dama*).
He said, beginning with “By truth,” and so forth. *Indriyasaṃvara* (restraint of the faculties) is the taming or the restraining of the six sense-faculties, including the mind;
thus it is *dama* (taming). It is *paññā* (wisdom), because it tames and pacifies evil states such as lust.

It is the *uposatha* called *dama*, because it tames, pacifies, and suppresses the defilements of action such as killing living beings. He said, “In this [uposatha], it is *dama* because it tames and disciplines ill-will, cruelty, and so forth.”
Furthermore, in the Sutta, patience (*khanti*) should be understood as “taming” (*dama*). “Tranquility” (*upasama*) is a synonym for that very taming;

therefore, it is both “taming” in the sense of subduing ill-will and the like, and “tranquility” in the sense of the pacification of those very same states—thus, it is “taming-and-tranquility,” which is patient endurance (*adhivāsana-khanti*).
In this regard, one who has performed their duty with respect to patience becomes a refuge for the great multitude upon going to that country.
Therefore, in order to clarify his life story (apadāna) starting from its origin, the passage beginning with “But who was this Puṇṇa?
was commenced. “Therein” means in this Sunāparanta country. “An unsuitable dwelling” means a residence not conducive to the application of meditation.

“Two brothers” refers to those whose property was undivided and whose business dealings were joint. Thus he said, “Among them,” and so forth. “Wandering on a journey through the country” means traveling through the districts while taking goods for sale.
Thinking, “We shall perform worship of the Buddha, worship of the Dhamma, and worship of the Saṅgha,” they were inclined toward that. “It reached as far as the marrow of the bones”:
the word “Buddha,” having entered the range of hearing for the first time, gave rise to no small measure of rapture and joy;
it remained reaching as far as the marrow of the bones, having cut through the skin, hide, and other tissues with exquisite forms born of rapture. It was released.
It was employed by way of being sold. "The meditation subject does not appear" means it does not enter the path of development (*bhāvanāvīthi*).
"It is unsuitable for me" means it is not beneficial or conducive to my development of the meditation subject.

There is no one at all capable of walking [the meditation path] because the attention of development cannot be sustained due to being overwhelmed by the great sound of the ocean waves. Therefore he said, "The ocean waves," and so forth. "He" refers to the Makuḷa monastery.
Traveling with great speed, they passed beyond their intended route and reached a certain island.
"Having raised a storm" means that by generating a great circle of wind, he stirred up the great ocean in that region and raised a mighty tempest.
The Elder, remembering the younger brother’s words, "Please attend to us," would attend to them from time to time; therefore—
Even then he adverts; it is with reference to this that it was said: “having adverted at that very moment. “In the presence” means in the place of the head.
“They announced” means they proclaimed; they acknowledged, saying, “We are lay followers. “By this” means by this portion relinquished by me.
“Circular hall” (maṇḍalamāḷa) means a dwelling similar to a circular maṇḍala-hall. “Attendants” means those who go along as the remainder.

Making room for Saccabandha, he said, "Of those numbering four hundred and ninety-nine. On that day... [he] took [the lot]; therefore, that elder was placed at the head of those taking the lots first.

"Having gone to the merchant village" means having gone to the vicinity of the merchant village. "The Buddha-festivity" (*buddhakolāhala*) refers to the curiosity that arises in beings upon approaching the Buddhas.
"In the Great Fragrant Chamber itself" means in the Great Fragrant Chamber within the Jetavana Mahāvihāra. "Should be attended" means should be served.
"Perfume woods" refers to fragrant woods such as sandalwood, agarwood, salal, and so forth. The remainder is easy to understand.
This concludes the *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Puṇṇovādasutta*.
4. Commentary on the *Nandakovādasutta*.
398. By means of the exhortation of the Elder Nandaka, he took upon himself the burden of the Saṅgha for the sake of training those bhikkhunīs who were to be disciplined by him.
Therefore, he said, “But this,” and so forth. That which proceeds or occurs is a *pariyāya*;
thus he said, “*Pariyāyena* means ‘in turn’. *Assa* refers to the Elder Nandaka. He caused others to speak [on his behalf] because there was no opportunity for himself.
"Exhorting in turn" means that the nuns who are capable of exhorting do so by rotation; this is "exhortation in turn.
The mind becomes one-pointed and serene through the reverence and great respect established by her former conduct, and through the affection rooted in her household life.
"Gotamī" refers to Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī. "Of the merchant" refers to the merchant of Bārāṇasī.

"Those four Paccekabuddhas. He asked, "What indeed? because his mental continuum had been long cultivated through meritorious deeds and he possessed great reverence and esteem for the Paccekabuddhas. "Is it possible even for those in poverty to do so?
he asked, meaning that the hut built by those in poverty according to their means was sufficient for you to dwell in.
"Give hand-labor" means "give after performing manual labor. "Having explained the benefit" means [saying] the benefit by such statements as:
"Service rendered to such great queens will be for our long-term welfare;
and the gift of a dwelling place indeed brings great fruit and great benefit, bringing great prosperity in the place where one is reborn," and so forth.
Having explained [this]. "Having exhorted with a stern admonition" means: having threatened her with fear, saying, "While they are doing this very work, why do you not do it?
Do you not know that you are the wife of my eldest slave?
If you do not perform the manual labor being done by everyone else, such-and-such suffering will come upon you. "Being a hundredfold, a hundredfold" means...
He gave one hundred and one sons of slaves, having gathered them together and each having built a separate hut.

"Together with the surrounding requisites for walking meditation" means together with the places for walking meditation, standing at night, standing during the day, eating, and other such attendant facilities. "Having groomed and prepared" means having made them ready.
"He had them assigned" means he had them relinquished [to the recipients]. "Having exchanged" means having bartered for them. "The three robes" means those worth a thousand [pieces of gold].
Having made three robes, he gave them. "From time to time" (*kālena kālam*) means at various times; the sense is "at some time.
"While established in kingship" means while established in a kingship that benefits all living beings.
"The elder Nandaka too" refers to the chief slave at that time, who later went forth as the elder Nandaka and attained arahantship.
"The daughter of the eldest slave-girl" ... [etc] ... refers to Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, who stood in the position of chief queen.
"This venerable Nandaka" means that this very Venerable Thera Nandaka [is meant] by way of his origin.
"These many bhikkhunīs" means that these five hundred bhikkhunīs [are meant] by way of their origin.
399. By way of cause means by way of method; that is, by way of practice that is not perverted. For preceding stages of practice are the causes for subsequent ones.

"Seen according to its true nature" means as if it were directly perceived through its actual mode of being. 401. "Of that same nature" means corresponding to that [feeling] by virtue of being its condition.

403. "Impermanent first and foremost": the impermanence of its shadow is established even earlier than the object itself. For there is nothing whatsoever that arises in dependence upon what is impermanent which could be called permanent.

“Without damaging” means without destroying. To show by way of contrast how the cutting of the other parts occurs without destroying the body of flesh and the body of skin, it is said, “Therein,” and so forth.
“Causing the skin to adhere” means causing it to stick to the skin, making it connected to the skin. “Having bound the skin” means not tearing it open at the time of the incision.
"Having bound it with skin. "Without having done so" means without having effected the destruction of the flesh and skin;

that is, having separated them from one another by cutting away the underlying flesh and so forth. In this context, "underlying flesh" (*vilimansa*) refers to the flesh attached to the skin, which they also call "covered *kilomaka*.
"Sinews" (*nhāru*) refers to fine sinews. "Binding" (*bandhana*) refers to the connection between the skin and the flesh. Thus he said:

“Only the flesh smeared upon all hides. “Only the internal defilements” means only those defilements that have become internal because they have arisen within the mind and are included within the continuum of a being. 405.
“The effort directed toward that” should be regarded as a mere illustration; for it is like a man cutting [wood] with an axe.
When cutting, the place of the cut must be observed; the state of its being struck back must be desired;
the absence of bodily fever must be desired; its steadiness must be desired; and equanimity toward other functions must be desired.

Thus, for the yogi who cuts away defilements with wisdom, there arise the factors of enlightenment consisting of mindfulness, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity, together with the power of energy.
"It should be desired," he said: "In this way, it is not possible... [omission] ...without the six [factors].
(407) "For that reason" means: because that teaching of the Dhamma was suitable for those bhikkhunīs, yet due to the weakness of their practice, their aspiration did not reach fulfillment;
however, if there were another such teaching, through the strength of their repeated practice, [the goal would be reached].
"They will have their intentions fulfilled; for that reason, you too should exhort those bhikkhunīs with that very same exhortation. 415.
"The very last of all" means the youngest of them all was a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*); the meaning is that there were none among them who were not noble ones (*anariya*).
Therefore he said: "But the rest... [up to] ...and those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*). "If it is so" refers to a bhikkhunī who, though her taints are not yet destroyed, is of such a kind.

It exists. This being so, he challenges [the opponent] with the underlying intention: "Even if one possesses the state of a *sukkhavipassaka* (dry-insight practitioner), if the state of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) exists, then in the Noble Discipline their intentions are not yet fulfilled. He asks, "In what way are their intentions fulfilled?

The other states the reason—that it is through the fulfillment of aspiration—and clarifies that point with the words beginning, "For one who... Here, "fulfillment of aspiration" means the fulfillment of purpose in that regard.
The intention is that there is no complete perfection of qualities. Therefore he said, "When indeed... and so forth.

By this, it should be understood that because of the difference between the foundational jhāna and the jhāna attained through the contemplation [of insight], the distinction between the enlightenment factors, path factors, and jhāna factors in the Noble Path occurs by way of the underlying tendency (ajjhāsaya) active at the time of a person’s insight;
thus the meaning is illustrated. The rest is easy to understand.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning of the Commentary on the *Nandakovāda Sutta* is completed.
5. Commentary on the *Rāhulovāda Sutta* 416.
"Bringing liberation to maturity" means bringing to full development the state of Arahantship, which consists of the liberation that is the subsiding of the defilements (*kilesa*). Entirely...
They are called "conducive to the ripening of liberation" because they mature, perfect, and cool it. "Dhammas" here refers to causal dhammas. Therefore he said:
"by way of the cause for purification"; the meaning is: by way of accomplishing the purification known as Arahantship.
As the faculties beginning with faith become purified, they gradually, according to the sequence of the paths, completely liberate the mind from lack of faith and the other defilements.
They achieve liberation as the supreme fruit. Their purification, however, comes about through avoiding fools, attending upon the wise, and reflecting on those qualities that inspire confidence.
Therefore, showing that fifteen factors are intended here, he said, "For it has been said," and so forth.
In this context, "persons lacking faith" refers to individuals devoid of faith. For by relying on them, faith never arises;
rather, by following their views, one’s lack of faith increases all the more.
Therefore, they should be avoided from afar, like a dangerous road. Furthermore, "lack of faith" (assaddhiya) is that which is opposed to faith regarding matters that are not to be believed.

The defiled states (*saṃkilesadhammā*) should be understood as those that arise in the mode of resolute conviction (*adhimuccanākāra*). "In persons endowed with faith" means in persons who have perfected faith.
For, by relying on them, faith arises regarding objects worthy of faith that had not yet arisen, and having arisen, it attains further increase and abundance.
And "objects worthy of faith" refers to the Jewels beginning with the Buddha, as well as kamma and the fruits of kamma.
"Of one who serves" means of one who practices in order to produce and increase the perfection of faith that is currently being obtained. The remaining phrases are synonyms for that same term.
Alternatively, "of one who serves" means of one who approaches; "of one who associates with" means of one who shows devotion toward their practice.
"Of one who attends upon" means of one who stands near them by way of carrying out their advice and instructions. These are called the "inspiring discourses."
The *Sampasādanīya Sutta* and others, which are associated with the qualities of the Buddha and so forth and which induce confidence, are [the third way].
For one who reflects upon them, confidence that has not yet arisen toward the Buddha and the rest arises, and that which has already arisen reaches further increase and fullness.
"By these three ways" means by these three aforementioned reasons. Cultivation occurs through the distancing of opposing factors and through each being easily offered.
They attain development. The faculty of faith becomes purified; by virtue of bringing about the path and its fruit, it remains and reaches purification.
In this same manner, the meaning should be understood for the remaining terms as well.
However, this is the distinction: "the lazy" refers to those who are indolent and have abandoned their burden in regard to right practice. "The energetic" refers to...

In one who has exerted energy and is practicing rightly. "In the right endeavors" (*sammappadhāne*) refers to the four types of purposeful striving that occur by way of the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states, and so forth.
"Of one who reviews" means of one who reviews the practice.

For, by reviewing those [states], having overcome sluggishness, one correctly applies the element of initiative and so forth for the sake of the arising of unarisen [wholesome states] through the proper method and the perfection of mindfulness.
It leads to further increase. When the mind is unconcentrated—resembling a startled deer or a startled ox—it is distracted.

When the mind is properly concentrated through access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*) and absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*), it is well-composed. Regarding "jhānas and liberations" (*jhāna-vimokkha*):

this refers to the jhānas beginning with the first, characterized by applied and sustained thought (*savitakka-savicāra*), as well as the first and subsequent liberations (*vimokkha*). For their successive reviewing occurs in each higher stage.

It leads to ultimate composure. "Lacking wisdom" (*duppañña*) means devoid of wisdom; it refers to one who is entirely destitute of wisdom due to the absence of learning, inquiry, hearing, and reflection upon the Noble Dhamma.
"Possessing wisdom" (*paññavanta*) means endowed with both the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*) and the wisdom of the Path (*magga-paññā*).

"The profound course of knowledge" (*gambhīra-ñāṇacariya*) refers to the profundity of knowledge regarding the divisions of the aggregates, bases, elements, truths, dependent origination, and so forth.
It is a place for practice, or rather, it is where the movement of profound knowledge proceeds.
For there, reflective contemplation dispels delusion and leads to the arising of wisdom not yet arisen, and to its further increase.
"In the collection of discourses" means in the body of suttas. Previously, the causes for the purification of the faculty of faith and the others were called "the states that ripen emancipation."

Here, showing other qualities such as faith and so forth, he says, “And others too,” and so on. In that context, the fact that faith and the rest are conducive to the ripening of liberation has already been shown;
however, there is no need to state that perceptions such as impermanence are conducive to the ripening of liberation, because they belong to the category of insight (vipassanā).
Therefore, he says: “These five perceptions partake of penetration. “Good friendship and so forth” refers to good friendship.
These five qualities—restraint by virtue, talk on effacement, arousal of energy, and penetrative wisdom—are [the fruits of] having virtuous friends and so forth.
This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the *Meghiya Sutta-aṭṭhakathā*.
Regarding the phrase "while surveying the world": it means while specifically surveying with the Buddha-eye the world of sentient beings who are to be converted by a Buddha.
419. Because the faculties of the Venerable Rāhula were fully matured, the deities who had established their aspirations stood watching him, thinking:
"When indeed will he attain the further destruction of the taints?
But when the Teacher reflected thus, at that very moment those deities, sharing his same inclination, waited for that specific occasion at all times.
Having seen that assembly, those deities gathered together in a certain Andhavana forest.
Because it functioned as the duty of seeing the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths for the householder Upāli and the wanderer Dīghanakha,
the first path among those who had attained the stream-entry (sotāpatti) was called the "Dhammacakkhu" (Eye of the Dhamma), owing to its preeminent quality for the purpose of such vision.

However, since the three lower fruits of knowledge among the fruits of knowledge of one with a Brahma-like lifespan are preeminent, the *Brahmāyusutta* refers to those three fruits as the "Eye of Dhamma. Here, moreover,

it is stated that the venerable Rāhula’s knowledge of the path and his knowledge of the fruit are preeminent for the purpose of seeing, and that the knowledge attained by those deities is likewise preeminent.
“In this sutta, it should be understood that the four paths and the four fruits are the ‘eye of Dhamma.
But is there any distinction in the disciples’ knowledge of the realization of the truths? Yes, there is.
And that distinction may indeed consist in some slight difference arising from the mode of occurrence of the insight leading to emergence during the prior stage. This is the meaning.”

In the Abhidhamma, this should be explained by the statement, "But it is not as it is for one who has attained through vision," which illustrates the distinction of one who has attained through vision over one liberated by faith with respect to the abandonment of defilements.

But did all those deities attain the four fruits simultaneously, like the Venerable Rāhula, with a single state of mind? Showing that this was not so, he said, "For in that case... and so forth. How many?
"But those deities," he said; thus [begins] the passage starting with "And of them.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Obscure Meaning) for the commentary on the *Rāhulovāda Sutta* is completed.
6. Commentary on the *Chachakka Sutta*.
420. "Good in the beginning" (*ādikalyāṇa*): either because its initial portion is good, it is "good in the beginning"; that which is good in the beginning is *ādikalyāṇa*.
And the state of being good in the beginning is to be desired through the removal of faults. For that which is entirely free from faults is indeed possessed of complete virtues;
thus it is called "faultless" (*niddosa*). The word "having made" (*katvā*) means "having made it good, having made it auspicious."
It should also be applied to the first two phrases. For here, the mode of teaching is grasped by the word *kalyāṇa* (beautiful/excellent). Therefore he said:

"The excellence of the dhamma to be taught is shown. However, in the second interpretation of the meaning, the excellence of the dhamma to be taught is stated in its primary sense, while the other [excellence] follows by implication. Thus: "beautiful in the middle and beautiful in the conclusion."

The same method applies here as well. And this praise of the teaching was spoken—beginning with “Thus the Blessed One, the Noble Lineage”—in order to show that it is a practice customary among the Buddhas.
The inclusion of the word *dhamma* is also a praise of the teaching; thus it is said, “by nine phrases.
Knowledge of feeling as it truly is is the function of the Path, and its means is insight (*vipassanā*); therefore he says: “together with insight...”

“...to be known by means of the Path. It is to be penetrated through non-delusion regarding its production by means of the function of full understanding (*pariññā*) and clear comprehension (*abhisamaya*), etc.
Only the mind of the three planes is mentioned because the sphere of comprehension (*sammasana-ṭṭhāna*) is intended here.

This same method applies to the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*) and so forth. Or rather, the inclusion of the base of mental phenomena is due to its status as a “base,” not because it is entirely non-internal.
"Craving arisen at the moment of impulsion conditioned by resultant feeling" means that craving arises from the moment of unwholesome impulsion,
thus experiencing and relishing in this way by depending on the thirty-six types of resultant feeling.
(422) "A separate connection" is stated with the intention that there is no possibility of a connection such as *yathānusandhi* (connection according to the subject matter) and so forth.

"Below" means that by demonstrating how consciousness, contact, feeling, and craving exist in dependence upon conditions, the dependence upon conditions of the eye-base and so forth, as well as the form-base and so forth, is illustrated;
for there can be no arising of what is not produced by conditions in the absence of those conditions.
And whatever exists in dependence upon conditions is impermanent because it is subject to arising; whatever is impermanent is suffering; and whatever is suffering...
Thus, by means of the five aggregates and the six sextets, the characteristic of non-self has been elucidated in terms of its actual meaning through the resolution of the compact mass.

Desiring to elucidate it also by way of its specific nature (*sarūpato*), the Blessed One—showing it both through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative exclusion (*vyatireka*) by means of that same method of resolving the compact mass of the six sextets—said: "The eye..."
By saying, "He who would say 'self,'" and so forth, the teaching has been elucidated according to its proper sequence. Therefore he said, "Of those explained above," and so on.
However, previously, by means of the six sets of six, there was merely a demonstration of their analytical separation;
the characteristic of non-self (*anattalakkhaṇa*) was not fully elucidated. But here, it is with the intention that the characteristic of non-self is elucidated in its true nature (*sarūpato*).

This indicates the existence of another investigation. Although the state of non-self (*anattabhāva*) is indeed found within all four truths—since all phenomena are non-self—nevertheless, it is said that these two methods proceed by way of comprehension (*sammasana*):
"for the purpose of showing the state of non-self in two truths. "It does not occur" means that it does not accord with the logic known as "arising" (*upapatti*).
"This is the meaning here," he said, "it is not tenable. For one who maintains the doctrine of self (*attavādin*), [the self] is considered "permanent, stable, and eternal";
yet the eye is impermanent because it possesses the quality of arising. Since it exists by way of conditions, therefore:

"If anyone should say, 'The eye is the self,' that is not logically possible," and so forth. The eye, which is the basis for the view of a personal identity (*sakkāyavatthu*), is non-self because of its impermanent nature, just as...
The eye is impermanent because its mode of existence is dependent on conditions, just like a jar;

the eye exists in dependence on conditions because it is subject to arising and so forth, just like a jar. "It passes away" means it passes away through the disappearance of its own nature at the moment of dissolution.
Therefore, he said: "it ceases."
424. Since the cycle of kamma is rooted in the cycle of defilements, and the cycle of result is rooted in the cycle of kamma;
and since the arising of defilements is preceded by the grasping of craving and so forth, he said, "in order to show the cycle by way of the three graspings.
Furthermore, since the phenomena belonging to the side of craving are the truth of the origin, while the eye and so forth are the truth of suffering, it was therefore stated:

“...in order to show the round of existence by means of two truths. It should be understood that the graspings of craving, conceit, and views are intended here because they constitute the way leading to identity (*sakkāya*).
Since the act of grasping itself—such as “This is mine”—is what is meant here by “contemplation,” he says:

“He contemplates by means of the three graspings. “By way of the opposites of the three graspings” refers to the contemplations of suffering, impermanence, and non-self, which are the opposites of the graspings beginning with craving.
The meaning is: by way of those [three], or by way of the opposites of those three verses, by way of unraveling, and by way of non-arising.

The construction is: "to show the turning away (vivaṭṭa) by way of the opposites. Regarding the phrase "the practice leading to the cessation of personality" (sakkāyanirodhagāminī paṭipadā), since the phenomenon of cessation has been shown here in its own form, he says: "to show the cessation... etc. "Words of negation" means words of rejection.

425. The statements regarding the non-clinging to craving and so forth are spoken specifically with reference to craving and views, because it is only in the case of craving and views that there exists the occurrence of delight and so on.
He says, "The meaning of 'not abandoned' is the meaning of 'underlying tendency' (anusaya)," explaining:

"It underlies (anuseti), thus it is not abandoned. For when defilements such as lust are not abandoned by the Noble Path and have become firmly established, they are called an underlying tendency; [this occurs] when the cause is obtained.
Because it is capable of arising when [the conditions] are present. As for what should be said regarding this, that has already been stated above.

"Of the suffering of the round and the suffering of the defilements" means of both the suffering of the round and the suffering of the defilements. For Nibbāna with residue remaining is the ending of the suffering of the defilements, while Nibbāna without residue remaining is the ending of the suffering of the round.
"Of these" means of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*). "By way of rejection" means by way of abandoning, that is, by way of causing them not to occur.
"Having abandoned ignorance" means having brought about the state of non-occurrence for ignorance without remainder.
Granted that even the knowledge of the lower paths is indeed true knowledge (*vijjā*) that abandons ignorance, yet that knowledge does not effect the abandonment of ignorance without remainder.
It does not exist; however, when the knowledge of the supreme path has arisen, not even a trace of ignorance remains.
Therefore, he said, "having generated the knowledge of the path to arahantship," to indicate that this very [knowledge] is the abandoner of ignorance. 427.
While the Tathāgata himself was teaching by means of his own Buddha-power, sixty bhikkhus attained arahantship.
"This is not wonderful; what then is wonderful?"—to this he said, "This," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "even as they were speaking":
here the word *iti* has the sense of manner, meaning "in this very manner. "Attained indeed" is to be construed as: "sixty bhikkhus attained indeed [arahantship].
This too is not wonderful, for in the presence of the Teacher, disciples have achieved great direct knowledge and mastered the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
"In such and such a way they teach the Dhamma with its wonders. Therefore he said: "For those disciples have attained the great direct knowledges (mahābhiññā).
Regarding "the great pavilion" (mahāmaṇḍapa): they say it was a large cloth pavilion constructed to accommodate the great assembly of bhikkhus that took place right in front of the Lohapāsāda.
"In those places" refers to those aforementioned locations, such as the great pavilion and so forth.
In these instances, the phrase "there was a great elder" (*mahāthero atthi*) should be brought forward and connected [to each case].
Having heard of the virtues of the Elder Deva, the Great Elder’s mind became serene; likewise, being pleased by the excellence of the robes, he said, "But you, bathe him.
And as for "in the lower palace," it refers to the Uposatha Hall in the Kalyāṇiya Mahāvihāra—sometimes in the lower palace and sometimes in the upper palace.
"At one time, he told [the story]. Some say that by the power of the deity, a great assembly of Cūḷanāga attained direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).
Others say that the Elder was himself of great psychic power, and therefore he caused that very large assembly to attain direct knowledge.

"From there, from there" means in each respective direction. "Only one" means just a single person, not many; the meaning is that there were only a few worldlings (*puthujjana*). The rest is easily understood because it follows the method already explained below.
The elucidation of the hidden meaning of the *Chachakkasutta* commentary is completed.
7. *Mahāsaḷāyatanikasuttavaṇṇanā*:
It is called the *Mahāsaḷāyatanika* because it proceeds by taking the great sixfold sense bases (*saḷāyatana*) as its subject; and as for their greatness:
They should be understood as such because, when grasped in an unwise manner, they pervade the vast world-system and lead to great harm;
whereas when grasped wisely, they lead to great benefit, welfare, and happiness. "Indicator" (*jotaka*) means that which makes known.

429. Even the knowing through insight (*vipassanā*) that has reached its peak is indeed knowing according to reality (*yathābhūta*), because it serves as the proximate cause for knowing by way of the Path (*magga*).
He said: "One who does not know by means of the path together with insight.
They "go to growth" means that through the convergence of conditions, they go to successive growth within the series of existence, birth-origins, destinations, stations, and abodes of beings.

Having become such, like the states of serenity and insight brought to proficiency, they are further brought to mastery; and like the meditative absorptions and direct knowledges, they have attained mastery.

Having sacrificed, they cause [the defilements] to increase further and further; thus he said, "they reach mastery. For indeed, at times they remain simply because they have not been abandoned, even though a longing for existence has not been produced.
Unwholesome states for the most part proceed and increase through the perception of destruction by means of the sense-base of vision (*dassanāyatana*).
"Distress of the five doors" refers to those [states] accompanied by the impulsion (*javana*) of the five doors.
"Unwholesome distresses. In this way, the distresses pertaining to the mind-door are to be understood.

"Torments" refers to those associated states that are more powerful than the distresses and which cause torment to both the associated phenomena and their support (the body). "Fevers" refers to those even more powerful than the torments, which burn those very same things.

430. "Sensory pleasure of the five doors" does not mean pleasure based solely on the sensitivity of the physical body. "Pleasure of the mind-door" means pleasure based on consciousness pertaining to the mind-door.
There is no mental pleasure whatsoever, because it is already included by the inclusion of bodily pleasure.
The statement that there is neither entering nor emerging by means of five-door javana is said with reference to the Path in order to show its occurrence through mind-door javana;
it is not, however, for the purpose of dispelling any suspicion regarding that [five-door process]. Even to produce mere intimation...
If it is asked: "How is it a condition for the attainment of *asamāpatti*, and yet how is it possible for the Blessed Buddhas?

Even so, in their proximity, there is simply no occurrence of five-door consciousness, because at that time, such a prior mental application (*pubbābhoga*) is impossible. By this very [reasoning], regarding those who are unskilled in the noble Dhamma...
The objection that [mental consciousness] would incur the same functional activity as the cognition of a pot or similar objects is to be understood as rejected.

This is because, by virtue of each respective prior attention (*ābhoga*), the mental consciousness—which arises subsequently to the five-door-determined mental consciousness—discriminates the specific qualities such as color and shape regarding their respective objects. Thus, it is said: "It exists merely upon having arisen."
Five-door javana is unable to perform any such function as determining the object; it merely arises for a moment. This is what is referred to by the phrase "contemplating danger," and so forth.
431. "Of one possessing wholesome consciousness... having become...
means of one who possesses mental pleasure associated with wholesome consciousness that leads to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī) and is accompanied by insight (vipassanā).
"Pure from the beginning" means pure even before the arising of the path or the commencement of insight. Therefore he said:

"They are indeed completely pure from the very start. "The factors that cause [the path] to operate everywhere" refers to the purification of virtue, the concentration of the mind, the application to insight, and the abandoning of defilements to be abandoned by the path—thus, to every function of the requisites for the path.
The factors that cause [the path] to be produced. "The eightfold" means it is either eightfold when consisting of the first jhāna, or sevenfold when consisting of the second jhāna.

By taking this very passage from the Sutta—namely, "the view of one who has become thus," and so forth—he says that the supramundane path is fivefold, because only the five beginning with right view are mentioned in that context. He, thus...

One who speaks thus is a caviller (*vitaṇḍavādī*). "By the very next statement" means by the immediately following statement, beginning with "the view of one who has become such," namely by the statement beginning with "thus for him.
"Should be refuted" means it should be rejected. For this statement, "the noble eightfold path," directly rejects the fivefold nature of the noble path. If...
Thus, regarding the question of what purpose is served by the inclusion of only five factors there—beginning with the phrase “the view of one who has become such”—he says:
“And further,” etc. One who possesses the Noble Path develops right speech; therefore he says, “he abandons wrong speech.
For at the very moment when right speech reaches the fulfillment of its cultivation, at that same moment wrong speech is abandoned.
They fulfill it by means of that very abstinence, for without the abstinence of total eradication, the full understanding of suffering and the other [noble truths] are impossible.
From the very beginning, they must be entirely pure, because meditation succeeds only for one who is established in perfectly pure virtue.
To support the aforementioned point through another text, it was said: "And also in the Subhadda Sutta," and so forth.
The intention is that in many hundreds of suttas, only the eightfold path is mentioned, not a fivefold one.

Since right mindfulness accomplishes the four functions beginning with the contemplation of the body at the moment of the path, he says, "the four foundations of mindfulness are associated with the path," showing them as being fourfold; it is not by way of their being associated with all four paths.
This same method applies to the right efforts and so forth as well. Because they do not overstep one another, the pairings of the Noble Path are like a yoke and a team;
they are bound together with one another, thus they are called "yoked. Therefore he said: "yoked in a single moment.

For it is at the very moment of the Noble Path that serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), having become simultaneous, proceed with an equal burden. For this very reason he said: "For these," and so forth.

The statement that "concentration occurs at one moment and insight at another" is said with reference to their predominance in their respective functions at those various stages, and not otherwise; for there is no concentration devoid of wisdom, nor is there insight devoid of concentration.
However, in the Noble Path, they occur simultaneously because of their equal strength and single flavor. "Fruition-liberation" (phala-vimutti) means...
The liberation that is the fruit of arahantship. The remainder is easily understood because it follows the method already explained below.
The exposition of the hidden meaning of the commentary on the Mahā-Ṣaḷāyataniya-sutta is completed.
8. Commentary on the Nagaravindeyya-sutta.
435. "They conduct themselves in what is even and uneven" means that they conduct, perform, and practice bodily evenness as indeed even, and bodily unevenness as indeed uneven.
However, because that evenness and unevenness are mutually contradictory and dissimilar, they cannot coexist at one and the same time;
therefore, it is said: "At one time even, at another time uneven. For even conduct...
This was said because it was previously illuminated by right conduct (*samacariyā*).
437. They are called *ākārā* because they indicate, make known, or awaken the intended meaning; thus he says, "What are the *ākārā*?
What are the causes? *Anubuddhiyo* means inferential knowledges (*anumāṇa-ñāṇāni*), for that [knowledge] [relates to] an object as it has been seen.
It is called "anvaya" (concomitance) because it follows or pursues by way of being seen. "By way of green grass, campaka groves, and so forth" means:
by way of grass resembling a green woolen blanket, and by way of blooming campaka groves resembling golden cloths;
and by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the presence of sounds and tastes is indicated here, such as the sound of the *kīcaka* bamboo and the sweetness of various fruits.
"It should be understood" means that by way of the *campaka* flower itself, the existence of the "fragrance of contact" (*phassagandha*) has also been stated. Therefore he said:

"The five strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*), beginning with visible forms, exist. Having stated, "This was said with reference to the forms of women and so forth," whether these forms and the rest are bound to the sense faculties (*indriyabaddha*) or not bound to the sense faculties (*anindriyabaddha*), all of them are "strands of sensual pleasure" because they serve as the objective causes for the arising of defilements.

Having in mind this very objection, he says, "For those... and so forth, showing that forms and other objects belonging to a woman of a different class are specifically the cause for the arising of defilements.
Therein, "those" refers to forms and the rest. The word "hi" (for) has the sense of a reason; by it, he supports the aforementioned point: "Because..."
“They persist by seizing the mind of a man; therefore, this was said with reference to the forms of women and so forth.
“The mind of a man”: having seized—that is, taken hold of—the wholesome mind of a man belonging to the four planes, making it as if it were contained within one’s own fist.
For in such expressions as “having seized the herd of elephants,” *pariyādāna* means grasping. “The perception of impermanence... [and so on].
In such passages as, "When cultivated and frequently practiced, it completely consumes all sensual lust," *pariyādāna* means exhaustion;

here, however, both meanings [exhaustion and grasping] are applicable. Now, in order to establish the aforementioned point by means of a sutta itself, the words beginning with "As it has been said" (*yathāha*) were spoken.
Therein, in phrases such as "I do not, monks," the particle *na* has the sense of negation. The word "I" (*aham*) is the Blessed One’s designation of himself.
"Bhikkhus" is how he addresses the bhikkhus. "Another" means something other than the form of a woman, which is what must now be stated.
"Even a single form" means even one form. "I do not perceive" refers to the perception by means of knowledge;
this should be connected by bringing the negative particle (*na*) from below. This is the meaning here: "Bhikkhus, when I am looking thoroughly with the knowledge of omniscience..."
“I do not see even a single other form [that does so]. “That which thus persists, having taken possession of a man’s mind”:

that form which, for a man who values form, persists by taking hold of and exhausting all wholesome states of consciousness, preventing them from arising. “Such as the form of a woman” means the physical body of a woman.

The word *rūpa* has many meanings, such as "aggregate" (*khandha*) and so forth; however, in this context, it should be understood as the visible-form base (*rūpāyatana*) consisting of the color-element (*vaṇṇadhātu*) within the fourfold origination of a woman.
The statement, "Bhikkhus, the form of a woman stands seizing the mind of a man," was spoken for the purpose of strengthening the preceding point.
The preceding passage, "Just as this, bhikkhus, is the form of a woman," was stated by way of a simile.
This statement should be understood as an illustration of the sense of "exhaustion" (pariyādāna). The remainder is easy to understand.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Nagaravindeyya Sutta* is completed.
9. Commentary on the *Piṇḍapātapārisuddhi Sutta*.

438. Because the General of the Dhamma intended [this] as a period of seclusion (*paṭisallīyana*), and because it was stated later in the text, "Venerable sir, I now dwell frequently in the dwelling of emptiness (*suññatāvihāra*)," he said, "'Seclusion' refers to the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
"Serene" means especially clear. "By way of their locus" means by way of the locus in which the faculties are established.
Is it not the case that those sense-faculties are clear by their very nature? True, they are.

However, this was not said with reference to such clarity; rather, it was said with reference to the attainment of a superior and more refined state by the remaining material phenomena of the mental continuum, which arise from the material qualities born of consciousness (*cittaja-rūpa*) manifested through peaceful and sublime meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
It has been stated. "From the attainment of the fruit" means from the attainment of the fruit entered into by way of the contemplation of emptiness (*suññatānupassanā*).
"The abiding of great persons such as the Buddhas" is *mahāpurisavihāra*. Therefore he said: "The abiding of the Buddha... [etc. ...the abiding.

"Starting from the abiding" means, in the case of an enclosed monastery, starting from the enclosure; and in the case of one not enclosed, starting from the place where an enclosure would be appropriate.
"Starting from"—some, however, say "starting from within the monastery. "As far as the village threshold" means the inner threshold of the village.
"Having wandered through the sequence of houses" means having wandered for alms.
"As far as the exit at the city gate" means as far as the place of exit at the city gate. "As far as the monastery" means as far as the interior of the monastery.

“The path turned back from” means the path of retreat. Although it occurs in the manner of striking against an object, that which is associated with resistance (*paṭigha*) proceeds as if striking against the mind;
thus he said, “the class of defilements that strike against the mind.
“Training day and night” refers to this very right practice that abandons lust and the other [defilements], both by day and by night.
By training step by step and increasing [one's practice] higher and higher.

Regarding the phrase "Have the five strands of sensual pleasure been abandoned by me?": here, the abandonment of the strands of sensual pleasure means the abandonment of the desire and lust associated with them.
For it has been said: "The variegated things remain just as they are in the world; yet herein the wise subdue their desire."

"Various reviewing by a single bhikkhu" means that for one and the same bhikkhu, there are various reviews as they appear in the Canon, such as: "Have the five strands of sensual pleasure been abandoned by me?
and so forth. "Various bhikkhus" means several individual bhikkhus. "Various reviews" refers to the various reviews mentioned above.
Now, this very point briefly stated [is explained as follows]:
In order to show this in detail, the passage beginning with “How? was stated. Therein, it was said, “he reviews”; but how does he review?

To this he says, “Have they been abandoned? and so forth. “Having exerted energy” means having undertaken the fourfold energy of right striving (*sammappadhāna*) and having increased insight (*vipassanā*).
The ellipsis to be supplied is: “having attained the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*) immediately after the path. Immediately after the fruit...
One who "searches" while established on that path of non-returning— having emerged from the attainment of fruition and begun insight for the sake of the supreme path (the path of Arahantship)—
does so in that very seat; and because he attains the path of Arahantship before long by intensifying his insight,
he is said to have "attained the path immediately after the fruition," since there was no period of dwelling in insight due to the non-occurrence of the phenomena subject to cessation.

“Emerging from that” means emerging from the fruit immediately following the path. For one who has emerged from what is immediately subsequent to the path is as if they have emerged from the path itself;
thus it is so stated. Regarding the phrase “the path immediately after the fruit,” here “fruit-immediate” (*phalānantara*) means that which has the fruit as its immediate [precedent].
By both phrases—“the fruit-immediate” and “the path”—the paths and fruits of the non-returner (*anāgāmin*) are indicated.

And "he speaks thus" is how the meaning should be understood here. "The same method applies to the hindrances and so forth"—here, the application should be understood by way of such [questions] as, "Have the five hindrances been abandoned by me?
Regarding the word "of these," it refers here to these [categories]: the hindrances, the five aggregates of clinging, the foundations of mindfulness, and so on.
"Abandoning and so forth" refers to abandoning, full understanding, development, and realization. "There is various reviewing" means those various acts of reviewing.

The meaning is "does not eat. Regarding the phrase "in these reflections," it refers to these twelve kinds of reflection, beginning with the reflection on the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*).
One reflects upon one reflection because the task is accomplished by means of just one among the twelve methods.
Another monk reflects upon another [reflection]. For this word *eka* has the sense of "another" in such expressions as "some [people] here" (*ittheke*).
It departs. However, there can also be a fourfold reviewing here, such as "the reviewing of various bhikkhus" and "the various reviews of various bhikkhus.
Yet, because there is no realization (*abhisamaya*) by means of these two, both of them have not been mentioned in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*). The rest is easily understood.
The exposition of the hidden meaning (*līnatthappakāsanā*) for the commentary on the *Piṇḍapātapārisuddhisutta* is completed.
10. Commentary on the *Indriyabhāvanāsutta*: 453.
“Named thus”: [it refers to] that which has received the name “Gajaṅgalā” by way of the feminine gender, located in the Middle Country.
In the market town that served as a boundary post, they say there was a tree named Suveḷu, which is a species of *nicala* tree.
However, with the intention of indicating that it was distinct from others, it is described as "a species of tree.

The taming (*damana*) of the eye and ear—meaning their restraint from their respective objects—is the cultivation of the faculties (*indriyabhāvanā*). And this occurs through not seeing and not hearing at all; thus he said: "With the eye..."
“He does not see forms; he does not hear sounds with the ear. For the intention is that since vision and hearing exist, those [faculties] are merely untamed and undeveloped.
And because the eye and ear grasp what is not yet reached, they are ill-guarded; thus the brahmin rejects their very apprehension of objects.
“Unrivaled” means not shared with the tenets of other sects.
"Ālayanti" means the aspect of the desire to speak; this is the meaning.

454. "Vipassanupekkhā" (equanimity of insight) refers to the equanimity consisting of insight that has become neutral during the discernment of the impermanent nature and so forth of formations, once the three characteristics have been seen by the knowledge of insight in one who has commenced insight practice. Furthermore, because it has reached a specific stage of development...
It is peaceful and sublime compared even to the lower stages of insight, let alone to the equanimities associated with eye-consciousness and so forth;
therefore he said: "This is peaceful, this is sublime. It is insatiable because it does not produce satiety through the flavor of such peaceful and sublime cultivation. For this very reason he said:
“For a bhikkhu who has entered an empty place, whose mind is peaceful, there is a superhuman delight as he clearly penetrates the Dhamma.
Here, “itī” means “in this manner,” referring to the way that will be explained. “This bhikkhu” means this bhikkhu who has initiated insight meditation.
The construction [is as follows]: “In the eye-door, regarding a visible object” means in a visible object that has come into the range of the eye-door.

“Pleasant” means that which functions by way of being pleasant. “Pleasant and unpleasant in the neutral” means that which functions both by way of being pleasant and by way of being unpleasant toward a desirable-neutral [object];
thus it is called “pleasant-unpleasant. Therefore he said: “Neither pleasant nor unpleasant.”
By the term "agreeable," the state of being agreeable is grasped; by the term "not agreeable," both the state of being agreeable and the neutral state are obtained in part.

Therefore, it is said, "agreeable and disagreeable. Having thus shown the ordinary mode of occurrence of the consciousness that takes that as its object, according to the specific qualities found in the object, [the author now proceeds] by way of its negation to [describe] that of the Noble One.
In order to show the unsurpassed development of the faculties (*indriyabhāvanā*) within the Vinaya, it is said:

“That his mind might be attached,” and so forth. Herein is the construction: that his mind might be attached to a desirable object, or feel aversion toward an undesirable object, or be deluded regarding a neutral object.
“Having restrained” means having prohibited. “Having encompassed” means by means of knowledge through full comprehension (*parijānanavasena*).
"Having grasped [them] and fully understood them through the full understandings of knowing, scrutinizing, and abandoning.

"He establishes insight in equanimity" means that he gradually generates the equanimity of insight (*vipassanupekkhā*), brings it to the state of equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*), and establishes it there. "One who possesses vision" does not merely indicate the existence of the physical eye of flesh;
rather, it indicates its existence in an eminent sense, as in the case of expressions such as "one who possesses virtue" (*sīlavā*).
He said: "One who has eyes is one endowed with eyes, one whose vision is purified.
(456) It is slightly inclined; having been high in the middle, it is slightly inclined, not bent at the edges. Therefore he said: "Standing up like the pole of a chariot.
(461) "Repulsive" refers to an unattractive object. "Perceiving the non-repulsive" means not perceiving it as repulsive. That state of perceiving the non-repulsive...
To demonstrate this, it was said: "Either by suffusing with loving-kindness," and so forth. In that context, one should construe it as follows:

regarding an unrepulsive and desirable object designated as a "being," either by suffusing with loving-kindness or by resolving according to the elements; and regarding an object designated as "formations" (saṅkhāra), by resolving according to the elements.
"He dwells perceiving the unrepulsive" means through the desire for welfare and the contemplation of the intrinsic nature of phenomena.
Having become one who does not perceive repulsiveness, he dwells in the maintenance of the postures.

Regarding an agreeable object that is not repulsive and is designated as "sentient," he does so either by means of the pervasion of foulness—thinking it is merely a collection of impurities such as head-hairs and so forth—or by way of attention to it as foul.
Or else, he does so by applying the thought that this mere form and non-form is impermanent and conditioned. For that very reason, [he considers it] as "suffering, subject to change."

"Attending to it, he dwells perceiving repulsiveness. Regarding "the remaining phrases": this refers to the two remaining phrases that follow in the sequence beginning with "in the repulsive and the non-repulsive," and so forth.

For there, having taken desirable and undesirable objects together, it is stated how—just as for beings what is first established as repulsive later appears through a different state by way of the mode of grasping.
Or it appears as non-repulsive. And that which first appears as non-repulsive later appears as repulsive;
regarding both of these, if one whose taints are destroyed so desires, he may dwell perceiving them as non-repulsive or perceiving them as repulsive according to the method already described.
"Avoiding both" means avoiding the object that appears according to its intrinsic nature and according to the power of meditation as having the intrinsic nature of repulsiveness.
Having abandoned and not grasped both that which has a nature of being agreeable and that which has a nature of being disagreeable, he says:
"In all objects, desiring to dwell as neutral, what does one do? Having stated this, he speaks—"in the desirable...
[and] in the undesirable... one becomes depressed"—showing the method of practice therein. Now, regarding the meaning just stated, according to the *Paṭisambhidāmagga-pāḷi*:
In order to clarify this, he said, "For it has been said," and so forth. Its meaning follows the method already explained above.

"Mindful" (*sato*) means possessing mindfulness due to the attainment of the fullness of mindfulness. "Clearly comprehending" (*sampajāno*) means acting with clear comprehension due to the attainment of the fullness of wisdom.

"Having seen a form with the eye" (*cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā*) refers either to the visual consciousness capable of seeing forms—which is conventionally designated as "the eye" by way of its instrument—or to the eye itself as the instrument.

Having seen a form, he is neither glad; this is by way of rejecting the joy based on the household life and [experiencing] the feeling of joy in activity belonging to the side of renunciation. And regarding these:
“But otherwise, Ānanda, in the discipline of the Noble One, there is the unsurpassed development of the faculties,” and so forth.

—“And how, Ānanda, is one a trainee (sekha) practicing the path? and so forth; and by the threefold methods presented beginning with: “And how, Ānanda, is one noble (ariya), with faculties developed? and so forth.
Herein, by the mention of the “agreeable,” there is the inclusion of wholesome and unwholesome states associated with joy (somanassa);
by the mention of the “disagreeable,” there is the inclusion of unwholesome states associated with grief (domanassa); and by the mention of the “both agreeable and disagreeable,”...
Because those associated with equanimity toward formations are included [in the first method], it is stated in the first method that "defilement applies; non-defilement applies.

For in the first method, since the worldling (puthujjana) is intended, even that which is dissociated from the defilements of corruption is appropriate. However, in the second method, because of such statements as "he... pe... is reckoned," it is said that "first, defilement applies."

It has been stated. Because the one in training (*sekkha*) is intended here, it is said that "defilement (*saṃkilesa*) is also applicable" due to the fact that his defilements have not yet been abandoned.
In the third method, because the Arahant is intended, it is said that "only the third [alternative], which is free from defilement (*nikkilesa*), is applicable.
However, in the section on those in training, the similes beginning with "a man with sight" were spoken in order to make known a single meaning. Therefore...
The noble ones’ development of the faculties is the establishment in equanimity regarding insight after having suppressed lust and the other defilements that have arisen at the eye-door.

The first method is presented from the perspective of one practicing insight; the second, from the perspective of a trainee (*sekha*); the first and second, from the perspective of the fundamental meditation subject for both trainees and worldlings;
and the third, from the perspective of the noble abiding of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).

[The Buddha] arrived. It should be understood that this is the distinction: in the first method, wholesome [states] are spoken of with reference to the worldling (*puthujjana*); in the second method, they are spoken of with reference to the trainee (*sekkha*);
and in the third method, functional-indeterminate (*kriyā-abyākata*) states are spoken of with reference to the one beyond training (*asekkha*).
From the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the *Indriyabhāvanāsutta* is completed.
The commentary on the Saḷāyatanavagga is finished.
The sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) on the latter fifty suttas is completed.
